The case markers that start in a plosive have voiced allomorphs intervocalically and after nasals. table [htp] centering tabular llp 8cm case & marker & function nominative& Ø&intransitive subject, transitive patient, ditransitive theme and goal, citation form, location (restricted use), copular topic and predicate ergative&=ŋa&transitive subject instrumental&=ŋa&instrument, ditransitive theme, temporal reference genitive&=ka &possession, material locative&=pe &location, ditransitive recipients and goals, temporal reference ablative&=phaŋ &source arguments comitative&=nuŋ &coordination, associated referents, source arguments of some verbs tabular Case markers (Group I) centering table We know from other Kiranti languages that case markers can be stacked to yield more specific functions (e.g., Ebert1994The-structure ; Dirksmeyer2008Spatial ; Schikowski2013_Thesis ). Generally, composite case markers are common in Tibeto-Burman languages DeLancey1985_Etymological . In Yakkha, the locative or the ablative case marker can be added to the genitive of a proper noun to yield the meaning at/from X's place . The ablative is also historically complex (see case-abl below). Several Kiranti languages have a (generally optional) dative marker -lai (e.g., Bantawa Doornenbal2009A-grammar, Puma Bickeletal2007Two-ways, Camling, Athpare and Thulung ( Ebert1994The-structure ), which is homonymous with the Nepali dative marker –lāī and probably a loan. Yakkha, however, does not employ this marker. It uses other strategies to mark semantic roles typically associated with dative marking: recipients and goals are either in the nominative or in the locative, and experiencers appear in various frames of argument realization, most prominently the Experiencer-as-Possessor frame. In the following, the cases of Group I and their functions will be introduced. More detailed information on argument realization and transitivity is found in Chapter verb-val.
summary:
The passage defines classical case as morphological marking on nouns or noun phrases showing their syntactic relation to predicates or to other nouns, and explains that Yakkha has two kinds of case-related elements: Group I clitic case markers on noun phrases and Group II markers that are more flexible and less phonologically dependent. It states that Yakkha Group I has seven cases, with nominative unmarked and the others expressed by enclitics attached to the rightmost noun phrase element, and notes that some case markers can stack to create more specific meanings.

The passage also explains that case marking may appear on dependent clauses in Yakkha, paralleling patterns found in Kiranti and Tibeto-Burman languages, though its historical origin is unclear. Finally, it notes that Yakkha lacks a dedicated dative marker and instead uses nominative, locative, or other argument-structure strategies to express roles such as recipients, goals, and experiencers.

text: The nominative is morphologically and functionally the unmarked case in Yakkha.Functional unmarkedness does not imply morphological unmarkedness, as research on marked-S languages has shown Handschuh2011_thesis, Brown2001_Nias. In the Yakkha case system, morphological and functional unmarkedness coincide. Participants in the nominative appear in their citation form, without any further marking. Intransitive subjects (S), transitive patients (P), ditransitive theme (T) and goal arguments (G), topic and comment of copular clauses, and to a certain extent locations, too, can be in the nominative and thus unmarked in Yakkha. With the discovery of ergativity, the term absolutive came into use relatively recently to refer to the case of intransitive subjects and transitive objects when these have the same case (see McGregor2009_Ergativity and Haspelmath2009_Terminology for summaries of the historical gestation of the term ergative ). Since then, research on ergativity has revealed that the system is far from uniform, and optional in many languages, other factors such as reference and information structure playing a greater role than had been expected. Haspelmath mentions the problem that the terminology nominative-accusative-ergative-absolutive refers to an ideal system which is rarely found Haspelmath2009_Terminology . Both nominative and absolutive refer to the functionally unmarked case in a system, and their application usually extends well beyond marking S and P arguments. Therefore, I do not see the need to maintain the distinction between the terms nominative and absolutive , since the unmarked case in an ergative system and the unmarked case in an accusative system have probably more shared properties than properties distinguishing them. Since nominative is the older term, it will be used in this work. Example shows S, P, T and G arguments in the nominative.To keep the glosses as short and straightforward as possible, the nominative is generally not glossed. . . ka maŋcwa=be khe-me-ŋ=na 1sg water =loc go -npst-1sg=nmlz.sg I go to fetch water. . nasa=ci ŋ-und-wa-ci fish =nsg 3pl.A- pull _out -npst-3nsg.P (They) pull out the fish. . ka nda cakleʈ pi-meʔ-nen=na 1sg[erg] 2sg sweet give -npst-1>2=nmlz.sg I will give you a sweet. Yakkha shows a typologically common nominative/ergative syncretism: transitive subjects that are represented by a first or second person pronoun always appear unmarked (cf. case-erg). Furthermore, both topic and comment in identificational copular constructions (see ), and the figure in existential/locative copular constructions (see ) are in the nominative. . . na ak=ka paŋ (om) this 1sg.poss=gen house ( cop ) This is my house. . ka=go arsale leʔlo! 1sg=top person _from _year _eight ctr.excla I was born in the year eight (B.S.), man! 06 _cvs _01.027 .nnakha=e maŋcwa=ca m-ma-ya-n that =loc water =add neg- be -pst[3sg]-neg There was no water, too. 42 _leg _10.009 Nominative arguments are also found in motion verb constructions, where a locative would be expected on the goal of the movement (see ). This option exists only for typical and frequent goals of movement, such as villages, work places, a school, a weekly market etc. The respective nouns are never modified (see , which was elicited in analogy to a sentence from the corpus, and which is well-formed only with a locative). Complements of verbs stating existence or location ( be at X ) can generally not occur unmarked, but exceptions in the colloquial register are possible (see ). The nouns in the nominative thus share features with incorporated nouns, although on other grounds they are not incorporated. Since the nouns mostly refer to names of places or landmarks, they refer to highly individuated participants, while incorporated nouns are often rather generic. . . Poklabuŋ tas-a-ma-c-u=hoŋ, Poklabung [loc] arrive -pst-prf-du-3.P=seq When they arrived in Poklabung, ... 22 _nrr _05.017 .ka ʈhuŋkha khy-a-ŋ=niŋ, 1sg steep _slope [loc] go -pst-1sg=ctmp When I was heading to the steep slopes, ... 40 _leg _08.036 . . uŋci=ga ten*(=be) khy-a-ma-ci, 3nsg=gen village *(=loc) go -pst-prf-du They went to their village, ... 22 _nrr _05.037 .tumok waiʔ-ŋa=na Tumok [loc] be [npst]-1sg=nmlz.sg I am in Tumok. (said on the phone)
summary: In Yakkha, the nominative is both morphologically and functionally the unmarked case, and it is used for a wide range of arguments and clause roles, including S, P, T, G, copular topics and comments, and sometimes locations. The passage argues that, since nominative and absolutive both denote the functionally unmarked case and their uses extend beyond S/P alignment, the distinction between the terms is not necessary here, so the older term nominative is retained. It also notes a nominative/ergative syncretism, especially with first- and second-person transitive subjects, and that some motion and locative expressions allow unmarked place names or frequent goals.

text: Transitive and ditransitive A arguments are marked by the ergative =ŋa (see ), except when they are first or second person pronouns, which display an ergative/nominative syncretism (see ). . . na, jaba, na mamu=ŋa luŋkhwak pok-ma n-yas-u-n, this when this girl =erg stone raise -inf neg- be _able -3.P[pst]-neg This one, when this girl could not raise the stone, ... 37 _nrr _07.039 .ka a-ma=ŋa khaʔla ly-a-ŋ: 1sg 1sg.poss- mother =erg like _this tell [3sg.A]-pst-1sg.P Mother told me the following: ... 42 _leg _10.011 . .jeppa nna len ka a-ma=nuŋ a-na=ga ceʔya y-yen-u-ŋa-n=na=ŋa, really that day 1sg[erg] 1sg.poss- mother =com 1sg.poss- eZ =gen matter neg- obey -3.P[pst]-1sg.A-neg=nmlz.sg=erg.cl Really, that day, because I did not listen to my mother's and my elder sister's warnings, ... 42 _leg _10.051 . iya nniŋda, eh, njiŋda yoŋ-me-c-u-ga, what 2pl[erg] oh 2du[erg] search -npst-du-3.P-2.A Whatever you (dual) look for, ... The speaker is correcting himself from plural to dual pronoun. 22 _nrr _05.084 In Yakkha, first or second person reference can also be instantiated by full nouns instead of pronouns, which is unusual from the perspective of Indo-European languages. One may have a sentence with first or second person verbal person marking, but the structural position of the pronoun is occupied by a noun, as shown in .Flexible agreement is discussed in flex-agr. On the principles behind agreement in Tibeto-Burman see Bickel2000On-the-syntax. In such participant configurations, there is overt ergative marking on the noun. To make a long story short, the differential agent marking is mainly determined by word class, but also by reference. . .phu=na mamu=ŋa yakkha ceʔya nis-wa-g=hoŋ maŋ-di-me-ŋ=naǃ white =nmlz.sg girl =erg Yakkha language know -npst-2=seq be _surprised -V2.give-npst-1sg=nmlz.sg I am surprised since you, a white girl, know Yakkhaǃ . a-phaŋ=ŋa men=na, a-koŋma=ŋa=le ta-ga=na raecha 1sg.poss- MyZH =erg neg.cop[3]=nmlz.sg 1sg.poss- MyZ =erg=ctr bring [pst;3.P]-2.A=nmlz.sg mir Not the uncle, but you, auntie, really brought her here (the second wife)! 06 _cvs _01.042 The examples in show that the ergative marker attaches to the final element of the phrase, whether two nouns are conjoined by a comitative (see and (b)) or whether the final element is a participle, as in . The comitative marker may function as a coordinator, much like English and . The verbal person marking is triggered by the collective number features of both nouns (dual in (a), and nonsingular in (b)). The negated form yyogan is found in all scenarios with third person acting on first, except for 3sg>1sg . . .lalubaŋ=nuŋ phalubaŋ=ŋa mamliŋ tas-a-ma-c-u Lalubang =com Phalubang =erg Mamling arrive -pst-prf-du-3.P Lalubang and Phalubang arrived in Mamling. 22 _nrr _05.041 .a-ma=nuŋ a-na=ŋa y-yog-a-n=niŋ=bi, 1sg.poss- mother =com 1sg.poss- sister =erg neg- search [3A;1.P]-sbjv-neg=ctmp=irr If my mother and sister had not searched for me, ... 42 _leg _10.052 . beuli=ga=ca u-nuncha parne=ŋa chata ham-met-wa bride =gen=add 3sg.poss- younger _sibling falling =erg umbrella spread -caus-npst[3A;3.P] Someone who is a younger sister of the bride, too, spreads an umbrella over her. 25 _tra _01.053 For several Tibeto-Burman languages, ergative marking has been described as optional and depending on pragmatic factors (see e.g., LaPolla1995_Ergative for a comparative account; Tournadre1991_Rhetorical on Lhasa Tibetan; Coupe2007_Mongsen on Mongsen Ao; Hyslop2011_Kurtop on Kurtöp). Yakkha, however, has a strictly grammaticalized system of ergative marking; the ergative is obligatory on A arguments (under the above-mentioned conditions), which is in line with the findings on other Kiranti languages. Doornenbal2009A-grammar notes the same for Bantawa. Bickel2003Belhare mentions an alignment split in Belhare that leaves first person singular pronouns unmarked. Also non-Kiranti languages like Newari, Chepang and Kham have stable grammaticalized ergative marking LaPolla1995_Ergative, while this is not as clear for Classical Tibetan DeLancey2011_Optional. The differential marking found on first and second person pronouns in Yakkha is determined by reference and word class, not by pragmatics. On a final note, the ergative marker is also employed in adverbial clause linkage (see Chapter adv-cl).
summary:
In Yakkha, transitive and ditransitive A arguments normally take the ergative marker =ŋa, but first- and second-person pronouns show ergative/nominative syncretism. Full nouns can also refer to first or second persons, and in such cases they receive overt ergative marking; thus, differential agent marking depends mainly on word class and also on reference, not on pragmatics.

The ergative marker attaches to the final element of a phrase, including coordinated phrases, and verbal person marking reflects the collective number of the participants. The passage also emphasizes that Yakkha has a strictly grammaticalized ergative system, unlike languages where ergative marking is optional, and notes that the ergative marker is used in adverbial clause linkage as well.

text: Yakkha exhibits an ergative-instrumental syncretism, which is not unusual, especially not in Kiranti. By formal criteria, except for one exception discussed below, the two cases cannot be distinguished. Functionally, though, they are distinct: the ergative marks animate agent arguments, while the instrumental typically marks inanimate participants like instruments , effectors, forces and causes . . . chom=na phiswak=ŋa hot-haks-u=na pointed =nmlz.sg knife =ins pierce- V2.send-3.P[pst]=nmlz.sg He pierced it with a pointed knife. . kisiʔma=ŋa solop miyaŋ eg-haks-uks-u fear =ins immediately a _little break -V2.send-prf-3.P[pst] Out of fear, he immediately broke off a little (from the stick). 04 _leg _03.023 The medium for communication is also marked by the instrumental . In this usage, an allomorph =ŋ is possible.Note the employment of exclusive vs. inclusive morphology in example (a). The speaker narrates the event from the perspective of the person who made the deontic statement, thus choosing the exclusive pronoun, despite the fact that the person she addresses is included. This shows that clusivity in Yakkha is not necessarily determined by including or excluding the addressee, but also by other people present in the speech situation. In other Eastern Kiranti languages like Belhare, Chintang or Limbu, this function is taken over by a mediative/perlative marker -lam ( Bickel2003Belhare ; Schikowski2012_Morphology ; Driem1987A-grammar ). A perlative case is not attested in Yakkha, at least not in the variety spoken in Tumok. . . aniŋ=ga ceʔya=ŋ=bu chem lum-biʔ-ma=na=lai 1pl.excl.poss=gen language =ins=rep song tell -V2.give-inf[deont]=nmlz.sg=excla She says we have to sing a song in our language. (reporting on the deontic statement of a person not included in the group) 06 _cvs _01.102 . eŋ=ga ceʔya=ŋ sarab pi-ci=ha leks-a 1pl.incl.poss=gen language =ins curse give -3nsg.P[3A;pst]=nmlz.nsg become [3sg]-pst It happened that it (the sun) cursed them (the Linkha clan members) in our language. 11 _nrr _01.031 The instrumental also indicates temporal reference (see ). On a side note, it is very likely that the adverbial clause linkage markers -saŋ and =niŋ(a) (both marking cotemporality) are based on the ergative/instrumental case etymologically. . .wandik=ŋa ta-meʔ=na next _day =ins come [3sg]-npst=nmlz.sg He will come tomorrow. . khiŋbelaʔ=ŋa this _time =ins at this time
summary: Yakkha shows ergative-instrumental syncretism: the ergative and instrumental are formally identical in most cases, though they differ in function. The ergative marks animate agents, while the instrumental marks inanimate participants such as instruments, causes, forces, and also the medium of communication; it can additionally express temporal reference. The passage also notes that Yakkha lacks a separate perlative case in the Tumok variety, unlike some other Eastern Kiranti languages.

text: The genitive case is marked by the suffix =ka (mostly realized as [ga] as result of the voicing rule, see voicing). It is used for possessive constructions, linking a possessor to a head noun (see ). As mentioned in poss on possessive pronouns, the possessee may be inflected by a possessive prefix, as in and . The possessive inflection may occur in addition to a genitive-marked possessor, or may replace it, as in . . . limbukhim=ci=ga taŋme a _clan =nsg=gen daughter-in-law a daughter-in-law of the Limbukhims 37 _nrr _07.002 . isa=ga u-chya? who =gen 3sg.poss- child Whose child (is it)? . m-ba m-ma=ci 2sg.poss- father 2sg.poss- mother =nsg your parents The head noun can also be omitted. The structure shown in is similar to a headless relative clause. Genitive-marked attributes may also be linked recursively to a head noun (see ).The example also shows that, at least in spoken language, discontinuous phrases are possible, since the adverb uhile belongs to the verb, but occurs inside the noun phrase. . . heko=na patti=ga=ci other =mmlz.sg side =gen=nsg those (children) from the other one (i.e., the other wife) 06 _cvs _01.033 . aniŋ=ga liŋkha=ga uhile utpati mamliŋ=be leks-a=na=bu 1sg.excl.poss=gen a _clan =gen long _ago origin Mamling =loc happen [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg=rep Our Linkha clan originated long ago in Mamling, they say. 11 _nrr _01.002 Relational nouns functioning as spatial adpositions also require the genitive, illustrated by . They are used in a possessive construction to which a locative must be added (see ; cf. also postpos). . .ʈebul=ga mopparik table =gen under under the table . saptakosi=ga u-lap=pe a _river _confluence =gen 3sg.poss- wing =loc on the shores of the Saptakosi 37 _nrr _07.044 The genitive is also employed to mark nominal modifiers referring to the material which the head noun is made of, as shown in . . . kolenluŋ=ga cuʔlumphi marble =gen stele a/the stele made of marble 18 _nrr _03.001 . siŋ=ga saŋgoŋ wood =gen stool a/the wooden stool . plasʈik=ka jhola=be plastic =gen bag =loc in a plastic bag 13 _cvs _02.045 .chubuk=ka caleppa ashes =gen bread bread of ashes A punishment for children: smearing ashes on their cheeks and slapping them. 40 _leg _08.056
summary:
The genitive case is marked by the suffix =ka, usually realized as [ga] by voicing, and it is used mainly in possessive constructions to link a possessor to a head noun. The head noun may also take possessive prefix marking, which can occur alongside a genitive possessor or replace it, and the head noun may be omitted in constructions resembling headless relative clauses.  

Genitive-marked forms are also used with relational nouns functioning like spatial adpositions, where a locative is added, and to mark nominal modifiers indicating the material something is made of. The passage also notes that genitive-marked attributes can be recursive and that spoken language allows discontinuous phrases inside noun phrases.

text: Yakkha has only one locative case marker =pe ([be] when voicing applies; it can be further reduced to [we] or simple [e]). Kiranti languages typically exhibit a four-fold distinction of deictic locative case markers that respond to the hilly topography of the environment. E.g., Camling, Bantawa, Puma, Thulung, Khaling Ebert1994The-structure; Yamphu Rutgers1998Yamphu ; Belhare Bickel2001Deictic . Such a case system consists of (i) one generic locative and three further markers to locate items (ii) above, (iii) below or (iv) on the same level as the deictic origin. Termed vertical case in Ebert1994The-structure ; altitudinal case in Dirksmeyer2008Spatial . While other Eastern Kiranti languages such as Limbu and Athpare also lack those altitudinal cases ( Ebert1997A-grammar , Driem1987A-grammar ), Belhare, seemingly the closest relative of Yakkha, displays them Bickel2001Deictic . The locative marks the spatial coincidence of an entity defined as figure with an environment or landmark defined as ground Levinsonetal2006_Grammars . It has a very general meaning, covering relations of containment, proximity and contact, translatable as in , at and on . Examples are provided in . . .khorek=pe cuwa bowl =loc beer There is beer in the bowl. .nwak=ka o-hop=pe bird =gen 3sg.poss -nest =loc in the nest of the bird .o-thok=pe toŋ-meʔ=na 3sg.poss -body =loc fit [3sg]-npst=nmlz.sg It suits/fits on her body. The basic locative construction Levinsonetal2006_Grammars , the answer to the question Where is F? is a copular construction with wama (with the suppletive nonpast stems waiʔ, wɛʔ, wei) be, exist (see ). The same construction (with different information structure) is generally used to introduce topics in the beginning of narratives (see and ). . .wa=ci kaŋyoŋ=be ŋ-waiʔ=ya=ci chicken =ngs chicken _basket =loc 3pl- be [npst]=nmlz.nsg=nsg The chicken are in the chicken basket. (a basket with small opening, to transport chicks) .panckapan=ga kerabari=be eko mãɖa luŋkhwak wɛʔ=na a _region =gen banana _plantation =loc one huge stone exist [3sg;npst]=nmlz.sg In the banana plantations of Pā̃ckapan, there is a huge rock. 39 _nrr _08.01 . eko ten=be eko maghyam wei-sa=na one village =loc one old _woman exist [3sg;npst]-pst=nmlz.sg In a village, there was an old woman. 01 _leg _07.060 Destinations of motion verbs and verbs of caused motion are generally marked by the locative, illustrated by . As explained above in case-nom, in certain scenarios the locative marking on the destinations of motion verbs can be omitted. . .khali puŋda=we kheʔ-m=ha only jungle =loc go- inf[deont]=nmlz.nsg Their only option was to go to the forest. 22 _nrr _05.045 .ŋkhiŋbelak=pe phopciba=ca ok-saŋ hop=pe pes-a-khy-a-ma that _time =loc owl =add shriek -sim nest =loc fly [3sg]-pst-V2.go-pst-prf That time, the owl flew back to its nest, shrieking. 42 _leg _10.042 . khokpu=ga siŋ=be thaŋ-ma=ga cog-a-ŋ fig =gen tree =loc climb -inf=gen do -pst-1sg I tried to climb the fig tree. 42 _leg _10.020 .beula=ga paŋ=be beuli ŋ-ghet-u=hoŋ, groom =gen house =loc bride 3pl.A- take _along -3.P[sbj]=seq They take the bride into the groom's house and ... Example shows three-argument constructions with locative-marked G arguments. Both inanimate and animate G arguments (i.e., goals and recipients) can be in the locative. Depending on the frames of argument realization, the locative is obligatory for some verbs, but optional for others (cf. three-arg for a discussion of three-argument frames, alternations and differential object marking). . . ka a-cya=ci iskul=be paks-wa-ŋ-ci-ŋ=ha 1sg[erg] 1sg.poss -child =nsg school =loc send- npst-1sg.A-nsg.P-1sg.A=nmlz.nsg I send my children to school. .uŋ=ŋa ka=be mendhwak haks-wa=na 3sg=erg 1sg=loc goat send [3sg.A;3.P]-npst=nmlz.sg He sends me a goat. Ownership can be expressed by a verb of existence and the possessor in the locative (see ). The existential verb has a suppletive form ma for negated forms . . . ŋga=be yaŋ waiʔ=ya? 2sg.poss=loc money exist [3sg;npst]=nmlz.nsg Do you have money? . eŋ=ga=be yaŋ m-ma-n=ha 1pl.incl.poss=gen=loc money neg- exist [3;npst]-neg=nmlz.nsg We do not have money. (said among own people) It is not surprising to find the locative marking extended to temporal reference. However, the more frequent marker in this function is the instrumental =ŋa. The locative in might well be a Nepali calque, since, except for na, all words in are Nepali loans. . . na tihar din=be this a _hindu _festival day =loc on this Tihar day 14 _nrr _02.026 . uncas sal=be thirty-nine year =loc in the year thirty-nine 06 _cvs _01.013 There are also some fixed expressions with the locative, shown in . . . maŋcwa=be khe-me-ka=na=i? water =loc go -npst-2=nmlz.sg=q Do you go to get water (from the well)? 13 _cvs _02.066 .daura=be khe-me-ŋ=na fire _wood =loc go -npst-1sg=nmlz.sg I go to get fire wood. There is a secondary locative marker =ge =ghe,Both forms are equally acceptable, and semantic differences could not be detected. used only with human reference, to express the notion at X's place (see ).The word maiti in (b) is a Nepali loan and refers to the natal home of a married woman. The morpheme =ge is a contraction of the genitive =ga and the locative =pe, a structure calqued from Nepali, where one finds e.g., tapāĩ-ko-mā at your place (you- gen-loc ), mero-mā at my place (mine- loc ). . .isa=ge? who =loc At whose place? . bagdata nak-se kheʔ-ma pʌryo, mapaci=ghe, maiti=ci=ghe kheʔ-ma=hoŋ, marriage _finalization ask _for -sup go -inf[deont] have _to .3sg.pst , parents =loc natal _home =nsg=loc go -inf[deont]=seq One has to go and ask for the Bagdata (ritual), one has to go to the parents, to the wife's family, and ... 26 _tra _02.013
summary: Yakkha has a single locative case marker, =pe, unlike many Kiranti languages that have a four-way “vertical” or altitudinal locative system marking generic location, above, below, and same level. The locative denotes general spatial coincidence and can express containment, proximity, contact, destinations of motion, goal/recipient arguments, possession with existential verbs, and some temporal or fixed expressions. A secondary locative =ge/ =ghe occurs only with human reference meaning “at X’s place” and is a contraction influenced by Nepali.

text: The ablative =phaŋ (or [bhaŋ] due to voicing) marks the source of movement or transfer (see ). Etymologically it could be the result of stacking an older ablative =haŋ upon the locative marker =pe. Various other Kiranti languages have such complex ablative markers based on the locative marker, too Ebert1994The-structure . In this light it might also be noteworthy that Grierson lists an ablative -bohuŋ for a Yakkha dialect spoken in the beginning of the 20th century in Darjeeling Grierson1909Linguistic. A possible cognate to the older marker =haŋ is the Belhare ablative =huŋ =etnahuŋ Bickel2003Belhare .The form =etnahuŋ is most probably also combined of a locative and an ablative marker. . .taŋkheŋ=bhaŋ tuknuŋ percoʔwa uks-a-ma, sky =abl thoroughly lightning come _down [3sg]-pst-prf Strong lightning came down from the sky. 21 _nrr _04.017 .nna=be ŋ-hond-u-n-ci-n=oŋ nna lupluŋ=bhaŋ tumhaŋ lond-a-khy-a=na that =loc neg- fit -3.P-neg-3nsg.P=seq that cave =abl Tumhang come _out -pst[3sg]-V2.go-pst=nmlz.sg As they did not fit there anymore, Tumhang came out of that cave. 27 _nrr _06.005 The ablative is also used to signify the starting point for a measurement of distance, as in . . i let u-cya=ŋa u-ma paŋ=bhaŋ maŋdu ta-meʔ-ma mit-uks-u one day 3sg.poss- child =erg 3sg.poss- mother house =abl far arrive -caus-inf think -prf-3.P[pst] One day, the son wanted to bring his mother far away from the house. 01 _leg _07.067 The medium of motion and the technical medium of communication can also be marked by the ablative, in parallel to the functions of the Nepali ablative bāṭa. . .kaniŋ nawa=bhaŋ hoŋma kakt-wa-m-ŋa=na 1pl[erg] boat =abl river cross -npst-1pl.A-excl=nmlz.sg We will cross the river by boat. . kithrikpa=ŋa solop maik=phaŋ lu-ks-u-ci policeman =erg immediately microphone =abl call -prf-3.P[pst]-3nsgP The policeman immediately called out their names with the microphone. 01 _leg _07.166 .thawa=bhaŋ to ŋ-khy-a-ma=niŋ=go mamu nnhe=maŋ wɛʔ=na=bu ladder =abl up 3pl- go -prf=ctmp=top girl there =emph exist [3sg]=nmlz.sg=rep When he climbed up on the ladder, the girl was right there (they say)! 22 _nrr _05.111 It is not unusual for Tibeto-Burman languages to display syncretisms between locative, allative and ablative DeLancey1985_Etymological. In the majority of the Yakkha data, the Yakkha ablative marks the source, but there are quite a few examples with an ablative form (or an adverb derived by an ablative) marking the goal of a movement. Thus, Yakkha shows a syncretism between ablative and allative, to the exclusion of the locative. . .heʔnang khe-ks-a-ga=na? where [abl] go -V2.cut-pst-2=nmlz.sg Where are you about to go? .yondhaŋ khy-a across [abl] go -imp Go there. Go from there. Just like the secondary locative =ge =ghe, the ablative shows a secondary form =ghaŋ that is used only with human reference, illustrated by . Furthermore, the sentences in example show that the ablative is not sensitive to topographic information. There is just one marker, used irrespective of directions and elevation levels with respect to the deictic center. . . lumba=ghaŋ ukt-u-ŋ-ci-ŋ, lumbapasal=bhaŋ Lumba =abl bring _down -3.P[pst]-1sg.A-3nsg.P-1sg.A shop _of _Lumba =abl I brought them down from Lumba (a person), from the Lumba shop. 36 _cvs _06.049 .yaŋliham=bhaŋ=jhen, koi. lowland =abl=top some From the lowlands (local lowlands, not the Tarai), some people. 36 _cvs _06.465 In some interrogative words and adverbs one can still see that they were composed of some root and an older ablative marker, e.g., in nhaŋ from here/and then and heʔnaŋ heʔnhaŋ where from .Both forms heʔnaŋ and heʔnhaŋ are equally acceptable to the speakers, and semantic differences could not be detected. . . heʔnaŋ tae-ka=na, mamu? where _from come [npst]-2=nmlz.sg , girl Where do you come from, girl? . mondaŋ ky-a-ŋ=na below [abl] come _up -pst-1sg=nmlz.sg I came up from below. The ablative is generally not used for temporal reference. There is a postposition nhaŋto that covers this function (cf. postpos below).
summary:
The ablative marker =phaŋ (or voiced [bhaŋ]) marks the source of movement or transfer, and may historically reflect a combination of an older ablative =haŋ with the locative =pe. It is also used for starting points of distance and for means or instruments of motion and communication, though in some cases it can mark the goal of movement as well, showing a syncretism between ablative and allative.  

The language has a secondary human-specific ablative form =ghaŋ, and the same marker is not sensitive to topographic distinctions. The ablative is generally not used for temporal reference, which is instead expressed by the postposition nhaŋto.

text: The comitative marker =nuŋ is cognate to Limbu -nu, Thulung -nuŋ Ebert1994The-structure , Wambule -no Opgenort2004A-Grammar , Bantawa -nin Doornenbal2009A-grammar , Chintang -nɨŋ Schikowski2012_Morphology . It can be used as a nominal coordinator, functionally similar to English and (symmetrical, with nouns of the same status, as defined in Haspelmath2004_overview ). An example is given in , a story title of the commonly found pattern X and Y . Thus, by its very nature, this case marker can be found inside noun phrases, coordinating two nominal heads. The other case markers attach to the coordinate structure as a whole (see ). The marker is phonologically bound to the first component of the coordinate structure. Examples and serve to show that both parts of the coordinate structure contribute features to the person and number marking on the verbs. In the verb is marked for dual number, determined by the proper noun ɖiana and by the omitted pronoun ka I . In the first person inclusive verbal marking is triggered by both nniŋda and kaniŋ. . . suku=nuŋ kithrikpa Suku =com policeman Suku (a girl's name) and the policeman 01 _leg _07.143 . a-ma=nuŋ a-na=ga ceʔya 1sg.poss- mother =com 1sg.poss- sister =gen matter the warnings of my mother and sister 42 _leg _10.051 .hakhok=ŋa am-me-ŋ-ci-ŋ=ba, ɖiana=nuŋ am-me-ŋ-ci-ŋ, asen=ca later =ins come _over -npst-excl-du-excl=emph Diana =com come _over npst-excl-du-excl yesterday =add Later, we will come of course, Diana and I, we will come; yesterday (we came), too. 36 _cvs _06.376 .la, nniŋda=nuŋ kaniŋ haku cuŋ-iǃ alright 2pl=com 1pl now wrestle -1pl[incl;sbjv] Well, now let us wrestleǃ 39 _nrr _08.12 The comitative is also used to mark peripheral participants that somehow accompany the main participants or that are associated with them (see ). . .tabek, kacyak, mina kondarik, caprak nhaŋ chomlaki=nuŋ puŋda=be lab-a-cog-a-ŋ-ci-ŋ khukuri _knife, sickle, small spade, spade and _then split _bamboo =com jungle =loc hold -pst-V2.make-pst-excl-du-excl Carrying khukuri, sickle, spades and split bamboo, we went into the jungle. (literally: made into the jungle )This V2 is only found in this one example so far, and thus, it is not treated in Chapter verb-verb on complex predicates. 40 _leg _08.008 .ka=nuŋ kheʔ-ma=na kamnibak 1sg=com go -inf[deont]=nmlz.sg friend a friend who has to walk with me Some frames of verbal argument realization (both intransitive and transitive) require the comitative on their arguments, such as cekma talk , toŋma fit/agree/belong to , kisiʔma be afraid , nakma ask and incama buy (from) (see ). . .mimik, ka=nuŋ seppa, u-ppa=nuŋ=go banda, n-jeŋ-me-n=na a _little 1sg=com restr.emph 3sg.poss- father =com=top closed neg- talk [3sg]-npst-neg=nmlz.sg A little, just with me – with her father, nothing, she does not talk to him. 36 _cvs _06.278 .limbu=ci=ga=nuŋ toŋ-di-me=ppa, eŋ=ga=go [...] aru=ga=nuŋ n-doŋ-men Limbu _ethnic.group =nsg=gen=com agree -V2.give-npst[3sg]=emph 1pl.incl.poss=gen=top [...] other =gen=com neg- agree [3sg]-npst-neg It is like the language of the Limbus, our (language). [...] It does not fit to the others. 36 _cvs _06.256--58 The comitative also plays a role in the derivation of some adverbs, as shown in (cf. adv). Furthermore, it is also found in clause linkage (cf. com-cl). .khumdu=nuŋ nam-ma tasty =com smell -inf to smell tasty
summary:
The comitative marker =nuŋ is cognate with similar markers in several related languages and can function as a nominal coordinator like English *and*, linking two nouns of equal status within a noun phrase. Unlike other case markers, it is phonologically attached to the first coordinate, and both coordinated parts can jointly determine person and number agreement on the verb.

Beyond coordination, =nuŋ also marks accompanying or associated peripheral participants and is required by certain verbal argument frames with both intransitive and transitive verbs. It also appears in some adverbial derivations and in clause linkage.

text: The markers of Group II are quite heterogenous; they do not define a class as such. They can appear bound to their host or independently, i.e., stressed like a separate word. Their phonological weight is also greater than that of the markers of Group I; all of them are at least disyllabic. The case markers of Group II have a greater flexibility with regard to hosts they can select. Not only nominals are possible, but also adverbials. Some markers of Group II are not attested with nominal complements at all, like khaʔla towards . Furthermore, a number of the markers of Group II have hybrid word class status; they can also be used as adverbs. Some markers were borrowed into the language from Nepali, like samma until or anusar according to . table-postpos provides a summary of all Group II markers and their functions, described in detail in the following sections. table [htp] centering tabular ll marker & function khaʔla&directional, towards ; manner like nhaŋto&temporal ablative, since, from X on haksaŋ&comparative, compared to haʔniŋ&comparative, compared to loʔa&equative, similative, like hiŋ&equative (size) as big as maʔniŋ&caritive, without bahek [nep]& exclusive, apart from samma [nep]&terminative, until, towards anusar [nep]& according to lagi [nep]&benefactive, for tabular Case markers (Group II) centering table
summary: Group II markers are heterogeneous and do not form a single class: they may be bound to a host or appear independently with stress, and they are generally heavier phonologically than Group I markers, being at least disyllabic. They are also more flexible in the kinds of hosts they take, occurring with nominals and adverbials, and some can function as adverbs; several markers were borrowed from Nepali.

subsubsection: The direction and manner marker khaʔla
text: The directional/manner marker khaʔla towards, in the way of is not attested with nouns, it only attaches to deictic adverbs. The directional reading is found when khaʔla attaches to demonstrative adverbs typically occurring with motion verbs (see ). Etymologically, it is a combination of a demonstrative kha with an older allative or directional case marker. Cognates of such a marker are attested in several Kiranti languages: -tni in Bantawa Doornenbal2009A-grammar and Puma Sharma2005Case, -baiʔni -ʔni in Chintang Schikowski2012_Morphology . . . to=khaʔla ky-a! up=towards come _up -imp Come up! 01 _leg _07.329 .ŋkha limbu=ci yo=khaʔla ŋ-khy-a those Limbu _person =nsg across=towards 3pl- go -pst Those Limbus went away (horizontally). 22 _nrr _05.017 .nniŋga=go, mo, mo=khaʔla=ca nis-uks-u-ŋ=ha 2pl.poss=top down down=towards =add see -prf-3.P[pst]-1sg.A=nmlz.nsg Your (home), below, downwards, I have seen it, too. Downwards could be any location outside the Himalayas. 28 _cvs _04.334 The manner reading is found when khaʔla attaches to demonstratives (see ). . .ijaŋ bhasa n-jiŋ-ghom-me=ha? hoŋ=khaʔla=maŋ baʔlo! why language 3pl- learn -V2.roam-npst=nmlz.nsg that _very=like =emph emph.excla Why do they walk around learning languages? Just like that! 28 _cvs _04.324 .nna=khaʔla, mamu, i cok-ma=ʔlo, hamro des? that=like girl what do -inf=excla our country (It is ) like that, what to do, girl, with our country? 28 _cvs _04.163 The marker khaʔla also has a homonymous adverbial counterpartAdverbial in the sense that it occurs independently, without nominal complements, and in the function of modifying verbs. with a purely manner reading: like this , e.g., khaʔla om It is like this.
summary: The marker **khaʔla** means “towards” or “in the way of,” but it does not attach to nouns; instead, it occurs only with deictic adverbs. It has a directional sense with demonstrative adverbs used with motion verbs, and a manner sense with demonstratives meaning “like that,” while an independent homonymous adverb **khaʔla** means “like this” and modifies verbs.

text: The marker nhaŋto (occasionally also bhaŋto) usually attaches to nouns or adverbs with temporal reference and marks the beginning of time intervals, regardless of whether they extend from a point in the past, present or future, as the examples in illustrate. Example shows that it may also attach to demonstratives. The etymology of this marker is still transparent. It is composed of a demonstrative na with an (older) ablative -haŋ and the deictic adverb to up , yielding a phrase up from here . This points towards a conceptualization of time as beginning below and flowing upwards. So far, this is just an educated guess, supported by the uses of some complex predicates, such as a combination of see and bring up , best translated as having remembered . . .asen=nhaŋto yesterday =temp.abl since yesterday .mi wandik=nhaŋto a _little later =temp.abl from a bit later on .lop=nhaŋto=maŋ now =temp.abl=emph from now on 01 _leg _07.030 .nna=nhaŋto sumphak cilleŋ n-leks-u that =temp.abl leaf face _up 3pl.A- turn -3.P[pst] From that (event) on, they turned around the leaf plate to the proper side. 22 _nrr _05.132 This marker is occasionally also found as clause-initial coordinator used similarly to , which reflects the historical stage prior to becoming a bound marker. The previous clause is referred to by a demonstrative (not in these, but in plenty of other examples), resulting in a structure nna, nhaŋto that, and then upwards , and eventually the clause-initial coordinator got reanalyzed as requiring a complement of some kind. . .nhaŋto, garo n-cheŋd-et-wa=na, to=khaʔla and _then wall 3pl.A- mason -V2.carry.off-npst=nmlz.sg up=towards And then they mason the wall, upwards. 31 _mat _01.093 .nhaŋto phuna=chen seg-haks-u-ŋ=hoŋ and _then white =top choose -V2.send-3.P[pst]-1sg.A=seq And then, I sorted out the white (bread), and ... 40 _leg _08.060 Marginally (in one case, to be precise), a synonymous marker nhaŋkhe, paraphrasable as from then on hither , was found with the same function. .nhaŋkhe u-ma heʔniŋ=ca issisi n-jog-uks-u-n and _then 3sg.poss- mother when =add bad neg- do -prf-3.P[pst]-neg And then, he never did his mother bad again. 01 _leg _07.082
summary:
The marker **nhaŋto** (and sometimes **bhaŋto**) attaches mainly to nouns or temporal adverbs and marks the beginning of a time interval, whether the reference point is in the past, present, or future. Its transparent etymology suggests a composition of a demonstrative plus an ablative and the deictic adverb *to*, roughly meaning “up from here,” which may reflect a conceptualization of time as beginning below and flowing upward.

The marker can also appear clause-initially as a coordinator, a use that likely preserves an earlier stage before it became a bound marker. A synonymous form, **nhaŋkhe**, occurs marginally with the same meaning, paraphrasable as “from then on hither.”

text: The two comparative markers haksaŋ and haʔniŋ mark the standard in comparative and in superlative constructions. They are used interchangeably without any functional difference. Since they are treated in detail in Chapter adj-adv, three examples shall suffice here. Examples and show comparative constructions, shows a superlative construction. The comparative markers can attach to all kinds of hosts, even to verbs. Etymologically they must have been converbal forms, since Yakkha has the converbal and adverbial clause linkage markers -saŋ and =niŋ, both indicating cotemporality. The structure of the Yakkha comparative markers could be calqued upon the structure of the Nepali comparative marker bhanda, which is a converbal form of the verb bhannu to say . The identity of a possible verbal stem hak in Yakkha, however, could not be determined. Synchronically, the meaning of compare is expressed by a complex verb themnima. A likely candidate could be the verbal stem haks, which basically means send/send up , but is also used with the meaning weigh . . . nda haʔniŋ pak=na? 2sg compar be _unripe =nmlz.sg Is he younger than you? . heko=ha nwak=ci haksaŋ miyaŋ alag (...) sa=na=bu other =nmlz.nsg bird =nsg compar a _little different (...) cop.pst=nmlz.sg=rep He was a bit different from the other birds, they say. 21 _nrr _04.002 . ghak haʔniŋ mi=na mima all compar small =nmlz.sg mouse the smallest mouse (of them all) 01 _leg _07.003
summary: The passage says that the comparative markers **haksaŋ** and **haʔniŋ** are used interchangeably to mark the standard in both comparative and superlative constructions, and they can attach to many kinds of hosts, including verbs. It argues that these markers were probably once converbal forms, possibly modeled on Nepali **bhanda**, although their exact historical source in Yakkha is uncertain. Synchronically, the idea of “compare” is expressed by the complex verb **themnima**.

subsubsection: The equative and similative marker loʔa
text: The equative/similative loʔa marks the standard of an equation. It can have adverbial and nominal complements (a numeral in ), even clausal, when they are embedded to verbs of perception or cognition. Example shows that the resulting equative phrase can be “fed” into a nominalization itself and thus made a referential phrase. The equative/similative marker is cognate to the comitative and adverbial clause linkage marker -lo lok loʔ in Belhare Bickel1993Belhare. The same marker is known as manner suffix in Bantawa Doornenbal2009A-grammar. There is one lexicalized instance of loʔa, the adverb pekloʔa pyakloʔa usual(ly) , still morphologically transparent: its literal meaning would be like much/like many . . .khem loʔa before like like before . kaniŋ ka-i-wa=niŋa eko loʔa kheps-wa-m 1pl say -1pl-npst=ctmp one like hear -npst[3.P]-1pl.A When we say it, it sounds the same! 36 _cvs _06.478 .khem loʔa=na mekan! before like =nmlz.sg neg.cop.2sg You are not like someone from just before! (said to someone who was a little tipsy but claimed to come right from work) In a manner typical for Tibeto-Burman languages, this marker extends its function to clauses.See also DeLancey1985_Etymological and Genetti1991From. In it takes over the function of a complementizer. . ka luʔ-meʔ-nen-in=ha loʔa cog-a-ni 1sg[erg] tell -npst-1>2-2pl=nmlz.nsg like do -imp-pl.imp Do as I tell you. 14 _nrr _02.019
summary: The equative/similative marker **loʔa** marks the standard of comparison and can take adverbial, nominal, and even clausal complements, especially with verbs of perception or cognition. The passage also notes that this marker can be nominalized to form a referential phrase and that, in a Tibeto-Burman pattern, it extends to clause linkage and complementizer-like functions; one lexicalized adverb, **pekloʔa pyakloʔa** ‘usually,’ remains morphologically transparent.

subsubsection: The equative marker for size hiŋ
text: The equative case for size is etymologically related to the deictic adverb khiŋ (which is etymologically composed of the demonstrative kha and hiŋ). Attached to a noun phrase that functions as standard of comparison, this case marker indicates that an object is as big as the object referred to by the noun to which hiŋ attaches, as shown in . In this example, the whole phrase is nominalized and functions as the nominal predicate of a copular clause. . m-muk a-laŋ hiŋ=na (om) 2sg.poss- hand 1sg.poss- foot as _big _as =nmlz.sg ( cop ) Your hand is as big as my foot.
summary: The equative case marker for size is etymologically related to the deictic adverb *khiŋ*, itself composed of the demonstrative *kha* and *hiŋ*. When attached to a noun phrase serving as the standard of comparison, it means that one object is as big as the object named by that noun phrase; in the example, the resulting phrase is nominalized and used as the nominal predicate in a copular clause.

text: The privative maʔniŋ is historically complex, similar to haʔniŋ above. It is composed of the negative existential copular stem ma (in third person singular, zero-marked) and the cotemporal adverbial clause linkage marker =niŋ (see ). In the same way as we have seen above for loʔa already, the privative phrase can be nominalized to serve as a nominal modifier, as shown in . . .i=ŋa cama niʔ-m=ha, maŋcwa maʔniŋ? what =ins rice cook -inf[deont]=nmlz.nsg water without How (in what) shall we cook rice, without water? 13 _cvs _02.108 .wariŋba maʔniŋ=ha khyu tomato without =nmlz.nsg curry _sauce curry sauce without tomatoes in it
summary: The privative *maʔniŋ* is historically composed of the negative existential copular stem *ma* and the cotemporal clause-linkage marker *=niŋ*, making it structurally similar to *haʔniŋ*. Like *loʔa*, the privative phrase can be nominalized and used as a nominal modifier, as in expressions meaning “without water” or “curry sauce without tomatoes.”

text: The benefactive/purposive postposition lagi (from Nepali lāgi), like in its source language, requires the genitive case. It can attach to proper nouns or to nominalized clauses like the infinitive in . The genitive is, however, also found on purposive infinitival clauses without the postposition (see maga); it might well precede the point in time when lagi entered the Yakkha language. . .hoʔiǃ ak=ka lagi iya=ca tuʔkhi n-jog-a-n enough! 1sg.poss=gen for what =add trouble neg- do -imp-neg No, thanks. Do not bother about me (at all). 01 _leg _07.186 . heʔniŋ-heʔniŋ=go yuncama=le cok-ma haʔlo when-when =top laughter =ctr do -inf[deont] excla Sometimes one just has to joke around, man! 36 _cvs _06.263 Another postposition from Nepali is anusar according to (from Nepali anusār ). It is typically found with nominalized clauses (see ). . .ka-ya=na anusar say [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg according _to according to what was said/promised 11 _nrr _01.012 . ka nis-u-ŋ=ha anusar 1sg[erg] see -3.P[pst]-1sg.A=nmlz.nc according _to according to what I know/saw 25 _tra _01.169 The terminative postposition samma is used to specify the endpoint of an event (see ). This postposition is also found in clause linkage, in combination with native adverbial subordinators. . aniŋ=ga ceʔya hen samma man=ha=bu 1pl.excl.poss=gen language now until neg.cop=nmlz.nc=rep Our language has not been established until now (they say). 07 _sng _01.06 The exclusive postposition bahek apart from serves to single out a referent to which the predication made in the sentence does not apply (see ). . taŋcukulik bahek=chen, heŋ-nhak-ni-ma, jammai, kha ya-muŋ=ca, ghak heŋ-nhaŋ-ma pig-tail apart _from =top cut -V2.send-compl-inf[deont] all this mouth-hair =add all cut -V2.send-inf[deont] Apart from the pig-tail one has to cut it off, all, this beard too, all has to be cut off. (context: funeral description) 29 _cvs _05.058 In all the postpositions from Nepali, the phonological contrast between open-mid /ʌ/ and open /a/, which is present in the source language, is neutralized to open and long /a/.
summary: The passage describes several postpositions borrowed from Nepali in Yakkha. Benefactive/purposive **lagi** requires genitive marking and can attach to proper nouns or nominalized clauses; **anusar** “according to” typically occurs with nominalized clauses; **samma** “until” marks the endpoint of an event and can also appear in clause linkage; and **bahek** “apart from” singles out a referent excluded from the predicate. It also notes that the Nepali vowel contrast between /ʌ/ and /a/ is neutralized in these borrowings to open, long /a/ in Yakkha.

text: Yakkha has a class of relational nouns, in which specific meanings like root are metaphorically extended to indicate more general spatial relations like under . Usually, they occur in a possessive construction with the complement noun in the genitive and a possessive prefix attaching to the relational noun, which also hosts a locative case marker, as in and . Relational nouns expressing spatial relations are a common source for case markers and postpositions in Tibeto-Burman DeLancey1985_Etymological . . . phakʈaŋluŋ=ga u-sam=be Mount _Kumbhakarna =gen 3sg.poss- root =loc at the foot of Mount Kumbhakarna 18 _nrr _03.001 . caram=ga u-lap=pe camokla=nuŋ ambibu=ga u-thap ŋ-weʔ-ha yard =gen 3sg.poss- wing =loc banana =com mango =gen 3sg.poss- plant 3pl- exist [npst]=nmlz.nsg At the edge of the yard there are some banana trees and mango trees. 01 _leg _07.176 Relational nouns can also be found without the inflectional morphology between complement and relational noun, in a compound-like structure, as in .The person marking for third person on the main verb here is exceptional, since it refers to a first person participant. The expected regular first person inflection (ipsamasaŋna) would be possible as well. We know that such impersonal inflection is an alternative and frequent way to express first person nonsingular patients in Yakkha. This example is, however, the only instance in the corpus where this strategy is used for first person singular subject of an intransitive verb. It is not only the locative but also the ablative which may attach to a relational noun, as shown in . In this particular example, the ablative marking indicates a movement along a trajectory above the table. . . hakhok=ŋa ka cend-a-ky-a-ŋ=hoŋ so-ŋ=niŋa=go ka luŋkhwak-choŋ=be ips-a-masa later =ins 1sg wake _up -pst-V2.come _up-pst-1sg=seq look -1sg=ctmp=top 1sg stone-top =loc sleep [3sg]-pst-pst-prf Later, when I woke up and looked around, (I realized that) I had been sleeping on a rock. 42 _leg _10.043 .chalumma=ŋa phuaba ʈebul-choŋ=bhaŋ bol lept-u-bi=na second _born _girl =erg last _born _boy table-top =abl ball throw -3.P[pst]-V2.give=nmlz.sg Chalumma threw the ball over the table to Phuaba. relnoun provides a summary and the original lexical nouns that are the bases for each relational noun. In , the relational noun is reduplicated, since the relation described is not one of location at the riverside, but one of movement along the river. table [htp] centering tabular lll relational noun & gloss & lexical meaning choŋ chom &above, on, on top of& top, summit sam &below& root lum &in, between& middle yum &next to& side hoŋ &inside& hole lap&next to (upper part) & wing laŋ &next to (lower part) & leg heksaŋ &behind, after & backside ondaŋ &in front of, before & frontside chuptaŋ &to the right of & right side pheksaŋ &to the left of & left side tabular Relational nouns centering table . hoŋma=ga u-lap-ulap lukt-a-ma river =gen 3sg.poss- wing -redup run [3sg]-pst-prf He ran along the shore of the river. 01 _leg _07.216 The two relational nouns heksaŋ and ondaŋ can, additionally, occur as adverbs. In the current corpus, they are mainly used adverbially (see ). As these examples show, heksaŋ and ondaŋ , in contrast to the other relational nouns, can also be used with a temporal interpretation. . .n-heksaŋ=be cuwa ta=ya 2sg.poss- behind =loc beer come [3sg;pst]=nmlz.nsg Some beer has arrived behind you. .tabhaŋ panc hapta heksaŋ ta-meʔ=na son-in-law five week behind come [3sg]-npst=nmlz.sg The son-in-law comes five weeks later. .heksaŋ so-ŋ-ci-ŋ uŋci n-nis-u-n-ci-ŋa-n later look [pst]-1sg.A-3nsg.P-1sg.A 3nsg neg- see -3.P[pst]-neg-3nsg.P-1sg.A-neg Later, when I looked for them, I did not see them. 41 _leg _09.050 Furthermore, there are spatial adpositions, presenting an orientation system that is based on the uphill/downhill distinction. They are treated in geomorph-postp, together with the other word classes that are based on this topography-based system. Yakkha does not have a perlative/mediative lam or lamma case or postposition which is found in many of the surrounding languages.E.g., in Chintang Schikowski2012_Morphology; Belhare Bickel2003Belhare; Limbu Driem1987A-grammar, Athpare, Yamphu, Camling, Thulung Ebert2003Kiranti. There is also no postposition for the relation around . This can only be expressed adverbially with ighurum . This adverb has its origin in a noun ighurum round , which still exists synchronically in Yakkha. . mi em-saŋ huŋ-ca-saŋ ighurum yuŋ-i-misi-ŋ fire get _warm -sim bask -V2.eat-sim around sit -1pl-prf.pst-excl [...], we had sat around the fire, getting warm. 40 _leg _08.033
summary: Yakkha has a set of relational nouns whose lexical meanings are metaphorically extended to spatial relations such as “under,” “on top of,” “inside,” and “behind.” They usually appear in possessive constructions with a genitive complement and possessive prefix, and they can take locative or ablative case; some, especially *heksaŋ* and *ondaŋ*, also function adverbially and can have temporal readings. The language also has topography-based spatial adpositions, lacks perlative/mediative and “around” postpositions, and expresses “around” only adverbially with a noun-derived form.

section: The structure of the noun phrase
text: The basic function of noun phrases is to establish reference. They occur as arguments of verbs, as complements of postpositions and as predicates in copular constructions. They may host morphology such as case and number markers and various discourse particles. Noun phrases are potentially complex; both coordinate and embedded structures can be found inside the noun phrase. Noun phrases can be headed by a lexical noun or by a pronoun, a demonstrative, a numeral, a quantifier or an adjective. Noun phrases that are not headed by a lexical noun are more restricted in the kind of modifying material they may contain. Noun phrases can also be headless, consisting just of some non-nominal material and a nominalizing device. Hence, no element in a Yakkha noun phrase is obligatory. The default structure for headed noun phrases is head-final. Deviations from this pattern reflect discourse requirements, as will be discussed below. In noun phrases that are headed by personal pronouns or demonstratives, modifiers follow the head. Noun phrases with more than two modfiying elements are exceedingly rare.
summary: Noun phrases primarily serve to establish reference and can function as verb arguments, postpositional complements, or predicates in copular constructions, while also carrying case, number, and discourse particles. They may be headed by various word classes or be headless, and no single element is obligatory; the default order is head-final, though pronoun- and demonstrative-headed noun phrases place modifiers after the head. Complex noun phrases are possible but rare, especially those with more than two modifiers.

section: The structure of the noun phrase
text: Possessive phrases minimally consist of a noun (referring to the possessee) which is marked by a possessive prefix (indexing the possessor, see ). If there is an overt possessor, marked by the genitive, the possessive prefix is generally optional (see ), except for inherently possessed nouns such as core family terms and some other nouns implying part-whole relations. The possessive prefix may, however, also co-occur with a possessive pronoun, but only when the possessor has singular reference (see unacceptable ). Recursive embedding is possible as well, but not found beyond two levels of embedding in the currently available data . . . (ak=ka) a-cya=ci ( 1sg.poss=gen ) 1sg.poss- child =nsg my children 21 _nrr _04.027 . ghak=ka ɖaŋgak=ci all =gen stick =nsg everyone's sticks 04 _leg _03.024 .eŋ=ga (*en-)na-nuncha=ci 1pl.incl.poss=gen (* 1pl.inc.poss- )eZ-yZ =nsg our sisters 41 _leg _09.015 .beuli=ga u-kamnibak bride =gen 3sg.poss- friend a friend of the bride 25 _tra _01.089 .eko khokpu=ga u-thap=ka u-sam=be one fig =gen 3sg.poss- plant =gen 3sg.poss- root =loc below a fig tree 42 _leg _10.015
summary: Possessive phrases minimally consist of a noun for the possessee marked by a possessive prefix indexing the possessor. If an overt genitive possessor is present, the prefix is usually optional, except with inherently possessed nouns such as kin terms and part-whole nouns; the prefix can also co-occur with a possessive pronoun only when the possessor is singular. Recursive possessive embedding is possible, but the available data show no more than two levels of embedding.

section: The structure of the noun phrase
subsection: Other modifiers: adjectives, numerals, quantifiers, demonstratives
text: Below, examples with numerals (see ), demonstratives (see and ), adjectives (see and ) are shown. The examples also illustrate nominal morphology such as case markers, attaching to the rightmost element of the phrase, and optionally followed by discourse particles like the additive focus marker =ca or the restrictive focus marker =se. . .eko a-muk=phaŋ one 1sg.poss- hand =abl from one of my hands 40 _leg _08.022 .na tumna=ŋa this elder =erg this elder one 40 _leg _08.055 .ŋkha u-hiruʔwa=ci those 3sg.poss- intestine =nsg those intestines 40 _leg _08.039 .onek=ha ceʔya=ca joking =nmlz.nsg matter =add jokes, too 40 _leg _08.057 .heko=na whak=pe other =nmlz.sg branch =loc on another branch 42 _leg _10.032 .honna=ga=se ɖaŋgak that _very =gen=restr stick only that person's stick 04 _leg _03.025 When the head noun is a pronoun or a demonstrative, the modifier is usually a quantifier or a numeral, and it follows the head. Occasionally other material elaborating on the identity of the pronominal referent is found as well, as in . . . iya-iya nis-u-ga=na, ŋkha ghak yok-met-a-ŋ=eba what-what see -3.P[pst]-2.A=nmlz.sg that all search -caus-imp-1sg.P=pol.imp Please tell me everything you saw. 19 _pea _01.005 .kaniŋ ghak chups-i-ŋ=hoŋ 1pl all gather -1pl-excl=seq As we all had gathered, ... 41 _leg _09.054 .uŋci hip-paŋ 3nsg two -clf.hum the two of them .kaniŋ yakkhaba yakkhama=ci 1pl Yakkha _man Yakkha _woman =nsg we Yakkha people
summary: The passage shows that numerals, demonstratives, and adjectives can modify nouns in noun phrases, with case markers attaching to the rightmost element of the phrase and optional discourse particles such as =ca and =se following them. It also notes that when the head noun is a pronoun or demonstrative, the modifier is usually a following quantifier or numeral, though other identifying material can sometimes appear as well.

section: The structure of the noun phrase
text: In and , examples of relative clauses are given, constructed with the nominalizers -khuba and =na/=ha (treated in Chapter ch-nmlz). They can be of considerable length and internal complexity. In , three coordinated relative clauses serve to modify the same head noun, whaŋsa steam . Enumerations of coordinated items, with the comitative marker functioning as a coordinator (between the last two items if there are more than two), are common in Yakkha. These relative clauses are not embedded into one another; there are three different smells (or steams ), not the smell of yams that are cooked together with fried bread and sauce, which also would not make sense semantically, since whaŋma can only refer to boiling something solid in water. They are joined by apposition and a comitative between the latter two relative clauses. This pattern of coordination is common. In , the relative clause is preceded by an adjective and contains a complement-taking verb with an embedded infinitive. . .ka haksaŋ tum=na yapmi 1sg compar elder =nmlz.sg person a person senior to me 40 _leg _08.078 . khaʔla otesraŋ=ha pachem=ci! like _this reverse =nmlz.nsg young _boy =nsg Such naughty boys! 40 _leg _08.075 .caleppa leps-a=ha, ni-ya=ha macchi=nuŋ khi whaŋd=ha whaŋsa bread deep _fry [3sg]-pst=nmlz.nc fry [3sg]-pst=nmlz.nc chili _sauce =com yam boil [3sg;pst]=nmlz.nc steam the steam of deep-fried bread, fried chili and boiled yams The lexeme macchi is a loan from the Nepali source word marej pepper . In Yakkha, it refers to chili peppers, but also to hot pickles and sauces. 40 _leg _08.046 .issisi, khem-ma=i me-ya-m=ha ceʔya ugly hear -inf=foc neg- be _able -inf=nmlz.nc talk ugly talk that one cannot listen to 36 _cvs _06.600 Headless noun phrases, identical to headless relative clauses, are presented in . . . khi khoŋ-khuba=ci yam dig -nmlz=nsg people digging yam 40 _leg _08.009 .to=na up =nmlz.sg the upper one Some nouns take clausal complements (see noun-compl).
summary: The passage describes Yakkha relative clauses formed with the nominalizers **-khuba** and **=na/=ha**, noting that they can be long and internally complex. It gives examples of coordinated relative clauses modifying the same noun, often linked by apposition and the comitative marker, and also mentions headless noun phrases that are structurally like headless relative clauses. Some nouns can additionally take clausal complements.

section: The structure of the noun phrase
text: If nouns are coordinated in a noun phrase, they can either be juxtaposed (see ), or, by means of the comitative case marker, be attached to the penultimate noun (see ). The comitative may also coordinate adjectives. Example shows again that several levels of embedding are possible: the coordinated nouns may themselves be modified and these modifers may also be coordinated by =nuŋ. Apposition is used comparatively often; instead of using some more general term, one often finds long enumerations of things. This could be a stylistic device to create suspense in narratives, as exemplified in . . .yarepmaŋ, likliŋphuŋ nam-ma=niŋ=ca ibibi sokma ta-ya=na fern, mugwort smell -inf=ctmp=add very _much breath come [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg When we sniffed at fern and mugwort plants, we regained quite some energy. 40 _leg _08.018 .paŋkhi=nuŋ puŋdakhi cultivated _yam =com wild _yam cultivated yam and wild yam 40 _leg _08.025 .paŋ=be phu=ha=nuŋ makhur=ha caleppa, macchi, khicalek=nuŋ cuwa py-a house =loc white =nmlz.nc=com black =nmlz.nc bread, pickles, rice _dish =com beer give -pst[1.P] At home, they gave us white and black bread, pickles, khichadi and beer. 40 _leg _08.051 .uŋci=ŋa tabek, siŋ, phendik, lom-ma n-darokt-u 3nsg=erg khukuri wood axe take _out -inf 3pl.A- start -3.P[pst] They started to take out khukuri knives, wooden clubs and axes. 41 _leg _09.038 Modifying material, too, can be coordinated by juxtaposition. Interestingly, when two sub-compounds are in apposition, the head noun of the first compound can be omitted, as shown in . . . phu-nuncha na-nuncha=be pak=na elder _brother-younger _sibling elder _sister-younger _sibling =loc be _unripe =nmlz.sg the youngest among the brothers and sisters 40 _leg _08.052 . hoŋkhaʔla khi-ma=ha tu-ma=ha ceʔya like _that _very fight -inf=nmlz.nc wrestle -inf=nmlz.nc matter the issue of fighting and wrestling like just told 41 _leg _09.072 .tondigaŋma liŋkhacama-puŋda=ci a _forest _name a _forest _name-forest =nsg the Tondigangma and Linkhacama forests 40 _leg _08.011
summary: Nouns in a noun phrase can be coordinated either by simple juxtaposition or by attaching the comitative case marker to the penultimate noun, and adjectives may also be coordinated with the comitative. The passage notes that coordination and modification can be layered, with coordinated nouns themselves modified and those modifiers coordinated by =nuŋ. Apposition is frequent and often takes the form of long enumerations rather than a more general term, which may serve a suspense-building narrative function; in some appositional compounds, the head noun of the first compound may be omitted.

section: The structure of the noun phrase
text: Concerning the combinatory potential inside the noun phrase, there seem to be only few restrictions. The average noun phrase, however, shows maximally two modi -fying elements, as illustrated below: num-adj-N in , dem-num-N in , dem-adj-N in , poss-num-N in , poss-dem-N in , dem-Quant in . Other possibilities found are poss-adj-N , adj-RC-N , num-RC-N , dem-RC-N , poss-num-N . The only recognizable tendency found was that of putting demonstratives first, although this is not a categorical rule. . .eko maɖa tiʔwa one big pheasant one big pheasant 40 _leg _08.036 .na eko luŋkhwak=chen this one stone =top as for this one stone 37 _nrr _07.007 .na makhruk=na caleppa this black =nmlz.sg bread this black bread 40 _leg _08.053 .chubuk=ka hic=ci caleppa ashes =gen two =nsg bread two breads of ashes 40 _leg _08.071 .paghyam=ga ŋkha sala old _man =gen that talk that talk of the old man 40 _leg _08.076 . kha ghak casak this all uncooked _rice all this uncooked rice 01 _leg _07.016 When the noun phrase is headed by a pronoun, only quantifiers or numeral modifiers are possible, and they follow the head, as has been shown above in example iyaiyadem. From these possibilities, the following (idealized) schema for a maximal noun phrase can be inferred (see np-max ). As it was said above, the noun phrase is rather unrestricted, so that it is highly conceivable that noun phrases with an internal structure deviating from this schema can be found. figure tabular lllllll &&&&&N& dem&poss&NUM&ADJ&RC&PRON/&NUM/ &&&&&dem&QUANT tabular Schema of the maximal noun phrase figure
summary: The passage says that noun phrases in this language are generally quite unrestricted in their internal combinatory structure, though most contain at most two modifiers. A weak tendency is for demonstratives to occur first, but this is not a fixed rule; when the noun phrase is headed by a pronoun, only quantifiers or numeral modifiers can follow it. Based on these patterns, an idealized maximal noun-phrase schema is proposed, though the author notes that actual noun phrases may deviate from it.

section: The structure of the noun phrase
subsection: Information structure inside the noun phrase
text: When the order of head and attribute is reversed in a noun phrase, one can notice an increase in assertiveness to the right end of the phrase. In , for instance, an assertion is made about an old man who has the habit of making jokes, a fact which sets the scene for what is to come: the old man plays a prank at the protagonist of the story. In , the asserted information is not so much the fact that a market takes place, because the narrative is temporally embedded in a season known for events such as markets and fun fairs, but rather the fact that it is a comparatively big market. Modifying material to the right of the head noun is restricted to one element (as in Belhare, see Bickel2003Belhare ). . .nna ighurum=be a-pum laktaŋge=ca wa-ya=na that round =loc 1sg.poss- grandfather humorous =add exist [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg In that round, a humorous old man was there, too. 40 _leg _08.034 . inimma maŋpha ma=na pog-a-ma market quite big =nmlz.sg rise [3sg]-pst-prf Quite a big market took place. The noun inimma is a neologism and not widely in use. 01 _leg _07.145 Elements inside the noun phrase can also be focussed on or topicalized, as the following examples show. In akkago is a contrastive topic, in a (hypothetical) argument where one person brags about how many friends he has in contrast to the other person. In , there is a contrastive focus marker inside the noun phrase, added because the assertion is made in contrast to a presupposition claiming that the opposite be true. . .ak=ka=go ibebe=ha ghak kamnibak=ci khaʔla=hoŋ ŋ-waiʔ=ya=ci 1sg.poss=gen=top everywhere =nmlz.nsg all friend =nsg like _this =seq 3pl- exist [npst]=nmlz.nsg=nsg As for mine, I have friends everywhere, like this. 36 _cvs _06.355 .na=go aniŋ=ga=le kham, nniŋda nhe wa-ma n-dokt-wa-m-ga-n=ha this =top 1pl.excl.poss=gen=ctr ground 2pl[erg] here live -inf neg- get -npst-2pl.A-2-neg=nmlz.nsg This is our land, you will not get the chance to live here. 22 _nrr _05.012
summary:
When the head and attribute order is reversed in a noun phrase, the asserted or contrastive information tends to appear toward the right edge of the phrase. The passage illustrates this with examples where the key claim is not merely that something exists or happens, but a more specific property such as a humorous old man or a particularly big market.

It also notes that modifying material to the right of the head noun is limited to a single element. In addition, elements inside the noun phrase can be marked for focus or topic, including contrastive topics and contrastive focus markers.

text: This chapter describes the elements that can be found in the noun phrase, mo -di -fying or replacing a head noun. It is structured as follows: pers-pron deals with the personal pronouns, poss-pron discusses the possessive pronouns, and dem-pron the demonstratives. sec-indef shows how indefinite reference is expressed, sec-quant deals with numerals and other quantifying elements. interr then focusses on interrogative forms, including non-nominal interrogatives.
summary: The chapter surveys the elements that can appear in a noun phrase by modifying or replacing a head noun. It is organized into sections on personal pronouns, possessive pronouns, demonstratives, indefinite reference, quantifiers and numerals, and interrogative forms, including non-nominal interrogatives.

text: Yakkha personal pronouns are used to refer to persons, typically to participants whose reference has already been established in discourse. They can take the structural position of a noun phrase (of any participant role) or they can function as heads of noun phrases, although the possibilities to be modified are restricted; relative clauses and demonstratives are not possible, for instance. Possible modifiers are quantifiers and numerals, but they follow the pronominal head, in contrast to noun phrases with nominal heads, which are mostly head-final. Pronouns, like noun phrases in general, are not obligatory, and they are frequently dropped in Yakkha. The pronouns distinguish person and number. Clusivity, which is found in possessive pronouns, possessive prefixes and in the verbal inflection, does not play a role in the personal pronouns (compare and ). An overview of the personal pronouns is provided together with the possessive pronouns in poss below. The first and second person pronouns distinguish singular, dual and plural number. The morpheme -ci conveys a dual meaning in the first and second person pronouns, as opposed to -ni for plural. In the third person, -ci simply has a nonsingular meaning.Note that in contrast to the pronominal paradigm, the verbal inflection distinguishes dual number also in the third person (cf. verb-infl). . . kaniŋ khe-i-ŋ=a 1pl go [pst]-1pl-excl=nmlz.nsg We (without you) went. . kaniŋ khe-i=ha 1pl go [pst]-1pl=nmlz.nsg We (all) went.
summary: Yakkha personal pronouns refer to already established discourse participants and can function as noun phrases, either as standalone heads or in other NP positions, though they allow only limited modification; quantifiers and numerals may follow the pronoun, but relative clauses and demonstratives are not permitted. The pronoun system marks person and number, with singular, dual, and plural distinctions in first and second person, but clusivity is not expressed in personal pronouns; instead, the dual is marked by -ci and plural by -ni, while in third person -ci simply indicates non-singular number.

section: Possessive pronouns and nominal possessive inflection
text: The possessive pronouns modify a head noun, indicating the possessor of the thing that is referred to by the noun (see ). Since the head noun can be omitted when its reference has been established already, the possessive pronoun can also be the sole element in a phrase (see ). The possessive pronouns resemble the personal pronouns slightly, but they are sufficiently different and irregular so that they establish a separate paradigm. Except for the third person nonsingular form, the roots all look slighty different from the corresponding personal pronouns. They all host the genitive enclitic =ga, though. The possessive pronouns distinguish number and person, including clusivity, a category that is absent from the personal pronoun paradigm. The inclusive forms have no parallel in the personal pronouns. poss provides an overview of personal and possessive pronouns and possessive prefixes. The capital /N/ stands for an unspecified nasal that assimilates to the following consonant in place of articulation. . .ak=ka kucuma sy-a-ma=na 1sg.poss=gen dog die [3sg]-pst-prf=nmlz.sg My dog has died. .ak=ka=ca sy-a-ma=na 1sg.poss=gen=add die [3sg]-pst-prf=nmlz.sg Mine has died, too. table ! centering tabular llll & personal pronoun & possessive pronoun & possessive prefix 1sg &ka & akka & a- 1du.excl & kanciŋ & anciŋga & anciŋ- 1pl.excl & kaniŋ & aniŋga & aniŋ- 1du.incl & kanciŋ & enciŋga & enciŋ- 1pl.incl & kaniŋ & eŋga & eN- 2sg & nda & ŋga & N- 2du & njiŋda & njiŋga & njiŋ- 2pl & nniŋda & nniŋga & nniŋ- 3sg & uŋ & ukka & u- o- 3nsg & uŋci & uŋciga & uŋci- tabular Personal and possessive pronouns, possessive inflection centering table
summary: Possessive pronouns function as modifiers of a head noun to mark the possessor, but they can also stand alone when the noun is recoverable from context. They form a separate paradigm from personal pronouns because they are irregular and differ in form, and they mark person, number, and clusivity; all take the genitive enclitic =ga, and the inclusive forms have no counterpart in the personal pronouns.

section: Possessive pronouns and nominal possessive inflection
text: Alternatively to using possessive pronouns, relationships of possession can also be expressed by attaching a possessive prefix to the head noun, that refers to the possessee. The prefixes index the number and person of the possessor. Their form is similar to the possessive pronouns, which suggests that they have developed out of them. The nasals in the 1pl.incl prefix eN- and in the 2sg prefix N- assimilate in place of articulation to the first consonant of their nominal host (see ). The third person singular prefix u- has the allomorph o- before stems containing /e/ or /o/. The possessees can also be nouns referring to sensations, as in . The difference between using a pronoun or a prefix lies in the information structure. If the possessive relationship is focussed on, the pronoun has to be used. . .n-yupma 2sg.poss- sleepiness your sleepiness .m-ba 2sg.poss- father your father .eŋ-gamnibak 1pl.incl.poss- friend our friend Possessive prefixes only attach to nouns, and thus, they are affixes, not clitics. In co-compounds (see ), and if two nouns are conjoined in a noun phrase (see ), both nouns host the possessive prefix.Admittedly, all examples of co-compounds or coordinated nouns with possessive marking in the current data set are from the domain of kinship terms. . .u-ppa u-ma=ci=ca 3sg.poss- father 3sg.poss- mother =nsg=add her parents, too 01 _leg _07.152 .a-ma=nuŋ a-na=ŋa y-yog-a-n-niŋ=bi 1sg.poss- mother =com 1sg.poss- sister =erg neg- search -sbjv[1.P]-neg-neg.pl=irr If my mother and sister had not searched for me, ... 42 _leg _10.052
summary:
Possession can be expressed not only with possessive pronouns but also with possessive prefixes attached to the possessed noun, and these prefixes mark the person and number of the possessor. Their forms resemble the pronouns, suggesting a historical development from them; some prefixes show regular phonological alternations, and the third-person singular prefix has an allomorph before stems with /e/ or /o/.

The choice between pronoun and prefix depends on information structure: if the possessive relation is focused, the pronoun must be used. Possessive prefixes attach only to nouns, so they are affixes rather than clitics, and in co-compounds or coordinated noun phrases both nouns can carry possessive marking, though the examples given are all kinship terms.

section: Possessive pronouns and nominal possessive inflection
text: Certain nouns nearly always appear with possessive prefixes, even when no clear possessor has been mentioned in the preceding discourse. They can hardly be expressed without belonging to another entity or person. The semantic domains which are relevant for obligatory possession are consanguineal kinship, spatial relations (relational nouns), body parts and other part-whole relations that are not body parts in the strict sense, such as otheklup half or ochon splinter . So far, 118 obligatorily possessed nouns could be found, which makes up roughly 9 % of the nominal lexicon. In Bickeletal2005_Obligatory on obligatorily possessed nouns, this phenomenon is defined as “words for which an inflectional category of possession is obligatorily present”. In the current Yakkha data at least some exceptions can be found, so that I conclude that obligatory possession is rather a gradual phenomenon in Yakkha. More data would be necessary in order to explain apparent exceptions and thus to paint a clearer picture of obligatorily possessed nouns in Yakkha. Some of the obligatorily possessed nouns are listed in inalien . Since obligatory possession is also found in the expression of spatial relations, several adverbs and relational nouns originate in obligatorily possessed nouns (cf. adv). table [htp] tabular ll 2 c consanguineal kinship acya& child aphu& elder brother ana& elder sister aphaŋ& father's younger brother akoŋma& mother's younger sister tabular tabular ll 2 c spatial and temporal relations ucumphak& day after tomorrow ulum& middle, center (relational noun) oʈemma& plains uyum& side (relational noun) okomphak& third day after today tabular tabular ll 2 c body parts unabhak& ear umik& eye unamcyaŋ& cheek unacik& face utamphwak& hair umuk& hand uʈaŋ& horn ulaŋ& leg uya& mouth, opening ophok& stomach osenkhwak& bone uʈiŋ& thorn, fishbone tabular tabular ll 2 c part-whole relations opoŋgalik& bud uchuk& corner upusum& crust uyin& egg otheklup& half okhop& husk of rice uhup& knot ukhuppa& lid, cover ophetrak& petal ochon& thorn, splinter oyok& place uwha& wound tabular Some obligatorily possessed nouns table With kinship terms, the first person singular possessive prefix is the default option, e.g., in the citation forms in elicitations, in general statements and in vocatives (as using names to address people is considered impolite). There are some lexicalized terms like a-mum grandmother , a-pum grandfather , a-na elder sister , characterized by a shift of stress to the first syllable. Recall that prefixes generally do not belong to the domain to which stress is assigned.
