summary:
The V2 **-ca “eat”** has both grammaticalized and lexicalized uses. It functions as a reflexive marker with detransitivizing effects, and also appears in autobenefactive derivations and lexical compounds where the subject is typically the intended beneficiary; in these autobenefactive cases, the verb may become intransitively inflected, but the P argument can still be expressed and is usually less central.

The passage also notes that **-ca** occurs in many non-compositional lexicalized predicates, especially involving bodily sensations, social interaction, and self-beneficial or enjoyable actions. Its transparent literal “eat” use may be the historical source for these grammatical and metaphorical meanings, and some examples even suggest adversative uses.

text: as well be expressed in two independent clauses. The verbs participating in the CP share all arguments, which motivates the choice of a CP instead of two clauses. . ka makkai ŋo-c-wa-ŋ=ha 1sg[erg] corn fry -V2.eat-npst[3.P]-1sg.A=nmlz.nsg I make popcorn and eat it. Having looked at the whole range of functions of the V2 -ca eat , it is obvious that perceiving this marker merely as a syntactic valency-decreasing device is not justified. Rather, the common core of all the uses of this V2 is the volitionally and beneficially affected agent (with the exception of a few adversative usages). The affectedness of the agent is also a property of the literal meaning of the verb eat. As pointed out in Naess2009_How , it is central to the semantics of eat and drink verbs. Næss argues that this semantic property of the event also makes it less prototypically transitive, as the agent shares the property of affectedness with patient arguments. Thus, the A and the P are not maximally distinct in eat and drink verbs. Verbs of eating often exhibit properties typical of intransitive verbs crosslinguistically, which possibly also gave rise to the grammaticalization of -ca into detransitivizing markers of reflexivity, autobenefactive, adversative notions and reciprocality (see refl3) in Yakkha. The extreme polysemy of the V2 -ca is not at all surprising, as the activity of eating is universal to human existence, and is thus expected to be a rich source for metaphors Newman2009_A-cross-linguistic. The use of eat in the expression of experiental events is a prominent pattern in Central and South Asia generally, that is thus found in other Tibeto-Burman languages, and in Indo-Aryan languages ( Hooketal2009_The-semantic , Pramodini2010_Eat ). While the grammaticalization to passive markers is also found elsewhere Heineetal2002_World , the use of eat as marker of reflexivity is, to my best knowledge, not yet reported for other languages, although such a development is, for the reasons laid out above, very plausible.
summary: The passage argues that the V2 marker **-ca ‘eat’** in Yakkha should not be analyzed simply as a valency-decreasing device, because its various uses share a semantic core: the agent is volitionally and beneficially affected, except in some adversative cases. This affectedness is also part of the meaning of eating and drinking verbs more generally, which helps explain why such verbs are less prototypically transitive and may develop into markers of reflexivity, autobenefactive, adversative, and reciprocal meanings. The text further notes that using **eat** to express experiential events is common in Central and South Asia, while reflexive uses of **eat** as a grammatical marker appear to be rare but plausible.

text: The marker -siʔ is not a verb historically, but it behaves according to the V2 pattern, triggering the recursive inflection and being part of the infinitives, which is why it is mentioned here as well (see below for its historical development). The morpheme is found with detransitivizing function as a middle marker (see and middle), but also in less transparent intransitive verb-verb combinations, that will be shown in this section. The grammatical and lexical functions of -siʔ all share the semantic feature of indicating unintentional or involuntary actions. All verbs derived by the middle involve animate or human subjects. . .kamala=ŋa sakhi phaps-u=na Kamala =erg thread entangle- 3.P[pst]=nmlz.sg Kamala entangled the thread. .mendhwak=ci phaps-a-sy-a-ci goat =nsg entangle- pst-mddl-pst-[3]du The two goats lost their way. The component of unintentional actions is best illustrated in . The simple verb tupma meet is intransitive and inherently reciprocal (see ). The middle specifies that the event happened spontaneously and unintentionally (see ). The examples in show further middle verbs. . .wandik tub-i? tomorrow meet -1pl[sbjv] Shall we meet tomorrow? .tub-a-sy-a-ŋ-ci-ŋ=ha meet- pst-mddl-pst-excl-[1]du-excl=nmlz.nsg We (dual) ran into each other. . .cuwa=ŋa hipt-a-sy-a-ga=na=i? beer =ins choke- pst-mddl-pst-2=nmlz.sg=q Did you choke on the beer? .ka kolem=na=be sos-a-sy-a-ŋ=na 1sg slippery= nmlz.sg=loc slide -pst-mddl-pst-1sg=nmlz.sg I slipped on the slippery ground. . chimd-a=nuŋ chimd-a=nuŋ tops-a-sy-a-ŋ=na ask- pst[3sg]=com ask- pst[3sg]=com confuse -pst-mddl-pst-1sg=nmlz.sg As she asked and asked, I got confused. Example shows lexicalized predicates containing -siʔ, all from the experiential domain. A look at the independent meanings of the lexical roots here shows that the semantics of these predicates are non-compositional, and non-transparent. . .cond-a-sy-a=bi=ba praise [3sg]-pst-mddl-pst=irr=emph She would have been happy. 13 _cvs _02.056 .ŋond-a-sy-a-ga=na=i? remain- pst-mddl-pst-2=nmlz.sg=q Do you feel shy? The middle marker is also used in imperatives, with the function of turning commands into implorations. By using the middle, the speaker acknowledges the affectedness of the addressee, or he implies that it is against the addressee's will (e.g. in ). In this function, the volition of the subject is allowed and even required, as and show. . . pog-a! stand _up- imp Stand up! .pog-a-sy-a stand _up- imp-mddl-imp Please, stand up. (to a person who was not willing to stand up) .yok-t-a-by-a-sy-a, so-t-a-by-a-sy-a search- ben-imp-V2.give-imp-mddl-imp , look -ben-imp-V2.give-imp-mddl-imp Please search her (the missing girl) for us, look for us. 22 _nrr _05.084--5 As for the etymology of the marker, it behaves like a V2 in the Kiranti languages, but it is a reconstructed suffix already in Proto-Tibeto-Burman. A sibilant suffix with middle semantics is well attested in many Tibeto-Burman languages, e.g. in Dulong-Rawang and Padam LaPolla1996_Middle and in languages of the West Himalayish branch Matisoff2003Handbook . The verbal behavior of the marker is a Kiranti innovation, resulting from reanalysis of a suffix to a verbal stem, under the pressure to have a structure that is analogous to the other verbal operations that are marked by V2s in Kiranti languages (see Bickel2003Belhare for the same development in Belhare). In some Kiranti languages the marker has reflexive and reciprocal semantics, e.g. in Limbu Driem1987A-grammar , in Kulung Tolsma1999A-grammar and in Chintang Bickeletal2010Ditransitives . In Thulung and Wambule it is found as a detransitivizer or stativizer ( Lahaussois2003_Thulung , Opgenort2004A-Grammar ). The middle marker in Yakkha does not have a stativizing effect on the temporal structure of the verb (reconstructed as a proto-function of this morpheme, Matisoff2003Handbook ). Most of the verbs have ingressive-stative Aktionsart, which is why they are usually marked for past while referring to present (stative) events.
summary:
The marker **-siʔ** is historically not a verb, but in Kiranti it behaves like a **V2** because it triggers recursive inflection and appears in infinitives. Its main functions are as a **middle marker** and in various intransitive verb-verb combinations, and in all cases it conveys the sense of **unintentional or involuntary action**, often with animate or human subjects.

The passage also notes that **-siʔ** appears in lexicalized predicates from the experiential domain, where the meaning is non-compositional, and in **imperatives** it softens commands into implorations that acknowledge the addressee’s affectedness. Etymologically, it is a reconstructed Proto-Tibeto-Burman suffix whose verbal behavior is a **Kiranti innovation** caused by reanalysis to match other V2-marked verbal operations.

text: The V2 kheʔ go is found with intransitive telic verbs, emphasizing their orientation towards an end point, or the irreversibility of an event. Example , for instance, was uttered to emphasize that the subject is already fast asleep, implying that it is useless to try and wake up that person. The other examples in illustrate the application of this V2 to indicate irreversible intransitive events. . . ips-a-khy-a=na fall _asleep -pst-V2.go[3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg She has fallen asleep (better not wake her up). .a-ma sy-a-khy-a, i cok-ma=na? 1sg.poss- mother die -pst-V2.go[3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg what do -inf=nmlz.sg My mother has died, so what to do? 06 _cvs _01.020 .wa bhale ka-ya-khy-a cock cock call -pst-V2.go[3sg]-pst The cock crowed already. Context: the time is over and the protagonist loses his bet. 11 _nrr _01.011 . ulippa paŋ hor-a-khy-a=na old house crumble -pst-V2.go[3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg The old house crumbled down. The development of a motion verb into a marker of telicity is common; the motion semantics get extended to a movement in time and changes-of-state in general. Examples that involve literal motion events are, however, also fairly frequent with -kheʔ, as the verbs in illustrate. In these examples, the lexical verb denotes the kind of motion, and the V2 specifies the direction away from a point of reference. . . chemha phom-khem-me=ha liquor spill [3sg]-V2.go-npst=nmlz.nc The liquor will spill. . uimalaŋ=be sos-a-khy-a=na steep _slope _downwards =loc lie _slanted [3sg]-pst-V2.go-pst=nmlz.sg He slipped on the steep slope (landing on his back and sliding off). . kakkulik kaks-a-khy-a=na rolling fall [3sg]-pst-V2.go-pst=nmlz.sg She tumbled down (in somersaults). 06 _cvs _01.020 . nhaŋ pes-a-khy-a-ma and _then fly [3sg]-pst-V2.go-pst-prf And then he has flown away. 21 _nrr _04.030 .limbu=ci nhaŋ n-las-a-khy-a-ma Limbu _group =nsg after _that 3pl- return -pst-V2.go-pst-prf The Limbus went back afterwards. 22 _nrr _05.035 Lexicalized complex predicates are possible as well. In , the combination of khus steal and V2 -kheʔ go has acquired the meaning escape, without an action of stealing being implied. As in the examples in , the V2 specifies also the direction away from a point of reference. The same is possible with the V2 -ra come to indicate that someone comes fleeing from a location further away. .ŋ-khus-a-khy-a-n=na neg- escape -pst-V2.go[3sg]-pst-neg=nmlz.sg He did not escape. In some instances, the V2 -kheʔ retains its original lexical meaning, and simply means go , as in the sequence of events shown in . The transitive verbs fry and eat have been detransitivized to synchronize the argument structure with the final verb go . So far, this is the only instance where the participants do not bear equal relations to the verb, as the location where the frying and the eating take place is in a source relation to the action of going. .camraŋ=be cama i=ya n-ni-ca-ya-khy-a-ma=hoŋ Camrang =loc food what =nmlz.nc 3pl- fry -V2.eat-pst-V2.go-pst-prf=seq After they have fried and eaten some food in Camrang and gone away, ... 22 _nrr _05.034 The whole range of -kheʔ in CPs, thus, represents a con -tinuum from the lexical meaning of go , via unspecific motion away from a point of reference, to a grammaticalized and regular telic function, by metaphorically extending a movement in space to a movement in time.
summary: The V2 *-kheʔ* ‘go’ occurs with intransitive telic verbs to emphasize endpoint orientation and the irreversibility of an event, as in falling asleep, dying, or crumbling down. It also appears in motion events to mark movement away from a reference point, and in some lexicalized complex predicates such as *khus + -kheʔ* ‘escape,’ where the original meaning of ‘go’ may be retained in some contexts. Overall, its uses form a continuum from literal motion to a grammaticalized telic marker that extends spatial movement metaphorically to temporal change and completion.

text: The V2 -ra (*ta) come (from further away) specifies an event in terms of a motion towards a point of reference, while being unspecified for the uphill/downhill distinction. The lexical source verb is tama, but initial /t/ becomes [r] intervocalically in all V2 stems. . .arap=phaŋ khus-a-ra-ya=na Arab _countries =abl escape [3sg]-pst-V2.come-pst=nmlz.sg He came escaping from (working in the) Arab countries. . cuncula [...] ten=be las-a-ra-ya-ma Cuncula [...] village =loc return [3sg]-pst-V2.come-pst-prf Cuncula has returned home. 01 _leg _07.307 .dharan men-da-le hiks-a-ra-ya=na Dharan neg- reach-cvb turn _around [3sg]-pst-V2.come-pst=nmlz.sg Without reaching Dharan, he turned around and came back. An actual movement in space is not implied here either, equal to -kheʔ discussed above. The function of -ra can also be metaphorically extended, just as in the English translation (see ). . hiŋ-a-ra-ya=na survive [3sg]-pst-V2.come-pst=nmlz.sg He came back to life.
summary: The V2 suffix **-ra** (from lexical *tama* ‘come’) marks an event as motion toward a point of reference, but it does not specify uphill versus downhill movement. In these examples, it can describe actual returning movement as well as metaphorical “coming back” uses, such as “came back to life,” and the initial /t/ of the source verb becomes [r] intervocalically in V2 stems.

text: The lexical source verb of -raʔ (*taʔ) refers to bringing something from further away, and this meaning component is preserved in the CPs, too. It specifies transitive events for directedness towards a point of reference. As such, the V2 can either modify a motion verb (see ) or express a sequence of events (see ). . .nhaŋ ak=ka kamnibak=ci hip-paŋ tikt-u-ra-wa-ŋ-ci-ŋ and _then 1sg.poss=gen friends =nsg two -clf.hum lead -3.P-V2.bring-npst-1sg.A-3nsg.P-1sg.A And I will bring along two of my friends. 14 _nrr _02.24 .eko phuŋ chikt-u-ra=na one flower pluck [3sg.A;pst]-3.P-V2.bring=nmlz.sg She plucked a flower and brought it. It is also possible to turn a transitive verb into a motion verb by adding -raʔ (see ). Since the stem momd cover is transitive, the V2 has to be transitive, too. . eŋ=ga ten khibrumba=ŋa momd-u-ra=na 1pl.incl=gen village fog =erg cover [3sg.A;pst]-3.P-V2.bring=nmlz.sg The fog came (lit.: brought) covering our village.
summary: The lexical source verb *-raʔ* (*taʔ*) means “bring something from further away,” and this sense is retained in the CPs, where it marks transitive events directed toward a reference point. The V2 can either modify a motion verb or express a sequence of events, and adding *-raʔ* can also turn a transitive verb into a motion verb.

text: If intransitive motion is directed downwards and towards a point of reference, the V2 -uks come down is used to specify this path. . taŋkhyaŋ ka-ya=na=hau. ikhiŋ=na! hor-uks-heks-a=na sky speak [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg=excla such =nmlz.sg burst -V2.come.down-V2.cut-pst=nmlz.sg It thundered, indeed. Such a loud one! It (the sky) is about to break down on us. 13 _cvs _02.088--89
summary: For intransitive motion that moves downward toward a reference point, the language uses the V2 form **-uks** ‘come down’ to mark the path. The example describes thunder with the sky “bursting down,” conveying that the sky is about to break on the speakers.

text: The V2 -ukt bring down denotes caused motion down and towards the deictic center, both with monotransitive and ditransitive verbs. The resulting CP has the argument realization of the indirective frame, showing agreement with the T argument (cf. Chapter verb-val). This verb is compatible with the adverb mo downhill (versus yo and to), although this would be a somewhat redundant expression. Note that in combination with CV or CVʔ stems that also have /u/ as stem vowel, the stems fuse into one syllable, as shown in . . .ŋ-gamnibak (mo) tikt-ukt-u 2sg.poss- friend (down) guide -V2.bring.down-3.P[imp] Bring your friend down here. .ʈhuŋkha=bhaŋ siŋ khu-kt-u-m-ŋ=ha steep _slope =abl wood carry -V2.bring.down-3.P[pst]-1pl.A-excl=nmlz.nc We brought down fire wood from the steep slopes.
summary: The V2 suffix **-ukt** ‘bring down’ expresses caused motion downward and toward the deictic center, and it can combine with both monotransitive and ditransitive verbs. The resulting CP follows an **indirective argument realization pattern**, agreeing with the **T argument**, and it is compatible with **mo** ‘downhill,’ though that combination is somewhat redundant. When attached to CV or CVʔ stems with the vowel /u/, the stems fuse into a single syllable.

subsection: The V2 -ap (motion towards, from close nearby)
text: The V2 -ap come denotes intransitive motion towards a point of reference, crucially from close nearby and from the same level with respect to the inclination of the hill, e.g. from a neighbouring house which is on the same elevation level. Such predicates are compatible with the adverb yondaŋ, which refers to sources on the same level. .yo=na paŋ=bhaŋ las-a-ab-a=na across =nmlz.sg house =abl return- [3sg]-V2.come-pst=nmlz.sg She came back from the house across.
summary: The V2 *-ap come* expresses intransitive motion toward a reference point, specifically from a nearby source at the same elevation, such as a neighboring house on the same level. This use is compatible with *yondaŋ*, an adverb indicating sources on the same level, as shown in the example meaning “She came back from the house across.”

subsection: The V2 -apt (caused motion towards, from close nearby)
text: The V2 -apt bring expresses caused motion towards a point of reference, from nearby and from the same elevation level with respect to the hill, in analogy to the intransitive -ap above. The resulting CP has the argument realization of the indirective frame (cf. three-arg-frame). As example illustrates, this V2 is also used for small-scale movements. . .ŋ-gamnibak tikt-apt-u 2sg.poss- friend guide -V2.bring-3.P[imp] Bring your friend here. .jhola peʔleʔle und-apt-u-ga=i bag ideoph pull -V2.bring-3.P[imp]-2=emph Pull out the bag (from behind the heap of clothes, towards oneself). The transitivity of the two verbal stems has to match. In , no literal bringing of the substance is involved, at least not if bringing is understood as carrying something in a container outside one's own body. .nhaŋ chemha=ca uŋ-apt-a-ŋ-c-u-ŋ=ba and _then liquor=add drink -V2.bring-pst-excl-du-3.P-excl=emph We drank liquor and came (lit.: brought it) here. 36 _cvs _06.398
summary:
The V2 **-apt** ‘bring’ expresses caused motion toward a reference point from nearby and from the same elevation level, parallel to the intransitive **-ap**. It yields a CP with the argument structure of an indirective frame and is also used for small-scale movements, such as bringing a friend here or pulling a bag out toward oneself.  

The two verbal stems must match in transitivity, and in some uses the verb does not imply literal carrying in a container; for example, “we drank liquor and came here” is described literally as “brought it” here.

subsection: The V2 -ris (caused motion to a distant goal)
text: The V2 -ris (*tis), with the lexical meaning place, invest (e.g. place a pot on the fire, invest money in some project), indicates caused motion towards a distant goal, implying that the object will remain there. The resulting predicate again exhibits the argument realization of the indirective frame (cf. Chapter verb-val). This V2 is not specified for the vertical dimension, and it is compatible with adverbial specifications for either mo down , to up or yo across , but naturally not with adverbials expressing proximity to the deictic center. In both examples, two V2 are involved. The V2 -a -na leave fuses with the inflectional material (/-u-a-u/) to result in [o]. . .ŋ-gamnibak u-paŋ=be tikt-u-ris-o 2sg.poss- friend 3sg.poss- house =loc lead -3.P-V2.place-V2.leave[3.P;imp] Deliver your friend at his home. . uŋci-ten=be ikt-u-ris-o 3nsg.poss- village =loc chase -3.P-V2.place-V2.leave[3.P;imp] Chase them to their village.
summary: The V2 **-ris** (*tis*), meaning “place” or “invest,” denotes caused motion toward a distant goal and implies that the object remains there. This predicate takes the **indirective frame** and is not specified for vertical direction, so it can combine with adverbials like “down,” “up,” or “across,” but not with those expressing proximity to the deictic center. The examples show that two V2s occur together, with **-a-na** “leave” fusing with inflectional material to form the final verb form.

text: The V2 -bhes has the lexical meaning send [towards] , bring [towards] . It signifies that caused motion takes place on the same elevation level and towards the point of reference, for either small-scale or large-scale movements. Example shows transfer from a very short distance, the application of the blessing on the forehead (by sticking cooked rice on the forehead). Example shows the employment of this V2 for a large-scale movement. This V2 is only compatible with adverbs derived from the root yo across . . .ʈika ʈal-a n-jog-u-bhes-u=hoŋ blessing _on _forehead stick -nativ 3pl.A- make -3.P-V2.bring-3.P[pst]=seq After they applied the blessings, ... (as remembered by a bride who got blessed) 25 _tra _01.049 . nhaŋ, nna, lalubaŋ=nuŋ phalubaŋ ŋ-ikt-a-bhes-uks-u-ci and _then that Lalubang =com Phalubang 3pl.A- chase -pst-V2.bring-V2.prf-3.P-3nsg.P And then, they chased Lalubang and Phalubang here. 22 _nrr _05.023
summary: The V2 **-bhes** means “send/bring toward” and marks caused motion toward the point of reference at the same elevation level, whether over a very short distance or a larger one. It is illustrated by use in applying blessings to the forehead and in a larger-scale motion example, and it is only compatible with adverbs derived from the root **yo** “across.”

text: The V2 -end ( -nen before consonants)Cf. the citation forms leʔnemma, lepnemma and huʔnemma for the examples in leendu. has the lexical meaning apply, insert . As a V2, it indicates caused motion downwards, as shown by the examples in . Here, the motion is not specified for the direction towards or away from a point of reference. . . u-laŋ=ci leʔ-end-u-ci=ha 3sg.poss- leg =nsg drop -V2.insert-3.P[pst]-3nsg.P=nmlz.nsg It (the plane) lowered its landing gear. . nhaŋ phoʔ n-lept-end-wa and _then ideoph 3pl.A- throw -V2.insert-npst[3.P] They throw it down swiftly (the fishing net). 13 _cvs _02.009 . hut-end-u-ŋ=na push -V2.insert-3.P[pst]-1sg.A=nmlz.sg I pushed him down. The V2 -end can also express caused motion downwards as a result of another action (see ). Furthermore, using this V2 may also convey regret. Saying pegenduŋna ( I shattered it ) sounds more regrettingly than the underived peguŋna. . . tabek=ŋa siŋ=ga u-whak cen-end-u=na khukuri _knife =ins tree =gen 3sg.poss-branch chop -V2.insert-3.P[pst]=nmlz.sg He cut down the branch with a Khukuri knife. (Cut-and-break clips, Bohnemeyeretal2010_cut ) . u-sa seps-end-u 3sg.poss- fruit pluck -V2.insert-3.P[imp] Get the fruits down (plucking).
summary:
The V2 **-end** (with **-nen** before consonants) has the lexical meaning **“apply, insert”** and, as a V2, it marks **caused downward motion**. In this use, the motion is downward but does not specify motion toward or away from a reference point, as in examples meaning “lowered its landing gear,” “throw it down,” “pushed him down,” and “cut down the branch.”

The passage also notes that **-end** can express downward motion **as a result of another action**. In addition, this V2 may convey **regret**, since forms like **pegenduŋna** sound more regretful than the underived **peguŋna**.

subsection: The V2 -ket (caused motion up and towards)
text: The V2 -ket bring up , signifies caused motion up and towards a reference point (see ). There is a corresponding intransitive stem -keʔ come up , but it has not been found yet as V2. . .na eko=ŋa=go thend-u-get-uks-u=ba this one =erg=top lift -3.P-V2.bring.up-prf-3.P[pst]=emph Someone has lifted it up (carried it up in one's hands). 37 _nrr _07.082 . thithi end-u-get-uks-u=na upright insert -3.P-V2.bring.up-3.P[pst]-prf=nmlz.sg He inserted it upright at an elevated place. 37 _nrr _07.083 The movement upwards may also happen on a very small scale. In , for instance, the speaker does not refer to someone plucking further downhill, but just one meter below herself. In Kiranti languages, the topography-based specification of events reaches a level of much greater distinction than speakers of European languages are generally used to (cf. Chapter ch-geomorphic, and Bickel1999Cultural, Bickel2001Deictic, Ebert1999The-up---down, Gaenszle1999Travelling ). . maŋkhu seps-u-get-u=ha garlic pluck -3.P-V2.bring.up-3.P[pst]=nmlz.nsg She plucked and brought up the garlic. Furthermore, at least one example suggests that bring up can also be understood metaphorically, as referring to a movement in time, where the past is equated with lower altitude. The postposition nhaŋto since in this example literally means and then up , providing support to this hypothesis. Further support for the hypothesis that the past is conceptualized as below comes from an idiomatic Noun-Verb Predicate, setni keʔma, literally bring up the night , which refers to staying awake until the morning. . nna namda ka piccha nhaŋto nis-u-get-u-ŋ=na. that festival 1sg[erg] child since see-3.P-V2.bring.up-3.P[pst]-1sg.A=nmlz.sg I have been attending this festival since childhood. 41 _leg _09.006
summary:
The V2 stem **-ket** means “bring up” and indicates caused motion upward toward a reference point, with a corresponding intransitive stem **-keʔ** meaning “come up.” The passage shows that this upward motion can refer even to very small spatial differences, and in Kiranti languages such topography-based distinctions are especially fine-grained.  

It also suggests a metaphorical extension in which upward motion refers to time, with the past conceptualized as lower; this is supported by examples such as **nhaŋto** “since” literally meaning “and then up” and the idiom **setni keʔma** “bring up the night,” meaning to stay awake until morning.

text: The V2 -haks -nhaŋ send (things) expresses caused motion away from a point of reference (see ), and away from the agent (in contrast to -khet carry off described below). Although its lexical meaning is send (things) , as a V2 it is also used with animate T arguments, including human referents. . .ka mima o-hoŋ=be hut-haks-u-ŋ=na 1g[erg] mouse 3sg.poss- hole =loc push -V2.send-3.P[pst]-1sg.A=nmlz.sg I pushed the mouse (back) into her hole. .ʈebul=be cuwa tug-haks-u=ha table =loc beer wipe -V2.send-3.P[pst]=nmlz.nsg She wiped the beer from the table. Despite the ablative semantics of the verbs, the locative is the standard case choice with this verb. . luŋkhwak luŋkhwak seg-haks-u stone stone chose -V2.send-3.P[imp] Sort out stone by stone (from the grains). .wasik ta-ya=hoŋ hoŋma uks-a, ŋkhoŋ yokhaʔla chekt-haks-a=na rain come[3sg]-pst=seq river come _down[3sg]-pst and _then across block -V2.send-pst[3sg]=nmlz.sg After the rain, a river came down, and we redirected it. The verb chekthaksana is detransitivized and passive-like structurally, but this structure can also express first person nonsingular agents (see detr-pass). Like the V2s -kheʔ go and -khet carry off , -haks also conveys telicity and actions with irreversible consequences, as illustrated by the examples in . This V2 was particularly prominent in the data elicited with the cut-and-break clips Bohnemeyeretal2010_cut. . .solop miyaŋ eg-haks-u-su immediately a _little break -V2.send-3.P[pst]-pst.prf Immediately he broke off a little. 04 _leg _03.079 . a-yaŋ cum-haks-u-ŋ=ha 1sg.poss- money hide -V2.send-3.P[pst]-1sg.A=nmlz.c I mislaid my money. . hu-haks-u=na accuse -V2.send-3.P[pst]=nmlz.sg He accused her. This is probably a metaphorical use of huʔ burn . . a-phu=ŋa cekt-haks-u=ha 1sg.poss- eB=erg talk -V2.send-3.P[pst]=nmlz.nc My elder brother did/finalized the talking. Context: wedding negotiations. 36 _cvs _06.363 .a-niŋwa=be=ha ceʔya lu-haks-u=ha 1sg.poss- mind =loc=nmlz.nc matter tell -V2.send-3.P[pst]=nmlz.nc She blabbered out my secret thoughts. The V2 -haks may also attach to the lexical verb haks, an option that has not been found with other V2s so far. It implies that something was sent via an intermediate station, e.g. another house where the adressee has to go and get his things, or via a post office. . salen haks-haks-u=na message send -V2.send-3.P=nmlz.sg He sent the message (via some institution). Furthermore, this V2 is frequently used when the P or T argument of a verb is human (discussed in detail in t-sap). This is surprising because the lexical verb haks send implies inanimate T arguments. There is a strong tendency for referentially high objects (mostly P and T; as G arguments are expected to be referentially high anyway) to occur in a complex predicate construction, and one V2 choice for this is obviously -haks. . . i=ca n-lu-n-ci-n=ha, so-haks-u-ci se=ppa what =add neg- tell -neg-3nsg.P-neg=nmlz.nsg look -V2.send-3.P[pst]-3nsg restr=emph He did not say anything to them, he just glanced at them. 34 _pea _04.044 .kaniŋ na=haŋ iŋ-nhaŋ-ma=na 1pl[erg] this =abl chase -V2.send-inf[deont]=nmlz.sg We have to chase him away from here (this place). 21 _nrr _04.010 . kaniŋ lon-nhaŋ-ma sin 1pl take _out -V2.send-inf[deont] cop.1pl.incl He has to expel us.
summary: The V2 **-haks** ‘send (things)’ expresses caused motion away from a reference point and away from the agent, and unlike the related verb **-khet** ‘carry off’ it can also take animate, including human, T arguments. Although it has ablative meaning, it typically appears with the **locative** case, and it often conveys telicity and irreversible consequences; it is also common with high-referential or human objects in complex predicates.

subsection: The V2 -khet (caused motion along with A)
text: The V2 -khet -kheʔ -(h)et indicates that the object is carried off or is in some way separated from its original location, remaining with the A argument. The lexical source verb is khet carry off . In the infinitives, the form is always -kheʔ, while in the inflected forms, the V2 surfaces as -het or even -et. These predicates either express a manner of caused motion away from a reference poin, as in and , or a sequence of doing something and literally carrying off the object, as in and . .ghak yaŋ-het-i=nuŋ=ga wasik all flush -V2.carry.off-compl=com=gen rain a rain that flushed away everything 38 _nrr _07.076 . jaŋgal=be sa-het-u=hoŋ forest =loc lead _by _rope -V2.carry.off-3.P[pst]=seq He led it (the goat) into the jungle, ... 20 _pea _02.026 . yubak coŋ-kheʔ-ma goods shift-V2.carry.off-inf[deont] The goods have to be unloaded and carried off. . khus-het-uks-u=ha hola steal -V2.carry.off-prf-3.P[pst]=nmlz.nsg probably He probably stole it and carried it off. 20 _pea _02.014 Like -raʔ bring described above, -khet carry off can also be used metaphorically, carrying various interpretations. In , it is employed to satisfy the requirement of matching valency within a CP. The verb -kheʔ go would be impossible here because it is intransitive, while uŋ drink is transitive. The same holds for transimpersonal verbs (see and (c)).Transimpersonal verbs always show transitive person marking, but an overt A argument cannot be expressed. With such verbs the V2 has to be transitive. In these examples, -khet has a telicizing effect, similar to the effect of -kheʔ go in intransitives. The lexical stems lokt and hand have ingressive semantics, i.e. when they are inflected for past, they refer to ongoing events. After -khet has been added, they are oriented towards the end point, as these examples show. . .khem uŋ-het-u-ŋ=na before drink-V2.carry.off-3.P[pst]-1sg.A=nmlz.sg I had drunken it before and left. . maŋcwa lokt-het-u=ha water boil-V2.carry.off-3.P[pst]=nmlz.sg The water boiled down. . micuʔwa hand-het-u=na bamboo _torch burn-V2.carry.off-3.P[pst]=nmlz.sg The bamboo torch burned down. Another interpretation of -khet was found e.g. with cognition verbs such as miʔma think, hope, want, remember , but also with other verbs. In the V2 functions as a marker of degree, intensity or excessiveness. . . nna hoŋ=be iha=le weʔ=na bhoŋ soʔ-ma mit-het-u-ŋ that hole =loc what =ctr exist [3sg]=nmlz.sg comp look -inf think -V2.carry.off-3.P[pst]-1sg.A I badly wanted to see what was inside that hole. 42 _leg _10.024 .maŋpha tas-het-u=ha very _much arrive -V2.carry.off-3.P[pst]=nmlz.nc It became very/too much.
summary:
The V2 **-khet/-kheʔ -(h)et** denotes carrying something off or separating it from its original location, with the object remaining with the A argument; its lexical source is **khet** ‘carry off’. In infinitives it appears as **-kheʔ**, while in inflected forms it may surface as **-het** or **-et**, and it can express caused motion away from a point or the sequence of doing something and physically carrying the object away.  

The marker also has metaphorical uses, including fulfilling valency requirements in certain clauses, giving transimpersonal verbs a transitive V2, and adding a telicizing effect. In some contexts, especially with cognition and other verbs, it marks degree, intensity, or excessiveness.

subsection: The quasi-V2 -a -na (do X and leave object)
text: The marker -a -na expresses that the action was carried out at a location not identical to the point of reference and that the subject has returned, leaving the object there, like for instance in pheʔnama drop someone at X and eʔnama enroll someone (e.g. in a boarding school). There is no corresponding independent simple verb ama or nama, but there is the complex verb naʔnama with the meaning to leave , which looks as if the first verb and the V2 are identical. This marker, due to its limited phonological content, undergoes several morphophonological operations, like ablaut and the insertion of consonants, so that it is not always easy to distinguish -a from other morphological material in the verbal inflection. When the first suffix following the stem contains a consonant, the V2 surfaces as -na, e.g. in naʔnanenna I left you . If the stems are followed by the suffix -u, the sequence /-u-a-u-/ will be realized as [-u(ʔ)o], [-o(ʔ)o] or simply [o] (see ). If there is the underlying sequence /-a-a/, it will either be realized as [aya] or as [aʔa] (see ). Furthermore, the ablaut (/a/ to [o]) triggers a change of [-uŋha] in the suffix string to [-oŋha]. . . tisuona /tis-u-a-u=na/ place -pst-V2.leave-1sg.P-2.A=nmlz.sg You delivered him (and returned). . nyubak kamalabe haktoʔoksoŋha /n-yubak kamala=be/ /hakt-u-a-uks-u-ŋ=ha/ 2sg.poss- goods Kamala =loc send -3.P-V2.leave-prf-3.P[pst]-1sg.A=nmlz.nsg I have sent your goods to Kamala (so you can get them there). . umaŋachen (...) lambu lambu yaksaŋnuŋ seula eksaŋ yuksoʔokso /u-ma=ŋa=chen (...) lambu lambu yaksaŋ=nuŋ/ /seula ek-saŋ yuks-u-a-uks-u/ 3sg.poss- mother =erg=top (...) road road grass =com green _stalk break -sim put -3.P-V2.leave-prf-3.P[pst] His mother (...) broke off some gras and stalks along the road and left them (to help the son orient himself back home). 01 _leg _07.072 . . tisayaŋgana /tis-a-a-ŋ-ga=na/ place -pst-V2.leave-1sg.P-2.A=nmlz.sg You delivered me (and returned). . pasupatinathpe phesaʔaŋna /pasupatinath=pe phes-a-a-ŋ=na/ Pashupatinath =loc bring -pst-V2.leave-pst-1sg.P=nmlz.sg He brought me to Pashupatinath (and returned without me).
summary: The marker **-a-na** indicates that an action was carried out at a location different from the reference point, and that the subject returned while leaving the object there, as in meanings like ‘drop someone off’ or ‘enroll someone somewhere.’ Although there is no independent simple verb **ama** or **nama**, there is a complex verb **naʔnama** ‘leave,’ and the marker undergoes several morphophonological changes, including ablaut and consonant insertion, which can make it hard to identify in inflected forms.

text: The V2 -nes lay marks continuative events, i.e., events that are ongoing for longer than expected, and which are not oriented towards an end point. It is found with both transitive and intransitive verbs (see .) Examples (a) to (c) show the combination of -nes with activity verbs, and example shows that in ingressive-stative verbs, the contintuative applies to the resulting state. . .wasik n-da-me-n=niŋa nam phen-a=na phen-a=na, phen-a-nes-a=na rain neg- come -npst-neg=ctmp sun shine [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg shine [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg shine -pst-V2.lay-[3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg While there is no rain, the sun was shining and shining, it kept shining. 38 _nrr _07.075 . leʔnamcuk kei m-mokt-u-nes-uks-u=ha whole _day drum 3pl.A- beat -3.P-V2.lay-prf-3.P[pst]=nmlz.nsg They have kept playing the drums the whole day long. . whaŋma=ŋa lupt-u-nes-u=na sweat=erg disperse -3.P-V2.lay-3.P[pst]=nmlz.sg She kept sweating (e.g. after a long run). . ka=ca hiŋ-a-nes-a-ŋ=na 1sg=add survive -pst-V2.lay-pst-1sg=nmlz.sg I have survived, too.
summary: The V2 suffix **-nes** marks a **continuative** event, meaning an action or state that continues longer than expected and is not directed toward a final endpoint. It occurs with both transitive and intransitive verbs, including activity verbs, and with ingressive-stative verbs it applies to the resulting state, as in examples meaning “kept shining,” “kept playing the drums,” “kept sweating,” and “have survived, too.”

text: The V2 -nuŋ adds a continuative reading, similar to the function of -nes described above. I tentatively suggest the verb yuŋ sit as the etymological source of this V2. Firstly, the grammaticalization of sit into a continuative marker would be a very common development historically, and secondly, I have shown that the insertion of a nasal occurs in vowel-initial and /h/-initial V2s, so that replacing /y/ with [n] seems plausible, too. So far, all examples found with this V2 were intransitive or detransitivized (see ). Punctual events, like in , get an iterative reading when -nuŋ is added. States and activities can also be extended by means of -nuŋ (see , ). In several instances, the two V2s -nuŋ and -nes seem to be interchangeable without any change in meaning. However, while -nes is more frequently combined with past tense, -nuŋ is typically found in nonpast contexts. The exact difference between -nuŋ and -nes cannot be established with certainty yet. . .a-laŋ=ci ŋ-aŋ-khe-nuŋ-me=ha 1sg.poss- leg =nsg 3pl- descend -V2.go-V2.sit-npst=nmlz.nsg My legs keep falling down (from the seat). . heʔniŋ=ca ŋonsi-nuŋ-meʔ=na when =add feel _shy -V2.sit[3sg]-npst=nmlz.sg She is always shy. . tek leŋ-nuŋ-meʔ=na clothes exchange -V2.sit[3sg]-npst=nmlz.sg She keeps changing her clothes.
summary: The V2 -nuŋ adds a continuative meaning, and the author tentatively links it etymologically to the verb yuŋ ‘sit,’ since grammaticalization of ‘sit’ into a continuative marker is typologically common and nasal insertion in certain V2s could account for the form. It appears mainly with intransitive or detransitivized verbs, can give iterative or extended-state/activity readings, and is often interchangeable with -nes, though -nuŋ is more typical in nonpast contexts while -nes more often occurs with past tense.

text: The function of the V2 -bhoks has developed from the lexical meaning split . Adding this V2 to a lexical verb results in a punctual reading, or in the implication that an event happens suddenly and unexpectedly (see ). .a-nabhak yokt-u-bhoks-u-ŋ=na 1sg.poss- ear prick -3.P-V2.split-3.P[pst]-1sg.A=nmlz.sg Suddenly I pierced through my ear (after trying some time and then applying too much pressure). With telic verbs, the event is distilled to an end point (see ), while with activities and ingressive-stative verbs, like in , the initial point of an event is emphasized by -bhoks. . . luŋkhwak thend-u-bhoks-u-ŋ=na stone lift -3.P-V2.split-3.P[pst]-1sg.A=nmlz.sg I lifted the stone (with great difficulties, at once). . mi mi=na et-u-ŋ=na, khatniŋgo ma leks-a-bhoks-a=na fire small =nmlz.sg perceive -3.P[pst]-1sg.A=nmlz.sg but big become [3sg]-pst-v2.split-pst=nmlz.sg It seemed to me that the fire was small, but suddenly it flamed up. . .cumabya=ha ceʔya haku khom-bhoŋ-ma hidden =nmlz.sg language now dig -V2.split-inf[deont] We have to start digging out the (our) hidden language now. . okt-a-bhoks-a-ma-ŋ=ba, hab-a-bhoks-a-ma-ŋ=ba shriek -pst-V2.split-pst-prf-1sg=emph cry -pst-V2.split-pst-prf-1sg=emph Suddenly I shrieked, I broke out in tears. 13 _cvs _02.034
summary: The V2 **-bhoks** has developed from the lexical meaning **“split”** and, when added to a lexical verb, it typically creates a **punctual** reading, often implying that an event happens **suddenly and unexpectedly**. With **telic verbs**, it highlights the **endpoint** of the event, while with **activities** and **ingressive-stative verbs** it emphasizes the **initial point** or sudden onset of the event.

text: The V2 -heks is used when the event denoted by the main verb is about to begin, as shown in . Its literal meaning is cut, saw . Note, again, that because of the inceptive semantics of many verbs, it is usually the past form that is used. The V2 may attach to verbs of any temporal structure, and restrictions on the semantics of the arguments (e.g. animacy or volition) were not encountered. With activities and states, the V2 conveys that the activity or state is about to start. With telic verbs, the V2 conveys that the end point is approaching. Example shows a combination of a completive notion and the immediate prospective notion. . . o-theklup leks-heks-a=na 3sg.poss- half become -V2.cut[3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg Almost half (of the book) is finished. . sabun mend-heks-a=na soap finish -V2.cut[3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg The soap is about to be finished. . ucun=na lambu(=be) tas-heks-u-m=na nice =nmlz.sg way(=loc) arrive -V2.cut-3.P[pst]-1sg.A=nmlz.sg We are about to get to the nice road. . .la ʈoŋnuŋ leks-heks-a=na moon full become -V2.cut[3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg The moon is about to be full. . hops-i-heks-u-ŋ=ha sip -compl-V2.cut-3.P[pst]-1sg.A=nmlz.nc I am about to finish (the soup). This V2 has a second meaning, translatable as do separately . The corresponding construction in Nepali is [ V.stem ]-dai garnu . This usage of -heks is often found in commands, for instance when the speaker encourages the hearer to start or go on with some activity while the speaker leaves the speech situation (see ). . .yuŋ-heks-a sit-V2.cut-imp Sit down (while I leave for a moment). . co-heks-u eat-V2.cut-3.P[imp] Keep eating (without me). . thukpa hops-heks-wa-ŋ=ha soup sip-V2.cut-npst[3.P]-1sg.A=nmlz.nsg I am sipping soup (noone else does).
summary:
The V2 *-heks* has an inceptive or immediate prospective meaning: it is used when the event expressed by the main verb is just about to begin. It can attach to verbs of any temporal type, with no observed restrictions on argument semantics, and with activities and states it marks the onset of the activity or state, while with telic verbs it indicates that the endpoint is approaching.  

The same V2 also has a second meaning, glossed as “do separately,” similar to Nepali *[V.stem]-dai garnu*. In this use it often appears in commands, where the speaker asks the hearer to continue or begin an action independently.

text: The V2 -ghond has the literal meaning of roam, wander around . This marker refers to actions and events that happen distributed over various locations, in the same manner as has been analyzed for the cognate Belhare marker -kon -gon Bickel1996Aspect . This V2 may attach to intransitive and transitive stems, and can be inflected either way, too (see ). . .heʔne maŋdu maŋdu kha luplum=ci=be wa-ya-ghond-a i-ya-ghond-a=niŋ=ca, ... somewhere far far those den =nsg=loc exist -pst-V2.roam-pst revolve -pst-V2.roam[3sg]-pst=ctmp=add While he also used to live and walk around somewhere far, far away, in those caves, ... 18 _nrr _03.013 .na maghyam heʔniŋ=ca sis-u-ghond-wa=na this old _woman when =add kill -3.P-V2.roam-npst=nmlz.sg This old woman always walks around drunken. (lit. she walks around being killed) . ijaŋ yoniŋ-kheniŋ n-jiŋ-ghom-me=ha? why thither-hither 3pl- learn -V2.roam-npst=nmlz.nsg Why do they walk around learning (languages)? Note that in , the experiencer is treated like s standard P argument by case and the verbal person marking (indexed by the 3.P suffix). This does not prevent the experiencer argument from taking part in complex predication, which usually synchronizes the argument structure of the single components of one CP. This again shows the importance of generalized semantic roles as parameter along which the syntax of Yakkha is organized. Example from a conversation clearly shows that the first verb is the semantic head, and that -ghond has lost its lexical meaning walk around . It merely adds the notion of spatial distribution. In the answer , the speaker refers to the event in question without using the V2. . .ŋkha i=ya het-u-ghond-wa-ga? that what =nmlz.nsg cut -3.P-V2.roam-npst-2 What are you cutting (at various places)? (said reproachfully) 28 _cvs _04.321 .are haʔlo, ijaŋ me-heʔ-ma? abbuiǃ hey excla why neg- cut -inf[deont] excla Goodness, why not to cut? Holy crackers! 28 _cvs _04.323
summary: The V2 marker **-ghond** originally means ‘roam, wander around’ and is used for actions or events distributed over several locations, comparable to a cognate marker in Belhare. It can attach to both intransitive and transitive stems, and the text shows that in complex predicates it no longer contributes its literal meaning but instead adds a sense of spatial distribution while the first verb serves as the semantic head.

text: The V2 -siʔ is always inflected transitively. It is probably etymologically connected to sis kill . In the Nepali translations, the predicates were paraphrased using mārnu kill . In a CP, -siʔ means avoid, prevent . The lexical verb denotes an action that prevents something else from happening, like catch in and , and scold in . The event which shall be avoided is not necessarily expressed overtly; it is usually obvious from the utterance context. . .picha kaŋ-kheʔ-ma n-dokt-u-n=na, u-ma=ŋa lab-i-si=na child fall -V2.go-inf neg- get -3.P[pst]-neg=nmlz.sg , 3sg.poss- mother =erg catch -compl-V2.prevent[3.P;pst]=nmlz.sg The child could not fall down because its mother held it. .lukt-heks-a=na, lam-siʔ-ma=na run -V2.cut-pst[3sg]=nmlz.sg catch -V2.prevent-inf[deont]=nmlz.sg She is about to run away, we have to hold her. . mokt-heks-uksa=na, nhaŋ thind-i-si-ŋ=na beat -V2.cut-pst.prf[3.P]=nmlz.sg and _then scold -compl-V2.prevent[3.P;pst]-1sg.A=nmlz.sg He was about to beat him, so I scolded and stopped him.
summary: The V2 **-siʔ** is always transitivized and is probably etymologically related to **sis** ‘kill’; in Nepali translations, it is paraphrased with **mārnu** ‘kill’. In a CP, **-siʔ** expresses **‘avoid, prevent’**, with the lexical verb describing the action used to stop something else from happening, as in examples meaning ‘hold’, ‘catch’, or ‘scold’ to prevent an expected event. The prevented event is often not overtly stated because it is clear from context.

text: The V2 -soʔ means look , and it is used as experiential marker, translatable with try X and find out oneself (see ). Note that this is not a complementation strategy, as one cannot express clauses like I found out that X did Y or I tried to X by means of this V2. Yakkha utilizes complement taking predicates to convey such meanings. The V2 is also not a means to express a conative, since it neither reduces the valency nor implies that the attempt fails (see Vincent2013_Conative for an overview of the different usages of the term conative ). The crucial meaning component of -soʔ is experiencing something by trying out oneself . The grammaticalization of perception verbs to such a marker is common in South Asian and South East Asian languages. . .liŋmi=ŋa chapt-u-so! straw =ins thatch -3.P-V2.look[3.P;imp] Try and thatch (the roof) with straw! (said as advice against tin roofs) . kheps-u-so! listen -3.P-V2.look[3.P;imp] Listen and find out! . chimd-u-ŋ-so-ŋ? ask -3.P-1sg-V2.look-1sg.A[3.P;sbjv] May I ask and find out? This V2 behaves exceptional with regard to the material that can stand between the verbal stems. Usually the first verbal stem can be inflected only by one suffix, and only if the suffix consists of a vowel. However, as shown in , the inflection on the first stem can include a nasal, if a nasal is available in the inflection.
summary:
The V2 -soʔ, meaning “look,” functions as an experiential marker expressing ‘try X and find out oneself,’ but it is not a complementation strategy or a conative marker. Its core meaning is experiencing something through one’s own attempt, and this type of grammaticalization from perception verbs is common in South and Southeast Asian languages.  

The marker also behaves unusually in that the first verbal stem in the construction can take a nasal-inflected suffix, whereas verbal stems normally allow only one suffix and only if it contains a vowel.

text: This chapter deals with idiomatic combinations of a noun and a verb. These predicates occupy a position somewhat between word and phrase. Lexically, a noun-verb predicate always constitutes one word, as its meaning is not directly predictable from its individual components (with varying degrees of metaphoricity and abstraction). But since the nouns enjoy considerable morphosyntactic freedom, speaking of noun incorporation here would be misleading. About 80 noun-verb predicates are attested so far, with rougly two thirds referring to experiential events. There are two main morphologically defined patterns for noun-verb predicates. In the first pattern (Simple noun-verb predicates) the predicate consists of a noun and a verb that are juxtaposed in N-V order, such as lam phakma open way, give turn or tukkhuʔwa lamma doze off (discussed in simple-noun-verb). The same pattern is also used as a strategy to incorporate Nepali nouns into the Yakkha morphology, with a very small class of light verbs, namely cokma make , wama exist, be and tokma get , cf. cop. The second pattern (the experiencer-as-possessor construction) is semantically more restricted and also different morphologically. It expresses experiential events, with the experiencer coded as possessor, as for instance hakamba keʔma yawn (lit.: (someone's) yawn to come up). This pattern is discussed in nv-comp-poss.
summary: The chapter examines idiomatic noun-verb combinations that are intermediate between words and phrases: they are lexically single words because their meanings are not fully compositional, but the noun component remains morphosyntactically independent, so they are not true cases of noun incorporation. About 80 such predicates are known, with roughly two thirds expressing experiential events, and they fall into two main patterns: simple N-V sequences and a more restricted experiencer-as-possessor construction.

text: Most of the simple noun-verb predicates are relatively transparent but fixed collocations. They denote events from the semantic domains of natural phenomena, e.g. nam phemma shine [sun] , taŋkhyaŋ kama thunder (lit. sky—call ), some culturally significant actions like kei lakma dance the drum dance and also verbs that refer to experiential events and bodily functions, such as whaŋma tukma feel hot (literally: sweat/heat—hurt ). Experiential concepts are, however, more frequently expressed by the experiencer-as-possessor construction. There is no clear explanation why some verbs expressing bodily functions, like chipma chima urinate belong to the simple noun-verb predicates, while most of them belong to the experiencer-as-possessor frame. Some verbs show synonymy across these two classes, e.g., the two lexemes with the meaning sweat : whaŋma lomma (literally: sweat—come out , an experiencer-as-possessor predicate, with the experiencer coded as possessor of whaŋma) and whaŋmaŋa lupma (literally: sweat- extsc ins —disperse , a simple noun-verb predicate). simple-nv-tab provides some examples of simple noun-verb predicates. Lexemes in square brackets were not found as independent words beyond their usage in these compounds. Some verbs, like weather verbs (e.g., nam phemma shine [sun] and wasik tama rain ) and some experiential predicates (e.g., wepma sima be thirsty and whaŋma tukma feel hot ), for instance, do not allow the expression of additional arguments; their valency is zero (under the assumption that the nouns belonging to the predicates are different from full-fledged arguments). If overt arguments are possible, they behave like the arguments of standard intransitive or standard transitive verbs. They trigger agreement on the verb, and they take nominative or ergative case marking (see frames). table [htp] center ! tabular lll predicate & gloss & literal translation cabhak lakma & do the paddy dance &(paddy – dance) chakma pokma & troubled times to occur &(hardship – strike) chipma chima& urinate &(urine – urinate) cuŋ tukma& feel cold &(cold – hurt) himbulumma cama & swing &(swing – eat) hiʔwa phemma & wind blow &(wind – be activated [weather]) hoŋga phaŋma & crawl &([ stem ] – [ stem ]) kei lakma & do the drum dance &(drum – dance) laŋ phakma & make steps &(foot/leg – apply) lam phakma & open way, give turn &(way – apply/build) lambu lembiʔma & let pass &(way – let–give) muk phakma & help, serve &(hand – apply) nam ama & sit around all day &(sun – make set) nam phemma & be sunny &(sun – be activated [weather]) phiʔma phima& fart &(fart – fart) sak tukma& be hungry &(hunger – hurt) setni keʔma& stay awake all night &(night – bring up) sokma soma& breathe &(breath – breathe) susuwa lapma& whistle &([whistle] – call) tukkhuʔwa lapma & doze off &([ stem ] – call) ( lamma) & & taŋkhyaŋ kama & thunder &(sky – call) uwa cama & kiss &(nectar/liquid – eat) wa lekma & rinse &(water – turn) wasik tama & rain &(rain – come) wepma sima & be thirsty &(thirst – die) wepma tukma& by thirsty &(thirst – hurt) wha pokma & septic wounds to occur &(septic wound – infest) whaŋma tukma & feel hot &(heat/sweat – hurt) yak yakma & stay over night &([ stem ] – stay over night) yaŋchan chiʔma & regret &([ stem ] – get conscious) chemha=ŋa sima & be intoxicated, be drunken &(be killed by alcohol) cuŋ=ŋa sima & freeze &(die of cold) sak=ŋa sima & be hungry &(die of hunger) whaŋma=ŋa lupma & sweat &(heat/sweat – disperse/strew) tabular Simple noun-verb predicates center table The predicates vary as to whether the noun or the verb carries the semantic weight of the predicate, or whether both parts play an equal role in establishing the meaning of the construction. In verbs like wepma sima be thirsty (lit. thirst—die ) or wasik tama rain (lit. rain—come ), the noun carries the semantic weight,This is the reason why noun-verb collocations have also become known as light verb constructions (after Jespersen1965_Modern, who used this term for English collocations like have a rest). while in verbs like kei lakma drum —dance , cabhak lakma paddy—dance , the nouns merely modify the verbal meaning. The nouns may stand in various thematic relations to the verb: in wepma sima be thirsty , the noun has the role of an effector, in predicates like hiʔwa phemma wind—blow it is closer to an agent role. In saya pokma head-soul—raise , Raising the head soul is a ritual activity undertaken by specialists to help individuals whose physical or psychological well-being is in danger. it is a patient. There are also a few constructions in which the noun is etymologically related to the verb, such as chipma chima urinate , sokma soma breathe and phiʔma phima fart (cognate object constructions). The nouns in these constructions do not contribute to the overall meaning of the predicate. Semantically empty nouns are also attested in the experiencer-as-possessor construction (cf. below). They are called eidemic in Bickel1995In-the-vestibule, Bickel1997The-possessive; and “morphanic” (morpheme orphans) in Matisoff1986Hearts. Concerning stress assignment and the voicing rule (see stress and morphophon), noun and verb do not constitute a unit. Both the noun and the verb carry equal stress, even if the noun is monosyllabic, resulting in adjacent stress, as in ˈsak.ˈtuk.ma. As for voicing, if the initial stop of the verbal stem is preceded by a nasal or a vowel, it remains voiceless. This stands in contrast to the verb-verb predicates (see Chapter verb-verb), which are more tightly fused in other respects, too. Compare, for instance, cuŋ tukma be cold (N+V, cold—hurt ) with ham-biʔma distribute among people (V+V, distribute—give ). There are different degrees of morphological fusion of noun and verb, and some nouns may undergo operations that are not expected if they were incorporated. They can be topicalized by means of the particle =ko (see ), and two nouns selecting the same light verb may also be coordinated (see ). Such examples are rare, though. Note that is from a collection of proverbs and sayings, in which rhythm and rhyming constraints could lead to
summary: The passage describes simple noun-verb predicates as mostly transparent but fixed collocations used to express natural phenomena, culturally significant actions, and some experiential or bodily events. In some predicates the noun carries the main semantic load, in others it mainly modifies the verb, and in a few cases the noun is semantically empty or cognate with the verb; the construction shows less tight morphological fusion than verb-verb predicates, though overt arguments can behave like ordinary intransitive or transitive arguments when present.

text: the insertion of particles such as =ko. In most cases the noun and verb occur without any intervening material. The noun may also be modified independently, as the spontaneously uttered sentence in shows. Typically, the predicates are modified as a whole by adverbs, but here one can see that the noun may also be modified independently by adnominal modifiers. The modifying phrase is marked by a genitive, which is never found on adverbial modifiers. . .makkai=ga cama, chiʔwa=ga khyu, cabhak=ko lak-ma, a-ŋoʈeŋma=jyu maize =gen cooked _grains nettle =gen curry _sauce paddy =top dance -inf 1sg.poss- female _in-law =hon Corn mash, nettle sauce, let us dance the paddy dance, dear sister-in-law. 12 _pvb _01.008 .kei=nuŋ cabhak lak-saŋ ucun n-joŋ-me drum =com paddy dance -sim nice 3pl- do -npst They have a good time, dancing the drum dance and the paddy dance. The interpretation of dancing the paddy dance with drums can be ruled out here, because the drums are not played in the paddy dance. 01 _leg _07.142 . a-phok tuk=nuŋ=ga sak tug-a=na 1sg.poss -stomach hurt =com=gen hunger hurt -pst[3sg]=nmlz.sg I am starving. (Lit.: A hunger struck (me) that makes my stomach ache. ) Some of the nouns may even trigger agreement on the verb, something which is also unexpected from the traditional definition of compounds, which entails that compounds are one unit lexically and thus morphologically opaque (see e.g. Fabb2001Compounding ). Example and are different in this respect:Many Yakkha verbs have inchoative-stative Aktionsart so that the past inflection refers to a state that still holds true at the time of speaking. while predicates that contain the verb tukma hurt are invariably inflected for third person singular (in other words, the noun whaŋma triggers agreement; overt arguments are not possible), predicates containing sima die show agreement with the overtly expressed (experiencer) subject in the unmarked nominative .The same argument realization is found in the Belhare cognates of these two verbs Bickel1997The-possessive. For the details of argument realization in Yakkha see Chapter verb-val. Some meanings can be expressed by either frame (compare and ), but this is not a regular and productive alternation. . .whaŋma tug-a=na sweat hurt [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg I/you/he/she/it/we/they feel(s) hot. .ka wepma sy-a-ŋ=na 1sg thirst die -pst-1sg=nmlz.sg I am thirsty. .wepma tug-a=na thirst hurt [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg I/you/he/she/it/we/they is/are thirsty. Note that if wepma in were a regular verbal argument, an instrumental case would be expected, since it is an effector with respect to the verbal meaning. And indeed, some noun-verb predicates require an instrumental or an ergative case on the noun (see ).Yakkha has an instrumental/ergative syncretism. Therefore, in intransitive predicates =ŋa is interpreted as instrumental; in transitive predicates it is interpreted as ergative. . . (chemha=ŋa) sis-a-ga=na=i? (liquor =erg ) kill -pst-2.P=nmlz.sg=q Are you drunk? . sak=ŋa n-sy-a-ma-ŋa-n=na hunger =ins neg- die -pst-prf-1sg-neg=nmlz.sg I am not hungry. Some verbs participating in noun-verb predicates have undergone semantic changes. Note that in the nouns sak and chemha do not have the same status with regard to establishing the semantics of the whole predicate. The verbal stem sis kill in (a) has already acquired a metaphorical meaning of be drunk, be intoxicated (with the experiencer coded like a standard object). The noun is frequently omitted in natural speech, and if all arguments are overt, the experiencer precedes the stimulus, just like in Experiencer-as-Object constructions (see and Chapter tr-objex). The same development has taken place in Belhare Bickel1997The-possessive . In contrast to this, the stem si in (b) is not polysemous; the noun is required to establish the meaning of the construction. . ka macchi=ŋa haŋd-a-ŋ=na 1sg pickles/chili =erg taste _hot -pst-1sg.P=nmlz.sg The pickles/chili tasted hot to me. Despite a certain degree of morphosyntactic freedom, the nouns are not full-fledged arguments. It is not possible to demote or promote the noun via transitivity operations such as the causative or the passive, or to extract it from the noun-verb complex via relativization (see ungrammatical ). . .*lakt-i=ha cabhak dance -1pl[pst]=nmlz.nsg paddy Intended: the paddy (dance) that we danced .*tug-a=ha sak hurt [3sg]-pst=nmlz.nsg hunger Intended: the hunger that was perceivable To sum up, simple noun-verb predicates behave like one word with respect to lexical semantics, adjacency (in the overwhelming majority of examples), extraction possibilities for the noun (i.e. the lack thereof). They behave like two words as far as clitic placement (including case), coordination, modifiability, stress and voicing are concerned. Thus, they are best understood as lexicalized phrases.
summary:
The passage argues that simple noun-verb predicates in Yakkha are best analyzed as lexicalized phrases rather than true compounds or single words. Although the noun and verb are usually adjacent and act like one unit in lexical meaning and extraction behavior, they still behave like two words with respect to clitic placement, case marking, coordination, modifiability, stress, and voicing.

It also shows that the noun in these constructions is not always a fixed argument: it can sometimes trigger verbal agreement or be marked by instrumental/ergative case, and some verb stems have developed specialized or metaphorical meanings. Overall, the constructions display a mixed pattern of word-like and phrase-like properties.

text: Following a general tendency of languages of South and Southeast Asia, Yakkha has a dedicated construction for the expression of experiential concepts, including emotional and cognitive processes, bodily functions, but also human character traits and their moral evaluation. In Yakkha, such concepts are expressed by predicates that are built from a noun and a verb, whereby the noun is perceived as the location of this concept, i.e. the “arena” where a physiological or psychological experience unfolds Matisoff1986Hearts . These nouns are henceforth referred to as psych-nouns, but apart from referring to emotions and sensations, they can also refer to body parts and excreted substances. Example illustrates the basic pattern: .u-niŋwa tug-a=na 3sg.poss- mind hurt [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg He was/became sad. The verbs come from a rather small class; they denote the manner in which the experiencer is affected by the event, many of which refer to motion events. The experiencer is morphologically treated like the possessor of the psych-noun; it is indexed by possessive prefixes. The expression of experiential concepts by means of a possessive metaphor is a characteristic and robust feature of Kiranti languages (cf. the possessive of experience in Bickel1997The-possessive, emotive predicates in Ebert1994The-structure , and body part emotion verbs in Doornenbal2009A-grammar ), but this is also found beyond Kiranti in South-East Asian languages, including Hmong-Mien, Mon-Khmer and Tai-Kadai languages Matisoff1986Hearts, Bickel2004The-syntax. In other Tibeto-Burman languages, such as Newari, Balti and Tibetan, for instance, experiencers are marked by a dative Beyer1992_Tibetan, Genetti2007_Newari, Read1934Balti, an option which is not available, at least not by native morphology, in most Kiranti languages. Experiencer-as-possessor constructions are not the only option to express experiential events. The crosslinguistic variation that can be found within experiential predicates is also reflected in the language-internal variation of Yakkha. We have seen Simple Noun-Verb predicates in simple-noun-verb above. Other possibilities are simple verbal stems like haŋma taste hot/have a spicy sensation (treating the experiencer like a standard P argument), eʔma perceive, like, have an impression, have opinion (treating it like a standard A argument) and the historically complex verb kisiʔma be afraid (treating it like a standard S argument). Verbs composed of several verbal stems may also encode experiential notions, such as yoŋdiʔma be scared (shake-give). It is the possessive experiencer verbs though that constitute the biggest class of experiential predicates. About fifty verbs have been found so far (cf. Tables tab-exp1 and tab-exp2), but probably this list is far from exhaustive. This section is organized as follows: the various possibilities of argument realization within the experiencer-as-possessor frame are introduced in poss-e1 introduces, poss-e3 looks at the principles behind the semantic composition of possessive experiential predicates, and poss-e2 deals with the morphosyntax of these predicates and with the behavioral properties of experiencers as non-canonically marked S or A arguments.
summary:
Yakkha has a dedicated set of predicates for experiential meanings such as emotions, sensations, bodily functions, and character traits, usually built from a noun plus a verb. In the main pattern, the noun functions as the “arena” of the experience and the experiencer is marked like a possessor through possessive prefixes, a construction that is especially characteristic of Kiranti languages.  

The language also allows other experiential predicate types, including simple verbal stems and more complex verbs, but possessive experiencer verbs form the largest class, with about fifty identified so far.

text: A basic distinction can be drawn between predicates of intransitive valency and transitive or labileSee also labile. valency (see Tables tab-exp1 and tab-exp2 at the end of the section). Within this basic distinction, the verbs can be further divided into various subframes of argument realization. In all classes, the experiencer is marked as possessor of the psych-noun, i.e., as possessor of a sensation or an affected body part. In the class of intransitive verbs, the psych-noun triggers third person marking on the verb, as in and . Intransitive verbs usually do not have an overt noun phrase referring to the experiencer; only the possessive prefix identifies the reference of the experiencer. When the experiencer has a special pragmatic status, and is thus marked by a discourse particle, it can be overtly expressed in eitherthe nominative or in the genitive (compare example kacaayupma and ukkaseopomma below). As this is quite rare, the reasons for this alternation are not clear yet. In some cases, the noun is conceptualized as nonsingular, triggering the according number markers on the verb as well (see ). One verb in this group is special in consisting of two nouns and a verb. Both nouns take the possessive prefix (see ). Their respective full forms would be niŋwa and lawa. It is not uncommon that the nouns get reduced to one syllable in noun-verb predicates. . .a-pomma=ci ŋ-gy-a=ha=ci 1sg.poss- laziness =nsg 3pl- come _up -pst=nmlz.nsg=nsg I feel lazy. .a-niŋ a-la sy-a=na 1sg.poss- mind 1sg.poss- spirit die [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg I am fed up/annoyed. The transitive group can be divided into five classes (cf. tab-exp2 on page tab-exp2 ). In all classes, the experiencer is coded as the possessor of the psych-noun (via possessive prefixes), and hence this does not need to be explicitly stated in the schematic representation of argument realization in the table. In Class (a) the experiencer is realized like a standard transitive subject (in addition to being indexed by possessive prefixes): it triggers transitive subject agreement and has ergative case marking (only overtly marked if it has third person reference and is overt, which is rare). The stimulus is unmarked and triggers object agreement (see ). Class (b) differs from class (a) in that the psych-noun triggers object agreement, invariably third person and in some cases, third person plural (see ). No stimulus is expressed in class (b). This class has the highest number of members. . . uŋ=ŋa u-ppa u-luŋma tukt-uks-u=na 3sg=erg 3sg.poss- father 3sg.poss- liver pour -prf-3.P=nmlz.sg He loved his father. (lit.: He poured his father his liver. ) .a-yupma=ci cips-u-ŋ-ci-ŋ=ha 1sg.poss- sleepiness =nsg complete -3.P[pst]-1sg.A-3nsg.P-1sg.A=nmlz.nsg I am well-rested. (lit.: I completed my sleep(s). ) Predicates of class (c) show three possibilities of argument realization. One possibility is an unexpected pattern where the stimulus triggers object agreement, while the psych-noun triggers subject agreement, which leads, oddly enough, to a literal translation my disgust brings up bee larvae in . Despite the subject agreement on the verb, the psych-nouns in this class do not host an ergative case marker, an option that is available, however, for verbs of class (d). The experiencer is indexed only by the possessive prefix in this frame; overt experiencer arguments were not found. The stimulus can be in the nominative or in the ablative in class (c), but if it is in the ablative, the verb is blocked from showing object agreement with the stimulus, showing 3>3 agreement instead (see ). The third option of argument realization in class (c) is identical to class (a) (cf. the comments in and (b)). Reasons or conditions for these alternations, for instance in different configurations of the referential properties of the arguments, could not be detected. . .thaŋsu=ga u-chya=ci a-chippa ket-wa-ci=ha bee =gen 3sg.poss- child =nsg 1sg.poss- disgust bring _up -npst-3nsgP=nmlz.nsg I am disgusted by the bee larvae. (same: thaŋsuga ucyaci achippa ketwaŋciŋha - (1 sg >3 pl , class (a))) .njiŋda=bhaŋ a-sokma hips-wa=na! 2du=abl 1sg.poss- breath whip- npst[3A>3.P]=nmlz.sg I get fed up by you. (same: njiŋda asokma himmeʔnencinhaǃ - 1 sg >2 du , class (a)) In class (d), the psych-noun also triggers transitive subject agreement, and it exhibits ergative marking. The object agreement slot can be filled either by the stimulus or by the experiencer argument (see ). There are (at least) two concepts, saya and lawa, that are related to or similar to soul in Yakkha and the Kiranti metaphysical world in general. Gaenszle2000Origins writes about these two (and other) concepts in Mewahang (also Eastern Kiranti, Upper Arun branch): quote The concept of saya is understood to be a kind of “vital force" that must be continually renewed (literally: “bought") by means of various sacrificial rites. [...] The vital force saya makes itself felt [...] not only in subjective physical or psychic states but also, and in particular, in the social, economic, religious and political spheres - that is, it finds expression in success, wealth, prestige and power. The third concept, lawa (cf. Hardman1981The-psychology , Hardman_phd_Conformity ) is rendered by the Nepali word sāto ( soul ). This is a small, potentially evanescent substance, which is compared to a mosquito, a butterfly or a bee, and which, if it leaves the body for a longer period, results in loss of consciousness and mental illness. The shaman must then undertake to summon it back or retrieve it. Gaenszle2000Origins quote Class (e) is exemplified by . Here, the experiencer is the possessor of a body part which triggers object agreement on the verb. Some verbs may express an effector or stimulus overtly. Others, like ya limma taste sweet cannot express an overt A argument, despite being inflected transitively (see ). This pattern is reminiscent of the transimpersonal verbs (treated in tr-imp). . .a-lawa=ŋa naʔ-ya-ŋ=na 1sg.poss- spirit =erg leave -V2.leave-pst-1sg.P=nmlz.sg I was frozen in shock. (lit.: My spirit left me. ) . (cuŋ=ŋa) a-muk=ci khokt-u-ci=ha (cold =erg ) 1sg.poss- hand =nsg chop -3.P[pst]-3nsg.P=nmlz.nsg My hands are tingling/freezing (from the cold). (lit.: The cold chopped off my hands. ) .a-ya limd-u=na 1sg.poss- mouth taste _sweet
summary: The passage describes how Yakkha psych-predicates vary in argument structure, contrasting intransitive, transitive, and labile valency patterns. In all classes, the experiencer is encoded as possessor of the psych-noun, but verbs differ in how the experiencer, stimulus, and psych-noun control case marking and agreement; some classes show experiencer subject agreement, others object agreement, and some allow multiple realizations, though the conditions for these alternations are often unclear. It also notes that several psych-nouns are tied to concepts similar to “soul” or “vital force,” such as *saya* and *lawa*, which are culturally important in the Kiranti world.

Many of the transitive verbs are attested also with intransitive inflection without further morphological marker of decreased transitivity, i.e. they show a lability alternation (see ). . .n-lok khot-a-ŋ-ga=na=i? 2sg.poss -anger scratch -pst-1sg.P-2.A=nmlz.sg=q Are you angry at me? . o-lok khot-a=na 3sg.poss- anger scratch [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg He/she got angry. For two verbs, namely nabhuk-lemnhaŋma dishonor (self/others) (lit.: throw away one's nose ) and nabhuk-yuŋma uphold moral (lit.: keep one's nose ), there is one more constellation of participants, due to their particular semantics. The experiencer can either be identical to the agent or different from it, as the social consequences of morally transgressive behavior usually affect more people than just the agent (e.g. illegitimate sexual contacts, or an excessive use of swearwords). This concept is particularly related to immoral behavior of women. It is rarely, if ever, heard that a man threw away his nose . The morphosyntactic consequences of this are that the verbal agreement and the possessive prefix on the noun may either have the same conominal or two different conominals. Taken literally, one may throw away one's own nose or throw away somebody else's nose (see ). Note that due to the possessive argument realization it is possible to have partial coreference, which is impossible in the standard transitive verbal inflection (cf. verb-infl). . . u-nabhuk lept-haks-u=na 3sg.poss- nose throw -V2.send-3.P[pst]=nmlz.sg She dishonored herself. . nda eŋ=ga nabhuk(=ci) lept-haks-u-ci-g=haǃ 2sg[erg] 1pl.incl.poss=gen nose( =nsg ) throw -V2.send-3.P[pst]-3nsg.P-2.A=nmlz.nsg You dishonored us all (including yourself)!
