text: The geomorphic postpositions are formally identical to the adverbs described in geodeixis. They take nominal complements that are marked by the genitive case (see case-gen). The possessive prefix is, however, not possible on these postpositions, which distinguishes them from relational nouns (cf. postpos-2). relnoun-topo provides an overview on the postpositions. table [htp] centering tabular lll postposition & gloss & internal structure mopparik &right below& downhill-side[Nep.] topparik &right above& uphill-side[Nep.] yopparik &right across& across-side[Nep.] mokhaʔla &below, downwards& uphill- dir tokhaʔla &above, upwards& uphill- dir yokhaʔla &across, away& across- dir mondaŋ &from below& downhill- abl tondaŋ &from above& uphill- abl yondaŋ &from the same level& across- abl moʔmorok &a bit below& toʔtorok &a bit above& yoʔyorok &a bit further away& kheʔkherek &a bit closer& tabular Geomorphic postpositions centering table The postpositions mopparik and topparik indicate a relation of parallel planes located above/below each other, such as stacked books or floors of a house (see ). Example shows a corresponding adverbial in a (semi-transparent) ablative form.In analogy to these examples, one could assume that there is also a directional topparikhaʔla/mopparikhaʔla to indicate directedness towards an upper/lower level, but such forms do not exist. Probably, topparik (and related forms) also have a directional meaning. The same is possible with yopparik and khepparik on the horizontal level. If the speaker wants to express that an object is oriented towards a particular direction, the directional forms tokhaʔla, mokhaʔla, yokhaʔla and khekhaʔla are used; orientation away from another object is indicatd by the ablative forms tondaŋ, mondaŋ, yondaŋ and khendaŋ (see ). . .ʈebul=ga mopparik table =gen right _below below the table (on a lower level, e.g. on the ground) .kanciŋ mopparindaŋ ky-a-ci=ha 1du from _right _below come _up -pst-du=nmlz.nsg We came up from the lower floor. . .ʈebul=ga tokhaʔla table =gen upwards above the table (e.g. a lamp installed on the wall) . ʈebul=ga mondaŋ chwigam kept-u=na table =gen from _below chewing _gum glue -3.P[pst]=nmlz.sg Someone stuck chewing gum below the table. The partly reduplicated forms moʔmorok, toʔtorok and yoʔyorok convey that an object is located a bit in the respective direction, from the perspective of the object referred to by the complement noun (see ). . .uŋci-paŋ=ga moʔmorok eko hoŋma wei-sa=na 3nsg.poss- house =gen bit _downhill one river exist -pst[3sg]=nmlz.sg A bit downhill from their house there was a river. 01 _leg _07.283 .hon=na yuktham=ga yoʔyorok kheʔkherek that _very =nmlz.sg place =gen bit _further bit _closer around that place/the surroundings of that place 01 _leg _07.269
summary: The geomorphic postpositions are formally identical to certain adverbs and take nominal complements marked with the genitive case, but unlike relational nouns they cannot take the possessive prefix. They express spatial relations such as below, above, across, and slight movement or position in those directions, with separate directional and ablative forms used for orientation toward or away from another object. Some forms, such as *mopparik* and *topparik*, refer to stacked vertical planes, while partly reduplicated forms like *moʔmorok* indicate a location a little in the relevant direction.

text: Several motion verbs have also lexicalized the uphill/downhill distinction, as shown in example and in deic-verb . Event specification with regard to the topography is highly frequent. Even though neutral forms are available (also included in the table), the pragmatically expected forms are those specifying the event for the mo/to/yo distinction. This specificity reaches well beyond classical motion events. Small-scale motions, too, like putting, repairing, stacking, looking, turning or calling are often precisely specified with respect to their spatial orientation. This is achieved by means of complex predicates with different function verbs (see and V2-table in Chapter verb-verb). Motion away from a point of reference is not specified with respect to the topography, there are only the neutral verbs go and carry off . This is unexpected pragmatically: in motion events towards a point of reference, the speaker and the hearer are usually identifiable, and with them, the direction of the movement. In motion events away from a point of reference, as in go and carry off , the direction of the movement is less predictable, and therefore, it would be more important pragmatically to specify events of going with regard to the topography-based distinctions. table [htp] centering tabular lll & come & bring neutral &ta come (from a greater distance)& taʔ bring neutral &kheʔ go & khet carry off up &keʔ come up & ket bring up across &ap come (same level, small distance)& apt bring down &uks uŋ come down &ukt bring down tabular Geomorphic distinctions in motion verbs centering table . .kanciŋ to tub-i=hoŋ uks-a-ŋ-ci-ŋ=hoŋ yo tas-a-ŋ-c-u-ŋ=ba 1pl up meet -1pl=seq come _down -pst-excl-du-excl=seq across arrive -pst-excl-du-3.P-excl=emph Having met uphill (many people), we (two) came down (home) and arrived across (at a neighbour's house on the same level as the speaker's home). 36 _cvs _06.395 .na eko=ŋa=go thend-u-get-uks-a=ba, nna, om leks-a=niŋa this one =erg=top lift -3.P-V2.bring _up-3.P-prf-pst=emph that bright become -pst[3sg]=ctmp One of them lifted it (the rock) and carried it up (holding in his hands, not carrying on his back), while the sun came out. 37 _nrr _07.086 These topography-specific verbs are only compatible with suitable adverbial expressions. For instance, apma come over can only be used with yondaŋ from a location on the same altitude level . Interestingly, this verb is also used when coming over implies climbing down 800 meters, crossing a river and then climbing up on the other side again.
summary: The passage explains that many motion verbs have lexicalized topography-based distinctions, especially uphill/downhill and related mo/to/yo contrasts, and that these forms are pragmatically preferred even though neutral verbs also exist. It also notes that such precise spatial specification extends beyond major motion events to smaller actions, often through complex predicates, while motion away from a reference point is less specifically marked and is only expressed by neutral verbs like *go* and *carry off*.

text: The frames introduced in frames show various alternations. Different types of alternations have to be distinguished: some just change the argument realization, e.g. differential case marking, which is triggered by pragmatic factors such as scenario classes. Other alternations, e.g. the inchoative-causative lability, change the argument structure. The labile verbs will be discussed in labile, three-arg deals with the alternations among the three-argument frames.For alternations found among the experiencer-as-possessor predicates see nv-comp-poss.
summary: The passage notes that the frames introduced earlier exhibit several kinds of alternations, which must be distinguished. Some alternations only affect argument realization, such as differential case marking triggered by pragmatic factors like scenario classes, while others, such as inchoative-causative lability, alter argument structure. It also indicates where related discussions can be found: labile verbs in labile, three-argument frame alternations in three-arg, and experiencer-as-possessor predicate alternations in nv-comp-poss.

text: Labile verbs are characterized by variable transitivity of the same verbal stem, which is not brought about by means of a morphological derivation. Letuchiy2009Labile classifies labile verbs into different types: the inchoative/causative alternation, the reflexive alternation, the reciprocal alternation, the passive (extremely rare) and the converse type. According to this classification, Yakkha has the inchoative/causative The inchoative/causative type is equated with labile in Haspelmath1993More, whose definition of labile verbs is more restrictive. and the reflexive. Furthermore, Yakkha shows morphologically unmarked detransitivizations that can have both passive and antipassive interpretations, but they do not change the semantic roles of the arguments and hence they are not lexical alternations. They are treated below in trans-op on transitivity operations. Letuchiy acknowledges the passive-type as labile, but considers unmarked antipassives quasi-lability, because his crucial defining feature for lability is a change of the semantic roles. But if semantic role change is required, his inclusion of the passive alternation is misleading. In passives, the semantic roles do not change; the undergoer of beat does not have different semantic roles in the active vs. the passive voice. The current lexical database contains 77 labile verbs. The inchoative/causative alternation is patient-preserving; the reflexive alternation is agent-preserving (see also Letuchiy2009Labile ). As lability is defined by the absence of morphological marking, it is hard to tell which form of a labile pair is the basic form. The intransitive verb can be considered the basic form semantically and formally, as less participants are involved in the event, and as the verb hosts less inflectional morphology than the transitive verb.From a first impression, there are definitely also differences in frequency among the labile verbs. Some are rather used transitively and some intransitively, depending on which function of a verb is more plausible in natural discourse. The existing corpus is not big enough for significant statistic analyses. Inchoative/causative lability -1ex By far the majority of the labile verbs belong to the inchoative-causative class, a fact that goes along with the crosslinguistic findings in Letuchiy2009Labile. The intransitive verbs denote states or spontaneous changes of state. No agent or causer argument is entailed in the verbal semantics. Notably, inchoative ( anticausative in Creissels2012_Lability ) readings do not always express events that do not have an agent or a causer argument. Sometimes, the A is merely not relevant for a certain event, and thus it is not part of the underlying concept of the event, and has to be left unexpressed, as shown e.g. for facilitative readings of anticausatives in Tswana by Creissels (ibid.). In the corresponding transitive verb, a causer argument that brings about the event is added, and the P argument corresponds to the S of the intransitive verb. Examples , and show the inchoative verbs with S undergoing a spontaneous change of state, while , and show the corresponding transitive verbs with an A argument bringing about that change of state. The verb cimma, meaning both learn and teach , basically belongs to the same alternation, but it has one additional argument. The intransitively inflected verb has two arguments and the transitively inflected verb has three arguments (see itr-teach). . . dailo hos-a=na. door open [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg The door opened. . a-ppa=ŋa dailo hos-uks-u=na. 1sg.poss- father =erg door open -prf-3.P=nmlz.sg Father has opened the door. . siŋ eg-a=na. wood break [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg The piece of wood broke. .uŋ=ŋa siŋ eg-u=na. 3sg=erg wood break -3.P[pst]=nmlz.sg He broke the piece of wood. .phuama yupma=ci=bhaŋ cend-a=na. last-born _girl sleepiness =nsg=abl wake _up [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg Phuama woke from her sleep. .ka uŋ cend-u-ŋ=na. 1sg[erg] 3sg wake _up -3sg.P[pst]-1sg.A=nmlz.sg I woke her up. There are border cases of lability. In Yakkha, many events are expressed by complex predicates. In these predicates, the first stem contains the lexical verb, such as the labile stem khiks khiŋ stretch, grow in . The second verbal stem is from the closed class of function verbs (V2s, see Chapter verb-verb); they specify the verbal semantics, for instance with regard to the temporal structure. In , the V2 -kheʔ go emphasizes the telicity of the event. It is sensitive to transitivity, too. The V2 -kheʔ is only compatible with intransitive interpretations (see ungrammatical ). Thus, complex predication can have the secondary function of indicating transitivity features. . . ikhiŋ khiks-a( -khy -a)=naǃ how _much stretch [3sg]-pst(-V2.go-pst)=nmlz.sg How tall she becameǃ .a-laŋ=ci khiŋ( *-kheʔ )-ma=ci. 1sg.poss- leg =nsg stretch (*-V2.go)-inf[deont]=nsg Intended: I have to stretch my legs. Reflexive lability -1ex The stems of this class alternate between a transitive reading and an intransitive reading with reflexive semantics. Strictly speaking, no argument is removed in reflexives, but the A and P have identical reference and collapse into one single intransitive subject role formally Haspelmath2004_Valency . In the transitive reading, an external P argument is added. Typically, the verbs undergoing this alternation refer to actions involving the body. The examples in illustrate the reflexive alternation with three verb pairs. . . uŋci=ŋa men-ni-ma=nuŋ cum-a-ŋ=na 3nsg=erg neg- see -inf=com.cl hide -pst-1sg=nmlz.sg I hid, so that they cannot see (me). .ripu=ŋa khorek cum-u=na Ripu =erg bowl hide -3.P[pst]=nmlz.sg Ripu hid the bowl. . ka=ca mimiʔ wasiʔ-a-ŋ=hoŋ, ... 1sg=add a _little wash -pst-1sg=seq After washing myself a little, ... 40 _leg _08.050 .a-nuncha wasiʔ-wa-ŋ=na 1sg.poss- younger _sibling wash -npst[3.P]-1sg.A=nmlz.sg I wash my little sister. .a-chya (tek=ŋa) ept-a=na 1sg.poss- child (cloth =ins ) cover [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg My child covered itself (with the blanket). .yenda ept-a-n-u-m millet _mash cover -pst-pl-3.P[imp]-2pl.A Cover the millet mash.
summary: The passage describes labile verbs as stems that vary in transitivity without morphological derivation, and notes that Yakkha has mainly inchoative/causative and reflexive lability. It also distinguishes these lexical alternations from morphologically unmarked detransitivizations, which may have passive or antipassive interpretations but do not change semantic roles, and reports that the lexical database contains 77 labile verbs.

text: Alternations in three-argument verbs are mostly conditioned by pragmatic factors such as topicality or the referential properties of the arguments. My investigation of referentiality effects in three-argument verbs (see also Schackow2012_Referential ) has been inspired by the EUROBabel project Referential Hierarchies in Morphosyntax (RHIM) and a questionnaire on three-argument constructions, designed by Anna Siewierska and Eva van Lier (not published). Typically, in events with three arguments, the G arguments (goals, recipients) are animate, definite and thus also more topic-worthy, whereas the T arguments have a strong tendency to be inanimate, indefinite and thus less topic-worthy. Events in which this expected scenario is reversed are more marked pragmatically, and this could be reflected in the morphosyntax of the clause ( Dryer1986Primary, Siewierska2003Person , Haspelmath2004Explaining, Haspelmath2005Argument, Haspelmath2007Ditransitive , Malchukovetal2010Ditrans-overview ). Some of the referential effects are found exclusively in three-argument verbs in Yakkha, for instance a case of hierarchical agreement, where the T and the G argument compete for an agreement slot. One has to distinguish between argument-based alternations, i.e. effects that are conditioned by the referential properties of only one argument, and scenario-based alternations, i.e. effects that are conditioned by the properties of both T and G in relation to each other. The spray-load alternation -1ex One class of verbs shows alternations between the indirective and the secundative frame, also known as spray-load alternation Levin1993_English, Malchukovetal2010Studies, Malchukovetal2015_Valency. Either the T argument is in the instrumental case and the G triggers object agreement on the verb (for the secundative frame, see ), or the G argument is in the locative and the T triggers object agreement (for the indirective frame, see ). . . ka makai=ŋa dalo ipt-wa-ŋ=na 1sg[erg] corn =ins sack fill -npst[3.P]-1sg=nmlz.sg I filled the sack with corn. (secundative) . gagri=be maŋcwa ipt-u pot =loc water fill -3.P[imp] Fill the water into the pot. (indirective) The verb ipma fill in can only have inanimate G arguments. Verbs with a greater variability of possible arguments may show restrictions on this alternation. Some verbs, for instance, block the secundative frame when the G argument is inanimate, e.g. , which renders the indirective frame the only possibility (see ). In order to license the secundative frame, the G argument has to have the potential to be affected by the event . The verb lupma scatter, disperse, strew provides another example of this restriction. Again, the the secundative frame is the preferred option for animate G arguments, while the indirective is used when inanimate G arguments are involved (context: the preparation of millet beer). In , the G argument is non-overt, but it has human reference, which can be inferred from the context: a funeral. . . *ka maŋcwa luŋkhwak=ŋa lept-u-ŋ=ha 1sg[erg] water stone =ins throw -3.P[pst]-1sg=nmlz.nsg Intended: I threw a stone into the water. (*secundative) . ka lunkhwak maŋcwa=be lept-u-ŋ=na 1sg[erg] stone water =loc throw -3.P[pst]-1sg=nmlz.sg I threw a stone into the water. (indirective) . ka nda luŋkhwak=ŋa lep-nen=na 1sg[erg] 2sg stone =ins throw [pst]-1>2=nmlz.sg I threw a stone at/to you. (secundative) . . kham=ŋa lupt-u-ga=i soil =ins scatter -3.P[imp]-2=emph Cover him with sand. . yenda=be khawa lupt-u-g=ha=i? millet _mash =loc yeast disperse -3.P[pst]-2=nmlz.nsg=q Did you add the yeast to the millet mash? Alternations related to the animacy of G -1ex One could see in the spray-load alternation that the unmarked nominative is preferred for animate, sentient G arguments. For some verbs, this results in alternations between the double object frame and the indirective frame. In , the G argument is human, moreover it is a speech-act participant, and thus the highest on the referential hierarchy Silverstein1976Hierarchy. Hence, the double object frame is chosen, the verb agrees with G, and both T and G are in the nominative. In , the G has third person inanimate reference, and the frame changes to indirective, with G in the locative, and T triggering the agreement.There is no number hierarchy at work in these alternations. The number of T is not the crucial factor, but nonsingular was chosen to illustrate the agreement. . . ka nda sandhisa khuʔ-nen=na 1sg[erg] 2sg present bring [pst]-1>2=nmlz.sg I brought you a present. . uŋ=ŋa kitab(=ci) iskul=be khut-u-ci=ha 3sg=erg book (=nsg) school =loc bring -3.P[pst]-3nsg.P=nmlz.nsg He brought the books to school. Some verbs only change the case marking of G without changing the agreement. The verb hambiʔma distribute is a benefactive derivation of hamma distribute, divide, spread . In the typical scenario, the G argument is referentially high, the T argument is low, and the argument realization follows the double object frame, as in . When the G argument changes to inanimate reference, as in example , it has to be in the locative case, but the verb does not change to the indirective frame; and thus the agreement remains with G. Furthermore, instead of using the nonsingular marker =ci on the G argument ten village , it is marked for nonsingular number by reduplication, which indicates a plurality of subevents. This kind of plural marking is not encountered when the G argument is human, as shown in example . . . ka nniŋda phoʈo(=ci) ham-biʔ-meʔ-nen-in=ha 1sg[erg] 2pl photo (=nsg) distribute -V2.give-npst-1>2-2pl=nmlz.nsg I distribute the photos among you. . sarkar=ŋa yaŋ ten-ten=be ŋ-haps-u-bi-ci=ha government =erg money village-village =loc 3pl.A- distribute -3.P[pst]-V2.give-3nsg.P=nmlz.nsg The government distributed the money among the villages. . ka piccha=ci yaŋ haps-u-bi-ŋ-ci-ŋ=ha 1sg[erg] child =nsg money distribute -3.P[pst]-V2.give-1sg.A-nsg.P-1sg.A=nmlz.nsg I distributed the money among the children. Scenario-based alternations -1ex Not only case marking, but also the verbal person marking can be subject to reference-based alternations. The Yakkha verb agrees with only one object, so that there is the potential for competition between T and G arguments as to which argument will trigger the agreement. The universal tendency for agreement to be triggered by arguments that are speech act participants, animate or topical has already been mentioned by Givon1976Topic. This tendency can lead to hierarchical alignment of agreement, understood as agreement that is not determined by syntactic roles but by the referential properties of the arguments Nichols1992Language . This is well-studied
summary: The passage argues that alternations in three-argument verbs are largely driven by pragmatic and referential factors such as animacy, definiteness, topicality, and speech-act participation, with goal/recipient arguments typically higher on the referential hierarchy than theme arguments. It distinguishes argument-based alternations, which depend on the properties of one argument, from scenario-based alternations, which depend on how T and G compare to each other, and shows that Yakkha verb morphology can reflect these differences through case marking, agreement, and frame choice. Examples from Yakkha illustrate spray-load alternations and other patterns where animate or human G arguments favor double-object or secundative realizations, while inanimate G arguments often force indirective marking.

text: for monotransitive verbs, but not for three-argument verbs. The most prominent example for hierarchical alignment in ditransitives is the Yuman language Jamul Tiipay ( Miller2001A-grammar , discussed e.g. in Siewierska2003Person ). Two verbs of the double object class allow animate/human T arguments, namely soʔmeʔma show and cameʔma feed . Etymologically, both verbs are causatives, but they show the same behavior as non-derived verbs. Usually, the verb shows object agreement with G in this frame (see ), but when G has third person reference and T is a speech act participant (sap), the verb agrees with T instead of G. The case marking of G also changes to locative, so that the verb now belongs to the indirective frame (see ). . . a-ni-ŋa ka u-phoʈo soʔmet-a-ŋ=na 1sg.poss- elder.sister =erg 1sg 3sg.poss- photo show -pst-1sg.P=nmlz.sg My elder sister showed me her photo. (T[3]→G[sap]) . ka nda appa-ama=be soʔmeʔ-nen=na 1sg[erg] 2sg mother-father =loc show [pst]-1>2=nmlz.sg I showed you to my parents. (T[sap]→G[3]) This alternation is scenario-based, as it only applies in the T[sap]→G[3] constellation. In , both T and G are are speech-act participants, and the agreement remains with the G argument. This scenario is also pragmatically marked, which is why locative marking on G is possible (though not obligatory) here. . uŋ=ŋa ka nniŋda(=be) soʔmet-i-g=ha 3sg=erg 1sg 2pl(=loc) show [3sg.A;pst]-2pl-2=nmlz.nsg He showed me to you (plural). (T[sap]→G[sap]) In some contexts, this may yield more than one interpretation. As it is always the speech-act participant that triggers the agreement, a clause like in is ambiguous. Note that the two verbs differ with respect to the acceptability of the locative on G. The effects of the T[sap]→G[sap] scenario are summarized in t-sap-table . . ka nda kiba(*=be) cameʔ-meʔ-nen=na 1sg[erg] 2sg tiger (*=loc) feed -npst-1>2=nmlz.sg I will feed you to the tigerǃ (T-agr) OR I will feed the tiger to you! (G-agr) I made this into a rcc table. Is this OK? figure [htp] center tabular rcc & G[sap] & G[3] T[sap] & V-o[G], G- loc/nom & V-o[T], G- loc soʔmeʔma show & & V-o[T], G- nom cameʔma feed T[3] & 2 c V-o[G], G- nom tabular The effects of the T[sap]→G[3] scenario center figure The same T[sap]→G[3] scenario may also restrict alternations. The verb nakma (stem: nakt) ask, beg alternates (almost) freely between the double object frame (see ) and the indirective frame (see ). It is the only verb that shows this alternation. The argument encoding is conditioned by the question of which argument is central in a given discourse. . . ka nda chemha nak-nen=na 1sg[erg] 2sg liquor ask [pst]-1>2=nmlz.sg I asked you for liquor. . ka i=ya=ca n-nakt-a-ŋa-n! 1sg what =nmlz.nsg=add neg- ask -imp-1sg.P-neg Do not ask me for anything! 27 _nrr _06:25 . . uŋ=ŋa ka=be unipma nakt-u=ha 3sg=erg 1sg=loc money ask -3.P[pst]=nmlz.nc He asked me for his money. . uŋ=ŋa appa-ama=be ka nakt-a-ŋ=na 3sg=erg mother-father =loc 1sg ask -pst-1sg.P=nmlz.sg He asked my parents for me (i.e. to marry me). However, when the T is a speech act participant and the G is not, as in , the indirective frame is the only option. Clauses like the one in are ungrammatical. Thus, the particular scenario in which the T is a speech act participant and the G is a third person restricts the alternations in the argument realization of this verb. . *uŋci ka n-nakt-u-n-ci-n 3nsg 1sg neg- ask -3.P[imp]-neg-nsg.P-neg Intended: Do not ask them for me. The preceding section has shown how the argument realization in three-argument verbs can be conditioned by referential factors. The scenario T[sap]→G[3] leads to an obligatory change in person and case marking for the verbs soʔmeʔma show and cameʔma feed , and to a restriction in the alternation possibilities for the verb nakma ask, beg . Hierarchical alignment, partly combined with inverse marking, is also known from the verbal paradigms of other Tibeto-Burman languages, e.g. from rGyalrong Nagano1984A-historical, Rawang LaPolla2007Hierarchical, and to some extent from other Kiranti languages, too, like Hayu and Dumi Michailovsky2003Hayu, Driem1993A-grammar. In the Yakkha verbal person marking, however, hierarchical alignment as it is found in the three-argument verbs shown above is not found in the monotransitive paradigms.Several morphemes in Yakkha verbal person marking are scenario-sensitive, see verb-infl. However, the alignment of the verbal person marking in Yakkha is too heterogenous to be captured by one principle or one hierarchy. It also includes ergative, accusative, tripartite and neutral alignment (cf. also Witzlacketal2011_Decomposing for a Kiranti-wide study).
summary: The passage shows that in Yakkha, hierarchical alignment in three-argument verbs is scenario-sensitive: when a speech-act participant T is mapped to a third-person G, verbs like *soʔmeʔma* “show” and *cameʔma* “feed” change agreement and G marking, while the verb *nakma* “ask, beg” has its alternation restricted in the same scenario. In contrast, this kind of hierarchical alignment is not found in monotransitive paradigms, and Yakkha verbal person marking is too mixed to be explained by a single alignment principle or hierarchy, since it also includes ergative, accusative, tripartite, and neutral patterns.

text: This chapter deals with argument structure, valency alternations and transitivity operations in Yakkha. The term argument structure is understood here as the configuration of arguments that are governed by a particular lexical item Haspelmath2004_Valency . In frames, the different verb frames of argument realization are identified by the number of possible arguments and their case and agreement properties. Several verbs occur in more than one frame; their alternations are treated in valclass.Only predicates with nominal arguments are discussed in this chapter. For predicates taking clausal complements see Chapter compl. Apart from those alternations that result in straightforward classes, there are also transitivity operations that are more productive and not related to certain verb classes (see trans-op). One has to distinguish between operations that change the argument structure by adding or removing argument roles, and those that merely change the argument realization by changing the case or person marking properties for an argument. Many markers of transitivity operations have been verbs historically. They are also found as parts of lexically complex predicates, and the grammatical functions are often related to the lexical meanings of these markers. This multiplicity of functions can be viewed as a result of simultaneous grammaticalization and lexicalization processes of certain verbs (see also Chapter verb-verb).
summary: The chapter examines argument structure, valency alternations, and transitivity operations in Yakkha, focusing on predicates with nominal arguments. It distinguishes between verb frames based on the number of arguments and their case/agreement properties, and between operations that change argument roles and those that only alter argument realization. The passage also notes that many transitivity markers historically come from verbs and can still appear in complex predicates, reflecting ongoing grammaticalization and lexicalization.

text: Before starting with the description of the argument frames, some methodological and terminological remarks are in order. The argument frames are identified by three parameters: agreement, case and the question of how the verbal semantics interact with these two formal means. For this purpose, generalized semantic roles (gsrs) are identified for each predicate. Following Bickel2010_Grammatical, these roles are labelled as follows: A stands for the most agent-like argument of a transitive predicate,Yakkha does not exhibit differences between A arguments of two-argument and three-argument predicates, so that they do not have to be distinguished. P stands for the most patient-like argument of transitive predicates, S stands for the sole argument of intransitive predicates. For three-argument verbs, the most theme-like argument has the label T and the most goal-like argument has the label G . By relying on generalized semantic roles to identify the arguments of a predicate, one does not imply that these roles build coherent classes of arguments that are characterized by some common semantic or formal property. For example, locative-marked arguments can have the semantic role of a goal, a recipient, a location, a source or a stimulus). Crucially, gsrs make sense only in relation to the particular predicates or predicate classes. No further morphosyntactic consequences, e.g. pivots in some construction, can be inferred from these terms, as different types of pivots may occur in Yakkha syntax (see Chapters ch-nmlz, adv-cl and compl). The argument realization does not always match with the semantic transitivity, e.g. in transimpersonal verbs (see tr-imp). Nevertheless, a “standard” intransitive and a “standard” transitive frame could be identified, which are the most common frames of argument realization. As arguments are frequently dropped in Yakkha, many examples in this chapter come from elicited data. In the following, I will outline the two parameters of argument realization in Yakkha, which are person marking and case marking. As for person marking, Yakkha distinguishes intransitive and transitive inflectional paradigms (compare the marking of the verbs with regard to the role of the argument kaniŋ in ). Thus, there are three possible values: arguments may trigger intransitive (subject) agreement, transitive subject agreement or object agreement (the latter two being indicated as A or P in the glosses).For the function of the frequently occurring main clause nominalization see nmlz-uni-3. For the conditions of the nominative-ergative syncretism see case-erg. . .kaniŋ khe-i=ha 1pl go -1pl[pst]=nmlz.nsg We went. (S) .kaniŋ kei kheps-u-m=na 1pl[erg] drum hear -3.P[pst]-1pl.A=nmlz.sg We heard the drum. (A) .uŋci=ŋa kaniŋ kheps-a=ha 3nsg=erg 1pl hear -pst[1.P]=nmlz.nsg They heard us. (P) The agreement markers are not uniformly aligned, so that, for the purposes of this chapter, person marking is presented as tripartite, i.e. agreement with S is different from agreement with A and also different from agreement with P.The person marking on the Yakkha verb combines accusative, ergative, neutral and hierarchical alignment, see Chapter verb-infl on the verbal morphology. The reader should bear in mind that the indications in the glosses ( A, P ) refer only to the type of person marking, following a common labelling tradition for languages where the verbs show agreement with more than one argument. These labels facilitate reading the glosses, but they should not be conflated with the semantic roles of the verbal arguments, which can be S, A, P, T, G . To illustrate this with an example: the verb cimma learn is semantically transitive; it has an A argument (the learner) and a P argument (the thing learned, the knowledge acquired). The verb is, however, inflected with intransitive morphology (triggered by the semantic A argument, the learner), thus behaving like the verb in ex-gointr with respect to person marking. Arguments can be marked with an ergative, a nominative, a genitive, a locative, an instrumental and, albeit less commonly, with a comitative or an ablative. Yakkha has an ergative/instrumental syncretism; the case marking does not distinguish between agent and instrument, but subsumes both roles under the umbrella category effector VanValinetal1996The-case. In the following sections, schematic diagrams will illustrate the mapping of the semantic roles to the case and agreement properties for each argument frame. Altogether, 22 verb frames can be established. They can roughly be divided into intransitively inflected verbs, transitively inflected verbs, three-argument verbs, experiencer-as-possessor predicates, copular verbs and light verbs. In the schematic diagrams of the frames of argument realization, capital letters stand for the respective gsrs of a predicate. Labels like erg indicate the case marking. The agreement is indicated with s , a and o , with the corresponding gsr following in square brackets.The same notational convention is employed e.g. in Schikowski2014_Flexible.
summary: The passage explains that Yakkha argument frames are described using generalized semantic roles such as A, P, S, T, and G, together with case marking and verbal agreement, but these labels are only analytic tools and do not necessarily define uniform semantic or morphosyntactic classes. It emphasizes that person marking is tripartite rather than uniformly aligned, that case marking includes an ergative/instrumental syncretism, and that the language shows 22 overall verb-frame types, including intransitive, transitive, three-argument, experiencer-as-possessor, copular, and light-verb constructions.

text: S- nom V-s[S] In the standard intransitive frame, the subject is in the unmarked nominative case (not written in the glosses) and triggers agreement on the verb. Verbs such as imma sleep , posiʔma vomit and numa get well, recover belong to this frame. . . ka posit-a-ŋ=na 1sg vomit- pst-1sg=nmlz.sg I vomited. . nda nu-ga=na? 2sg get _well [pst]-2=nmlz.sg Are you fine? . n-yag-a-sy-a-ga-n=na=i? neg -feel _exhausted -pst-mddl-pst-2-neg=nmlz.sg=q Are you not exhausted?
summary: In the standard intransitive frame, the subject appears in the unmarked nominative case and controls agreement on the verb. Verbs like “sleep,” “vomit,” and “get well/recover” occur in this pattern, as shown by examples where the verb agrees with the subject and is followed by nominalizing or question particles.

text: A- nom P- loc/ins/abl/com V-s[A] Some experiencer verbs allow the expression of overt stimulus arguments, despite being identical to the standard intransitive frame in all other respects. The stimulus can be marked by various peripheral cases like the ablative, the locative, the instrumental and the comitative, as illustrated by example and . These experiencer verbs are typically etymologically complex (both Noun-Verb and Verb-Verb compounds), as they often have bisyllabic stems, and Kiranti languages, following a broader tendency in Southeast Asian languages, are typically characterized by monosyllabic morphemes Matisoff1990_Bulging. Some verbs of this frame have metaphorical meaning: to be hungry is expressed as in , without the intention to exaggerate or to be ironic. . . ka nda=bhaŋ/nda=nuŋ kisit-a-ŋ=na 1sg 2sg=abl/2sg=com be _afraid- pst-1sg=nmlz.sg I was afraid of you. . ka cokleʈ=pe kam-di-me-ŋ=na 1sg sweets =loc pine _over- V2.give-npst-1sg=nmlz.sg I pine over sweets. . sak=ŋa n-sy-a-ma-ŋa-n=na hunger =ins neg- die -pst-prf-1sg-neg=nmlz.sg I am not hungry.
summary: Some experiencer verbs can take an overt stimulus argument even though they otherwise look like ordinary intransitives. The stimulus may be marked with peripheral cases such as ablative, locative, instrumental, or comitative, and these verbs are often etymologically complex and bisyllabic, unlike the usual monosyllabic pattern of Kiranti languages. Some also have metaphorical meanings, such as the expression for “I am not hungry.”

text: A- nom P- loc V-s[A] Motion verbs are intransitively inflected, but they have two arguments, as they entail a mover (A) and the location or goal of the movement (P) in their conceptualization. This is also borne out by the natural language data: most of the motion verbs express the location overtly, marked by a locative. In a language that has generally more covert than overtly realized arguments, this can be counted as a strong indicator for the entailment of the locative argument in the verbal semantics. The location or goal can be expressed by an adverb, as in , or by a noun phrase (see - ). . . kucuma heʔne khy-a=na? dog where go [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg Where did the dog go? . koŋgu=be thaŋ-a=na hill =loc climb [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg He climbed on the hill. .saŋgoŋ=be yuŋ-a=na mat =loc sit _down [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg He sat down on the mat. . taŋkheŋ=be pes-a-khy-a=niŋ sky =loc fly [3sg]-pst-V2.go-pst=ctmp When he (the bird) flew into the sky, ... 21 _nrr _04.031 Under certain circumstances the locative on the goal argument can be omitted, e.g. when the location is a specific place with a name, or if it is a place that one typically moves to, such as villages, countries, the school, the work place and the like (see and Chapter case-nom).Example (a) refers to a marriage custom called bagdata, see Chapter social. Only unmodified nouns can appear without the nominative; if the reference of the noun is narrowed down and made definite, e.g. by a possessive or demonstrative pronoun, it has to take the locative case (see ). . . liŋkha=ci=ga teʔma bagdata nak-se mamliŋ ta-ya-ma a _clan =nsg=gen clan _sister finalization _of _marriage ask _for -sup Mamling come [3sg]-pst-prf A Linkha clan sister came to Mamling to ask for her bagdata (ritual). 37 _nrr _07.002 . hiʔwa pes-a=na wind fly [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg He flew (up) into the air. 21 _nrr _004.051 . nna*(=be)=go imin thaŋ-ma? that *(=loc)=top how climb -inf But how to climb to that (place)? 22 _nrr _05.098
summary:
Motion verbs are intransitively inflected, but semantically they take two arguments: a mover and a location or goal. The location/goal is usually overtly expressed with a locative-marked adverb or noun phrase, and this overt marking is treated as evidence that the locative argument is part of the verb’s semantics. 

The locative on the goal can sometimes be omitted, especially with named places or destinations people typically move to, but only unmodified nouns can appear without the locative. If the noun is made definite or more specific, such as by a possessive or demonstrative, it must take the locative case.

text: A- erg P- nom V-a[A].o[P] This frame characterizes the majority of the monotransitive verbs, such as nima see and mokma beat . The verb shows agreement with both A and P. The A argument is marked by an ergative case =ŋa (see ), except for first and second person pronouns, which exhibit an ergative/nominative syncretism (see also Chapter case-erg). Note that nouns with first and second person reference are possible in Yakkha (as if saying An old woman AM tired ; see also flex-agr). If they are A arguments of transitive verbs, they are marked by an ergative, other than the first and second person pronouns. The condition for the ergative/nominative syncretism is identical to this frame throughout all the transitively inflected frames. The P arguments are in the nominative case. . .isa=ŋa chemha tuks-u=ha? who =erg liquor spill -3.P[pst]=nmlz.nc Who spilled the liquor? . ka iya=ca ŋ-kheps-u-ŋa-n=ha 1sg[erg] what =nmlz.nc=add neg -hear- 3.P[pst]-1sg.A-neg=nmlz.nc I did not hear anything.
summary: The passage describes the most common monotransitive verb frame in which the verb agrees with both the A and P arguments. The A argument is marked with ergative case =ŋa, except for first- and second-person pronouns, which show ergative/nominative syncretism; P arguments are marked nominative.

text: A- nom P- erg V-a[P].o[A] Experiential events often show deviations from the standard marking patterns of argument encoding Bhaskararao2004_Nonnominative, Malchukov2008Split. There is one frame in Yakkha that is identical to the standard monotransitive frame, but the marking of A and P is reversed; the experiencer triggers object agreement on the verb, while the stimulus triggers subject agreement (zero for third person singular) and hosts the ergative case clitic. Notwithstanding the non-canonical agreement and case properties, the preferred constituent order is A-P-verb, and constructions with an S/A pivot, for instance, select the experiencer. The majority of the verbs belonging to this frame are related to the ingestion of food or to the consumption of other supplies, illustrated in . . . ka macchi=ŋa haŋd-a-ŋ=na 1sg pickles =erg taste _spicy -pst-1sg.P=nmlz.sg The pickles tasted hot to me. The Maithili loanword macchi has developed several meanings in Yakkha, namely chili plant , chili powder and hot pickle or sauce . . ka haŋha=ŋa khot-a-ŋ=na 1sg hot _spices =erg have _enough -pst-1sg.P=nmlz.sg I have enough spice (in my food). . nasa=ga ŋai=ŋa khikt-a-ŋ=na fish =gen stomach =erg taste _bitter -pst-1sg.P=nmlz.sg The fish stomach tasted bitter to me. Verbs that refer to being affected by natural or supernatural powers also follow the object-experiencer frame, e.g. teʔnima be possessed, suffer from evil spirit in . The verb be drunk is expressed as shown in . The stem sis literally also means kill with an animate, intentional A argument, but as the example shows, metaphorical meanings are possible as well. Notably, in this predicate, the stimulus is often omitted; sis has undergone a metaphorical extension towards the meaning of being drunk . . . puŋdaraŋma=ŋa teps-y-uks-u=na forest _goddess =erg be _possessed -prf-3.P[pst]=nmlz.sg He is possessed by the forest goddess. . (raksi=ŋa) sis-a-ga=na=i? liquor =erg kill -pst-2.P=nmlz.sg=q Are you drunk?
summary:
Yakkha has a special experiencer construction that reverses the usual A/P marking of a monotransitive clause: the experiencer behaves like an object in agreement, while the stimulus takes ergative case and controls subject agreement. Although the morphology is non-canonical, the default word order remains A-P-verb and the experiencer functions as the pivot in S/A constructions.

This frame is used mainly with verbs of tasting, eating, and consuming, as well as verbs for being affected by natural or supernatural forces. The passage also notes a metaphorical extension of the verb *sis* ‘kill’ to mean ‘be drunk,’ often without an overt stimulus.

text: S- nom V-a[3].o[S] The transimpersonal frame is similar to the object-experiencer frame. The verbs inflect transitively, but there is no overt A argument, the verbs show default third person singular subject agreement (zero). The sole argument is in the nominative and triggers object agreement on the verb. Diachronically there probably was an overt A, but the only remnant found synchronically is the agreement; all attempts at producing an overt A were regarded as ungrammatical. Malchukov2008Split notes that such constructions tend to be experiencer constructions crosslinguistically. In Yakkha, however, transimpersonal verbs are not experiencer verbs, as the subjects of these verbs are not typically animate, sentient beings. Verbs belonging to this frame often have change-of-state semantics, e.g. cikma ripen , lokma boil , homma swell , huʔma be blocked , ŋomma remain , shown in . . . a-nabhuk hut-u=na 1sg.poss- nose be _blocked -3.P[pst]=nmlz.sg I have a blocked nose. . a-laŋ=ci homd-u-ci=ha 1sg.poss- leg =nsg swell -3.P[pst]-nsg.P=nmlz.nsg My legs are swollen. . cama ŋond-u=ha rice remain -3.P[pst]=nmlz.nc (Some) rice remained. . cuwa cikt-u=ha beer ripen -3.P[pst]=nmlz.nc The beer is well-fermented. An agent or cause can only be expressed indirectly, via adverbial clauses such as in . .tumbuk poks-a=niŋa ten lus-u=na gun explode [3sg]-pst=ctmp village deafen -3.P[pst]=nmlz.sg When the gun exploded, the village was deafened (by the noise). A transitive structure, with an overt A argument can be achieved by a causative derivation . . . maŋcwa lokt-u=ha water boil -3.P[pst]=nmlz.nsg The water boiled. . kamala=ŋa maŋcwa lok-met-wa=ha Kamala =erg water boil -caus-npst[3.P]=nmlz.nsg Kamala boils water. Transimpersonal verbs are a solid class in Kiranti languages, found e.g. in Limbu Driem1987A-grammar , in Thulung Allen1975Sketch and in Bantawa Doornenbal2009A-grammar . In Yakkha, 29 transimpersonal verbs have been found so far. The following transimpersonal verbs have been found so far in Yakkha: chamma spread, increase , cemma get well, recover , choma tingle , cikma ripen , cipma rise (only for water), hekma get stuck, choke , heʔma be entangled, hang, snag , homma swell (stem: homd), homma fit into (stem: hond), huʔma be blocked , keŋma bear fruit , khakma freeze , khekt freeze, harden , khopma fit around something , leʔma flourish, be prosperous , lokma boil ,mopma be clouded, be dull , ŋomma remain , oʔma hatch , pheʔma bloom , phiŋma get clear , puʔma spill, overboil , sipma evaporate , suncama itch , tapma last long , wemma get intoxicated, be insolent , yeŋma be strong, be tough .
summary: The passage describes Yakkha transimpersonal verbs as transitive in inflection but lacking an overt agent, with the sole nominative argument triggering object agreement and the verb showing default third person singular subject agreement. Although they are crosslinguistically often experiencer constructions, Yakkha transimpersonal verbs are not experiencer verbs; instead, they typically denote change-of-state meanings such as ripen, boil, swell, or remain, and any agent or cause can only be expressed indirectly or through causativization. The passage also notes that this is a solid class in Kiranti languages and lists 29 such verbs identified in Yakkha.

text: A- erg P- loc V-a[A].o[3] One verb, tama arrive (at) , differs from the standard monotransitive frame in marking the P argument with the locative case. The object agreement slot is always filled by default third person object agreement: speech-act participants cannot be the objects of this verb. Rather, one would express such content as arrive at your place , with a third person object agreement. . lalubaŋ=nuŋ phalubaŋ=ŋa mamliŋ=be tas-a-ma-c-u Lalubang =com Phalubang =erg Mamling =loc arrive -pst-prf-du-3.P Lalubang and Phalubang have arrived in Mamling. 22 _nrr _05.041
summary: The verb **tama** ‘arrive (at)’ is exceptional in that it marks its P argument with the **locative case** rather than the usual object marking. Its object agreement position is always filled by **default third-person agreement**, so speech-act participants cannot be expressed as the object of this verb; to convey such meanings, the language uses a third-person object agreement instead.

text: S- erg V-a[S].o[3] In the semi-transitive frame, the verb is transitively inflected and the sole argument receives ergative marking, but overt objects are suppressed. The verb shows default 3sg object agreement, as in . The expression of the P (the excreted substance) is not just considered redundant, but unacceptable. See Li2007Splitergativity for a similar class of verbs in Nepali. This frame is like the mirror-image of the trans-impersonal frame discussed above. So far, however, the verb oma vomit in is the only member of this frame. . tug-a-by-a=na yapmi=ŋa os-u=ha get _sick -pst-V2.give-pst[3sg]=nmlz.sg person =erg vomit -3.P=nmlz.nc The sick person vomited.
summary: In the semi-transitive frame, the verb is inflected as transitive and the sole argument is marked ergative, while any overt object is suppressed. The verb takes default 3sg object agreement, and expressing the patient or expelled substance is not merely redundant but ungrammatical; at present, *oma* ‘vomit’ is the only verb attested in this frame.

text: A- nom P- nom V-s[A] This frame was found only for one verb, but it is listed for the sake of completeness. The verb cimma learn is inflected intransitively, although it takes two arguments. Both A and P are in the nominative, and A triggers the verbal person marking (see ). With transitive agreement morphology the verb becomes the ditransitive verb teach (see ). Except for the additional argument, this alternation is identical to the labile alternation discussed in labile. . . hari iŋlis cind-a=na Hari English learn [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg Hari learned English. . kamala=ŋa hari iŋlis cind-u=na Kamala =erg Hari English teach -3.P[pst]=nmlz.sg Kamala taught Hari English.
summary: The passage describes a special argument frame found only with the verb *cimma* “learn,” which is inflected intransitively even though it takes two arguments. In this frame, both A and P appear in the nominative, and A controls the verbal person marking. When transitive agreement morphology is added, the verb changes meaning to the ditransitive *teach*; aside from the extra argument, this alternation is like the labile alternation discussed elsewhere.

text: The case and agreement properties of the subjects of three-argument verbs are not different from those of monotransitive verbs. The argument realization of the T and G arguments, however, deserves a closer look. It is determined by both semantic roles and the referential properties of the arguments. The choice of the agreement triggering argument for the nominalizing clitics =na and =ha need not be the same as for the verbal agreement. The nominalizers are partly aligned according to the referential properties of the arguments and partly according to their role. This is discussed in detail in verb-infl and nmlz-uni-3 and will not figure prominently in the following treatment of three-argument frames.
summary: The subjects of three-argument verbs have the same case and agreement properties as the subjects of monotransitive verbs. However, the realization of the T and G arguments depends on both semantic roles and referential features, and the argument that triggers agreement with the nominalizing clitics =na and =ha may differ from the one that triggers verbal agreement. The nominalizers are therefore only partly role-based and partly sensitive to referential properties.

text: A- erg G- nom T- nom V-a[A].o[G] In the double object frame, both T and G arguments are in the nominative case. The verb agrees with the A and usually with the G argument, except for some pragmatically marked scenarios where T becomes the agreement trigger (see three-arg). The choice of the nominalizer on the finite verb depends on T when T has third person reference: singular T triggers =na, and nonsingular or non-countable T triggers =ha (compare and ). The verbs belonging to this frame are typically verbs of caused possession and benefactives (both derived and underived), and thus, the G arguments are typically animate in this frame. . . ka a-ni mendhwak hakt-wa-ŋ=na 1sg[erg] 1sg.poss -aunt goat send -npst[3.P]-1sg.A=nmlz.sg I send my aunt a goat. . ka nda eko cokleʈ piʔ-nen=na 1sg[erg] 2sg one sweet give[pst]-1>2=nmlz.sg I gave you a sweet. . ka nda pyak cokleʈ piʔ-nen=ha 1sg[erg] 2sg many sweet give[pst]-1>2=nmlz.nsg I gave you many sweets.
summary: In the double object frame, both the T and G arguments are marked nominative, while the verb agrees with A and usually with G, except in some pragmatically marked cases where T becomes the agreement trigger. When T is third person, the finite verb’s nominalizer depends on its number/countability: singular T takes =na, and nonsingular or non-countable T takes =ha. The verbs in this frame are typically caused-possession and benefactive verbs, so G is usually animate.

text: A- erg G- loc/abl/com T- nom V-a[A].o[T] The indirective frame is more frequent than the double object frame, i.e. there are more verbs that follow this frame. The G argument may have goal or source role and is marked by a locative (see ) or, occasionally, by an ablative or comitative case (see ), while the T argument is in the nominative and triggers object agreement on the verb (including the nominalizers). Mostly, caused motion is expressed by verbs of this frame. . . ka a-cya=ci iskul=be paks-wa-ŋ-ci-ŋ=ha 1sg[erg] 1sg.poss-child=nsg school=loc send-npst-1sg.A-nsg.P-1sg.A=nmlz.nsg I send my children to school. . ak=ka khorek cula=ga u-yum=be yuks-uks-u-ŋ=na 1sg.poss=gen bowl hearth=gen 3sg.poss-side=loc put-prf-3.P[pst]-1sg.A=nmlz.sg I have put my bowl next to the hearth. .ama=ŋa a-nuncha netham=be nes-u=na mother =erg 1sg.poss-younger _sibling bed=loc lay-3.P[pst]=nmlz.sg Mother laid my younger sister on the bed. . .khaʔniŋgo tuʔkhi leŋ-meʔ=niŋa heko=ha=ci=nuŋ yaŋ naŋ-ca-ma ucun men but trouble happen [3sg]-npst=ctmp other =nmlz.nsg=nsg=com money beg -V2.eat-inf nice neg.cop But in difficult times, it is not good to ask others for money. 01 _leg _07.257 . haku nhaŋto m-ban=uŋ nasa ŋ-in-wa-n-ci-ŋa-n=ha now temp.abl 2sg.poss- father =com fish neg- buy -npst-neg-3nsg.P-excl-neg=nmlz.nsg From now on I will not buy fish from your father. 01 _leg _07.208 The locative can also mark adjuncts, yielding clauses that look superficially identical to the indirective frame. However, the adjuncts have to be distinguished from locative-marked arguments. In , for instance, it is straightforward that the locative-marked noun phrases refer to circumstances (time, place, manner, quantity Tesniere1959Elements ) and are thus adjuncts. The decision whether a participant is an argument or an adjunct is, however, not that trivial for all the predicates. . . a-ppa=ŋa ka omphu=be nis-a-ŋ=na 1sg.poss- father =erg 1sg verandah =loc see -pst-1sg.P=nmlz.sg Father saw me on the veranda. . a-ma=ŋa tan=be tek akt-u=na 1sg.poss- mother =erg loom =loc fabric weave -3.P[pst]=nmlz.sg Mother wove (a piece of) fabric on the loom.
summary:
The indirective frame is more common than the double-object frame and is used by many verbs, especially those expressing caused motion. In this pattern, the G argument is marked by locative, ablative, or comitative case and can express goal or source, while the T argument is nominative and controls object agreement on the verb.

The passage also notes that locative case can mark adjuncts, creating clauses that superficially resemble the indirective frame. Such locative phrases are clearly adjuncts when they denote circumstances like time, place, manner, or quantity, though distinguishing adjuncts from locative-marked arguments is not always straightforward for every predicate.

text: A- erg G- nom T- ins V-a[A].o[G] The verbs of the secundative frame denote events of throwing, hitting, covering, applying, exchanging, events of creative or destructive impact. The T argument is marked by an instrumental case, but it is not always an instrument in the classical sense of “used by the agent to act on the patient” Andrews1985The-major, as shows. The G argument is in the unmarked nominative and triggers agreement on the verb (including the nominalizers). Some verbs of this frame may alternate with the indirective frame (the spray-load alternation , see three-arg). . . ka cabak=ŋa paŋge lend-u-ŋ=ha. 1sg rice =ins millet exchange- 3.P[pst]-1sg.A=nmlz.nsg I exchanged rice for millet. . u-ppa=ŋa hammana=ŋa picha ept-u=na 3sg.poss- father =erg blanket =ins child cover -3.P[pst]=nmlz.sg The father covered his child with a blanket. .eko phiswak=ŋa sum=ci ʈukra yub-u-ci=ha one knife =ins three =nsg piece cut -3.P[pst]-3nsg.P=nmlz.nsg He cut it into three pieces with a small knife. (Cut-and-break clips, Bohnemeyeretal2010_cut )
summary: The secundative frame is used for verbs expressing throwing, hitting, covering, applying, exchanging, and similar events of creative or destructive impact. In this frame, the T argument takes instrumental case but is not necessarily a classical instrument, while the G argument is in unmarked nominative and controls verb agreement; some verbs can also alternate with an indirective frame.

text: S- gen/nom poss- N V-s[3] A- gen/erg P- nom poss- N V-a[A].o[3] Experiential predicates are characterized by the core participant being emotionally or sensationally affected by the event. This makes the thematic role experiencer less agent-like, which is often reflected in the treatment of experiencer arguments as non-prominent (“downgrading” in Bickel2004The-syntax ), e.g. by non-canonical case marking or by deviating agreement patterns ( Levinetal2005_Argument , Naess2007_Prototypical ). We have already seen a class of experiential predicates in Yakkha that code their A arguments like standard objects. However, downgrading of an argument in one part of grammar,for instance, in case marking, does not necessarily imply downgrading in other domains, for instance access to pivothood or reflexivization Bickel2004The-syntax . Most experiential events in Yakkha, and generally in Kiranti languages, are expressed by complex predicates consisting of a noun and a verb, and the experiencer (i.e., the A argument) is coded as the possessor of the noun (see nv-comp-poss).See Bickel1997The-possessive for Belhare. The nouns that belong to such predicates denote sensations, feelings, character traits, moral qualities or affected body parts (hence, the term psych-noun). Noun-verb compounds for the expression of experiential events are not unique to Yakkha or Kiranti languages; they belong to a broader Southeast Asian pattern Matisoff1986Hearts. Morphosyntactically, the psycho-noun hosts a possessive prefix that refers to the experiencer. The noun may also trigger agreement on the verb (see for examples). Some psycho-nouns are conceptualized as nonsingular and thus trigger nonsingular verbal agreement. The predicates can be grouped into intransitively and transitively inflected verbs. Some verbs show alternations. The two schematic diagrams above only show the most common frames of the experiencer-as-possessor predicates, corresponding to and , respectively. In , the stimulus triggers object agreement. For a detailed description of the subframes and alternations see poss-e1. . . ŋ=ga yupma(=ci) n-yus-a(=ci)? 2sg.poss=gen sleepiness (=nsg) 3pl -be _full -pst(=nsg) Are you tired? . ŋ-khaep cips-u-ga=na=i? 2sg.poss- interest/wish complete -3.P[pst]-2.A=nmlz.nsg=q Are you satisfied? . nda ka ijaŋ n-lok khot-a-ŋ-ga=na? 2sg[erg] 1sg why 2sg.poss -anger have _enough -pst-1sg.P-2sg.A=nmlz.sg Why are you mad at me?
summary: Experiential predicates in Yakkha involve a core participant, the experiencer, who is emotionally or sensorially affected, and this role is often treated as less agent-like. In Yakkha and other Kiranti languages, many such events are expressed by noun-verb compounds in which the experiencer is coded as the possessor of a psych-noun, which may also control verbal agreement and can appear in both intransitive and transitive inflectional frames.

text: Copular clauses are different from the other clauses insofar as the predicate is a not verb but a nominal, adjectival or locative constituent Dryer2007Clause . The constituents in copular clauses do not have semantic roles. Yakkha has two copular frames which can roughly be characterized as the identificational and the existential frame.Such a two-way distinction in the copular frames is common in languages of the Himalayan region (see, e.g., Genetti2007_Newari on Newari, and Matthews1984Course on Nepali), but the exact distribution of the copular verbs probably differs from language to language. While the equational frame is expressed by a copular verb (that is lacking an infinitival form) or by a copular particle om that is not found elsewhere in simple clauses, the existential frame is expressed by two standard intransitive verbs: wama be, live, exist and leŋma become, happen, come into being .
summary: Copular clauses differ from other clauses because their predicate is nominal, adjectival, or locative rather than verbal, and the constituents in such clauses do not have semantic roles. Yakkha has two copular frames, roughly identificational and existential, a distinction common in Himalayan languages, though the distribution of copular verbs varies across languages. The equational frame is marked by a copular verb without an infinitival form or by the particle *om*, while the existential frame uses the intransitive verbs *wama* ‘be, live, exist’ and *leŋma* ‘become, happen, come into being’.

text: Two different forms participate in Frame (a): a copular verb that shows the expectable inflectional categories of person, number, tense/aspect and polarity, and a copular particle om that can also refer to any person, but is not inflected, apart from the nonsingular marker =ci (see ). They are used to equate or identify two entities, and to state class inclusion (see ). The forms of the copular verb are suppletive in the nonpast; in the past forms it has a stem sa (see cop-infl on the morphology of the copulas). The copular verb and the particle are optional, and thus they are often omitted. The particle is also used as affirmative interjection om yes . The domains of these two copular devices overlap, and in one instance they were found combined, too (see , where this combination seems to yield emphasis). . . ka khasi ŋan 1sg castrated _goat cop.1sg I am a castrated goat. 31 _mat _01.074 . ka isa om? 1sg who cop Who am I? .susma=nuŋ suman na nuncha om=ci Susma =com Suman eZ yB cop=nsg Susma and Suman are (elder) sister and (younger) brother. 01 _leg _07.035 .ka na puŋda=ga khuncakhuwa ŋan om! 1sg this jungle =gen thief cop.1sg cop I am the thief of this jungle! 01 _leg _07.335
summary: The passage describes two copular devices: an inflected copular verb and an uninflected copular particle om, which can refer to any person except for a nonsingular marker =ci. Both are used to equate or identify entities and to express class inclusion, and both are often omitted. The particle also serves as an affirmative interjection, and although the two copular forms overlap in use, they can sometimes occur together for emphasis.

text: Two verbs occur in Frame (b): the verb wama be, live, exist is a stative verb expressing existence. Its stem shows irregular behavior: the basic stem form is waiʔ waeʔ weʔ, and additionally ma can be found in some negated forms (see cop-infl for the inflection of the copulas). This verb can occur in the motion verb frame, expressing location or possession (see ). It can also be used to express a property of the copular topic, with an adjective as the predicate (see and ). . . ibebe pyak encho paŋ=ci m-ma-ya-nin=ha somewhere much long _time _ago house =nsg neg- exist -pst-pl.neg=nmlz.nsg Once upon a time there were no houses. The adverbial phrase ibebe is a fixed expression that originates in ibe-ibe somewhere-somewhere . 27 _nrr _06.001 . bani man=na habit exist .neg.npst[3sg]=nmlz.sg There is no (such) habit. .nna cuʔlumphi haku=ca ceŋgaceŋ waeʔ=na that stele now =add straight _upright be [3sg;npst]=nmlz.sg This stele stands straight upright even now. 18 _nrr _03.030 . piccha=go uhiŋgilik weʔ=na child =top alive exist npst[3sg]=nmlz.sg But the child is alive. 22 _nrr _05.087 The second verb of frame (b) is the ingressive-phasal verb leŋma (stem: leks) become, come into being, happen , shown in . Apart from this meaning it is also used to express non-permanent properties, as in .In (c), the property as such is of course permanent, but the subordinate clause puts the property in the perspective of a specific time. . . na=ga suru imin leks-a=na baŋniŋ this =gen beginning how become [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg as.for As for how she came into being... 14 _nrr _02.002 . hoŋkaʔla leks-a=hoŋ like _that become [3sg]-pst=seq As it became like that, ... 11 _nrr _01.019 .limlim lim=nuŋ leŋ-me. khuŋ-kheʔ-ma=niŋa li=nuŋ=ca n-leŋ-me-n sweet sweet =com become [3sg]-npst carry -V2.carry.off-inf=ctmp heavy =com=add neg- become [3sg]-npst-neg The sweet will be tasty. While carrying, it also will not be heavy. 01 _leg _07.044 Example from a pear story shows a nice minimal pair between the identificational and the existential copula (sana and waisa). The identificational copula only takes nominal predicates. The question word imin how is nominalized, and combined with the identificational copula. The existence of the snow is, however, expressed by the existential verb wama. .i=na, la, ʈhoŋ=ca imin=na sa=na, hiuŋ=le wai-sa, i=ya? what =nmlz.sg , filler , place =add how =nmlz.sg cop.pst[3sg]=nmlz.sg snow =ctr exist -pst[3sg] what =nmlz.nc What, well, what kind of place was it, there was snow, what was it? (Context: the speaker is unsure, because she is trying to understand what happens in the pear story film. Her interpretation of the distorted quality of the footage is that it must be a snowy place.) 19 _pea _01.002
summary: The passage describes two verbs in frame (b): **wama** ‘be, live, exist,’ a stative verb used for existence, location, possession, and some copular predicates, and **leŋma** ‘become, come into being, happen,’ an ingressive-phasal verb also used for non-permanent properties. It notes that **wama** has irregular stem forms and can appear in negated forms, while **leŋma** can be used where a property is viewed at a specific time. The passage also contrasts the existential verb **wama** with the identificational copula, which only takes nominal predicates.

text: The light verb strategy is commonly used to introduce Nepali verbs or light verb constructions into Yakkha. The construction is parallel to the Nepali source construction, but the Nepali light verbs are replaced by the Yakkha lexemes wama exist, be and cokma do . The resulting structure also gets formally adjusted to the Yakkha morphosyntax. In Nepali, some S/A arguments (e.g. of knowledge and experiential predicates) are marked by the dative -lāī (the Nepali translation of would be ma-lāī ali-ali thāhā cha), and the verb shows third person agreement with the noun in the nominative. But as there is no dative case in Yakkha, the result of the calquing is a nominative-marked subject and a light verb that triggers third person agreement. In light verb constructions which are not calques from experiential predicates, the verb agrees with the subject (S or A, see ). Although overt P arguments are possible, as nam sun in , the light verbs found so far are always inflected intransitively, and A arguments in the ergative case were not found. . . ka mimik thaha waeʔ=na 1sg a _bit knowledge exist [3sg]=nmlz.sg I know a little bit. 13 _cvs _02.022 . liŋkha=ci nam=nuŋ bʌgʌri n-jog-a a _clan =nsg sun =com bet 3pl- do -pst The Linkhas had a bet with the sun. 11 _nrr _01.003 The same strategy is also used for borrowing Nepali verbal stems into Yakkha (see , with the Nepali verb haraunu lose ). The Nepali stems are integrated into Yakkha by means of the suffix -a (also found in related languages, e.g. -ap in Belhare, Bickel2003Belhare ). The resulting lexeme hara is then treated like any other noun by the light verb. . ŋkhoŋ liŋkha baji=be har-a cog-a-khy-a and _then a _clan bet =loc lose -nativ do [3sg]-pst-V2.go-pst And then the Linkha man lost the bet. 11 _nrr _01.012
summary:
Yakkha commonly calques Nepali light-verb constructions by replacing Nepali light verbs with Yakkha verbs such as **wama** ‘exist, be’ and **cokma** ‘do’, while adjusting the whole construction to Yakkha morphosyntax. In calques of Nepali experiential predicates, Yakkha lacks the Nepali dative pattern, so the subject is nominative and the light verb shows third-person agreement; in other light-verb constructions, the verb agrees with the subject, and no ergative A arguments were found.  

The same strategy is used to borrow Nepali verbal stems: they are integrated with the suffix **-a** and then treated like nouns combined with a light verb, as in **hara** ‘lose’ with **cokma** ‘do’.

text: Yakkha does not have reflexive pronouns. The reflexive is constructed by a complex predicate with the V2 -ca eat . It indicates that the A and P argument of the predicate have identical reference. The resulting verb gets detransitivized with regard to case and person marking, as shown in . This construction can only express complete coreferentiality, so that propositions like I saved us can neither be expressed by the verbal morphology nor by the reflexive derivation in Yakkha. The various other functions of this V2 are treated in V2-eat. Apart from reflexive constructions, it also occurs in many lexicalized predicates with classical middle semantics, such as grooming and social interactions. Some of the labile verbs that are discussed in labile also show reflexive semantics when they are inflected intransitively, without attaching the reflexive marker. . nda (aphai) moŋ-ca-me-ka=na 2sg (self) beat-V2.eat-npst-2=nmlz.sg You beat yourself. The examples below show that the reflexive can also apply to a quantified noun phrase , to a question pronoun , and to negated propositions . There are no dedicated negative pronouns in Yakkha; negation is constructed by a question pronoun with the additive focus clitic =ca and verbal negation markers. In irrealis (question and negation) contexts, both singular and nonsingular inflection is possible, depending on the potential referents that the speaker has in mind (or what the speaker assumes the addressee has in mind). . .ghak sar n-so-ca-ya all teacher 3pl -look- V2.eat-pst All teachers looked at themselves. .isa u-chik ekt-a-ca-ya=na who 3sg.poss -hate make _break [3sg]-pst-V2.eat-pst=nmlz.sg Who is angry at himself? .isa=ca n-so-ca-ya-n=ha=ci who =add neg -look- V2.eat-pst-neg=nmlz.nsg=nsg Noone looked at themselves. In three-argument verbs, there are two potential candidates for coreference with A. Whether A controls G or T is a matter of the original frame of the verb. For double object verbs, coreference with T is ungrammatical (see ), while coreference with G is fine (see ). It seems crosslinguistically unexpected that the coreference of A and G is accepted, while the coreference of A and T is ungrammtical. Kazenin states the implicational universal that [...] if a language allows verbal marking of indirect reflexives, it allows verbal marking of direct reflexives as well. Kazenin2001_Verbal . It is not possible for T and G to be coreferential in the reflexive derivation, i.e. to express propositions like I showed him to himself (in the mirror) . . . *ka ama (aphai phoʈo=be) soʔmen-ca-me-ŋ=na 1sg[erg] mother (self photo=loc) show-V2.eat-npst-1sg=nmlz.sg Intended: I show myself to mother (on the photo). . ka (aphai) cokleʈ pin-ca-me-ŋ=na 1sg[erg] (self) sweet give-V2.eat-npst-1sg=nmlz.sg I give myself a sweet. As for three-argument verbs of the indirective frame, A can be coreferential with the argument in the nominative. This is illustrated by the verb thumma tie to . In the frame is shown for comparison. Example shows the reflexive, where the locative G argument is retained and the nominative T argument is coreferential with A, and thus unexpressed. The A argument changes its case marking from ergative to nominative. . .a-ppa=ŋa on siŋ=be thund-u=na 1sg.poss -father =erg horse tree =loc tie -3.P[pst]=nmlz.nsg My father tied the horse to the tree. .a-nuncha siŋ=be thun-ca-meʔ=na 1sg.poss -younger _sibling tree=loc tie-V2.eat[3sg]-npst=nmlz.sg My brother ties himself to a tree. Reflexivization is also possible with verbs of the experiencer-as-possessor frame (cf. exp and nv-comp-poss), as shown above in example uchik. In complex sentences, e.g. in embedded complement clauses, the reflexive V2 can mark the main verb, although the reflexive semantics actually apply to the predicate in the embedded clause (see ). The complement-taking predicate miʔma means want when it takes infinitival complements; its meaning in other constructions is hope, like, think (see also Chapter compl). This is, however, only possible in the type of complement construction that embeds infinitives, where the embedded and the main clause S/A argument are necessarily coreferential.Note that the ergative on A is retained in this construction, which suggests that the A argument belongs to the embedded transitive clause (a case of backward control). . uŋ=ŋa phoʈo cok-ma min-ca-meʔ=na 3sg=erg photo make -inf want- V2.eat[3sg]-npst=nmlz.sg She wants to take a photo of herself.
summary: Yakkha has no reflexive pronouns; reflexivity is expressed by a complex predicate with the V2 -ca ‘eat’, which marks the A and P arguments as having identical reference and detransitivizes the verb in case and person marking. This construction requires complete coreference and applies across different verb types, including some three-argument verbs, experiencer-possessor verbs, and certain embedded infinitival complement clauses, though some coreference patterns are ungrammatical.

text: The reciprocal is constructed by attaching the suffix -khusa to the stem of the lexical verb and employing the verb cama eat as auxiliary (see ). The lexical verb and the auxiliary have to be adjacent, but the degree of morphological fusion is lower than in the reflexive construction and complex predication in general. Inflectional prefixes attach to the auxiliary, not to the lexical verb. As the reciprocal expresses mutual actions, it is characterized by at least two participants that both simultaneously have the role of actor and undergoer. The reciprocal participants are fused into one noun phrase. The construction only applies to transitive verbs, and it always formally detransitivizes the predicate, by assigning the nominative case to the A arguments and by inflecting the auxiliary intransitively, even when the lexical verb is a three-argument verb, as in : here, the G argument is coreferential with A and hence it is omitted, while the T remains on the surface, retaining the case marking of its frame of argument realization (unmarked nominative in the double object frame). Contexts where reciprocals of double object verbs have coreferential A and T arguments are hard to imagine, and those proposed were rejected (see ungrammatical ). Inherently reciprocal verbs such as tupma meet , tuma fight , khima quarrel and cuŋma wrestle are intransitive in Yakkha; they do not permit the reciprocal operation. . . kanciŋ [...] sok-khusa=se ca-ya-ŋ-ci-ŋ 1du [...] look-recip=restr eat.aux-pst-excl-du-excl We (dual, excl) just looked at each other. (A=P) 40 _leg _08.070 . kanciŋ phuŋ pi-khusa ca-me-ci=ha 1du flower give-recip eat.aux-npst-1du=nmlz.nsg We (dual, incl) give flowers to each other. (A=G) . *kanciŋ ama(=be) soʔmek-khusa ca-me-ci=ha 1du mother(=loc) show-recip eat.aux-npst-[1]du=nmlz.nsg Intended: We showed each other to mother (e.g. on a photo). (*A=T) The antecedent of the coreferential argument always has to be the agent, as with the reciprocal of nis see, know , yielding introduce, get to see/know each other in . Coreferential T and G are possible, however, when the causative marker -met is attached to the auxiliary, so that the reciprocal construction serves as input to a causative construction (see ). The arguments that are fused into one noun phrase are the A and P arguments of the reciprocal construction, and simultaneously they are T and G arguments of the causative construction nikhusa cameʔma introduce to each other , which shows transitive person marking and ergative case marking on A. The causative verb nimeʔma, without the reciprocal, also exists; it is a three-argument verb with the meaning introduce (X to Y) . . . kanciŋ ni-khusa ca-me-ci=ha 1du see/know- recip eat .aux-npst-[1]du=nmlz.ns We will get to see/know each other. (A=P) . uŋ=ŋa uŋci ni-khusa ca-met-u-ci=ha 3sg=erg 3nsg see/know-recip eat.aux-caus-3.P[pst]-nsg.P=nmlz.nsg He introduced them (to each other). ([[A=P. recip ], G=T. caus ]) In the indirective frame (characterized by locative or ablative marking on the G argument, see three-arg-frame), the reciprocal construction can express coreference of A and T or A and G, regardless of the case and agreement properties of the arguments in the corresponding non-reciprocal predicate. The possibilities are restricted only by the verbal semantics, i.e. whether the T or the G argument is animate/human and thus eligible for being coreferential with A. In , the A argument is coreferential with T, while in , A is coreferential with G. . . uŋci hoŋma=be luŋ-khusa ca-ya-ci=ha 3nsg river =loc drown- recip eat .aux-pst-[3]du=nmlz.nsg They (dual) drowned each other in the river. (A=T) .uŋci yaŋ khu-khusa ca-me-ci=ha 3nsg money steal -recip eat .aux-npst-[3]du=nmlz.nsg They steal money from each other. (A=G) In the secundative frame (characterized by instrumental marking on the T argument, see three-arg-frame), animate or human T arguments are hardly conceivable, and thus, only instances with coreferential A and G could be attested, as shown in . .ibebe n-juŋ-a-ma, ikhiŋ=ga tabek=ŋa ce-ŋkhusa n-ja-ya=em, barcha-ŋa hok-khusa n-ja-ya=em, luŋkhwak=ŋa lep-khusa n-ja-ya, ikhiŋ=ga bhuiʈar=ŋa ap-khusa n-ja-ya. anywhere 3pl- fight -pst-prf so _big =gen khukuri _knife =ins cut -recip 3pl- eat .aux-pst=alt spear =ins pierce -recip 3pl- eat .aux-pst=alt stone =ins throw -recip 3pl- eat .aux-pst so _big =gen catapult =ins shoot -recip 3pl- eat .aux-pst=alt They fought so much, with knifes so big, whether they cut each other with knives, whether they stabbed each other with lances, they threw stones at each other, they shot each other with a really big catapult. 39 _nrr _08.21--2 Derived verbs can also serve as input to the reciprocal construction, as shown for the benefactive in and for the causative in . . .kanciŋ ʈopi pham-bi-khusa ca-me-ci=ha 1du cap knit -V2.give-recip eat .aux-npst-[1]du=nmlz.nsg We knit caps for each other. .kaniŋ cuwa=ŋa khoʔ-meʔ-khusa ca-i-wa 1pl beer=ins have _enough-caus-recip eat .aux-1pl-npst We serve each other beer. (Lit. We make each other have enough beer. )
summary:
The reciprocal in Yakkha is formed by adding the suffix **-khusa** to the lexical verb and using **cama** ‘eat’ as an auxiliary, with inflectional prefixes attaching to the auxiliary; the two parts must be adjacent but are less tightly fused than in reflexive and other complex predicates. It expresses mutual action between at least two participants fused into one noun phrase, applies only to transitive verbs, and detransitivizes the clause by marking the A argument nominative and inflecting the auxiliary intransitively. 

The construction can interact with different argument frames and with causative or derived verbs: in some cases A is coreferential with P, T, or G depending on the verb frame and semantics, while coreferential T and G become possible when the reciprocal is embedded under causative morphology. Inherently reciprocal verbs like ‘meet,’ ‘fight,’ and ‘quarrel’ are intransitive in Yakkha and

text: Middle verbs are characterized by denoting an event that“affects the subject of the verb or his interests”, to take up the definition by Lyons1969_Introduction .
