summary: The passage gives an example in which the verb is marked with a non-past first-person singular ending and a nominalizer, and it is glossed as “I sew a kurta for myself.” It illustrates the morphology of the sentence, including the verb suffixes and the nominalizer attached to the clause.

text: As pointed out in Dryer2007Clause , at least four perspectives come to mind when talking about clause types: (i) the distinction between declarative, interrogative, and imperative speech acts, (ii) the distinction between main and subordinate clauses, (iii) the properties of clauses and their constituents as building blocks of discourse, and (iv) types of clauses based on different kinds of predicates and their argument structure. The purpose of this chapter is to provide a bird's eye view from all four perspectives. An in-depth treatment of the argument structure can be found in Chapter verb-val, some aspects of information structure are dealt with in Chapter particles and subordinate clauses are the topic of Chapters ch-nmlz, adv-cl and compl. The chapter is structured as follows: simp-cl1 discusses general structural properties of simple independent clauses, simp-cl2 lays out constituent structure. Different types of illocutionary acts and how they affect the shape of a clause are discussed in simp-cl3. Finally, flex-agr introduces the regularities of agreement in Yakkha. In line with what is known about agreement in Tibeto-Burman languages in general, the agreement in Yakkha is less restricted than in Indo-European languages and does not require a complete matching between the referential features of the agreement markers and their controllers.
summary: The chapter surveys clause types from four perspectives: speech-act type, main versus subordinate clauses, discourse-building properties of clauses, and clause types defined by predicate and argument structure. It also outlines the chapter’s organization, covering simple clause structure, constituent structure, illocutionary effects on clause shape, and agreement in Yakkha. Yakkha agreement is presented as relatively less restricted than in Indo-European languages, since it does not require a complete match between agreement markers and their controllers.

text: Independent clauses present propositional content independently of other syntactic units. They are the unit in which any grammatical category of a language can be expressed, other than in dependent clauses (relative clauses, complement clauses or adverbial clauses), which are often restricted in some way. Some operators generally function on the level of an independent clause, like the mirative rahecha (a Nepali loan) or exclamative particles like baʔlo and haʔlo (see ). The reportative marker =bu is also found clause-finally (see ), but occasionally it is also found on embedded clauses containing indirect speech and on constituents inside the clause (see hearsay). Most markers, for instance information-structural particles and case markers, are found both on clausal constituents and on clauses, which is not unusual in Tibeto-Burman. There are, however, tendencies for certain markers to appear on noun phrases (e.g. the topic marker =ko, the contrastive focus marker =le, the emphatic marker =maŋ) or rather on clauses or both (case markers, several postpositions, the restrictive focus marker =se, the additive focus marker =ca, the reportative marker =bu). Another feature which distinguishes independent clauses is the clause-final afterthought position which is accompanied by an intonation break as a means to provide additional information about one of the (overt or omitted) referents (see ). All kinds of arguments are possible in the afterthought position. Yakkha has verbal clauses, copular clauses and verbless clauses, the latter reflecting a copular structure without a copula, usually with identificational or ascriptive semantics. . .n-so-ks-u=na rahecha baʔloǃ neg- look -prf-3.P[pst]=nmlz.sg mir excla Oh, he did not look into it! 34 _pea _04.039 . yondaŋ=ca khendaŋ=ca pik=ci=le n-du-ma-sim-me=ha=bu, ibebe=ga from _thither =add from _hither =add cow =nsg=ctr 3pl- step _on -inf-aux.prog-npst=nmlz.nsg=rep everywhere =gen Here and there, cows are trampling everywhere, it is said, everywhere. 39 _nrr _08.25 . . liŋkha=ci nam=nuŋ bʌgʌri n-jog-a, bʌgʌri a _clan =nsg sun =com bet 3pl- do -pst bet The Linkhas had a bet with the sun, a bet. 11 _nrr _01.003 . ŋkhaʔla lu-saŋ uŋ=ŋa nna, luŋkhwak, cuʔlumphi thukt-uks-u, nna kolenluŋ=ga like _that tell -sim 3sg=erg that stone stele erect -prf-3.P[pst] that marble =gen Telling them like that, he erected that stone, the stele, out of marble. 18 _nrr _03.021 . heksaŋ nna miyaŋ n-thog-haks-uks-u=na raecha, pik=ci=ŋa, goru=ci=ŋa later that a _little 3pl.A- hit -V2.send-prf-3.P=nmlz.sg mir cow =nsg=erg ox =nsg=erg Later, they hit off some of it (the stone), the cows, the oxen. 39 _nrr _08.03
summary: Independent clauses are presented as the basic unit for expressing propositional content and for realizing grammatical categories, while dependent clauses are often restricted in what they can express. The passage notes that some markers and particles are clause-level, others occur on noun phrases or both, and that independent clauses also have a distinctive clause-final afterthought position with an intonation break for adding information about a referent. It further distinguishes verbal, copular, and verbless clauses in Yakkha, with verbless clauses reflecting copular meaning without an overt copula.

text: Yakkha has a flat clause structure; there is no evidence for a unit like the verb phrase (verb and arguments). The unmarked constituent order is head-final in phrases and sov in clauses, with increasingly rhematic status towards the end of the clause. Focal information is often put in pre-verbal position (see ). Noun phrases are optional (see ), and clauses where all arguments are represented by noun phrases are rather rare. In complex clauses, the main clause is mostly in final position (see ). Yakkha is both head- and dependent-marking on the clausal level, since it has both case marking of arguments and verbal person indexing. . . ilen paŋdaŋba=ga u-niʔma mas-a-by-a-masa one _day landlord =gen 3sg.poss- money lose -pst-V2.give-pst-pst.prf[3] One day, the landlord's money got lost. . aniŋ=ga liŋkha=ga uhile utpatti mamliŋ=be leks-a=na=bu 1pl.excl=gen a _clan =gen long _ago origin Mamling =loc happen -pst=nmlz.sg=rep Our Linkha clan's origin, long ago, was in Mamling, they say. 11 _nrr _01.002 . tabaŋ hetne tas-wa-ga=na male _in-law where arrive- npst-2=nmlz.sg Where will (your) husband arrive? . .mund-y-uks-u-ga=na=i? forget -compl-prf-3.P-2=nmlz.sg=q Did you forget it? .tek whap-se khe-me-ŋ=na clothes wash -sup go -npst-1sg=nmlz.sg I go to wash clothes. sov is the default constituent order, but a fronted P argument is possible when it is more topical than the A argument, as in . Such examples are best rendered by English passive constructions. When the object position is filled by embedded direct speech, the preferred order is the one with the object preceding the A argument, as shown in . . . hoʈʌl=beʔ=ya cameŋwa cica=ci=ŋa m-bupt-wa=ha hotel =loc=nmlz.nsg food fly =nsg=erg 3pl.A- surround -npst[3.P]=nmlz.nsg The food in the hotel is surrounded by flies. 01 _leg _07.053 .ka, ka khaʔla ŋana=ba uŋ=ŋa lu-ks-u-ci 1sg 1sg like _this cop.1sg=emph 3sg=erg tell -prf-3.P-3nsgP I, I am just like this; it (the bird) told them (the other birds). 21 _nrr _04.006 Initial constituents often carry topic markers like =chen (a loan, from Nepali cāhĩ) or =ko. In , these particles mark contrastive topics. . .eŋ=ga=chen nna man=na 1pl.incl=gen=top that cop.neg=nmlz.sg We do not have that (custom). 29 _cvs _05.165 .kham=go m-bi-me=ha soil =top 3pl.A- give -npst=nmlz.nsg As for soil, they offer it (throwing it into the grave). In contrast to water, as one interlocutor had claimed before. 29 _cvs _05.159 In copular clauses the topic (referential or locational) naturally precedes the complement, which can be adjectival, nominal or locative (see ). Copulas in affirmative clauses are not obligatory. There are different copulas for equational/ascriptive and existential/locative complements. The details are discussed in cop. . .nhaŋ, henca-khuba=chen yakkha om and _then win -nmlz=top of _Yakkha _affiliation cop The winner is/will be Yakkha. (from a story where two groups fight about whether they are Yakkha or not) 39 _nrr _08.17 . haku camyoŋba nak-ma=na ʈhaun ma-n now food ask -inf=nmlz.sg place cop.neg-neg Now there is nowhere to ask for food. 14 _nrr _02.10 .u-yum=be waiʔ=na 3sg.poss- side =loc exist [3]=nmlz.sg It is next to it.
summary: Yakkha has a flat clause structure with no evidence for a separate verb phrase, and its default order is head-final in phrases and SOV in clauses, with the most rhematic information toward the end. The language is both head- and dependent-marking at the clausal level, using case marking on arguments and verbal person indexing, while noun phrases are optional and clauses with all arguments expressed as NPs are uncommon. Fronting is possible, especially for topical or contrastive material, and in copular clauses the topic typically precedes the complement, with different copulas used for equational/ascriptive versus existential/locative meanings.

text: Yakkha distinguishes declarative, imperative, hortative, and various types of interrogative and exclamative clauses. Independent declarative clauses either have a verbal or a copular predicate, as many examples in simp-cl1 and simp-cl2 have shown. Among the clauses with a verbal predicate, the declarative and interrogative clauses have to be specified for tense. There is one emphatic particle =pa (originating in a nominalizer) which is found in declarative, hortative and imperative clauses, but never in questions (see ). The exclamative force can be amplified by attaching the exclamative particle =ʔlo to =pa. The resulting unit expressing both emphasis and exclamative force is an independent word as far as stress is concerned, but the voicing rule still applies (see ). . .ɖuŋga=go ka-i-wa=ba, kaniŋ=go boat =top say -1pl-npst=emph 1pl=top We just say ɖuŋga , we. (speaker puzzled about not finding a Yakkha word for boat and having to use the Nepali word instead) 13 _cvs _02.006 .men=ba! cop.neg[3]=emph Of course not! .yo, nhe pi-haks-a-masa baʔlo! across here give -V2.send-pst-pst.prf[1.P] emph.excla (My father) over there had sent me here (in marriage), man! 06 _cvs _01.016 Much more frequent on declarative as well as on interrogative clauses are the clitics =na and =ha, originating from clausal nominalizations, a common development in Tibeto-Burman languages (and beyond). They are never found on hortatives, optatives or imperatives. Their function is hard to pin down by one neat term, but “assertive force” may give the reader an idea of their function. They occur more frequently than the emphatic =ba. They are discussed at length in Chapter ch-nmlz. Declaratives (and imperatives) can also be emphasized by another marker =i, as shown in . . .ca-i-ŋ=na=i eat -compl-1sg=nmlz.sg=emph I finished eating. 36 _cvs _06.241 .ab-a-ga=i! come -imp-2=emph Come! Other clause-final markers that have already been mentioned are the mirative and the reportative marker, the latter is frequently found in reported speech and in passed-down narratives, and in all other contexts where the speaker wants to free himself of the responsibility for the content of the utterance.
summary: Yakkha has distinct declarative, imperative, hortative, interrogative, and exclamative clause types. Independent declaratives may have verbal or copular predicates, and verbal declaratives and interrogatives must be marked for tense; several clause-final particles and clitics express emphasis or assertive force, including =pa, =na, =ha, and =i, while =ʔlo can be added to =pa to intensify exclamative force. The passage also notes that mirative and reportative markers occur clause-finally, with the reportative especially common in reported speech and narratives.

text: Hortative clauses are uttered when the speaker wants to urge or encourage someone to do something together. There is no dedicated hortative marker, the verb just appears in the main clause subjunctiveThere are two subjunctives in Yakkha: the main clause subjunctive and the dependent clause subjunctive, the latter being identical to the past inflection in most person configurations, cf. Chapter verbalmorph. first person dual or plural inflection and without any tense/aspect specification. shows an intransitive example, shows a transitive example with an additional particle au. It may occur in hortatives and imperatives, lending force to the request or order. The constituent order is like in declarative clauses, presuming overt arguments are there at all. In general, the subjunctive just expresses vagueness about some future event. If it is used with first person singular or with exclusive inflection, it becomes a permissive question, with the typical intonation contour of high pitch at the end of the clause (see ). With second or third person, the subjunctive can be rendered with you might [...] or he might [...] , and can express warnings (see ), threats and statements about possibilities in general. . .cuŋ-i, kaks-i wrestle -1pl[sbjv] make _fall -1pl[sbjv] Let us wrestle, let us fight! 39 _nrr _08.15 . a-na, a-ma=ŋa py-a=ha yaŋ=ŋa limlim inca-c-u, au? 1sg.poss- sister 1sg.poss- mother =erg give -pst[1.P]=nmlz.nsg money =ins sweets buy -du-3.P[sbjv] insist Sister, let us buy sweets with the money that mother gave us, shall we? 01 _leg _07.042 . . ka kheʔ-ŋa, au? 1sg go -1sg[sbjv] insist I am off, allright? .kaks-i-khe-i-gaǃ fall -pl-V2.go-pl-2[sbjv] You (plural) might fall downǃ .lem-nhaŋ-nen? throw -V2.send-1>2[sbjv] Shall I throw you out? The above-mentioned emphatic particle =pa in combination with hortatives is shown in . . .lamdhaŋ=ca khond-u-m=ba, aniŋ=ga ya=ca hond-u-m=ba field =add dig -3.P-1pl.A=emph 1pl.excl=gen mouth =add open -3.P-1pl.A=emph Let us dig our fields and also open our mouths. The exclusive is used here because the researcher was present during the song (a spontaneous song about the endangerment of the Yakkha language, and an encouragement for the hearers to speak the language), even though the people addressed are of the singer's group. It might also be due to the unnatural recording situation that the singer was not sure whom to address with her song. In later recordings, speakers vary as to whether they use the inclusive or the exclusive forms when the fieldworker is present, which can partly be attributed to including her and partly to ignoring her or forgetting about her presence. 07 _sng _01.14 .haku khe-ci=ba now go -du=emph Now let us (dual) goǃ The optative expresses the wish of the speaker for something to happen that is beyond his immediate control. It is constructed with subjunctive forms to which the marker -ni is added . Optative forms can also be found in purposive adverbial clauses (rendered by in order to [...] ). Verbal negation is possible in these forms as well. Full paradigms can be found in mood. . .siŋ pu-ni tree grow [3sg]-opt May the tree grow. .miʔ-ŋa-ni think -1sg.P-opt May he remember me.
summary:
Hortative clauses in Yakkha are used to urge or encourage joint action, and they are formed without a special hortative marker: the verb simply appears in the main-clause subjunctive, with normal declarative word order. The subjunctive in general expresses vagueness about a future event; with first-person singular or exclusive forms it can function as a permissive question, while with second- or third-person forms it can express warnings, threats, or possibilities, and an additional particle *au* may intensify hortative or imperative force.  

The optative is formed by adding *-ni* to subjunctive forms and expresses the speaker’s wish for something outside immediate control; it also appears in purposive clauses and can be negated.

text: Imperatives are uttered to make the addressee do something. Prohibitives are used to prevent the addressee from doing something. The imperative marker is -a,Often deleted as a strategy to avoid vowel hiatus. identical to the past marker, but the person inflection at least partly differs from declaratives, so that most forms are distinct from their past counterparts. Imperatives have a colloquial register and a polite register . The polite forms have an additional marker -eba, which has probably developed from the emphatic particles =i and =pa. They are used for elders, guests and other respected people. This is the only instance of grammaticalized politeness forms in the Tumok dialect of Yakkha.In Dandagaun village, people make politeness distinctions also in declaratives and questions. They use a calqued form from Nepali, which is discussed in honorific. . .hani ket-u! quickly bring _up -3.P[imp] Bring it up quickly! .naʔtorok naʔtorok ket-u-eba! a _bit _further _up a _bit _further _up bring _up -3.P[imp]-pol.imp Bring it a bit further up, please! Formally, prohibitives are negated imperatives (see mood for the morphology). The examples in contrast imperatives with prohibitives in the colloquial register. . .khy-a! go -imp Go! .ŋ-khy-a-n! neg- go -imp-neg Do not go! .kisa ab-a-n-u-m! deer shoot -imp-pl-3.P-2pl.A Shoot (plural) the deer! .maksa ŋ-ab-a-n-u-m-nin! bear neg- shoot -imp-pl-3.P-2pl.A-neg Do not (plural) shoot the bear! Arguments can be expressed overtly in imperatives, including S and A arguments. They are not calls or vocatives, since they are not set apart by an intonational break, and since vocatives may precede them, as in . If the person addressed by the imperative of a transitive verb is referred to by a noun and not by a pronoun, it will be marked by the ergative. . .lu, lu, mamu, nda=ca phat-a-ŋ init init girl 2sg=add help -imp-1sg.P Come on, come on girl, help me too! 07 _sng _01.01 .ka um-me-ŋ, nniŋda lakt-a-ni, nhaŋ kaniŋ ikhiŋ lakt-iʔ-wa 1sg enter -npst-1sg 2pl dance -imp-pl and _then 1pl how _much dance -1pl-npst I will enter (the basket), you (plural) dance. And how much we will dance! 14 _nrr _02.29 Occasionally, one finds the second person marker combined with the emphatic marker =i attached to the imperative, which increases the insistence of the request or command. This marker is also found on declarative clauses. . .mendhwak ghororo sa-ga=i! goat forcefully pull _with _rope [imp]-2=emph Pull the goat forcefully! .ab-a-ga=i! come _across -imp-2=emph Come here!
summary:
Imperatives in Yakkha are used to induce the addressee to act, while prohibitives are negated imperatives used to stop the addressee from acting. The imperative marker is -a, and polite imperatives add -eba, a form used for elders and other respected people; this is the only grammaticalized politeness system in the Tumok dialect, though Dandagaun also shows politeness distinctions in declaratives and questions through a Nepali-calqued form.  

Imperatives can overtly express arguments, including subject and agent, and transitive imperative subjects marked by nouns take ergative case. The text also notes that an emphatic =i may attach to imperatives to increase insistence.

text: Polar questions obligatorily host the clause-final clitics =na and =ha if they contain a verb,It is misleading, however, to perceive these clitics as markers of polar questions, because they occur in other clause types as well. and a particle i that is found both phonologically bound and unbound. When it occurs unbound, it carries its own stress and has an initial glottal stop prothesized (not written in the orthography), as all vowel-initial words have (see ). The conditions for the alternation between bound and unbound are not clear yet. The word order is the same as in declaratives. Polar questions are typically answered by repeating the (verbal or nonverbal) predicate (see ), or by one of the interjections om yes , and menna or manna for no (identificational and existential/locational, respectively).On a sociolinguistic side note, when meeting someone familiar (or calling on the phone, nowadays), one often asks whether the interlocutor has already eaten rice or drunken tea, depending on the time of day. . .nda yakkhama mekan=na=i? 2sg Yakkha _woman cop.2sg.neg=nmlz.sg=q Aren't you a Yakkha woman? 36 _cvs _06.547 .nda lak-ma miʔ-me-ka=na=i? 2sg dance -inf think -npst-2=nmlz.sg=q Do you want to dance? .ka i? 1sg q You mean me? .men=na=i, khaʔla so-nhaŋ-se i? neg.cop=nmlz.sg=emph like _this watch -V2.send-sup q In order to watch them (as they leave)? 36 _cvs _06.489 . .yakthu=i? enough =q Did you have enough? .yakthu enough. I had enough. In conversations, one often hears tag questions like mennai? isn't it? . They request a confirmation from the interlocutor that the propositional content of the preceding utterance is true (see examples in ). Sometimes they may just convey uncertainty on behalf of the speaker, since in , from a pear story, the interlocutor is not supposed to know about the content. . . to thaŋ-a-ŋ-ci-ŋ, men=na=i? up climb -pst-excl-du-excl cop.neg=nmlz.sg=q We climbed up, didn't we? 36 _cvs _06.267 . pi-uks-u, men=na=i? give -prf-3.P[pst] cop.neg=nmlz.sg=q She gave it to her, didn't she? 36 _cvs _06.381 . nhaŋ=ŋa khaʔla lukt-a-sy-a-ci, men=na=i? and _then =ins like _this collide -pst-mddl-pst-du cop.neg=nmlz.sg=q And then they collided like this, didn't they? 34 _pea _04.025
summary:
Polar questions in this language obligatorily take clause-final clitics =na and =ha if they contain a verb, but these are not exclusive markers of polar questions because they also occur in other clause types. The language also uses a particle i, which can appear either bound or unbound; when unbound it carries its own stress and an initial glottal stop, though the conditions for this alternation are still unclear.

Word order in polar questions is the same as in declaratives, and they are usually answered by repeating the predicate or by the interjections om for yes and menna/manna for no. The passage also notes the frequent use of tag questions like mennai?, which ask for confirmation of the preceding statement and can sometimes express the speaker’s uncertainty.

text: Disjunctive questions consist of two juxtapposed alternative scenarios, both marked by the alternation marker =em . If it attaches to a word that ends in /a/ or /e/, the first vowel gets deleted, e.g. /nhaŋ=le=em/ or afterwards is pronounced [nhaŋlem]. This marker is not only found in interrogative clauses. Occasionally, it also attaches to hypothetical clauses, not following the template of two juxtaposed alternatives, but rather expressing uncertainty (see ). Although the verb in this clause is marked for nonpast, and hence is in realis mood, the marker =em weakens the realis interpretation of this utterance, and thus it is best rendered with a subjunctive in the English translation. . .nniŋda yakkha om=em, men=em? 2pl of _Yakkha _affiliation cop=alt cop.neg=alt Are you (plural) Yakkha or not? 39 _nrr _08.10 .khumdu=em ŋ-khumd-in=em? tasty =alt neg- tasty -neg=alt Is it tasty or not? .nda i=ya=ca men-gap-khuba luʔ-ni-me-ŋ=n=em. 2sg what =nmlz.nsg=add neg- carry -nmlz tell -compl-npst-1sg.P=nmlz.sg=alt He might tell me: You have nothing. 36 _cvs _06.349
summary: Disjunctive questions consist of two juxtaposed alternatives, both marked with the alternation marker =em, which may cause deletion of a preceding final /a/ or /e/. Although it is mainly used in interrogative clauses, =em can also appear in hypothetical clauses to express uncertainty; in these cases it weakens the realis force of the verb, making a subjunctive-like English translation more appropriate.

text: Content questions contain one of the interrogative pro-forms introduced in interr. Question words remain in situ (see ), even in adverbial clauses such as and embedded clauses such as . The embedded clause in reflects direct speech (see the imperative and the person marking). Question words or phrases are often marked by the focus marker =le. In declaratives, it marks contrastive information, and it is also often found in mirative contexts. In questions, it implies that the speaker is particularly clueless and very eager to get the answer. . . ŋ=ga paŋ heʔne om? 2sg.poss=gen house where cop Where do you live? 01 _leg _07.160 .heʔna ceʔya yok-se ta-ya=na which matter search -sup come [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg Which language did she come to search for? . ka ina=le khut-a-ŋ ly-a-ŋ-ga=na? 1sg what .sg=ctr bring -imp-1sg.P tell -pst-1sg.P-2.A=nmlz.sg What did you tell me to bring (you)? The somewhat unusual verb form khutaŋ bring me! is found here because structurally, this is embedded direct speech. There is an interjection issaŋ that can be provided as an answer when the person asked does not know the answer either. It has a rising intonation contour just like questions, and means as much as I do not know or no idea , but often contains the subtext How am I supposed to know? , and is thus very similar in usage to the Nepali interjection khoi. It can be used as an answer to any question type. More information on the discourse-structural particles touched upon in this chapter can be found in Chapter particles.
summary:
Content questions use interrogative pro-forms that stay in situ, including in adverbial and embedded clauses. Question words or phrases are often marked with the focus marker =le, which in questions signals that the speaker is especially unsure and eager for an answer, while in declaratives it marks contrastive or mirative information.

The passage also notes that some embedded questions reflect direct speech, as shown by imperative and person-marking forms. An interjection issaŋ can be used as a response when the speaker does not know the answer, with rising intonation and a meaning like “I don’t know” or “no idea.”

text: Strictly speaking, exclamative clauses are not a distinct clause type because their formal structure is identical to interrogative clauses. They always contain the interrogative quantifier ikhiŋ (or its nominalized forms ikhiŋna/ikhiŋha) which is used to inquire about the size, amount or degree of nominal, verbal and adjectival concepts. Functionally, exclamations can be defined as declaratives with high expressive value, containing some extreme and especially remarkable information Koenig2007_Speech . Although they are questions syntactically, their falling intonation differs from that of questions, which have a rising intonation towards the end of the clause. . . ikhiŋ ucun, hen=na din=be tub-i=ha! how _much nice today =nmlz.sg day =loc meet -1pl=nmlz.nsg How nice (that) we met today! 10 _sng _03.003 .ka ikhiŋ pe-me-ŋ=na! 1sg how _much fly -npst-1sg=nmlz.sg How much (how high) I will flyǃ 21 _nrr _04.032 .ikhiŋ chippakekeʔ=na takabaŋǃ how _much disgusting =nmlz.sg spider What a disgusting spiderǃ
summary: Exclamative clauses are not treated as a separate clause type because they have the same formal structure as interrogative clauses and always contain the interrogative quantifier *ikhiŋ* (or its nominalized forms). Although they are syntactically questions, they function as highly expressive declaratives and are marked by falling intonation rather than the rising intonation typical of questions.

text: The syntax of the agreement in Yakkha and Tibeto-Burman in general is much more flexible than in Indo-European languages. As noted earlier by Bickel2000On-the-syntax, the purely identificational agreement that is known from Indo-Aryan is accompanied by associative (appositional and partitive) agreement types. In appositional agreement, the noun phrase that corresponds to the agreement marker is semantically an apposition to the antecedent of that marker, but syntactically it is the argument. In the clauses in the person value of the arguments is only revealed by the verbal person marking. The corresponding nouns provide additional information about the referent, while they are the arguments syntactically. We know that the ergative case is not overtly marked on arguments that are represented by first and second person pronouns. It is overtly marked on nouns with first or second person reference (see ), which shows that the differential agent marking is determined by a combination of person features and word class. . . mamu heʔne khe-i-g=ha girl where go [pst]-2pl-2=nmlz.nsg Where did you girls go? . kamnibak sori yuŋ-i=hoŋ uŋ-u-m friend together sit -1pl[pst]=seq drink -3.P-1pl.A[sbjv] Having sat down together, let us friends drink. . a-koŋma=ŋa=le ta-ga=na raecha 1sg.poss- aunt =erg=ctr bring [pst]-2.A[3.P]=nmlz.sg mir You, auntie, really brought her (the second wife)! 06 _cvs _01.042 .phu=na yapmi pham=na yapmi leks-a-ŋ=na white =nmlz.sg person red =nmlz.sg person become -pst-1sg=nmlz.sg I, the white person, turned red. The second type is partitive agreement, shown in . Here, the verbal person marking refers to a group of potential referents, while the noun phrase refers to the subset of actual referents. The verb here shows nonsingular number marking, although the referent of the A argument has singular number. With pronouns like who and none it is not always easy to determine the semantic number. In Yakkha, however, if one inquires about the identity of more than one person, one generally uses the nonsingular marker isa=ci. In this referential mismatch extends from an embedded clause into the main clause, as it is found on both the matrix verb kama say and the verb in the embedded speech khuma steal . The sentence is paraphrasable with But none of them said: we stole the money , although it is clear from the question pronoun (and from how the story proceeds) isa who that the purpose of the clause is to single out one referent. . . nniŋda sum-baŋ=be isa=ŋa yaŋ khus-uks-u-m-ga? 2pl three -clf.hum=loc who =erg money steal [pst]-prf-3.P-2pl.A-2 Who of you three stole the money? . khaʔniŋgo isa=ŋa=ca khus-u-m-ŋa=ha ŋ-ga-ya-ma-nin but who =erg=add steal [pst]-3.P-1pl.A-excl=nmlz.nc 3pl.A- say -pst-prf-pl.neg But none of them said: I stole the money. 04 _leg _03.018 .isa=ja n-nis-u-nin=na who =add neg- see -3.P[pst]-neg.pl=nmlz.sg None of them had seen her. 22 _nrr _05.071
summary:
The passage says that agreement in Yakkha and Tibeto-Burman is more flexible than in Indo-European languages and includes not only identificational agreement but also associative types such as appositional and partitive agreement. In appositional agreement, the noun phrase matching the agreement marker is an apposition semantically but functions as the syntactic argument, while partitive agreement involves verbal person marking that refers to a larger potential set even when the noun phrase denotes only a subset of actual referents.

It also notes that ergative marking is omitted on first- and second-person pronouns but overtly expressed on nouns with first- or second-person reference, showing that differential agent marking depends on both person and word class. Several examples illustrate referential mismatch between verb agreement and noun phrase meaning, including cases where nonsingular verbal marking appears with semantically singular referents and can extend across embedded and matrix clauses.

text: In Sino-Tibetan languages one commonly finds a pattern of syntactic nominalizations that participate in various constructions, creating noun phrases, nominal modifiers and relative clauses, but also nominalized embedded clauses, and independent main clauses. This convergence of functions has been referred to as the Standard Sino-Tibetan Nominalization (sstn) pattern Bickel1999Nominalization and has been widely studied Matisoff1972Lahu, DeLancey1989Relativization, Genetti1992Semantic, Genettietal2008_Nominalization, Saxena1992_Finite, Ebert1994The-structure, DeLancey1999Relativization, Bickel1999Nominalization, Watters2002A-grammar, Noonan2008_Nominalization, Doornenbal2008_Nominalization. DeLancey2011_Finite has even proposed nominalization as the major driving force for syntactic change in Tibeto-Burman. The nominalization processes found in Yakkha fit well into the broader Sino-Tibetan pattern, extending far beyond the derivation of lexical nouns. Their functions cover (a) the derivation of nouns, (b) the construction of relative clauses, adjectives and other adnominal modifiers, and (c) a function beyond reference: they may occur on finite embedded complement clauses, in auxiliary constructions, and in independent main clauses. The nominalization of main clauses serves discourse-structural purposes, as will be shown in nmlz-uni-3 below. Yakkha has three sets of nominalizers, one set for lexical nominalizations (marked by -pa and -ma, treated in nmlz-pa), and two for mainly syntactic nominalizations, namely the subject nominalizers -khuba and -khuma (treated in nmlz-khuba) and the universal nominalizers =na and =ha (see nmlz-uni). correlative briefly deals with correlative clause constructions.
summary: The passage explains that Sino-Tibetan languages commonly use syntactic nominalization in a wide range of constructions, including noun phrases, modifiers, relative clauses, embedded clauses, and even independent main clauses. It argues that Yakkha follows this broader pattern, with nominalizers used not only for deriving nouns but also for relative clauses and other clause types, and it distinguishes three nominalizer sets: lexical -pa/-ma, subject nominalizers -khuba/-khuma, and universal =na/=ha.

text: The first set contains the suffixes -pa -ba -wa and -ma, of which -pa (and its allomorphs) can be traced back at least to Proto-Bodic; it is found with nominalizing and related functions in Tibetan, Sherpa, Tamangic languages and other Kiranti languages DeLancey2002_Relativization, DeLancey2011_Finite, Genetti1992Semantic. In Yakkha, this set is used solely for lexical nominalizations, with -pa and its allomorphs for generic and male reference, while -ma is generally reserved for female reference (related to an old system of gender marking). Some exceptions where both -pa and -ma have generic reference were found, too. These nominalizers are mostly found in occupational titles, in names of mythical beings and gods, in zoological terms, in names for kinds of food and in kinship terminology (cf. appendix). Some examples are provided in table-pa . As this table shows, many of the forms are not transparent; their base or part of it does not occur independently. A few adjectives and adverbs were found with -pa, too, such as ulippa old and tamba slowly , but this is not the typical derivational pattern for adjectives or adverbs in Yakkha; the suffixes -pa and -ma are not productive in Yakkha. table [h] center tabular lll lexeme & gloss & bases kucuma& dog & – kiba & tiger & – hibumba& dung beetle &dung-roll-nmlz cikciŋwa& wasp & – caleppa& bread &eat-fry-nmlz miksrumba& blind person &eye-[ stem ]-nmlz cagaŋba& grain dish (Nep. ɖheɖo)&eat–[ stem ]-nmlz maŋgaŋba& ritual specialist &god-[ stem ]-nmlz camyoŋba& food &eat-[ stem ]-nmlz wariŋba& tomato & – khibrumba& fog, cloud & – tabular Lexical nominalizations with -pa and -ma center table
summary:
The suffix set -pa, -ba, -wa, and -ma is an old nominalizing system, with -pa traceable to Proto-Bodic and attested in Tibetan, Sherpa, Tamangic, and other Kiranti languages. In Yakkha, these suffixes occur only in lexical nominalizations: -pa/allomorphs generally mark generic or male reference, while -ma is usually used for female reference, though some forms show generic use for both.

These nominalizers are mainly found in occupational titles, mythological and divine names, zoological terms, food terms, and kinship vocabulary. Many forms are not transparent because their bases do not occur independently, and the suffixes are not productive in Yakkha, with only a few non-typical uses on adjectives or adverbs.

text: The default form of this nominalizer is -khuba, but -khuma is found occasionally with female reference. This marker derives nominals that may either modify a head noun (see ) or function as noun phrases themselves (see and (c)). Morphologically, it is an affix; it always attaches directly to the verbal stem. Syntactically, it has the whole phrase in its scope. . . heko=ha=ci mok-khuba babu other =nmlz.nsg=nsg beat -nmlz boy the boy who beats the others . heko=ha=ci mok-khuba other =nmlz.nsg=nsg beat -nmlz someone who beats others . mok-khuba beat -nmlz beater These nominals may be long and internally complex, as shown by the examples in . This makes -khuba different, for instance, from the English nomina agentis in -er. . . eŋ=ga yakkhaba=ga kha ceʔya yok-khuba Helihaŋ 1pl.incl.poss=gen Yakkha _person =gen this language search -nmlz Helihang Helihang, who searches for this language of us Yakkha 18 _nrr _03.032 . samundra=ga u-yum=be inca-khuba ocean =gen 3sg.poss -side =loc play -nmlz someone (who is) playing on the shores of the ocean 13 _cvs _02.057 In a relative clause structure, the constituent order is usually head-final, but postposed relative clauses are possible as well. Impressionistically, restrictive relative clauses (those that narrow down the reference of a head noun out of a set of possible referents) tend to occur preposed, while appositional relative clauses (those that add descriptive information about a noun) tend to occur postposed. . .eko yapmi kisa si-khuba one person deer kill-nmlz a man killing/having killed a deer . babu sem-khuba boy pluck-nmlz the boy who is plucking If the nominalization results in a noun, it may head NPs and host all nominal morphology: case, number and possessive prefixes. The examples in serve to illustrate that the resulting nominals can be modified or quantified just as simple nouns can. . .kha cyabruŋ-lak-khuba=ci these drum-dance -nmlz=nsg these drum-dancers 25 _tra _01.071 .jammai kam cok-khuba=ci all work do -nmlz=nsg all the workers 25 _tra _01.098 As the nominalizer attaches directly to the verbal stem, there is no tam marking on the verb, and the tam interpretation is retrieved from the context. The verb may host the negation marker men-, which is also found on other nonfinite verbal forms such as converbs and infinitives (see ). Another verbal property is illustrated in : the noun in -khuba may still be modified by adverbs. However, it is not clear yet whether nominal and verbal properties could occur simultaneously, e.g. in a phrase like jammai ʈhwaŋ namkhubaci all the awfully stinking ones . . . kaniŋ=nuŋ men-doŋ-khuba nwak 1pl=com neg -agree- nmlz bird the bird that does not belong to us/that is different from us 21 _nrr _04.004 . makhurna waghui loʔa ʈhwaŋ nam-khuba black chicken _droppings like [smelling] awfully smell- nmlz something black, smelling awfully, like chicken droppings 42 _leg _10.017 Complement-taking verbs with embedded infinitives can be in the scope of the nominalizer as well, as shows. The infinitive hiŋma support is embedded into yama be able to X . .hiŋ-ma ya-khuba babu=be kheʔ-ma support -inf be _able -nmlz boy =loc go -inf[deont] You have to marry a man who can support you. 28 _cvs _04.112 The constituents of the relativized clause can also be focussed on by means of the additive focus marker (see ), and they can be emphasized, as in , with ŋkhiŋ that much . . . sa=maʔniŋ=ca leŋ-khuba meat=without =add be _alright -nmlz someone who is fine even without (eating) meat .yapmi=ci=nuŋ=ca ŋkhiŋ sala me-leŋ-khuba=ci people =nsg=com=add that _much matter neg -exchange- nmlz=nsg They were of the kind that does not talk that much with people, too. 22 _nrr _05.046 A few lexicalized nominalizations with -khuba and -khuma can be found, too: khuncakhuba thief (steal-eat-nmlz), thukkhuba tailor (sew-nmlz), hiŋ -khuba husband , hiŋ -khuma wife (support-nmlz), yaben-pekkhuba diviner (sign-divine-nmlz). Note the parallelism of -khuba referring to generic/male nouns and -khuma referring to female nouns, as in the lexical nominalizations discussed in nmlz-pa. This suggests that -khuba and-khuma are historically complex.The syllable khu is also found in the reciprocal marker -khusa.
summary:
The nominalizer’s default form is **-khuba**, with **-khuma** appearing occasionally for female reference. It attaches directly to the verbal stem and can form nominals that either modify a noun like relative clauses or function as full noun phrases, taking nominal morphology such as case, number, and possessive prefixes; these forms can also be quite complex internally, including embedded infinitives, negation, adverbs, and focus marking.

In relative clause structures, the usual order is head-final, though postposed clauses also occur, with restrictive clauses tending to be preposed and appositional ones postposed. The passage also notes a small set of lexicalized nominalizations and suggests that the contrast between **-khuba** and **-khuma** may reflect an older gender distinction, since similar **khu** material appears in the reciprocal marker **-khusa**.

text: Descriptions of other Kiranti languages call equivalent constructions nomen agentis or active/agentive participle Tolsma1999A-grammar, Rutgers1998Yamphu, Ebert1997A-grammar, Ebert1999Nonfinite, Doornenbal2009A-grammar. One should note, however, that the nominalization may apply to verbs of any semantics, and the resulting nouns do not just refer to typical agents (see Bickel2004Hidden for the same point on closely related Belhare). Subjects of stative verbs like namma smell, emit odour , haŋma have spicy sensation or tukma be ill can also be the targets of this nominalization. The resulting nominal always refers to the S in intransitive verbs, and to the A for all transitive verbs (two-argument and three-argument), but never to any lower argument. This is illustrated by : S and A arguments are possible results of the nominalization, while P arguments are not (see ). Nominalizing morphology that indicates a grammatical relation is common in Kiranti languages, and it is also known e.g. from Dolakha Newari and from Kham (see Genetti1992Semantic , Ebert1999Nonfinite ). . .paip pek-khuba babu pipe break- nmlz boy the boy who broke/breaks the water pipe (A) . leŋ-khuba tabhaŋ become -nmlz son-in-law the prospective son-in-law (S) .*babu=ŋa pek-khuba paip boy =erg break- nmlz pipe Intended: the pipe that was/will be broken by the boy (*P) Non-canonically marked S and A arguments, e.g. possessive experiencers or locative marked possessors undergoing the nominalization have the same status as standard S and A arguments (i.e., in the ergative or nominative case and being indexed on the verb). In , the experiencer S argument is coded as possessor of the sensation, literally translatable as someone whose laziness comes up . In , the semantic relation expressed is possession, but it is coded with an existential construction and a combination of genitive and locative marking on the A argument. . . o-pomma kek-khuba yapmi 3sg.poss -lazyness come _up- nmlz person a lazy guy .kai=ga=be wa-ya, wa-khuba=ŋa me-wa-khuba m-bi-n-ci-nin some =gen=loc exist [3sg]-pst exist- nmlz=erg neg -exist- nmlz 3pl.A -give [pst]-c-3nsg.P-neg Some (people) had (food), and those who had (food) did not give it to those who did not have it. 14 _nrr _02.012
summary: The passage explains that in several Kiranti languages, nominalizations traditionally described as “agentive” can apply to verbs of any meaning, including stative verbs, and the resulting noun refers not just to typical agents but specifically to the S of intransitives and the A of transitives. It never refers to lower arguments such as P, and this grammatical-relation marking is also found when S or A are non-canonically marked, such as experiencer or possessive arguments.

subsection: Predicative use of the nominalized forms
text: Some examples even point towards a predicative use of the nominalized forms, as opposed to the expected referential use shown in the examples above. As we will see in nmlz-uni below, this function of -khuba is similar to what is found for the nominalizers =na and =ha. Shown below is a prime example to illustrate the function of nominalization as a discourse-structural device in Yakkha (see ). It is from a written narrative. The narrator remembers a fight with his brother. Both boys want to let out the chicks from the cage, and in the course of the fight, they accidentally kill them by squeezing them with the cage door. The nominalization is employed to yield a vivid narrative style, at a point where the event line approaches its climax, i.e., the accidental killing of the chicks. The verb of saying has to be set back against the content of the embedded direct speech, which contains the crucial information for what happens next. The fact that the nominalized form kakhuba the one who says occurs before the embedded direct speech supports this explanation. In the typical structure, the finite verb of saying would be the last element in the sentence. But as focal elements tend to come sentence-finally, and as the embedded speech here contains the focal information, the constituent structure is reversed. On a further note, the embedded speech itself contains a nominalizer =ha. This nominalizer has quite the opposite function here: it serves to put emphasis on the claim uttered by the boys (cf. nmlz-uni-3 below). The example nicely illustrates how nominalizers are employed to carve out a text by means of backgrounding and foregrounding chunks of information. .ka ka-khuba ka hon-wa-ŋ-ci-ŋ=ha!, a-phu ka-khuba ka hon-wa-ŋ-ci-ŋ=ha! 1sg say-nmlz 1sg open-npst-c-3nsg.P-1sg.A=nmlz.nsg, 1sg.poss- eB say-nmlz 1sg open-npst-c-3nsg.P-1sg.A=nmlz.nsg I said: “I will let them out!”, and my elder brother said: “I will let them out!” 40 _leg _08.065 Example is from a narrative account of what happened at a festival. The sentence describes some young men who feel ashamed of what they had done the night before when they were drunk. As such, the sentence which is nominalized by -khuba is rather like a comment, set apart from the main event line. . nhaŋ koi-koi sulemwalem leŋ-khe-khuba and _then some-some with _hanging _heads become-V2.go-nmlz And some of them hung their heads. 37 _nrr _07.074
summary: The passage argues that nominalized forms in Yakkha, especially -khuba, can have a predicative rather than referential function and can serve as discourse-structural devices. In narrative, nominalization helps create vividness by backgrounding some material and foregrounding key information, as shown in examples where nominalized speech and comments are set off from the main event line.

text: The nominalizers =na and =ha =ya have a wide range of functions. They are clitics, attaching to the rightmost element of a phrase, whether this is an inflected verb, a stem (of any word class), a case-marked phrase or a clause. The resulting nominal may fill the structural position of a nominal head, an adnominal modifier (adjectives, participles, relative clauses), a complement clause, or a finite, independent main clause. Nominalized main clauses have several and, at first sight, contradictory discourse functions. nmlz-uni-1 is concerned with uses of this nominalization in adnominal modification, while nmlz-uni-2 deals with complementation. nmlz-uni-3 discusses main clause nominalization. The markers =na and =ha =ya indicate singular and nonsingular number, respectively, shown in . The marker =ha also refers to non-countables, substances and more abstract concepts (see ). Example illustrates the same point with the interrogative root i. The interrogative root i is the base for many interrogative words. In isolation, it may be used to ask about states-of-affairs, as in i leksa? What happened? . The nominalizers turn the interrogative root into a pronoun, in order to inquire about a particular referent. This number distinction in nominalization is also found in Athpare and in Belhare, both also from the Greater Yakkha branch of Eastern Kiranti ( Ebert1997A-grammar , Bickel1999Nominalization ). . . pham=na wariŋba red =nmlz.sg tomato red tomato . pham=ha wariŋba=ci red =nmlz.nsg tomato =nsg red tomatoes . onek=ha ceʔya joking =nmlz.nc matter jokes . . i=na what =nmlz.sg what (presupposing one item) . i=ha what =nmlz.nsg/nc what (presupposing many items or mass reference) It should be emphasized for the following discussion that the traditional sense of the term nominalizer is too narrow with regard to Yakkha and in Sino-Tibetan nominalization in general (hence Bickel's (1999) term Standard Sino-Tibetan Nominalization). The markers =na and =ha do not regularly derive nouns, although one occasionally finds lexicalized expressions, such as chemha liquor (be transparent-nmlz), tumna senior (ripen-nmlz), pakna junior (be raw-nmlz), haŋha hot spice (taste hot-nmlz), bhenikna morning ritual (morning-nmlz). Rather, they turn any material into referential expressions, behaving identically or very much like noun phrases, either with or without a head noun. Etymologically, the nominalizers are related to a set of demonstratives: na this , kha these (see dem-pron). These demonstratives have exactly the same distribution with regard to number and mass/abstract reference as the nominalizers (compare examples and with ). . .na sambakhi this potato this potato . kha sambakhi=ci these potatoes=nsg these potatoes . kha kham this soil this soil . kha ceʔya this matter this matter/language So far, not many restrictions on the inflectional properties of the nominalized or relativized verb phrases could be detected. The only restriction is that certain clausal moods which are expressed by verbal inflection (optative, imperative) cannot be fed into the nominalization process. As far as person and tense/aspect marking is concerned, anything is possible. Example shows a verb inflected for the progressive. The nominalization may also apply recursively (see ). . .lop pok-ma-si-me=ha yaŋli now rise- inf-aux.prog-npst[3sg]=nmlz.nsg sprout the sprouts that are shooting now . heʔ=na=beʔ=ya=ci? which =nmlz.sg=loc=nmlz.nsg=nsg [The people] from which place?
summary:
The nominalizers =na and =ha =ya are clitics that attach to the rightmost element of a phrase and can nominalize verbs, stems, case-marked phrases, or whole clauses. The resulting forms may function as nominal heads, modifiers, complement clauses, or even independent main clauses; =na marks singular and =ha =ya nonsingular, with =ha also used for non-countable or abstract reference.  

The passage emphasizes that these markers do not primarily derive lexical nouns but instead create referential expressions much like noun phrases, and their behavior is linked historically to demonstratives with the same number/mass distinctions. The only notable grammatical restriction is that optative and imperative moods cannot be nominalized, while other person and tense/aspect forms can, and nominalization can even apply recursively.

text: The nominalizers are frequently found as relativizers. In contrast to the nominalizer -khuba, =na and =ha are almost unresticted with respect to grammatical relations. Core participants as well as non-core participants can serve as a relativization site for =na and =ha. The only thematic relation that has not been found is A, as A arguments get nominalized by -khuba.There is no direct negative evidence, unfortunately, but in the whole corpus of recorded language data (roughly 13.000 words), not a single instance of A arguments nominalized by =na or =ha was detected, neither did I hear it in conversations or elicitations. Thus, even if nominalization or relativization over A was possible, it would be a rather marked structure. In this respect, Yakkha is radically different from its neighbors, where the corresponding markers are unconstrained with respect to grammatical relations Ebert1997A-grammar, Bickel1999Nominalization. Relativizations on S arguments do occur, but they are much rarer than relativizations on objects or other kinds of participants, since this grammatical relation is also covered by the marker -khuba. The examples in show relativizations on core arguments. . .ci=ha maŋcwa be _cold =nmlz.nsg water cold water (S) .nda nis-u-ga=na chem 2sg[erg] know-3.P[pst]-2=nmlz.sg song a song that you know (P) . chemha yukt-u=na mamu liquor put _for-3.P[pst]=nmlz.sg girl the girl that was served liquor (G) . beula=ŋa khut-u=ha tephen groom=erg bring-3.P[pst]=nmlz.nsg clothes the clothes brought by the groom (T) 25 _tra _01.054 Some relativizations of objects have lexicalized into adjectives. Example is from the canonical transitive class. Example is originally from the class of transimpersonal verbs (cf. Chapter verb-val). In this class, the sole argument is expressed as the object of a morphologically transitive verb, and the verb shows default third person A marking, i.e. zero. An A cannot be expressed with transimpersonal predicates. . .a-na mi cend-u=na sa-ya=na 1sg.poss- eZ a _little wake _up-3.P=nmlz.sg cop.pst-pst[3sg]=nmlz.sg My elder sister was rather witty. 40 _leg _08.057 . ikhiŋ yeŋd-u=na yapmi lai! how _much be _tough-3.P=nmlz.sg person excla What a tough person! The relativization of non-core participants such as locations, temporal expressions or comitatives is illustrated by .Regarding (c), the question with whom one may eat is fundamental in the highly stratified Hindu society. subsubsection: Headless and internally headed relative clauses
text: Besides the adnominal modification, one often encounters headless relative clauses, i.e., noun phrases that lack a head noun (see ). The relative clause takes the structural position that would otherwise be filled by the head noun. . nhaŋ sapthakt-wa-c-u=na ibilag-ibilag khus-het-i-ya-ma-c-u=na and _then like -npst-du-3.P=nmlz.sg secretly- redup steal -V2.carry.off-compl-pst-prf-du-3.P=nmlz.sg And they (dual) secretly stole one (girl) whom they liked. 22 _nrr _05.064 The reference of the head noun is retrieved from the context, but there is a syntactic constraint, too. As A arguments may not undergo this kind of relativization, headless relative clauses are always interpreted as referring to the object of a transitive verb (see ) or as the sole argument of an intransitive verb (see ). As the S and the P arguments are treated identically, this is a case of ergative alignment in syntax. . .nna tas-wa=na=be yog-a-ca-n-u-m, nna=be that reach [3sg.A]-npst[3.P]=nmlz.sg=loc search -imp-du.A[imp]-3pl.P-3.P-2pl.A that =loc Look for it where it lands, in that (place). 22 _nrr _05.090 . nda cekt-a-ga=na ŋ-kheps-u-ŋa-n=na 2sg[nom ] speak-pst-2=nmlz.sg neg -hear-3.P[pst]-1sg.A-neg=nmlz.sg I did not hear what you said. (presupposing one word was said) In contrast to the almost unconstrained adnominal modification, headless relative clauses referring to non-core participants were not found. The absence of the head noun would make their interpretation rather difficult. For instance, leaving out din day from a clause like in is not possible. .na mamu=ŋa nna luŋkhwak khet-u=na *(din) i leks-a-ma=na baŋniŋ ... this girl=erg that stone carry _off-3.P[pst]=nmlz.sg *(day) what happen -pst [3sg] -prf=nmlz.sg about ... As for what happened on the day when the girl carried off that stone, ... 38 _nrr _07.042 While headless relative clauses show properties of noun phrases, such as number and case marking and the possibility of being referred to anaphorically by demonstratives (see nna in ), they do not have noun properties: there is no evidence for possessive prefixes attaching to the headless relative clause. Furthermore, the argument marking inside the headless relative clause remains as in simple clauses. There are, for instance, no genitives on core arguments, as e.g. in the English clause His talking annoyed me. A marginally occurring type of relative clause are internally headed relative clauses (called “circumnominal” in Lehmann1984Der-Relativsatz ). Internally headed relative clauses are relative clauses whose head noun is not extracted but remains in the same structural position as it would be in a main clause. This type has been reported for other Tibeto-Burman languages, too; see e.g. Bickel2005On-the-typological and Bickel1999Nominalization for closely related Belhare, DeLancey1999Relativization for Tibetan, and Coupe2007_Mongsen for Mongsen Ao. In Yakkha, this type is rather marginal. All examples are elicited, and natural data would be necessary for a better understanding of this structure. An example is shown in . The main verb tumma find can only take nominal, but not clausal complements. Thus one cannot, for instance, add the complementizer bhoŋ to the embedded verb, or interpret it as I found out that a man was killed by a tiger . The object can only be the noun yapmi person , so that the surrounding material must be a relative clause. .kiba=ŋa eko yapmi sis-u=na tups-u-ŋ=na tiger=erg one person kill-3.P[pst]=nmlz.sg find-3.P[pst]-1sg.A=nmlz.sg I found a man who was killed by a tiger. The ergative alignment found for headless relative clauses is also found for internally headed relative clauses. Relativizing over an A argument is ungrammatical and instead, a relative clause marked by -khuba was offered in the elicitation (see ). Example also resulted from the attempt to elicit a transitive clause relativizing over an A argument. The transitive verb was changed to an imperfective structure which, by means of an intransitively inflected auxiliary, is also (morphologically) intransitive. This suggests that the ergativity is the result of a morphosyntactic, not a semantic constraint. An A, at least in the third person, would carry an ergative marker, which would clash with the object properties that the noun has with respect to the main clause. On the other hand, the ergativity is not surprising anyway, as relativization by =na and =ha generally does not allow A arguments as head nouns. The difference to the more common head-final structure lies only in the exclusion of non-core participants such as locations or comitatives. . . eko yapmi kiba si-khuba tups-u-ŋ=na one person tiger kill-nmlz find-3.P[pst]-1sg.A=nmlz.sg I found a man who killed a tiger. (A: -khuba) . eko yapmi syau sem-ma-sy-a=na tups-u-o-ŋ=na one person apple pluck-inf-aux.prog-pst[3sg]=nmlz.sg find-3.P[pst]-V2.leave-1sg.A=nmlz.sg I found (and passed) a man who was plucking apples. (S) An ambiguity with finite complement clauses further complicates the analysis of headless relative clauses. All of the potential instances of internally headed relativization found in my corpus could also be complements of verbs of perception or cognition. As nothing is extracted in internally headed relativization, the constituent structure of the relative clause is identical to simple clauses, and one cannot distinguish structurally between I heard the one who was talking and I heard that someone talked . Both clauses refer to identical situations in the real world; one cannot hear that someone talks without actually hearing the person talking. One structural criterion to find out whether the embedded clause is a complement or a relative clause could be agreement. Example is from a narrative, while is made up in analogy, but with different number features. As the argument tori ( mustard , a mass noun) triggers =ha on the main verb oʔma be visible and eko phuŋ one flower triggers =na, one could infer that they are arguments of the main verb, rather than taking the whole clause to be the argument. However, one could as well interpret this behavior as long distance agreement out of a finite complement clause, which would not be surprising in Yakkha complementation (see Chapter compl). Hence, the question of how to distinguish internally headed relative clauses and complement clauses cannot be answered satisfactorily, at least not with perception verbs that allow both clausal and nominal complements. . . saptakosi=ga u-lap=pe tori phet-a=ha=ca ot-a=ha=bu, nna=bhaŋ a _river _confluence =gen 3sg.poss -side =loc
summary:
The passage describes headless relative clauses in Yakkha as noun phrases without an overt head noun, where the relative clause occupies the head position and the referent is recovered from context. These clauses behave like noun phrases in number, case, and anaphoric reference, but not like nouns, and they show an ergative pattern in which relativization over A arguments is ungrammatical while S and P arguments can be relativized.

It also notes that headless relatives referring to non-core participants were not found, and that internally headed relative clauses are rare and mostly elicited. These internally headed clauses preserve the head noun in its original position, but they share the same ergative restriction on A arguments and are difficult to distinguish from finite complement clauses of perception or cognition verbs.
