It also notes that constituents inside adverbial clauses can generally be focused, and that emphatic markers and constituent focus are more often found in inflected adverbial clauses, such as conditional and sequential clauses, than in converbal clauses.

text: In addition to conditional finite relations, clauses marked by bhoŋ may also express purposes, intentions, cognitive reasons and goals, or states of mind in general (see Bickel1993Belhare for a similar observation in Belhare). Purpose clauses frequently have optative finite forms, as if they were a direct quote from the subject of the main clause (see and ). Example , however, shows that the purpose clause can also take the perspective of the speaker. Purpose clauses may also be marked for indicative mood (see ), or have deontic finite forms (see ). The formal similarity between purposive and speech or thought representation structures (see utterance-pred) can be explained by the etymological origin of the marker bhoŋ. It is assumed that, as in Belhare Bickel1993Belhare, it developed from a combination of the reportative marker =pu and the sequential marker hoŋ.Bickel1993Belhare mentions the contracted form [muŋ] in Belhare, combined of the quotative marker mu (an allomorph of -bu -phu, which is cognate with Yakkha =pu), and the ablative/sequential marker huŋ (cognate to Yakkha =hoŋ). Since the reportative marker =pu is a clitic and gets voiced after vowels, this also explains why bhoŋ has a voiced initial despite being an independent word with regard to stress. . .nam phen-ni bhoŋ, nam=bhaŋ leŋ-ma=na; wasik ta-ni bhoŋ wasik=phaŋ luŋkhwak leŋ-ma=na. sun shine [3sg;sbjv]-opt purp sun =abl turn -inf[deont]=nmlz.sg rain come [3sg;sbjv]-opt purp rain =abl stone turn -inf[deont]=nmlz.sg In order for the sun to shine, it (the stone) has to be turned away from the sun. In order for the rain to come, the stone has to be turned away from the rain. 37 _nrr _07.116--7 .yaks-u-ni bhoŋ lept-u-ris-u-ŋ=na strike -3.P-opt cond throw -3.P-V2.place-3.P[pst]-1sg.A=nmlz.sg I threw it at him, so that it would hit him. .ap-ŋa-ni bhoŋ ka-ya-ŋ=na come -1sg-opt purp call -pst-1sg=nmlz.sg He called me, so that I would come. Purpose clauses have the same internal structure as complement clauses, but they function differently in that they adverbially modify the main clause, and hence are optional, whereas complement clauses function as obligatory arguments, without which the main clause would be incomplete. In , the purpose clause contains quoted speech, which is evident from the use of variables such as the speech-act participant pronoun nniŋda and the deictic adverb nhe. The conjunction bhoŋ in is ambiguous between a purpose marker and a quotative marker. Parellel structures with a purely quotative function of bhoŋ can also be found (see , translated with are in Nepali). . . nniŋda nhe wa-ma n-dokt-wa-m-ga-n=ha bhoŋ ikt-haks-a-ma-c-u-ci 2pl[erg] here live -inf neg- get _to _do -npst-2pl.A[3.P]-2-neg=nmlz.nsg purp chase- V2.send-pst-prf-du-3.P-3nsg.P You will not get the chance to live hereǃ, (they [dual] said) and chased them away. OR They chased them away, so that they would not get the opportunity to live there. 22 _nrr _05.012--3 . haku miyaŋ ŋkha yabenpekhuwa=ci=le soʔ-meʔ-ma=ci=em bhoŋ yabenpekhuwa=ci=ja n-soʔ-met-uks-u-ci now a _little those healer =nsg=ctr look -caus-inf[deont]=nsg=alt quot healer =nsg=add 3pl.A- look -caus-prf-3.P-3nsg.P Now we better show the matter to those healers; (they said) and they also showed it to the healers. 22 _nrr _05.072 Finally, clauses marked by bhoŋ are also found with main verbs such as soʔma look , kuma wait and yokma search , illustrated in . The activity in the main clause is done not in order to achieve whatever is expressed in the purpose clause, but with the goal to acquire knowledge or to achieve a state of mind about the proposition in the purpose clause. These clauses always contain indirect speech or questions (see also for another example of indirect speech). The perspective is anchored in the speaker and the speech situation, not in the subject of the clause. In , if the perspective of the subject had been taken, the verb tayamacuha should have been tayamacugha how much have you brought . . .paŋ=be a-ma=ŋa ikhiŋ ta-ya-ma-c-u=ha bhoŋ khesup so=niŋa house =loc 1sg.poss- mother =erg how _much bring -pst-prf-du-3.P=nmlz.nc purp bag look -[3.P;pst]=ctmp At home, when mother looked into the bag to see how much we had brought, ... 40 _leg _08.025 .m-ba=ŋa nasa ta-wa-ci=ha bhoŋ ku-ma=ŋa ku-ma=ŋa! 2sg.poss- father =erg fish bring -npst-3nsg.P=nmlz.nsg purp wait -inf[deont]=erg.cl wait -inf[deont]=erg.cl Because I have to wait and wait for your father to bring the fish! 01 _leg _07.205 . kucuma heʔne waiʔ=na bhoŋ yok-ma-si-me-ŋ=na dog where exist [npst;3sg]=nmlz.sg purp search -inf-aux.prog-npst-1sg=nmlz.sg I am looking for the dog (where the dog is). . jal hetne het-u=na bhoŋ hoŋma=ga u-lap-ulap lukt-a-ma net where get _stuck -3.P=nmlz.sg rep/purp river =gen 3sg.poss -wing 3sg.poss -wing run [3sg]-pst-prf He ran along the river bank (in order to see) where the net got stuck. 01 _leg _07.216
summary:
Clauses marked by **bhoŋ** can express not only conditionals but also purposes, intentions, cognitive reasons, goals, and other states of mind. Purpose clauses often use optative forms and may resemble quoted speech, though they can also appear with indicative or deontic forms; the marker is argued to come historically from a combination of reportative and sequential markers.

Purpose clauses have the same internal structure as complement clauses but differ in function because they adverbially modify the main clause and are optional. The passage also shows that bhoŋ can be ambiguous between purposive and quotative uses, and that with verbs like ‘look,’ ‘wait,’ and ‘search,’ it can express a speaker-anchored goal of gaining knowledge or a mental state rather than the subject’s purpose.

section: Sequential clause linkage and narrative clause-chaining in =hoŋ
text: The sequential marker =hoŋ indicates that the dependent clause event and the main clause event take place in a temporal sequence. This clause linkage marker is attached to the inflected verb (without =na or =ha) or to an infinitival form (see e.g. example camahong). Sequential clauses can be in the indicative or in the subjunctive. There is no constraint on the corefence of arguments, but the S/A arguments are shared in 60.8 % of the occurrences in the corpus (see ). Center-embedding is attested only marginally (2.0 % of 307 sequential clauses), shown in and (b). Center-embedding can be attested semantically or via the case marking of the arguments. In , the dual pronoun belongs to the last two verbs, while the sequential clause with tupma meet has plural reference. In , the subject is in the unmarked nominative that can only come from the intransitive main verb, and hence the transitive sequential clause must be center-embedded. Since overt arguments are rare, one cannot always assess the variable of center-embeddedness in the data. As and have already shown, the sequential clause may also entail a consecutive reading; is another example illustrating this. . .nam lom-me=hoŋ phoʈo khic-a cog-u-m. sun come _out -npst[3sg]=seq photo press -nativ do -3.P-1pl.A[sbjv] Let us take photos when the sun comes out. . nam=ŋa heco=hoŋ, liŋkha sarap pi=na. sun =erg win [pst;3.P]=seq Linkha spell give [pst;3.P]=nmlz.sg As the sun had won, it put a spell on the Linkha man. 11 _nrr _01.020 .nna tiʔwa=go majhya paghyam=ŋa napt-het-a-ŋ=hoŋ kobeŋ-kobeŋ lam-a-khy-a, ... that pheasant =top a _title old _man =erg snatch -V2.carry.off-pst-1sg.P=seq continously- redup walk [3sg]-pst-V2.go-pst That old Majhya snatched the pheasant from me and left quickly, ... 40 _leg _08.037 . mela=be [...] suku=ŋa u-ppa u-ma=ci=ca mund-y-uks-u-ci=hoŋ phaps-a-khy-a-ma. fair =loc [...] Suku =erg 3sg.poss- father 3sg.poss- mother =nsg=add forget -compl-prf-3.P-3nsg.P=seq entangle [3sg]-pst-V2.pst-pst-prf In the fun fair [...], Suku forgot her parents and got lost. 01 _leg _07.152 . . kanciŋ to tub-i=hoŋ uks-a-ŋ-ci-ŋ=hoŋ yo tas-a-ŋ-c-u-ŋ=ba. 1du up meet -1pl[pst]=seq come _down- pst-excl-du-excl=seq over _there arrive -pst-excl-du-3.P-excl=emph ‘After we (plural) had met, we (dual) went down and then we (dual) arrived over there.’ 36 _cvs _06.395 . paghyam=ca piccha nis-uks-u=hoŋ cond-a-sy-a-ma. old _man= add child see -prf-3.P=seq be _happy [3sg]-pst-mddl-pst-prf ‘The old man was happy, too, when he saw the child.’ 01 _leg _07.296 . chippakekek nis-u-ŋ=hoŋ yamyam ca-ŋ=ha disgusting see -3.P[pst]-1sg.A=seq [eating]hesitantly eat [pst]-1sg.A=nmlz.nc It smelled awfully, and so I ate hesitantly. Deriving from its sequential semantics, a secondary function can be observed as well: clauses marked by =hoŋ can also express chains of coordinated events in narratives, a function comparable to the narrative converb Nedjalkov1995Some. Some examples are shown in . The clause-initial conjunction nhaŋ(a) has a very similar function, and is historically derived from a demonstrative and the sequential marker. As shows, =hoŋ is not restricted to verbal hosts. It may attach to adverbs, nouns and demonstratives in non-verbal clauses (i.e. to predicates of copular clauses).The marker can, not function as a nominal coordinator. Nouns are coordinated by the comitative marker =nuŋ, though. . . nhaŋ ŋ-und-wa-ci=hoŋ pheri, haiko=na=be ŋ-khe-me=ha=ci. and _then 3pl.A- pull -npst-3nsg.P=seq again other =nmlz.sg=loc 3pl- go -npst=nmlz.nsg=nsg They go a bit further and then they pull them (the fish) out. 13 _cvs _02.13 . nhaŋ hattabatta lukt-ab-a=hoŋ muccok=hoŋ paŋ=be ta-ya, nhaŋa paŋ=be=hoŋ pheri lukt-ab-a=hoŋ sidhak end-a-bhy-a-ŋ=ba. and _then hastily run -V2.come-pst[3sg]=seq lifting _lightly =seq house =loc come -pst[3sg] , and _then house =loc=seq again run -V2.come-pst[3sg]=seq medicine apply -pst-V2.give-pst-1sg.P=emph Then, he came running quickly, he lifted me up, and came to the house, and then, as (we were) in the house, he came running again and applied medicine (on my wounds). 13 _cvs _02.053--54 . ka=ca om mit-a-ŋ=hoŋ n-sy-a=ha wa=ci solok ta-ŋ-ci-ŋ 1sg=add yes think -pst-1sg=seq 3pl- die -pst=nmlz.nsg chicken= nsg immediately bring [pst]-1sg.A-3nsg.P-1sg.A ‘I agreed and quickly brought the dead chicken.’ 40 _leg _08.072 The scopeof negation is less restricted than in the converbal clauses. It may reach over the whole sentence, or be restricted to the main clause. The first possibility is shown in , with the focus of the negation attracted by the sequential clause. Pure main clause scope can be found in sentences like . . .cama ca-ma=hoŋ sidhak men-ja-ma, ondaŋ=se ca-ma food eat -inf=seq medicine neg- eat inf[deont] before= restr eat -inf[deont] ‘You don’t have to take this medicine after eating, but before.’ . hiʔwa u-yin ind-wa=ci=hoŋ na u-yin=go m-beŋ-me-n air 3sg.poss- egg lay- npst=3nsgP=seq this 3sg.poss- egg= top neg- break -npst[3sg]-neg ‘After he has laid his eggs in the air, this egg does not break.’ 21 _nrr _04.040 For illocutionary operators all configurations are possible, and some sentences are even ambiguous, as . In addition, coordinative scope can be found, with the illocutionary force applying to each subclause separately (see the second reading of , and ).Coordinative scope has proven to be difficult to distinguish from overall scope in most cases, and was thus disregarded for the classification of clause linkage types here. Note that for the coordinative reading in imperatives the verb of the clause marked with =hoŋ has to be in subjunctive mood. The imperative lab-u=hoŋ is not possible in ). . . kamniwak sori yuŋ-i=hoŋ uŋ-u-m friend together sit -1pl=seq drink-3.P-1pl.A[sbjv] (We) friends having sat down together, let us drink. OR Let us friends sit down together and drink! .nda cattu=nuŋ lab-u-g=hoŋ tokhaʔla ky-a! 2sg firmly grab -3.P-2sg.A[sbjv]=seq upwards come _up -imp ‘Grab it firmly and come up!’ 01 _leg _07.329 An example of main clause scope is given in . Here, the first part of the sentence is uttered as a statement in surprise and it thus does not fall under the scope of the question in the main clause. In , though, the question word is part of the sequential clause, and the main clause is presupposed, as the question is not about whether the addressee survived, but how he was able to hold such a thin rope. . .sondu khaʔla=na cuŋ=be tek me-waʔ-le jal kapt-uks-u-g=hoŋ hetnaŋ ta-e-ka=na? Sondu like
summary: The sequential marker =hoŋ links a dependent clause to a main clause and indicates that the two events occur in temporal sequence. It attaches to an inflected verb or an infinitival form, can occur in indicative or subjunctive clauses, and does not require coreferent arguments, though shared S/A arguments are common and center-embedding is rare. The marker can also have secondary discourse functions, such as chaining narrated events, and it is not limited to verbs since it may attach to adverbs, nouns, and demonstratives in non-verbal clauses.

The coordinative reading of =hoŋ is also employed in a narrative strategy to build up continuity, known as tail-head linkage Ebert2003Equivalents . The previous clause, or just the verb, is repeated in a sequential clause, before adding new information in the main clause, as illustrated in . .ŋkhoŋ=ca a-chik ekt-a=na belak=ŋa esap-esap thaŋ-ma yas-a-ŋ. to thaŋ-a-by-a-ŋ=hoŋ khaʔla so-ŋ=niŋa=go eko maŋpha=na hoŋ nis-u-ŋ. afterwards =add 1sg.poss- anger make _break -pst=nmlz.sg time =ins swiftly-swiftly climb -inf be _able -pst-1sg up climb -pst-V2.give-pst-1sg=seq like _this look [pst]-1sg.A=ctmp=top one huge =nmlz.sg hole see [pst]-3.P-1sg.A Nevertheless, as I was so angry, that I managed to climb up. summary: The passage explains that sequential clauses can be focused as a whole, for example by the restrictive particle =se, as in a sentence meaning that someone will set off only after eating. It also shows that the coordinator-like use of =hoŋ is used in tail-head linkage, a narrative strategy where the previous clause or just the verb is repeated in a sequential clause before the main clause adds new information.

text: It is a crosslinguistically common pattern for concessive clauses to be constructed by means of an additive focus marker or a scalar operator Koenig1993_Focus . Yakkha employs this strategy, too, combining the sequential clause linkage marker =hoŋ (see above) with the additive focus marker =ca (see Chapter ptcl-additive), as shown in .Occasionally, the cotemporal clause linkage marker niŋ is found in concessive clauses, too. Concessive adverbial clauses indicate that the condition expressed in the adverbial clause is in contrast to the expected conditions, or that the condition is not relevant for the assertion to be true. As in the concessive is employed together with another converb (-saŋ), =hoŋ is proved to not have sequential semantics any more in concessive clauses. . . ropa lamdhaŋ=be cayoŋwa lin-ca-saŋ=hoŋ=ca cama=ŋa khot-u-co-nes-uks-u-ci paddy _field field =loc food plant -V2.eat-sim=seq=add food =erg be _enough -3.P-V2.eat-V2.lay-prf-3.P-3nsg.P Even though they ate what they planted in the field, the food was enough for them. 01 _leg _07.063 . marej end-a=hoŋ=ca khumdu sa pepper insert [3sg]-pst=seq=add tasty cop.pst[3] Even though pepper was added, it was tasty. . yok-ma=bu, cek-ma=i men-ni-ma=hoŋ=ca ceŋ-soʔ-ma=bu search -inf[deont]=rep speak -inf=emph neg- know -inf=seq=add speak -V2.look-inf[deont]=rep One has to search for it (the language). Even though one does not know it, one has to try and speak, she said. 07 _sng _01.11 In adv-cl-cond, speech-act conditionals have been introduced Thompsonetal2007_Adverbial. The same phenomenon is also found with concessive clauses. In , the speaker excuses himself for talking about sensitive topics despite the fact that women are present. .nhe, mamu wanne=hoŋ=ca, baru khaʔla cok-ma=na, nna, lakhe coŋ-siʔ-ma=na. here girl exist [3;npst]=seq=add instead like _this co -inf[deont]=nmlz.sg that castrated do -V2.prevent-inf[deont]=nmlz.sg Here - even though women are present - instead, one should do it like this, one should castrate them. 28 _cvs _04.228 Related to concessive clauses are exhaustive clauses. They contain a question word functioning as a pro-form that may stand for the greatest conceivable temporal extension in and for any conceivable location in . Such clauses can either be marked just by the additive focus marker, or by the concessive =hoŋca. . ikhiŋ kus-u=ca mima n-lond-a-ma-n how _much wait -3.P=add mouse neg- come _out -pst-prf-neg However much it waited, the mouse did not come out. 04 _leg _03.008 . heʔne khe-i-ga=hoŋ=ca [...] ka=ca hakt-a-ŋ au. where go -2pl-2=seq=add [...] 1sg=add send -imp-1sg.P insist Wherever you go, (...) send (a message) to me too. 01 _leg _07.276
summary: Yakkha forms concessive clauses by combining the sequential clause linker =hoŋ with the additive focus marker =ca, and sometimes uses the cotemporal linker niŋ as well. In these clauses, =hoŋ no longer has sequential meaning; instead, concessives express that the clause content contrasts with what is expected or is irrelevant to the truth of the main assertion. The passage also notes that related exhaustive clauses may be marked only by =ca or by =hoŋ=ca.

text: The marker =niŋ =niŋa combines clauses that refer to events that happen at the same time, but that do not necessarily have coreferential S or A arguments. The two forms occur in free variation; no phonological or functional motivation for the alternation could be found. The event in the main clause generally unfolds against the background provided by the adverbial clause, as e.g. in . Given its semantics, it is not surprising that the marker may host the topic particle =go (see ). The adverbial clause can be inflected for either one of the subjunctives (see mood), but also for different tenses in the indicative mood. Generic statements are in the infinitive, as in . As in the sequential construction, the S and A arguments do not have to be coreferential (see ), but in 37 % of the clauses they are. Center-embedding is as rare as in the sequential clause linkage pattern, but it is technically possible. . . uthamlaŋ uimalaŋ lam-ma=niŋa laŋ=ci n-sa-ma=ha=ci steeply _uphill steeply _downhill walk -inf=ctmp leg =nsg 3pl- become .pst-prf=nmlz.nsg=nsg While walking steeply uphill and downhill, the legs got stronger. .thawa=bhaŋ to ŋ-khy-ama=niŋ=go mamu nnhe=maŋ wet=na=bu ladder =abl up 3pl- go -prf=ctmp=top girl there =emph exist [3sg]=rep As they have gone up on the ladder, the girl is right there! 22 _nrr _05.111 The scope properties are similar to those of the sequential clauses. With regard to negation, overall and main clause scope are possible. Overall scope is shown in , and main clause scope in , which acquires a causal reading in addition to the basic cotemporal one. . .ta-ya-ŋ-ci-ŋ=niŋ cama n-ni-n=ha come -pst-excl-du-excl=ctmp food neg- cook [pst;3.P]-neg=nmlz.nsg ‘She wasn’t preparing food when we came.’ . pyak=ŋa m-phat-uks-u=niŋa, Tikule=ŋa i=ya=ca cokla cok-ma por-a n-jog-ama-n many= erg 3pl.A- help -prf-3.P=ctmp Tikule= erg what =nsg=add work do -inf must -nativ neg- do -prf[3sg]-neg ‘As so many helped him, Tikule did not have to do anything.’ 01 _leg _07.019
summary:
The marker =niŋ /=niŋa links clauses describing events that occur at the same time, even when the S or A arguments are not coreferential. The two forms are in free variation, and the adverbial clause can take subjunctive, indicative, or infinitival marking depending on the type of statement.  

This construction allows the topic particle =go, permits both overall and main-clause negation scope, and has scope properties similar to those of sequential clause linkage. Center-embedding is rare but possible, and about 37% of clauses show coreferential S and A arguments.

text: Counterfactual clauses are marked mostly by =niŋ for cotemporal clauses and occasionally by =hoŋ for sequential clauses. The adverbial clause can be infinitival or inflected for the subjunctive, and is often marked by the topic particle =ko (voiced [go] in intervocalic and postnasal position, see voicing). Furthermore, both the adverbial clause and the main clause host the irrealis marker =pi ([bi] due to the voicing rule). Clauses as in can only have a counterfactual reading (i.e. it is established knowledge at the time of speaking that the condition does not obtain); they cannot be understood hypothetically. The irrealis marker, however, also occurs in hypothetical statements. . . ka nis-u-ŋ=niŋ=bi ikhiŋ lu-ŋ=bi. 1sg[erg] know -3.P[sbjv]-1sg.A=ctmp=irr how _much tell -1sg.A[3.P;sbjv]=irr If I knew it, how much would I tellǃ . diana=ca piʔ-ma=hoŋ=go=bi cond-a-sy-a=bi=baǃ Diana =add give -inf=seq=top=irr be _happy -sbjv-mddl-sbjv[3sg]=irr=emph After giving them to Diana too, she would have been happy! 13 _cvs _02.075 . encho=maŋ jal lep-ma cind-a-ŋ-ga=niŋ=bi hen tuʔkhi n-ja-ya-ŋa-n loppi. long _ago =emph net throw -inf teach -pst-1sg.P-2.A=ctmp=irr today trouble neg- eat -sbjv-1sg-neg probably If we had gone, I would have sent it to you. 01 _leg _07.252 .nniŋ=ga ten a-sap n-thakt-u-n=niŋ=go=bi, ka n-da-ya-ŋa-n=bi. 2pl=gen village 1sg.poss-[stem] neg- like -3.P-neg=ctmp=top=irr 1sg neg- come -pst-1sg-neg=irr If I did not like your village, I would not have come here.
summary: Counterfactual clauses are usually marked by =niŋ for cotemporal clauses and sometimes by =hoŋ for sequential clauses, with the adverbial clause either infinitival or subjunctive and often marked by the topic particle =ko. Both the adverbial and main clauses take the irrealis marker =pi, but clauses of this type are interpreted only as counterfactual, not merely hypothetical, even though =pi also appears in hypothetical statements.

text: The clause linkage marker =lo does not figure prominently in the current corpus. It signals that a certain event takes place within the time span of another event, often interrupting it (see ), or having an effect contrary to the one expected (see ). The verb in the adverbial clause often includes the inceptive V2 -heks (see Chapter verb-verb), which signifies that the action has just begun and has not yet been not completed (see and ). With telic verbs, this implies that the event has not reached its end point yet . The marker is probably cognate with a comitative marker found e.g. in Belhare and Bantawa, which is also employed in clause linkage in Belhare Bickel1993Belhare, Doornenbal2009A-grammar. As the examples are limited for this kind of clause linkage, the description of this clause linkage strategy cannot go into further detail. . .a-ppa, eh, a-ppaǃ cekt-heks-a=lo swak wa-ya-by-ama 1sg.poss- father he 1sg.poss- father talk -V2.cut-pst=itp silent be -pst-V2.give-prf[3sg] He started calling: Father, hey, father!, when he suddenly fell silent. 01 _leg _07.179 .jal so-heks-u=lo mas-a-by-ama net watch -V2.cut-3.P=itp lose -pst-V2.give-prf[sbjv] As he was about to watch the net, it got lost. 01 _leg _07.217 .tokhaʔla khem-me, to khem-meʔ=lo pheri heko=na=ga u-cya leŋ-me. upwards go -npst[3sg] up go -npst[3sg]=itp again other =nmlz.sg=gen 3sg.poss- child become -npst[3sg] It flies up, and within the time it flies up, again this other one has a child (egg). 21 _nrr _04.046
summary: The marker =lo is a clause linkage device that is not frequent in the corpus; it indicates that one event occurs within the time span of another, often interrupting it or producing an unexpected opposite effect. In adverbial clauses, the verb often takes the inceptive V2 -heks, marking an action as just beginning and not yet completed, especially with telic verbs. The marker is probably cognate with a comitative marker found in languages such as Belhare and Bantawa.

text: This chapter deals with connectives on the text level. These are invariable particles that introduce grammatically independent sentences, but refer back to the content of the previous sentence (or sentences). These connectives are always sentence-initial. Some of them are also deictic temporal adverbs. They indicate relationships of temporal sequence, cotemporality, causality, or negativity. Many of these particles look as if they have been calqued upon Nepali connectives such as kinabhane because or tyaspachi afterwards, and then . Another possibility is that both languages follow a more general areal pattern. Other clause linkage markers occur clause-finally in Yakkha, as described in Chapters ch-nmlz, adv-cl and compl.
summary: The chapter describes sentence-initial, invariable connectives that link independent sentences by referring back to earlier discourse. These particles can express temporal sequence, simultaneity, causality, or negation, and some also function as deictic temporal adverbs. The text notes that their forms may reflect calquing from Nepali or a broader areal pattern, while other clause-linking markers in Yakkha appear clause-finally.

text: Sequential connectives have developed from demonstratives (na, kha, ŋkha) to which the sequential clause linkage marker =hoŋ has been added, exactly like the Nepali connective tyas-pachi. The following forms have been found, and are translatable with after this , after that , or more generally with and or and then : nhaŋ (na-hoŋ), khoŋ (kha-hoŋ) and ŋkhoŋ (ŋkha-hoŋ). It is likely that the form nnhaŋ exists, too, but as these forms are utterend sentence-initially and usually in very fast speech, such a distinction could not be established reliably. Examples are shown in and . The connective nhaŋ is by far the most frequent one, featuring 230 occurrences in the corpus (of 3012 clauses), while ŋkhoŋ is found only 17 times and khoŋ is found no more than 38 times. Occasionally, nhaŋ occurs as nhaŋŋa, marked by the instrumental marker in his function of indicating the time of an event. . .uŋ=ŋa pheri, lu, maiti=ci=be, ka haku bagdata=ca nakt-wa-ŋ-ci-ŋ=ha bhoŋ=cen eko ceʔya cekt-wa. khoŋ bagdata nak-se khe-meʔ=na. 3sg=erg again init natal _home =nsg=loc 1sg now marriage _finalization =add ask -npst-1sg.A-3nsg.P-1sg.A=nmlz.nsg compl=top one matter speak -npst[3A;3.P] and _then marriage _finalization ask -sup go [3]-npst=nmlz.sg She says: Well, now I will ask my parents for my bagdata, too. And she goes to ask for the bagdata. The bagdata ritual belongs to the marriage custom, see social. 26 _tra _02.011--2 .ah. ŋkhoŋ i n-jog-u=ha? yes and _then what 3pl- do -3.P[pst]=nmlz.nc Yes. And what did they do then? 20 _pea _02.011 . luŋkhwak hoŋ-ma pʌrne, nhaŋ khibak=ca ip-ni-ma pʌrne sa=bu. stone hole _out inf[deont] having _to and rope =add twist -compl-inf[deont] having _to cop.pst[3]=hsy He had to hole out a grinding stone, and he had to complete making a rope, too, it is said. 11 _nrr _01.007--8 The temporal ablative nhaŋto derived from the most frequent sequential connective nhaŋ. Its literal meaning is and then up . This connective is also found with complements (see postpos), referring to a point in time when an ongoing event has started. The event or activity does not necessarily have to go on at the time of speaking. The connective only signifies the initial boundary, as in English from then on . An example is provided in . . nhaŋto, garo n-cheŋd-et-wa=na, tokhaʔla from _then _on terace 3pl.A- mason -V2.carry.off-npst=nmlz.sg upwards From then on, they mason the terrace, upwards. 31 _mat _01.093
summary: Sequential connectives in this language developed from demonstratives plus the sequential clause-linkage marker =hoŋ, paralleling Nepali tyas-pachi. The forms nhaŋ, khoŋ, and ŋkhoŋ can mean “after this/that” or more generally “and/and then,” with nhaŋ by far the most frequent; a related temporal ablative, nhaŋto, comes from nhaŋ and means roughly “from then on,” marking the starting point of a time span.

text: The cotemporal connectives khaʔniŋ and ŋkhaʔniŋ nnakhaʔniŋ are constructed of deictic adverbs based on demonstratives and the cotemporal adverbial clause linkage marker, =niŋ (see ). .ŋkhaʔniŋ eko paŋ=ca m-ma-ya-n=niŋa tumhaŋ=ŋa paŋ cog-uks-u. that _time one house =add neg-cop-pst-neg=ctmp Tumhang =erg house make -prf-3.P At that time, when there was not even a single house, Tumhang built a house. 27 _nrr _06.038
summary: The cotemporal connectives *khaʔniŋ* and *ŋkhaʔniŋ nnakhaʔniŋ* are formed from deictic adverbs based on demonstratives plus the cotemporal clause-linking marker *=niŋ*. The example shows its use to mark a simultaneous time reference, meaning “at that time, when there was not even a single house, Tumhang built a house.”

text: Cotemporal connectives have developed into an adversative connective, indicating that the propositional content of the clause stands in contradiction or in contrast to some previous content, or that it restricts the previous information in some way. Their structure is transparent; they are cotemporal connectives marked by the standard topic marker =ko. In the speaker ponders about arranged marriages. The sentence, about a hypothetical groom, stands in contrast to an earlier (hypothetical) statement that he might leave a good impression or talk nicely. Example is self-explanatory. . .khaʔniŋgo imin=na, imin=na, i=na tha? but how =nmlz.sg how =nmlz.sg what =nmlz.sg information But how, how will he (a hypothetical husband) be, how to know? 36 _cvs _06.336 .kha liŋkha=ci=ŋa camyoŋba i=ya=go m-bi-ci, khaʔniŋ=go phophop=na sumphak, sumphak phophop n-jog-uks-u=hoŋ=se camyoŋba m-by-uks-u-ci these Linkha =nsg=erg food some =nmlz.nc=top 3pl.A- give -3ngs.P but upside _down =nmlz.sg leaf leaf upside _down 3pl.A- do -prf-3.P=seq=restr food 3pl.A- give -prf-3ngs.P These Linkhas gave them some food, but they gave it to them only after turning the leaf plates upside-down. 22 _nrr _05.047--8
summary: Cotemporal connectives have developed into adversative connectives that express contradiction, contrast, or restriction relative to prior information. They remain structurally transparent, since they are cotemporal connectives marked with the standard topic marker =ko. The examples show this use in contrasting a hypothetical groom’s behavior with earlier expectations, and in restricting a statement by specifying that food was given only after turning leaf plates upside-down.

text: The connective ijaŋbaŋniŋ because is used for causal clause linkage. It is constructed in parallel to the Nepali kina bhʌne, out of the interrogative word ijaŋ why and the textual topic marker baŋniŋ (see Chapter particles). An example is provided in . .ŋkhaʔniŋgo ka con-si-saŋ, ijaŋbaŋniŋ nna len=bhaŋto=maŋ ka heʔniŋ=ca chocholaplap n-jog-a-ŋa-n. but 1sg be _happy -mddl-sim because that day =temp.abl=emph 1sg when =add naughty neg- do -pst-1sg-neg But I was happy, because from that day on I never did mischievous things again. 42 _leg _10.053
summary: The connective **ijaŋbaŋniŋ** means **“because”** and is used to link causal clauses. It is formed in parallel with Nepali **kina bhʌne**, combining the interrogative **ijaŋ** “why” with the textual topic marker **baŋniŋ**.

text: The connective manhoŋ (also manoŋ, manuŋ) stands at the beginning of clauses that contain information about what happens when a previously mentioned condition has not been fulfilled, like English if not or otherwise (see ). It can be decomposed into the negated existential copula man and the sequential clause linkage marker =hoŋ. . .nhaŋ, henca-khuba=cen yakkha om, man=hoŋ, me-henca-khuba men=na. and _then win -nmlz=top Yakkha _person cop if _not neg- win -nmlz=top neg.cop[3]=nmlz.sg Then, the winner is Yakkha; otherwise, the loser, he is not. 39 _nrr _08.17 .ah, manhoŋ, adhi barkha khiŋ khoʔ-ni-me. yes if _not half year this _much be _enough -compl-npst[3sg] Otherwise (if the harvest is not enough), we can survive for as much as half a year. 28 _cvs _04.042
summary: The connective **manhoŋ** (also **manoŋ, manuŋ**) introduces clauses expressing what happens if a previously mentioned condition is not fulfilled, similar to English **“if not”** or **“otherwise.”** It is analyzable as the negated existential copula **man** plus the sequential clause marker **=hoŋ**.

text: Yakkha has a number of verbs that embed clausal complements. These com -ple -ment-taking verbs (ctps, cf. Noonan2007Complementation ) license several complement constructions, defined by the type of the embedded clause. The most salient formal distinction can be drawn between infinitival clauses and inflected clauses.I deliberately avoid the terms finite and nonfinite here, since finiteness is a problematic concept. The defining criteria are different across languages and across theoretical frameworks. In this case, finiteness would only be defined by the presence or absence of the verbal inflection, as inflected complement clauses are less finite than independent clauses. They lack many features such as clause-final marking for evidentiality or mirativity, certain mood inflections like the imperative, and detached positions. The infinitival clauses, on the other hand, are potentially equal to finite clauses in Yakkha: in one infinitival complement construction the main verb is optional (the deontic construction), so that the infinitive can present a full (deontic) predication (see obl). A typical infinitival complement construction is shown in . Inflected complement clauses show person, tense/aspect, mood inflection (indicative or subjunctive) and the nominalizing clitics =na or =ha (see , cf. nmlz-uni). In the case of embedded direct speech they may show any marking that is found on independent clauses as well, for instance the imperative (see ). . .ka kheʔ-ma mit-a-ŋ-na 1sg go -inf think -pst-1sg=nmlz.sg I want to go. .nda lam-me-ka=na mi-nuŋ-nen=na 2sg return -npst-2=nmlz.sg think -prf-1>2=nmlz.sg I thought that you will come back. .haku bagdata=ca py-a-ŋ-ni-ŋ bhoŋ eko binti bisa cog-wa-ci now finalization _of _marriage =add give -imp-1sg-pl-1sg comp one request request make -npst-3nsg.P “Now give me the bagdata, too!” she requests from them. The form pyaŋniŋ is more complex than expected from the Tumok data (see mood).The speaker's natal home is in Hombong village. 26 _tra _02.019 overview-all provides an overview of the complement-taking predicates of Yakkha. They are grouped according to the inflectional features of the embedded clauses and according to their semantics. Noonan2007Complementation lists the following semantic classes of complement-taking predicates: utterance predicates, propositional attitude predicates, pretence predicates, comment (factitive) predicates, predicates of knowledge or acquisition of knowledge, predicates of fearing, desiderative predicates, manipulative predicates, modal predicates, achievement predicates, phasal predicates and predicates of perception. In Yakkha, inflected complement clauses occur with utterance predicates, propositional attitude predicates and with predicates of perception. Infinitival complement clauses occur with a broader semantic range of ctps, as the Table shows. Most complement-taking verbs may also take nominal arguments, e.g. tokma, which can mean get something or get to do something . In addition to the complement-taking verbs, there are also some nouns that can embed clausal complements, such as ceʔya talk, matter or kisiʔma fear . table ! tabular p 6cm p 6cm infinitival complement & inflected complement 2 c Phasal tarokma begin & lepnima stop, abandon & tama be time to (lit. come )& 2 c Utterance Predicates & kama say &luʔma tell & chimma ask &yokmeʔma tell (about something) 2 c Propositional Attitude, Desiderative, Experiential miʔma like doing, want (lit. think )&miʔma think, hope, remember kaŋma give in, surrender (lit. fall ) &yemma emma agree (to propositions) poss-niŋsaŋ puŋma have enough, be fed up & consiʔma be happy about sukma intend, aim &kuma wait, expect leŋma be acceptable, be alright & poss-niŋwa wama hope kisiʔma be afraid &niŋwa hupma decide collectively 2 c Perception, Cognition, Knowledge nima know how to do & nima see/get to know muʔnima forget to do & muʔnima forget about something &khemma hear &eʔma have the impression that 2 c Modals yama be able & (copula/zero) have to & cokma try (lit. do )& 2 c Achievement tokma get to do (lit. get )& 2 c Pretence loʔwa cokma pretend & 2 c Permissive, Assistive (S-to-P ) piʔma allow (lit. give )& phaʔma help doing & cimma teach & soʔmeʔma show & tabular Overview of complement-taking predicates table Many complement constructions, especially those with infinitival complements, are characterized by the referential identity between an argument of the embedded clause and an argument of the matrix clause. This may be reflected by leaving an argument unexpressed in one clause (Equi-deletion). Traditionally, complement constructions with shared arguments are divided into raising and control constructions. Arguments can be shared with respect to morphological marking, agreement, or constituency properties, following Serdobolskaya's definition of raising Serdobolskaya2009_Raising . In control constructions, the shared argument belongs to both clauses semantically, whereas in raising constructions the shared argument belongs to the embedded clause semantically, despite being coded as argument of the main clause. Hence, in raising constructions an unraised alternative expressing the same propositional content is usually available, while in control constructions, there is only one option. The ctps taking infinitival complements are discussed in nonfin-comp, the verbs and nouns that take inflected complement clauses are dealt with in fin-comp.
summary:
Yakkha has many complement-taking predicates, and the main formal distinction is between infinitival and inflected complement clauses. Inflected complements show person, tense/aspect, mood, and nominalizing clitics, but are less clause-like than independent clauses; infinitival complements can in some cases express a full predication and occur with a wider range of verbs, while inflected complements are used especially with utterance, propositional attitude, and perception predicates.

The language also shows shared-argument complement constructions, where an argument of the embedded clause may be unexpressed because it is shared with the matrix clause. These are analyzed in terms of raising and control, with control involving semantic participation in both clauses and raising involving semantic membership in the embedded clause only.

text: In this section I discuss all constructions that follow the basic pattern of an infinitive followed by an inflected verb. I found 20 predicates that occur with embedded infinitives in Yakkha. Infinitival complement clauses are marked by the infinitive -ma to which, optionally, the genitive marker =ga may attach (see ). Other inflectional categories are not possible on these clauses. Apart from these basic features, the behavior of the various verbs that embed infinitives is far from homogenous, as will be shown below. . . ka kheʔ-ma(=ga) cog-a-ŋ=na 1sg go-inf(=gen) do-pst-1sg=nmlz.sg I tried to go. . kucuma=ŋa ka haʔ-ma(=ga) sukt-a-ŋ=na dog =erg 1sg bite -inf(=gen) aim[3sg.A]-pst-1sg.P=nmlz.sg The dog intended to bite me. The embedded infinitive depends on the main verb for all inflectional categories. One construction (expressing deontic modality) is exceptional in this respect, though (cf. obl). In this construction, the nonsingular marker =ci attaches to the infinitive when the object has third person nonsingular reference. The marker is aligned with the primary object (compare the intransitive example with transitive and ditransitive ). . . yapmi paŋ-paŋ=be nak-saŋ kheʔ-m=ha people house-house =loc ask- sim go- inf[deont]=nmlz.nsg The people have to go from house to house, asking (for food). (S) 14 _nrr _02.029 . thim-m=ha=ci scold- inf[deont]=nmlz.nsg=nsg They (the young people) have to be scolded. (P) . wa=ci piʔ-m=ha=ci chicken =nsg give- inf[deont]=nmlz.nsg=nsg It has to be given to the chicken. (G) The complement-taking verbs can be distinguished according to their valency and their argument realization. Some matrix verbs always have intransitive morphology, some always have transitive morphology, and some verbs assimilate to the valency of their embedded predicates. According to this, the agreement properties have the potential to differ. Yakkha infinitival complement constructions show long distance agreement (lda), i.e. the matrix verb shows agreement with an argument of the embedded clause. This is illustrated by example above: the constituent ka 1sg is the P argument of the embedded clause and triggers object agreement in the matrix verb sukma intend . lda is common for Kiranti languages; it has been described e.g. for Belhare Bickeletal2001Syntactic, Bickel2004Hidden and for Puma Schackow2008Clause. An overview of the infinitival complement types and their properties is provided in overview-infinitival below. In the following sections, these properties will be treated in detail. The case assignment has to be determined independently from the agreement properties. In the majority of the complement-taking verbs, the case assignment for the embedded arguments comes from the embedded verb. This means that in cases of shared reference it is not necessarily the embedded argument that is omitted, but rather the matrix argument (discussed below). Such structures are known as backward control, and received attention in the literature on control phenomena especially after an article on the Nakh-Dagestanian language Tsez by Polinskyetal2002_Backward. Thus, in several infinitival complement constructions the arguments show relations to both clauses simultaneously, so that the whole structure is better analyzed as monoclausal rather than as matrix clause and embedded clause.See Haspelmath1999Long-distance for a discussion on clause union in the Nakh-Dagestanian language Godoberi. This is the case when, for instance, case is assigned by the embedded verb, but agreement is triggered on the main verb.Yakkha also has a periphrastic imperfective construction that has developed from an infinitival complement construction, see tense. summary:
The passage describes Yakkha infinitival complement clauses, which are marked by the infinitive suffix -ma, optionally followed by the genitive =ga, and cannot take other inflectional categories. The language has 20 predicates that embed such infinitives, but these constructions vary in valency, argument realization, and agreement: in many cases the matrix verb shows long-distance agreement with an argument of the embedded clause, and case assignment is usually determined by the embedded verb.

It also notes that some constructions behave like backward control, where the shared argument may be omitted from the matrix clause rather than the embedded clause, so the structure can be analyzed as more clause-unified than biclausal. One deontic construction is exceptional because the nonsingular marker =ci attaches to the infinitive when the object is third person nonsingular.

text: Some complement-taking verbs assimilate in valency to the embedded verb. If the embedded verb is intransitive, the matrix verb shows intransitive agreement morphology; if the embedded verb is transitive, the matrix verb shows transitive agreement morphology. The verbs yama be able , miʔma like doing and cokma try belong to this class. The S/A arguments of embedded and matrix verb have to be coreferential. Sentences like I want him to go cannot be expressed by this construction. These predicates exhibit backward control. The S/A arguments are case-marked according to the properties of the embedded verb, i.e. nominative with intransitive verbs and ergative with transitive verbs. This indicates that the overtly realized arguments are those of the embedded verb. The verb yama is a modal verb, expressing abilities, as opposed to tokma, which expresses the possibility of an event as determined by other circumstances or participants. Example shows an intransitive complement clause. The respective transitive form nyaswaŋanna (supposing dummy object inflection of third person singular) would be ungrammatical here. Example and show transitive complement clauses. Both arguments trigger agreement in the matrix verb, and case is assigned by the embedded verb (notice the ergative in ). In , a three-argument verb from the double object class is embedded. The person inflection of the matrix verb is analogous to the inflection that is usually found in the embedded verb soʔmeʔma show , aligned with the primary object. . . ka nda=maʔniŋ hiŋ-ma n-ya-me-ŋa-n=na 1sg 2sg= without survive-inf neg- be _able-npst-1sg-neg=nmlz.sg I cannot survive without you. . ŋkha (...) them-ma n-yas-uks-u-n-ci-ni-n those (...) lift -inf neg- be _able -prf[pst]-3.P-neg-3nsg.P-3pl.A-neg They could not lift those (stones). 37 _nrr _07.029 .na mamu=ŋa luŋkhwak pok-ma n-yas-u-n this girl =erg stone wake _up -inf neg- be _able [3sg.A]-3.P[pst]-neg This girl was not able to wake up the stone. 37 _nrr _07.036 . ka nda a-den soʔ-meʔ-ma ya-meʔ-nen=na 1sg[erg] 2sg 1sg.poss -village show-inf be _able-npst-1>2=nmlz.sg I can show you my village. When yama is negated, occasionally an alternative infinitive marker -sa is found, as in . It is only attested with yama. .kanciŋ i=ca ka-sa y-yas-a-n-ci-ŋa-n 1du what =add say -inf neg- be _able -pst-neg-du-excl-neg We could not say anything. 40 _leg _08.027 Example and illustrate the same properties for the verbs miʔma want (lit.: think ) and cokma try (lit.: do ). . . paŋ=be ap-ma mit-a-ma-ŋ=na house =loc come-inf like-pst-prf-1sg=nmlz.sg I want to come home. (intransitive) 01 _leg _07.096 .suman=ŋa limlim inca-ma mit-uks-u Suman =erg sweets buy -inf like [3sg.A]-prf-3.P[pst] Suman wanted to buy sweets. (transitive) 01 _leg _07.040 . . siŋ=be thaŋ-ma=ga cog-a-ŋ tree =loc climb -inf=gen try -pst-1sg I tried to climb the tree. (intransitive) 42 _leg _10.020 . ŋkha them-ma n-jog-uks-u-ci those lift -inf 3pl.A- try -prf-3.P[pst]-3nsg.P They tried to lift those (stones). (transitive) 37 _nrr _07.029 The agreement pattern with the embedded object may also apply when the agreement triggering arguments and the embedded verb are not overt, as example from a conversation illustrates. . khuʔ-nen? – khatniŋgo n-yas-wa-ŋ-ga-n=naǃ carry- 1>2[sbjv] – but neg -be _able- npst-1sg.P-2sg.A-neg=nmlz.sg A: Shall I carry you? B: But you can't! The verb niŋsaŋ puŋma have enough, lose interest , an experiencer-as-possessor predicate (cf. nv-comp-poss) may also alternate in valency. In most cases, it is intransitively inflected, invariably with third person singular inflection . With transitive embedded verbs, however, it may optionally mirror the inflection of the embedded verb . . . nda=nuŋ kon-ca-ma a-niŋsaŋ puŋ-a-by-a=naǃ ikhiŋ koʔ-ma=le haʔloǃ? 2sg=com walk -V2.eat-inf 1sg.poss-[stem] lose _interest [3sg]-pst-V2.give-pst=nmlz.sg how _much walk -inf[deont]=ctr excla I have enough of walking with youǃ How much do we have to walk?ǃ . kha philim=ci (soʔ-ma) a-niŋsaŋ puŋ-y-uks-u-ŋ-ci-ŋ=ha those film =nsg (watch -inf ) 1sg.poss-[stem] lose _interest -compl-prf-3.P[pst]-1sg.A-3nsg.P-1sg.A=nmlz.nsg I have enough of (watching) those films.
summary: Some complement-taking verbs in this language match the valency and agreement pattern of their embedded verb: they take intransitive morphology with intransitive complements and transitive morphology with transitive complements. This class includes *yama* ‘be able’, *miʔma* ‘want/like’, and *cokma* ‘try’; the matrix and embedded S/A arguments must be coreferential, so constructions like “I want him to go” are not possible, showing backward control. The overt arguments are case-marked according to the embedded verb, and *niŋsaŋ puŋma* ‘have enough, lose interest’ shows a related but less regular alternation, optionally mirroring transitive embedded inflection.

text: Some complement-taking verbs always show transitive person inflection. Both subject and object of transitive embedded verbs are indexed on the matrix verb. When intransitive verbs are embedded, the embedded S argument triggers transitive subject agreement in the matrix verb, while the object agreement is default third person singular. Verbs belonging to this class are tokma get to do , tarokma begin , sukma aim, intend , lepnima stop, abandon and muʔnima forget . Except for tarokma all verbs may also take nominal complements. Example illustrates this pattern with the verb tokma. It expresses possibilities that are determined by other participants or conditioned by outer circumstances beyond the power and control of the subject (S or A). When three-argument verbs are embedded, the person marking on the matrix verb is analogous to the person marking usually found on the embedded verb (see from the double object class). The long distance agreement is obligatory, as evidenced by ungrammatical , where the number features of the embedded object and the person inflection of the matrix verb do not match. . . nda nhe uŋ-ma n-dokt-wa-ga-n=na 2sg here come _down- inf neg -get -npst[3.P]-2sg.A-neg=nmlz.sg You will not get the chance to come down here (i.e. we will not let you come down here). 21 _nrr _04.035 . ka kamniwak=ci sandisa khuʔ-ma tokt-u-ŋ-ci-ŋ=ha 1sg[erg] friend =nsg present bring- inf get- 3.P[pst]-1sg.A-3nsg.P-1sg.A=nmlz.nsg I got the chance to bring my friends presents. . *ka muŋ=ci im-ma tokt-u-ŋ 1sg[erg] mushroom =nsg buy -inf get- 3.P-1sg.A Intended: I got the chance to buy mushrooms. (correct: imma toktuŋciŋ) Example shows the transitive agreement with the embedded object for the verb tarokma begin . In , the verbal person marking is the only hint given on the number of the object argument, as the nonsingular marker on the noun is optional and often omitted, in this case because of the unspecific reference of the argument yakpuca. Example and serve to show that tarokma is not restricted to verbs with intentional agents. Case is assigned by the embedded verb, since the subjects of embedded intransitive verbs are in the nominative and not in the ergative. . . yakpuca yok-ma tarokt-a-ma-c-u-ci porcupine search- inf begin -pst-prf-du.A-3.P-3nsg.P They (dual) began to look for porcupines. 22 _nrr _05.014 . khap khap-ma=niŋa=go chiŋdaŋ khoŋ-ma, khap yoŋ-ma tarokt-uks-u roof cover -inf=ctmp=top main _pillar collapse -inf roof shake -inf begin [3sg.A]-prf-3.P[pst] While (Tumhang) made the roof, the pillar began to collapse, the roof began to shake. 27 _nrr _06.031 . nna mamu=ga o-phok tuk-ma tarokt-uks-u that girl =gen 3sg.poss- stomach hurt -inf begin [3sg.A]-prf-3.P[pst] That girl's stomach began to hurt. 37 _nrr _07.020 Another member of this class is the phasal verb lepnima stop, abandon (see ). The verb consists of two stems: the lexical stem lept throw and the marker ni i contributing completive semantics. This verb indicates the terminal point of an event, regardless of whether they are activities or states (as in ), or actual or habitual (as shows). The embedded object triggers object agreement on the matrix verb. . . a-nabhuk hup-ma n-lept-iʔ-wa-n=na 1sg.poss -nose be _blocked -inf neg -stop [3sg.A]-compl-npst[3.P]-neg=nmlz.sg My nose continues to be blocked. . ka uŋci cim-ma lept-i-ŋ-ci-ŋ=ha 1sg[erg] 3nsg teach -inf stop- compl-c-3nsg.P-1sg.A=nmlz.nsg I stopped teaching them. As with tarokma above, the semantics of lepnima do not imply conscious decisions and actions, as both sentences in show. Given the etymological relation to the lexical verb lepma throw , this is an unexpected finding. . . paŋ yoŋ-ma lept-i-uks-u house shake -inf stop [3sg.A]-compl-prf-3.P[pst] The house stopped shaking. 27 _nrr _06.036 . luŋdaŋ lupluŋ=be hom-ma n-lept-i-ci cave den =loc fit _into- inf 3pl.A- stop- compl[pst]-3nsg.P They did not fit into caves and dens any more. 27 _nrr _06.004
summary:
The passage describes a class of complement-taking verbs that obligatorily show long-distance transitive agreement, indexing both subject and object on the matrix verb. With intransitive complements, the embedded subject triggers transitive subject agreement while the object agreement is default third singular; with three-argument verbs, the matrix agreement parallels that of the embedded verb, and matching person features are required.  

It illustrates this pattern with verbs such as tokma ‘get to do,’ tarokma ‘begin,’ sukma ‘aim, intend,’ lepnima ‘stop, abandon,’ and muʔnima ‘forget,’ noting that some also take nominal complements. The examples show that case is assigned by the embedded verb, and that these matrix verbs can express situations not limited to intentional agents.

text: Complement-taking verbs with assistive or permissive semantics such as phaʔma help , piʔma give ( allow ), cimma teach and soʔmeʔma show follow a pattern where the G argument of the matrix clause has identical reference to the subject of the embedded clause. In other words, the matrix G argument controls the reference of the embedded S or A argument. The patients of teaching, allowing etc. are arguments of the matrix clause; hence, the agreement is not optional. For instance, a form like soʔmetuŋna (1>3) would not be acceptable in . These verbs realize their arguments according to the double object frame, i.e. the nominal G argument triggers object agreement on the verb; and the embedded clause has the role of the T argument . An example from natural speech is provided in . . . im-ma pim-meʔ-nen=na sleep- inf give- npst-1>2=nmlz.sg I allow you to sleep. . kondarik ok-ma soʔmeʔ-meʔ-nen=na spade dig -inf show -npst-1>2=nmlz.sg I will show you how to plough. .na yakkha=ga ceʔyamumma ghak heko=ci=ŋa ŋ-khus-het-u, cek-meʔ-ma m-bi-n-ci-nin=niŋa, ... this Yakkha =gen speech all other =nsg=erg 3pl.A- steal -V2.carry.off-3.P[pst] talk -caus-inf 3pl.A- give -neg-3nsg.P-3pl.A=ctmp When this language of the Yakkha people was all taken away by the others, when they did not allow them to speak it ... 18 _nrr _03.006 All verbs of this class can have either nominal or infinitival complements, as exemplified with cimma teach in . . . kamala=ŋa ka yakkha ceʔya cind-a-ŋ=na K. =erg 1sg Yakkha language teach [3sg.A]-pst-1sg.P=nmlz.sg Kamala taught me the Yakka language. . kei-lak-ma cim-meʔ-nen=na drum-dance- inf teach -npst-1>2=nmlz.sg I will teach you to dance the drum dance.
summary: Complement-taking verbs with assistive or permissive meanings, such as ‘help,’ ‘allow,’ ‘teach,’ and ‘show,’ take a matrix G argument that is coreferential with the subject of the embedded clause, so the matrix G controls the embedded S or A. Because the patient/recipient-like participant is an argument of the matrix clause, agreement on the verb is required and these verbs pattern with a double-object frame, where the nominal G argument triggers object agreement and the embedded clause functions as T. These verbs can take either nominal or infinitival complements.

subsection: The intransitively inflected verb kaŋma agree, give in
text: The verb kaŋma agree, be willing to, give in (lit.: fall ) always shows intransitive person inflection, regardless of the valency of the embedded verb. Hence, there is only one agreement slot and (at least) two potential candidates to trigger agreement when transitive verbs are embedded. For this verb, the choice of the agreement triggering argument is determined by pragmatics, not by syntax. It shows agreement with whatever argument of the embedded clause is more salient in the current stretch of discourse (see ). This is also the case for the subject-complement construction with the matrix verb leŋma be all right (cf. subjectcomplement below). With certain embedded verbs, agreement with A is pragmatically more common (e.g. with cama eat ), while with other verbs agreement with P is more common (e.g. with cameʔma feed ). Interestingly, A arguments in the ergative case are not allowed with this complement-taking verb, indicating that the matrix S argument controls the embedded arguments. This pragmatically conditioned behavior stands in contrast to Chintang and Belhare, where certain complement-taking verbs are restricted to P arguments alone, following a purely syntactic constraint Bickeletal2001Syntactic, Bickeletal2010Ditransitives. . . picha im-ma ŋ-gaŋ-me-n=na child sleep- inf neg -agree [3sg]-npst-neg=nmlz.sg The child is not willing to sleep. (S) . lukt-a-khy-a=ŋ, chuʔ-ma ŋ-gaks-a-n=oŋ run [3sg]-pst-V2.go-pst=seq tie -inf neg- agree [3sg]-pst-neg=seq As it (the cow) ran away, as was not willing to be tied, ... (P) 11 _nrr _01.011 .ka uŋ phaʔ-ma ŋ-gaks-a-ŋa-n=na 1sg 3sg help -inf neg- agree -pst-1sg-neg=nmlz.sg I was not willing to help him. (A)
summary: The verb *kaŋma* ‘agree, be willing to, give in’ always takes intransitive person inflection, even when the embedded verb is transitive, so agreement is controlled by a single slot rather than by syntax. The choice of which embedded argument triggers agreement is pragmatic: the verb agrees with whichever argument is most salient in discourse, though A is often selected with some verbs and P with others. Unlike in Chintang and Belhare, this construction does not impose a purely syntactic restriction, although ergative A arguments are not permitted.

text: Two verbs, namely tama be time to (lit.: come ) and leŋma be allright, be accepted (lit.: become ), take the whole proposition as their sole argument, usually showing third person singular person marking regardless of the referential properties of the embedded arguments, as shown in . This type of complement construction is referred to as subject complement construction. . . uŋ mit-a: haku eko paŋ cok-ma ta-ya=na 3sg think [3sg]-pst : now one house make- inf come [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg He thought: Now the time has come to build a house. 27 _nrr _06.006 . yun-ma leŋ-meʔ=n=em n-leŋ-me-n=n=em? sit _down -inf be _allright [3sg]-npst=nmlz.sg=alt neg- be _allright [3sg]-npst-neg=nmlz.sg=alt Is it allright to sit down (or is it not alright)? .liŋkha=ci hoŋliŋwa ca-ma n-leŋ-me-n=na a _clan =nsg a _kind _of _fish eat -inf neg- be _allright [3sg]-npst-neg=nmlz.sg The Linkhas are not allowed to eat the Honglingwa fish. It is also possible that one embedded argument gets raised and triggers agreement on the matrix verb (compare and ). . .n-dokhumak im-ma n-leŋ-me-n=na 2sg.poss- alone sleep -inf neg- be _allright [3sg]-npst-neg=nmlz.sg .n-dokhumak im-ma n-leŋ-me-ka-n=na 2sg.poss- alone sleep -inf neg- be _allright -npst-2sg-neg=nmlz.sg Both: You should not sleep alone. When transitive verbs are embedded, the choice of which argument to raise is determined by pragmatics, i.e. by the question which argument is pragmatically more salient .Information structure has not been studied in depth for Yakkha yet. Impressionistically, an argument can be raised either when the discourse is about that argument (i.e., the topic), but also when the reference of that argument is singled out against other possible referents (i.e., focus). Thus, transitive embedded clauses are potentially ambiguous, when there is no overt A argument in the ergative (see ). Such ambiguities are resolved by context. . .kaniŋ kha siau=ci ca-ma n-leŋ-me=ha=ci 1pl these apple =nsg eat -inf neg- be _allright -npst=nmlz.nsg=nsg We are not allowed to eat these apples. (P) .ka mok-ma n-leŋ-meʔ-ŋa-n=na! 1sg[erg/nom?] beat -inf neg- be _allright -npst-1sg=nmlz.sg It is not allright to beat me! (P) OR I should not beat (others). (A) The verb leŋma does not only occur with infinitival complements. It can be found following non-embedded structures such as converbal clauses (see ), and it is also found with nominal objects (see ), where it basically just means be, become . leŋma does not only express social acceptability, but also personal attitudes (see ). The clause providing the context for the expressed attitude is marked with a sequential marker followed by the additive focus particle, so that the clause acquires a concessive reading. The verb leŋma in the third person singular nonpast inflection (leŋmeʔna) has also developed into a fixed expression It's allright . . . ceʔya=ŋa=se ŋ-khas-iʔ-wa-n=na, cama men-ja-le n-leŋ-me-n=na language =erg=restr neg -be _full- 1pl-npst-neg=nmlz.sg , food neg- eat -cvb neg- be _alright [3sg]-npst-neg=nmlz.sg One will not be satisfied just by talking, there is no way but to eat food. . paŋ=be ta-meʔ-ma n-yas-u-ga-n bhoŋ, aniŋga=ca n-leŋ-me-n, ŋga=ca n-leŋ-me-n house =loc arrive -caus-inf neg- be _able- 3.P-2sg.A-neg cond 1p.excl.poss=add neg -be _alright [3sg]-npst-neg 2sg.poss=add neg -be _alright [3sg]-npst-neg If you cannot bring it (the stone) home, it will neither belong to us nor to you. 37 _nrr _07.013 . ka sa matniŋ=hoŋ=ca leŋ-meʔ-ŋa=na 1sg meat without =seq=add be _alright -npst-1sg=nmlz.sg I am fine also/even without (eating) meat.
summary: The verbs **tama** ‘be time to’ and **leŋma** ‘be allright, be accepted’ take an entire proposition as their sole argument and typically show third-person singular agreement, a pattern called **subject complement construction**. When an embedded clause is transitive, one argument may be raised to the matrix verb depending on pragmatic prominence, and **leŋma** can also occur in other constructions, where it expresses not only social acceptability but also personal attitudes and has developed a fixed expression meaning “it’s allright.”

text: Yakkha has an infinitival construction that expresses necessities, either with a deontic or with a dynamic reading. Deontic modality is understood as the expression of a moral obligation of an event, as assessed by the speaker or by someone else, if one reports on someone else's assessments of a situation (following the distinctions made e.g. in Nuyts2006_Modality or in Vanlinden2012_Modal ). In dynamic readings, the expressed necessity is not grounded in the attitudes of the speaker, but in the external circumstances of a situation. This construction is henceforth referred to as Necessitative Construction, since the deontic/dynamic distinction does not have syntactic consequences. In most cases, this construction simply consists of an infinitive to which one of the nominalizing clitics is added (either =ha or =na, see ).See nmlz-uni-3 for the functions and etymology of these nominalizers. Alternatively, the infinitive can also be followed by a copular auxiliary.See cop-infl for the forms of the copula. The third person present affirmative is zero. This is found when the argument is singled out pragmatically, which is tentatively analyzed as focus here . The auxiliary is obligatory in scenarios with first or second person objects. Although the occurrence of the auxiliary in this construction is conditioned by reference and pragmatics, it exhibits an interesting alignment pattern that is conditioned by syntactic roles and referential properties of the arguments (for details cf. below). Both verbs constitute a tightly-knit unit in the necessitative construction. Formally, it is thus rather a simple clause consisting of an infinitive and an auxiliary. . . ka kheʔ-ma=na 1sg go-inf[deont]=nmlz.sg . ka kheʔ-ma ŋan 1sg go-inf[deont] cop.1sg Both: I have to go. The following examples provide an overview of the different readings that the Necessitative Construction may have. The dynamic reading is exemplified in . Here, the conditions for the necessity of the event lie in the circumstances of the situation: in the fact that people are starving in , and in the fact that the stone should not get wet in , both from mythical narratives. Deontic examples are shown in . It is straightforward that both utterances express the attitude of the speakers. What these examples also show is that the infinitives in this construction can be inflected by the nonsingular marker =ci when the object has nonsingular number (see , also mentioned above). In three-argument constructions of the double-object frame, the G argument triggers =ci . . . wasik ta-ni bhoŋ wasik=phaŋ luŋkhwak leŋ-ma=na rain come [3sg]-opt cond rain =abl stone turn _over- inf[deont]=nmlz.nsg In case it rains, one has to turn the stone away from the rain. 37 _nrr _07.112 . yapmi paŋ-paŋ=be nak-saŋ kheʔ-m=ha people house-house =loc ask- sim go- inf[deont]=nmlz.nsg The people have to go from house to house, asking (for food). 14 _nrr _02.029 . .nna=haŋ=maŋ kaniŋ=ca eŋ=ga pama=ci pyak luŋma tuk-ma=ha=ci that =abl=emph 1pl=add 1pl.incl.poss=gen parents =nsg much liver pour -inf[deont]=nmlz.nsg=nsg So that is why we too have to love our parents very much. 01 _leg _07.086 . thim-m=ha=ci scold -inf[deont]=nmlz.nsg=nsg They (the young people) have to be scolded. . wa=ci piʔ-m=ha=ci chicken =nsg give- inf[deont]=nmlz.nsg=nsg It has to be given to the chicken. (G) It is not uncommon for constructions expressing deontic modality to develop further meanings. A directive speech act is shown in . The directive is somewhat related to the expression of an attitude, with the difference lying not in the semantics, but in the type of speech act (assertion vs. command). At least one example, taken from a narrative, also points towards an evidential usage of the Necessitative Construction . The context of this utterance is that a king named Helihang is said to have set out to search for the lost language of the Yakkha people. Before doing so, he erected a marble stele at the foot of Mount Kumbhakarna, in order to let his people know whether he was still alive. As long as this stele does not topple over, the people shall know that he is still alive, searching for their language. This example provides a bridging context between deontic and epistemic modality, as one can read it in two ways: either the people infer from the stele standing upright that their king is still alive (epistemic modality), or the people know that they are expected to think that he is still alive, as he told them so when he departed on his search for the language (deontic modality). . . ŋkha=ci ham-biʔ-ma=ci, ŋ-ga-ya=oŋ, those =nsg distribute -V2.give-inf[deont]=nsg 3pl- say -pst=seq , After they said: It has to be distributed among those (who do not have food), ... 14 _nrr _02.031 .nna ceŋ waiʔ=na=ŋa haku=ca kaniŋ i miʔ=m=ha baŋniŋ: (...) that upright be [3sg]=nmlz.sg=erg now =add 1pl what think -inf=nmlz.nsg about Since that (stele) stands upright, what we have to think even now, ... 18 _nrr _03.031 The negated forms of this construction, marked by prefix men-, express the necessity for an event not to happen (see and ). The deontic meaning has scope over the negation, not the other way around. Negating the necessity of an event is expressed by a construction involving a Nepali loan parnu fall/have to and the light verb cokma do . The negation of the infinitive is formally different from the negation in the verbal inflection, and identical to the negation in another uninflected form, the negative converb. . .nhaŋ cautara=ca men-jok-m=ha=ci, barpipal=ca men-lip-m=ha=ci and _then resting _place =add neg- make -inf=nmlz.nsg=nsg banyan _tree =add neg- plant -inf=nmlz.nsg=nsg And neither are they allowed to build resting places, nor to plant banyan trees. 11 _nrr _01.017 .chubuk=ka caleppa=chen isa=ŋa=ca heʔniŋ=ca men-ja-ma=na ashes =gen bread =top who =erg=add when =add neg- eat -inf[deont]=nmlz.sg No one should ever have to eat the bread made of ashes. 40 _leg _08.082 .iha=ca im-ma por-a n-joŋ-me-ŋa-n what =add buy -inf have _to -nativ neg- do -npst-1sg-neg I do not have to buy anything. 28 _cvs _04.187
summary: Yakkha has a necessitative infinitival construction that can express either deontic necessity, grounded in obligation or speaker attitude, or dynamic necessity, grounded in external circumstances. It usually consists of an infinitive plus a nominalizing clitic, optionally followed by a copular auxiliary; the construction can also take nonsingular marking on the infinitive in some argument configurations. Negated forms express that an event must not happen, while a different construction is used to negate the necessity itself.

text: After the basic morphological and semantic properties have been introduced, let us now turn to the argument realization in this construction. I will show how the nominalizing clitics attaching to the infinitive are aligned and how the copular auxiliary is aligned. cop-options shows the distribution of the two constructions over participant scenarios. The default option in my Yakkha corpus is the construction without the auxiliary.As for the auxiliary, elicited paradigms from different speakers on various occasions and plenty examples from unrecorded spontaneous discourse exist to illustrate its alignment. In scenarios with third person acting on third, it is the only option. In scenarios with first or second person objects, however, only the construction with the auxiliary is acceptable. table tabular llll A>P & 1 & 2 & 3 1 &-&inf+cop&inf+cop or &&&inf 2 &inf+cop&-&inf+cop or &&&inf 3- extsc erg &inf+cop&inf+cop&inf tabular Two options of the Necessitative Construction table copula shows the suppletive inflectional paradigm of the copula (present, affirmative). The forms resemble the agreement suffixes in the verbal inflection, so that I assume that there was a phonologically light stem in a earlier stage that got lost over time. Related person suffixes in Yakkha are -ŋ(a) for first person (exclusive), -ka -ga for second person, and -ci for the dual. The initial /s/ of the plural forms and the dual forms starting in nci cannot be related to the agreement morphology of Yakkha. Limbu though, the eastern neighbour of Yakkha, has a 3nsg object agreement marker -si Driem1987A-grammar . In the past paradigms, there is a stem sa, and the person inflection is regular (see cop-infl), but in the present forms the stem is zero. This copula does not have infinitival forms. An equational copula as such does not belong to the general morphological profile of Kiranti languages Bickel1999Nominalization . What is crucial for the following discussion of the data is that the copula has only one agreement slot. table [htp] center tabular llll & 1.excl & 1.incl & 2 sg & ŋan& &gan du & nciŋan&ncin& ncigan pl & siŋan& sin&sigan tabular Inflection of the copular auxiliary (present indicative, affirmative) center table As for the agreement of the auxiliary, with intransitive verbs it simply agrees with the embedded S argument, as shown in below. If transitive verbs are embedded, the agreement exhibits an intricate combination of hierarchical Hierarchical alignment is the morphological and syntactic treatment of arguments according to their relative ranking on the referential (...) hierarchies Siewierska1998On-nominal . With reference to agreement, this means that access to inflectional slots for subject and/or object is based on person, number, and/or animacy rather than (or no less than) on syntactic relations Nichols1992Language . and ergative alignment,Ergative alignment is given when S and P arguments are treated alike and differently from A arguments. as shown schematically in align-sum-cop . summary:
The passage describes argument realization in the Yakkha necessitative construction, focusing on how the nominalizing clitics on the infinitive and the copular auxiliary are aligned. The default form in the corpus lacks the auxiliary, but the auxiliary is required in scenarios with first- or second-person objects and is the only option in third-person acting on third-person contexts; the copula itself has a suppletive present paradigm and only one agreement slot.

With transitive verbs, the auxiliary shows hierarchical alignment in mixed speech-act-participant vs. third-person scenarios, but ergative alignment in local scenarios: it agrees with P rather than A, just as with intransitive S. The author also notes some speaker variation and suggests that certain rejected forms may reflect a face-preserving avoidance of explicit reference to second-person agents or first-person patients.

summary: The passage argues that Yakkha speakers often avoid explicitly mentioning participants in the Necessitative Construction, especially first-person nonsingular patients, as a face-preserving strategy; avoiding reference to second-person agents is described as innovative and limited to this construction. It then shows that agreement and nominalizer marking follow a mixture of reference-based and role-based alignment: the speech-act participant or higher-ranking argument usually triggers auxiliary agreement, while in reversed T–G relations the theme can index the auxiliary and the goal may receive locative marking.
