summary: The passage describes a hierarchical agreement pattern in which the suffix =ha attaches to the infinitive whenever either participant has nonsingular reference, regardless of which argument is the actor or patient. This is illustrated with examples showing that both singular and plural agents take =ha when the patient is nonsingular, and plural agents also trigger =ha with singular patients.

text: The alignment in the necessitative construction is centered around two factors: person (sap) and syntactic role (P), and the question of which selection principle applies is conditioned by different scenarios: speech-act participant reference is the relevant factor in mixed scenarios, and P is the relevant factor in local scenarios. The person marking in regular verbs supports this reasoning, as the alignment is more consistent across the columns (representing P) than across the rows (representing A) in the paradigm (cf. Schackow2012_Grammatical ). Speech-act participant markers are aligned different than the third person markers. sap markers show ergative or hierarchical alignment, while the third person is largely aligned accusatively. As I have shown above, the alignment of the nominalizing clitics =na and =ha is sensitive to participant scenarios. The distribution of tense-marking allomorphs is scenario-based, too (cf. tense). The distinction between speech-act participants and third persons figures as a factor in other constructions: the ergative case is not overtly marked on first and second person pronouns, and the verbal inflection has person markers that have underspecified speech-act participant reference, e.g. -m (for first and second person plural A arguments), -i (for first and second person plural S and P arguments). Hence, although the alignment of the necessitative construction is unique, the selection principles leading to this pattern can also be found in other domains of the grammar of Yakkha. Alignment splits serve as scenario classifiers in Yakkha (cf. also Bickel1992Motivation on Belhare).In search for a Yakkha-internal explanation of the pattern at hand it is tempting to attribute the hierarchical alignment to the defective paradigm of the copula: the absence of third person forms provides an empty slot that is filled by the material marking a speech-act participant. The absence of third person forms can, however, not explain the entire picture. Firstly, it does not account for the fact that the copula is obligatory when the object is a speech-act participant, but not when the subject is a speech-act participant. Secondly, there are also traces of hierarchical alignment in the verbal paradigm, although there are markers for the third person available. Scenarios of a 3.A>2.P type, for instance, largely neglect reference to the third person A argument (cf. verb-infl). Furthermore, the defective paradigm of the copula can also not explain the ergative alignment in local scenarios, i.e. why it is always the object that is indexed on the verb in these scenarios. Hierarchical patterns are a recurrent feature in other Tibeto-Burman languages that show person marking, too, e.g. in Rawang, Kham and in many of the Kiranti languages (cf. DeLancey1989Verb , LaPolla1992Dating , LaPolla2003_Overview , LaPolla2007Hierarchical , Ebert1987Grammatical , DeLancey2011_Notes , Watters2002A-grammar ). The particular pattern that was found in Yakkha has been attested, with varying degrees of transparency, in Tibeto-Burman languages of various geographic origins and sub-branches, reaching back to Tangut sources as early as the 12th century Kepping1975_Subject, Kepping1994The-conjugation. Watters2002A-grammar, who compared the person marking system of the Kham dialects with person marking in other Tibeto-Burman languages, found hierarchical patterns in Gyarong, Nocte and Western Kiranti languages with sap outranking third person and, crucially, with a preference for the object in conflicting scenarios (Nagano1984A-historical, cited in Watters2002A-grammar ). The alignment in the Yakkha necessitative construction also resembles Proto-Tibeto-Burman agreement as reconstructed in DeLancey1989Verb, who characterizes the system as “a split ergative agreement pattern in which agreement is always with a 1st or 2nd person argument in preference to 3rd person, regardless of which is subject or object.” DeLancey1989Verb .As noted earlier, Tibeto-Burman reconstruction and subgrouping are far from being settled, see, e.g., Thurgood1984The-Rung, DeLancey1989Verb, DeLancey2010_Towards, DeLancey2011_Notes, LaPolla1992Dating, LaPolla2012_Comments, Jacques2012_Agreement. Under the assumption that a sub-branch Rung exists (see the references from Thurgood and LaPolla), those Tibeto-Burman languages showing agreement would be related on a lower level than Proto-Tibeto-Burman. A potentially interesting side note in this respect is that the same alignment split (ergative and hierarchical, conditioned by a distinction of speech-act participant vs. third person) is also found in the verbal agreement of the Caucasian (Nakh-Daghestanian) language Dargwa Zuniga2007_From . The pattern is neither a one-off case, nor is it restricted to Tibeto-Burman. Of course, more cross-linguistic data would be necessary to be able to corroborate any functional-typological explanation for this alignment split. Indeed, it would be exciting to discover that this pattern is more widespread than assumed at this stage. According to Serdobolskaya2009_Raising, referential properties also play a role in raising constructions in some Uralic, Turkic and Mongolic languages languages, and she tentatively suggests this to be an areal feature. More data on other languages could help to answer the question if this feature really has an areal distribution. On a final note, the auxiliary in the necessitative construction is often replaced by the third person form of the Nepali auxiliary pʌrnu fall/have to , as shown in . In this calqued structure, the peculiar alignment pattern of the necessitative construction gets lost. .kʌhile-kʌhile mamu=ŋa=ca taʔ-ma=ci pʌrchʌ sometimes girl =erg=add bring- inf=nsg has _to Sometimes, the girl has to bring them (further wives), too. 06 _cvs _01.044
summary: The Yakkha necessitative construction shows a split alignment that depends on whether speech-act participants or third persons are involved: speech-act participants trigger ergative or hierarchical alignment, while third-person contexts are largely accusative, and local scenarios favor P-indexing. The author argues that this pattern is not unique to the necessitative construction but is reflected in other parts of Yakkha grammar and in other Tibeto-Burman languages, suggesting that the alignment split functions as a scenario classifier rather than being fully explained by the copula’s defective paradigm.

text: Inflected complement clauses are found with predicates of cognition like nima see, get to know , khemma hear , miʔma think, hope, consider, like (see cognition-pred) and utterance predicates such as luʔma tell, say , yokmepma tell (about) , chimma ask (see utterance-pred). overview-all (on page overview-all ) provides the list of all complement-taking predicates that embed clauses with inflected verbs in Yakkha. Complement clauses in Yakkha distinguish direct speech and indirect speech. In case of indirect speech, the clauses contain nominalized inflected verbs. In case of direct speech, the verbs are able to express the full range of verbal categories found in independent clauses. Some types of complement clauses are marked by the conjunction bhoŋ that also functions as a marker of conditional clauses, direct speech and purpose clauses. The latter seem to have developed out of clauses containing direct speech (see adv-cl-fin-purp). Some complement-taking verbs are polysemous, their semantics depending on whether they occur with an infinitival or with an inflected complement. The verb miʔma, for instance, means like (doing) with infinitival complements but think, hope, consider with inflected complements. The verb nima means know (how to do) with infinitival complements, but see, get to know with inflected complements. Some nouns may embed propositions as well, by means of the complementizer baŋna/baŋha (cf. noun-compl).
summary: Yakkha uses inflected complement clauses with cognition verbs such as “see,” “think,” “hope,” and “like,” as well as utterance verbs such as “tell” and “ask.” These complements distinguish indirect speech, which contains nominalized inflected verbs, from direct speech, whose verbs can show the full range of verbal categories found in independent clauses. Some complements are marked by bhoŋ, a conjunction also used in conditionals, direct speech, and purpose clauses, and some predicates change meaning depending on whether they take infinitival or inflected complements; additionally, some nouns can embed propositions via baŋna/baŋha.

text: The complement-taking predicates of cognition can be further classified into predicates of knowledge, perception, experience and propositional attitude. The most common predicate embedding inflected complements is nima to see or get to know something , exemplified in . The embedded verb is mostly in one of the indicative past tenses and has to carry one of the nominalizers =na or =ha (cf. Chapter ch-nmlz). The embedded subject obligatorily triggers agreement both on the embedded verb and on the main verb. On the main verb, it triggers object marking (see ). This can be explained from a semantic perspective: perceiving that a person is doing something implies perceiving that person. The argument realization in the complement clause is identical to that of independent clauses. The subject of the embedded clause receives ergative case marking when the embedded verb is transitive, although the A argument simultaneously triggers object agreement on the matrix verb. Such complements typically use an indicative past tense plus a nominalizer, and the embedded subject is cross-referenced both on the embedded verb and as object agreement on the matrix verb; when the embedded verb is transitive, the embedded subject also receives ergative case.  

Other verbs like **miʔma** ‘think’ and **eʔma** ‘perceive, have the impression’ show similar agreement patterns, but **miʔma** can take optative complements with a hope reading, while some experiential verbs introduce direct-speech complements with full inflection and a shift in perspective to the embedded subject. text: Utterance predicates distinguish between those that embed indirect speech (as already introduced in the predicates of cognition) and those that embed direct speech. Some verbs may occur with both indirect speech and direct speech, for instance miʔma think . Predicates embedding indirect speech or indirect questions are, for instance, yokmeʔma tell (about) and khemmeʔma tell, make hear (see ), while direct speech is embedded mainly by the predicates kama say, call and luʔma tell . The complement clauses of both types of utterance predicates can be marked by bhoŋ, the complementizer that is also found as a quotative marker and as conjunction on purpose clauses and conditional clauses.These uses of bhoŋ are parallel to the functional distribution of the Nepali conjunction bhʌne. This complementizer is frequently found in clauses containing indirect speech and indirect questions (see ), and rarely on clauses containing direct speech (see ). . . ak=ka kamniwak=ci, ka isa om, isa om bhoŋ uŋci=ŋa=ca n-yokme-me-ka-nin. 1sg.poss=gen friend =nsg 1sg who cop who cop comp 3nsg=erg=add neg -tell _about- npst-2-pl.neg My friends, they will also not tell you who I am. 14 _nrr _02.25 . philm=be=cen haku i=ya i=ya cok-ma-sy-a=na bhoŋ khem-meʔ-meʔ-nen=ba, ani. film =loc=top now what =nmlz.nc what =nmlz.nc do -inf-aux.prog[3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg comp hear -caus-npst-1>2=emph aunt I will tell you now what he was doing in the film, auntie. 34 _pea _04.007 .nna cuʔlumphi isa=ŋa thukt-u=na bhoŋ pyak pyak yapmi=ci=nuŋ ceʔya leks-a=ha. that stele who =erg erect -3.P[pst]=nmlz.sg comp many many people =nsg=com matter become [3sg]-pst=nmlz.nc Many people have discussed who erected that stele. 18 _nrr _03.002--3 Direct speech (quotes) may show the full range of tense, aspect and modal marking, and also any type of illocutionary force marking, clause-final exclamative particles and the like. The person marking on the embedded verb follows the perspective of the embedded subject, not the perspective of the speaker. Direct speech is generally embedded without any complementizer, as shown in the following examples, where kama say , luʔma tell , miʔma think and chimma ask function as matrix verbs (see , and note that presents an exceptional case without bhoŋ). . . khamba=ŋa a-tokhumak yep-ma n-ya-me-ŋa-n=na ka-saŋ por-a-khy-a=na pillar =erg 1sg.poss -alone stand -inf neg- be _able -npst-1sg-neg=nmlz.sg say -sim fall [3sg]-pst-V2.go-pst=nmlz.sg I cannot stand alone, said the pillar and fell down. 27 _nrr _06.17 . heko=ha nwak=ci=ŋa haku nda nhe uŋ-ma n-dokt-wa-ga-n=na n-lu-ks-u other =nmlz.nsg bird =nsg=erg now 2sg here come _down -inf neg- get _to _do -npst-2.A[3.P]-neg=nmlz.sg 3pl.A -tell- prf-3.P[pst] The other birds told him: Now you will not get the chance to come down here any more. 21 _nrr _04.035 . hetne=le ta-ʔi=ya m-mit-a-ma=hoŋ uŋci m-maks-a-by-a-ma=ca where =ctr come -1pl=nmlz.nsg 3pl- think -pst-prf=seq 3nsg 3pl -be _surprised- pst-V2.give-pst-prf=add They also wondered: Where on earth did we arrive? 22 _nrr _05.30 . hetniŋ-hetniŋ om=em men=em mit-wa-m=ha sometimes yes =alt no =alt think -npst[3.P]-1pl.A=nmlz.nc Sometimes we think: Is it (true) or not? .nani, i=na yubak?, n-chimd-uks-u. child what =nmlz.sg property 3pl.A- ask -prf-3.P[pst] Child, what thing (do you want)?, they asked her. 37 _nrr _07.006 .imin kaniŋ cin-a cok-meʔ-nen-in? bhoŋ elaba=ci=ŋa n-lu-ks-u-ci. how 1pl recognize -nativ do -npst-1>2-2pl quot a _clan =nsg=erg 3pl.A- tell -prf-3.P[pst]-3nsg.P How will we recognize you?, asked the Elabas (people of Elaba clan). 39 _nrr _08.11 In a few cases, the reportative particle =bu is also found on embedded speech (see for direct speech, and which could be either direct or indirect speech). . .por-a cog-a=bu lu-ya-n-u-m. study -nativ do -imp=rep tell -imp-pl-3.P-2.A Tell him to study. ( Tell him: study! ) 01 _leg _07.094 .kham=be=ca n-yuŋ-me-n, siŋ=be=ca man, hiʔwa=ga hiʔwa wait=na=bu ŋ-ga-me earth =loc=add neg- live [3sg]-npst-neg tree =loc=add neg.cop air =gen air exist [npst;3]=nmlz.sg=rep 3pl- say -npst It is neither living on the ground nor in the trees, it just lives in the air, they say. 21 _nrr _04.052 Example serves to illustrate that question words remain in situ in direct speech; they do not get extracted. Semantically, the question word belongs to the embedded clause because it is an argument of khuʔma bring . It is, however, the focus of the question and hence appears as question word. The particle =le serves as contrastive focus marker, and it emphasizes the cluelessness of the speaker in questions and his eagerness to get to know the answer. . nda ka ina=le khut-a-ŋ ly-a-ŋ-ga=na? 2sg[erg] 1sg what =ctr bring -imp-1sg tell -pst-1sg.P-2.A=nmlz.sg What did you tell me to bring?
summary: Utterance predicates in the language distinguish between verbs that embed indirect speech or indirect questions and those that embed direct speech. Indirect speech is commonly introduced by the complementizer bhoŋ and is associated with verbs such as yokmeʔma, khemmeʔma, and often miʔma, while direct speech is usually embedded without a complementizer, mainly with kama, luʔma, and also miʔma and chimma. Direct speech allows the full range of tense, aspect, modality, and illocutionary marking, with person marking following the perspective of the quoted speaker rather than the matrix speaker.

text: Nouns can embed finite complement clauses via the use of the complementizers baŋna (if the head noun has singular number) and baŋha (if the head noun has nonsingular number or non-countable reference). Example shows how baŋna links propositions to a head noun from the semantic domain of saying. In the head noun is from the experiential domain. As illustrates, the complement clause can be of considerable length and complexity. Narratives often conclude with a structure as shown in . . . na chuʔlumphi helihaŋ=ŋa thukt-u=na baŋna ceʔya this stele Helihang =erg erect -3.P[pst]=nmlz.sg comp matter the matter about how/when this stele was erected by Helihang 18 _nrr _03.004 .a-ma=ŋa moŋ-meʔ=ha baŋna kisiʔma=ŋa 1sg.poss- mother =erg beat -npst[1.P]=nmlz.nsg comp fear =erg Out of fear that my mother would beat us, ... 40 _leg _08.030 . nhaŋroŋ-hoknam=be me-wasiʔ-le me-wacek-le cameŋba ca-ma bhoŋ samba-nwak leks-iʔ-wa, phak men-semeʔ-le ca-ya bhoŋ phak loʔwa pombrekpa, chippakeppa leks-iʔ-wa baŋna eko lu-yukt-a=na ceʔya wɛʔ=na a _festival =loc neg -wash -cvb neg -wash -cvb food eat -inf cond vulture become -1pl-npst pig neg -greet -cvb eat -sbjv cond pig like lazy disgusting become -1pl-npst compl one tell -V2.put-3.P=nmlz.sg story exist [3sg]=nmlz.sg We have a saying that during Maghe Sankranti, if we eat without bathing, we will become a vulture, and if we eat without bowing down to the pig, we will become lazy and disgusting like a pig. 40 _leg _08.047 .nnakha lalubaŋ phalubaŋ=ci ŋkha liŋkha=ci iya ŋ-wa-ya, ŋkha=ci ghak eko n-leks-a=bu baŋna taplik om those Lalubang Phalubang =nsg those Linkha _person =nsg what 3pl- exist -sbjv those =nsg all one 3pl- become -pst=rep compl story cop Those Lalubang and Phalubang, those Linkhas, whatever happens, they all became one (they say), (this) is what the story is about. 22 _nrr _05.134 Such structures do not necessarily need a head noun, as example shows. . keŋ-khuwa u-thap-ka kolem=na sumphak baŋna na=maŋ om. bear _fruit -nmlz 3sg.poss- plant =gen smooth =nmlz.sg leaf comp this =emph cop This is what it means if we say: the high-yielding plant has smooth leaves. From the Nepali saying: hune biruwāko cillo pāt, for people who show a promising behavior from an early age on. 01 _leg _07.236 The complementizer is not only used to embed clauses, it may also link names to a head noun, translating as called or so-called (see and ). As shows, this structure does not necessarily need a nominal head either. The phrase marked by baŋna has nominal properties, like a headless relative clause. It can, for instance, host the nonsingular marker =ci and case markers. This shows again how complementation and nominalization are related in Yakkha (see Chapter ch-nmlz).Etymologically, the complementizer can be deconstructed into a root baŋ (of unknown origin) and the nominalizers =na and =ha. . . eko selele-phelele baŋna nwak one Selele-Phelele so-called bird the bird called Selele-Phelele 21 _nrr _04.001 . haŋsewa baŋha yakkha=ci Hangsewa comp Yakkha _person =nsg the Yakkha people called Hangsewa (a clan name) 39 _nrr _08.06 . jalangaja, mendenbarik baŋna=be Jalan-Gaja Mendenbarik so-called =loc in a place called Jalan Gaja, Mendenbarik (in Malaysia) 13 _cvs _02.063
summary: The complementizers **baŋna** and **baŋha** allow nouns to embed finite complement clauses, with **baŋna** used after singular head nouns and **baŋha** after nonsingular or non-countable heads. These clauses can be lengthy and complex, and the same forms can also link names to nouns in the sense of “called” or “so-called,” including in headless structures that show nominal properties such as plural and case marking.

text: This chapter provides an overview of operators on the discourse level. Syntactically speaking they are optional, but of course omitting them does not make sense from a discourse perspective. Particles are invariant morphemes and not part of the inflectional paradigm of the verb or the noun. Some particles attach to phrases (potentially including adverbial clauses), others attach to the end of a sentence and accordingly, their scope properties have the potential to differ (see tab-particles for an overview). It should be noted that the term particle does not make any statements about their nature, apart from the fact that they are uninflected. The operators discussed here can be phonologically bound, free, or have variable phonological status. Some of them can also be stacked to arrive at more specific discourse functions, which in some cases leads to new, phonologically unbound forms. The functions of the particles include indicating topicalized or focussed constituents of the sentence (cf. ptcl-top and ptcl-foc). Other particles rather have scope over a section of discourse that is bigger than one sentence, most prominently baŋniŋ. Some particles indicate the source of information (evidentiality markers) and the assessment of the speaker regarding the likelihood or reliability of a piece of information (epistemic markers). They are discussed, together with a marker of mirativity, in ptcl-evid. Exclamative particles are the topic of ptcl-excla. Further particles discussed here are the marker of alternatives, the marker of truth-value questions, the vocative and the insistive particles in ptcl-further. This chapter also contains an overview of the interjections found in Yakkha (interjections). Two further markers with discourse function have been discussed at length in nmlz-uni-3: the nominalizing clitics =na and =ha. Rarely, markers from Nepali are used as well, such as emphatic ni, the initiative lu, and the probability particle hola (paraphrasable with probably ). They are not discussed here. The only markers from Nepali that are found frequently enough to be considered in this discussion are the contrastive topic particle (see ptcl-top) and the mirative marker (see ptcl-evid). This chapter has the character of a descriptive overview, providing merely impressionistic conclusions. It does not present a theory of discourse marking in Yakkha, as an in-depth discourse analysis has not been undertaken for Yakkha yet. table [htp] tabular lll particle & function & domain =ko =go&topic&phrase, adv. clause =chen&contrastive topic&phrase baŋniŋ&textual topic, quotative&adv. clause =se&restrictive focus&phrase, adv. clause =ca&additive focus&phrase, adv. clause =pa =ba& emphasis&sentence =i& emphasis &sentence =le&contrastive focus&phrase =maŋ&emphasis&phrase =pu =bu&reportative& phrase, emb. clause loppi&probability/hypothetical &sentence =pi =bi&irrealis &clause rahecha&mirative&sentence lai&exclamative&sentence =ʔlo&exclamative&sentence hau&exclamative&sentence =em&alternation&clause i&truth-value question&sentence =u&vocative&phrase au&insistive& sentence tabular Overview of discourse particles table
summary: This chapter gives a descriptive overview of Yakkha discourse particles and other operators, noting that they are optional syntactically but important for discourse functions. These uninflected markers may attach to phrases or sentence-finally, vary in phonological status, and can be stacked; they signal functions such as topic and focus, evidentiality, epistemic meaning, mirativity, exclamatives, alternatives, questions, vocatives, and insistive force, with some operating over larger stretches of discourse. The chapter also mentions interjections, two nominalizing clitics with discourse functions, and a few borrowed Nepali markers, while emphasizing that no full theory of discourse marking in Yakkha is offered.

text: The topic particle =ko =go (alternation conditioned by the voicing rule, cf. voicing) marks the constituent in the sentence about which a question or assertion is made, and is thus only found once in a sentence. It attaches to constituents of any kind (see ), including adverbial clauses (see ). In , =go attaches to a possessive pronoun that refers to the protagonist of a narrative. The constituent marked for topic does not have to be given in a certain stretch of discourse; in for instance, the topic of the sentence is a newly introduced discourse topic. In the assertion is made about a certain time that is expressed by an adverbial. . . uk=ka=go pik=ci wai-sa=bu. 3sg.poss=gen=top cow =nsg exist -pst.prf=rep He had cows. 11 _nrr _01.005 . a-pum=go nu=na hola ni? 1sg.poss- grandfather =top get _well [3sg]=nmlz.sg probably ptcl The grandfather is fine, most probably? hola and ni are Nepali particles and they do not occur frequently (yet), so they are not discussed further here. 06 _cvs _01.083 .heʔnasen=go n-lit-a-ma-n=ha. thesedays =top neg- plant [3sg]-pst-prf-neg=nmlz.nc These days it has not been planted. 36 _cvs _06.094 . .nhe nis-u-ŋ=niŋ=go pako sa=na here see [pst]-3.P-1sg.A=ctmp=go old cop.pst[3sg]=nmlz.sg When I had seen him here, he was (already) old. 06 _cvs _01.088 .wa=ci ŋ-ga-ya=hoŋ=go om leks-a-khy-a chicken =nsg 3pl- call -pst=seq=top bright become [3]-pst-V2.go-pst The cocks crowed, and the day started. 37 _nrr _07.028 .massina=ci bhoŋ=go, massina=ca ŋ-und-wa=ci small =nsg cond=top small =add 3pl.A- pull -npst-3nsg.P If they (the fish) are small, they also pull them out. 13 _cvs _02.021 The constituent marked by =ko comes sentence-initially (see and ), or in a detached position. Example shows a right-dislocated topic in an afterthought which is marked by =ko that was probably uttered to correct the plural marking of the verb to dual in the pronoun. The same is illustrated below by and . . haku i=ya ka-m haʔlo, kanciŋ=go? now what =nmlz.sg say -1pl.A[sbjv] excla 1du=top Now what shall we say, I mean, the two of us? 13 _cvs _02.54 The topic particle is also involved in a fixed construction, where the finite main verb is preceded by its infinitival form, which is marked by the topic particle. This grammatical construction implies that a restriction applies to the propositional content expressed in the sentence (see the examples in ). In example , people discuss where one could purchase fish, and that even though a certain household might have fish, they probably do not have enough to sell them to others. The question in implies that things could have been worse, as the talk is about an arranged marriage. The construction does not only occur with verbs, but also with other word classes in predicative function (see ). The same structure occurs in Nepali with the infinitive in -nu and the topic marker ta. . .yo gumba=ci=ge=ca wa-ma=go wam-me=ha, across Gumba =nsg=loc=add exist -inf=top exist [3sg]-npst=nmlz.nsg Gumba's family over there has some (fish), (but ...) 13 _cvs _02.057 .we=ppa, wa-ma=go, ca-ma khoblek. cama=ŋa ŋ-khom-me-n. exist [3sg;npst]=emph exist -inf=top food eating _up _at _once food =erg neg- be _enough [1.P]-npst-neg There is, there is food, (but) it is eaten up quickly. We do not have enough food. 28 _cvs _04.169--70 .nhaŋ cekt-a-ci=ha, cek-ma=go? and _then speak -pst-du=nmlz.nsg speak -inf=top And then they talked, at least? (bride and groom) 36 _cvs _06.289 .khumdu=go khumdu, khatniŋgo haŋ=ha tasty =top tasty, but spicy =nmlz.nc It is tasty, but spicy. The topic particle is also part of the lexicalized adversative clause-initial connective khatniŋgo/ŋkhatniŋgo but , which historically is a combination of a temporal adverb meaning at this/that time and the topic marker.
summary: The topic particle =ko/=go marks the constituent that a sentence is about and appears only once per sentence; it can attach to almost any constituent, including adverbial clauses, and its form is conditioned by voicing. The topic-marked constituent may be newly introduced, can occur sentence-initially or in a detached/right-dislocated position, and is also used in a fixed construction where an infinitival form plus =go expresses a restriction on the proposition. The particle further appears in the lexicalized adversative connective khatniŋgo/ŋkhatniŋgo, historically built from a temporal adverb plus the topic marker.

text: In addition to the Yakkha topic marker =ko, the particle =chen (with a freely alternating allomorph [cen]), a borrowed form of the Nepali particle cāhĩ, can be employed (see loansphon). It has a stronger reading, marking contrastive topics in contexts where the speaker switches the topic or singles out one constituent (about which an assertion is made) against other constituents, as shown in . In , the protagonists of the story are marked by =chen, because the preceding content was about the people who chased them away. In contrast to =ko, =chen is restricted to constituents of clauses; it is not found on adverbial clauses. . . imin lak-m=ha baŋniŋ, ka=chen na doku=hoŋ=be u-me-ŋ, [...] nniŋda lakt-a-ni how dance -inf=nmlz.nsg about 1sg=top this basket =inside=loc enter -npst-1sg [...] 2pl dance -imp-pl As for how to dance, I will climb into this basket, [...] and you (plural) will dance. 14 _nrr _02.28--9 .nhaŋ khaci lalubaŋ=nuŋ phalubaŋ=chen khali puŋda=e kheʔ-m=ha and _then these Lalubang =com Phalubang =top only forest =loc go -inf[deont]=nmlz.nsg And then, those (guys) Lalubang and Phalubang only had the option to go to the forest. 22 _nrr _05.045
summary: The particle =chen, borrowed from Nepali cāhĩ and with an allomorph [cen], is used in Yakkha as a stronger topic marker than =ko. It marks contrastive topics or constituents singled out against alternatives, but unlike =ko it is restricted to clause constituents and does not occur on adverbial clauses.

subsection: The quotative and textual topic particle baŋniŋ
text: This particle marks the question or topic that a broader section of discourse is about (see ). The particle constitutes a stress domain by itself. The voiced initial could be a reflex of its formerly bound nature. Yakkha also has a complementizer baŋna, embedding clauses to nouns, sometimes also translating as so-called . Although the origin of baŋ is not clear, it looks as if a root of an utterance predicate has been nominalized to yield baŋna, and the cotemporal adverbial clause linkage marker =niŋ (see sim-finite) has been added to the same root to yield baŋniŋ. In fact, the particle in has the function of marking direct speech in much the same function as bhoŋ in purpose clauses and utterance predicates (see adv-cl-fin-purp and utterance-pred). In clauses with bhoŋ as a quotative marker, the subject of the main clause and the source of the utterance are coreferential. This is not the case for speech marked by baŋniŋ, as clearly shows. This example also shows that it is possible for the topic marker =ko to attach to baŋniŋ. . .nna ceŋ waiʔ=na=ŋa haku=ca kaniŋ i miʔ=m=ha baŋniŋ: (...) that [nom] upright be [3sg]=nmlz.sg=erg now =add 1pl[nom] what think -inf[deont]=nmlz.nsg about As that (stele) stands upright, what we have to think even now, ... 18 _nrr _03.031 .liŋkha=ŋa=bu i=ya i=ya men-jok-ma baŋniŋ: a _clan =erg=rep what =nmlz.nc what =nmlz.nc neg- do -inf[deont] about As for what things the Linkha clan is not allowed to do, (...) 11 _nrr _01.022 .maŋcwa=le apt-u baŋniŋ=go i=ha=le kheps-uks-u=ha? water =ctr bring -imp quot=top what =nmlz.nc=ctr hear -prf-3.P=nmlz.nc When we told her to fetch water, what the heck did she understand? 42 _leg _10.045
summary: The passage explains that a particle is used to mark the question or topic a larger discourse section is about, and that it forms its own stress domain. It also discusses Yakkha complementizers, especially baŋna and baŋniŋ, proposing that they may derive from a nominalized utterance predicate plus additional marking; baŋniŋ functions as a direct-speech marker, unlike bhoŋ, and unlike bhoŋ it does not require the main-clause subject and speech source to be coreferential.

text: Restrictive focus is expressed by the particle =se. It is attached to the constituent it focusses on. A sentence with a constituent being focussed by the restrictive marker expresses that out of a given set only this constituent fulfills the necessary condition for the proposition to be true. The restrictive focus marker thus has a semantic impact on the sentence, and does not merely add emphasis (see also Koenig1993_Focus ). . . ka=go na mamu hen=se nis-u-ŋ=na 1sg=top this girl today =restr know -3.P[pst]-1sg.A=nmlz.sg But I saw this girl only today! . hoŋkhiŋ=se that _much =restr That much only. 11 _nrr _01.42 .yakkhaba=ga=se cekt-uks-u-m Yakkha _person =gen=restr speak -prf-3.P[pst]-1pl.A We have only talked in the language of the Yakkha people. 36 _cvs _06.609 The restrictive focus marker can also be found on adverbial clauses (see ), and also inside adverbial clauses, as the focus domain generally extends into subordinate clauses in Yakkha (see ). . . sumphak phophop n-jog-uks-u=hoŋ=se camyoŋba m-by-uks-u-ci leaf upside _down neg- do -prf-3.P=seq=restr food 3pl.A- give -prf-3.P[pst]-3nsg.P They gave the food to them only after turning the leaf-plates upside-down. .nna mʌndata=se m-bi-wa-ci=nuŋ samma cahĩ, [...] that marriage _custom =restr 3pl.A- give -npst-3nsg.P=com.cl until top And as long as only the Mandata is given, ... (the wife does not belong to the husband's side). 26 _tra _02.007 The marker =se is also found in a construction that expresses very urgent requests or imperatives. In such constructions, an infinitival form, marked by the restrictive focus particle, precedes the inflected verb, as shown in . . oe chiŋdaŋ oe=maŋ, nda yep-ma=se yeb-a-sy-a! addr pillar addr=emph 2sg stand -inf=restr stand -imp-mddl-imp Oh, pillar, oh, if you only stood upright! 27 _nrr _06.023
summary: Restrictive focus in Yakkha is marked by the particle =se, which attaches to the constituent it focuses on and means that only that constituent satisfies the condition for the proposition to be true. The marker has a real semantic effect rather than merely adding emphasis, and it can occur on constituents in main clauses as well as on adverbial clauses and within subordinate clauses. It is also used in constructions expressing very urgent requests or imperatives, where an infinitival form with =se precedes the finite verb.

text: Additive focus is marked by the clitic =ca. In related languages, the cognate of this marker has aspirated /ch/ initially (e.g. in Bantawa and Belhare Doornenbal2009A-grammar, Bickel2003Belhare ). This marker expresses that content is added to some presupposed or previously activated content, or that some participant is included to the presupposed set of participants, as illustrated by . The marker attaches to constituents of any type, including adverbial clauses, as will be shown below. . . nda=nuŋ ka=ca khe-me-ŋ=na. 2sg=com 1sg=add go -npst-1sg=nmlz.sg I will also go with you. . kaniŋ=ca yakkha siŋan. 1pl=add Yakkha cop.1pl.excl We are also Yakkha people. 39 _nrr _08.08 . encho=ca ta-ya-ma=ga=na some _time _ago =add come -pst-2=nmlz.sg You have come before, too. 28 _cvs _04.164 The additive focus particle may also be attached to question words, yielding pro-forms that include all conceivable referents and thus have an exhaustive or ‘free-choice’ See Koenig1993_Focus . reading any or ever , as in . In this function, the additive focus particle is often combined with the sequential clause linkage marker =hoŋ (see and (c) and the following paragraph). . .hetna=ca tihar ta-meʔ=niŋa, na uŋci=ga yad=be khaʔla, nniŋda lakt-a-ni. which =add a _hindu _festival come [3sg]-npst=ctmp this 3nsg=gen remembrance =loc like _this 2pl dance -imp-pl.imp Whichever Tihar day comes, dance like this, in memory of them (goddess Sangdangrangma and her companions). Narrative 14 is about a Yakkha goddess called Saŋdaŋraŋma, also called Dokeni. Tihar is the Hindu festival of the goddess Laksmi, celebrated in October or November, and this celebration has been transformed to a Yakkha celebration in the Yakkha cultural sphere. The Hindu goddess of fortune, wealth and prosperity Lakṣmī is identified with Saŋdaŋraŋma. 14 _nrr _02.37 .na makhur=na caleppa hen imin=hoŋ=ca ca-ma=na. this black =nmlz.sg bread today how =seq=add eat -inf[deont]=nmlz.sg This black bread has to be eaten today, by all means. 40 _leg _08.056 . i=ya=hoŋ=ca cok-ma yas-wa-g=ha. what =nmlz.nc=seq=add do -inf be _able -npst-2=nmlz.nc You can achieve anything. 01 _leg _07.031 .iʔbeniŋ=ca what _time =add at any time 13 _cvs _02.005 Scalar notions, translatable with even , can also be marked by =ca (see the example in ), but constituents with a scalar reading are rare in the corpus. Such notions are expressed in concessive clauses increasingly (see adv-cl-conc), marked by the related particle =hoŋca, which is a combination of sequential clause linkage marker and additive particle (see ). In the scalar reading is combined with restrictive focus even if only . . . jammai, kha yamuŋ=ca, ghak heŋ-nhaŋ-ma. all this beard =add all cut -V2.send-inf[deont] All (hair), even this beard, one has to cut off all of it (while mourning). 29 _cvs _05.058 .ucun=na yapmi=ca ucun n-nis-wa-m-nin. nice =nmlz.sg person =add nice neg- see -npst-1pl.A-3pl.neg Even nice people will seem ugly to us (if we are forced to marry them). 36 _cvs _06.330 . liŋkha=ga teʔmaŋa=se=hoŋca, ... a _clan =gen clan _sister =restr=seq=add Even if it is only a Linkha sister (as opposed to a Linkha sister who will marry a Limbukhim guy), ... 37 _nrr _07.095 In a pattern that is common in the languages of South Asia (and possibly beyond), the additive focus marker is employed together with verbal negation to express exhaustive negation (i.e. to the greatest conceivable extent), which is often paraphrasable with English any . In this function, it is typically attached to interrogative words, as shown in . . . ka hetniŋ=ca m-man-diʔ-ŋa-n=na. 1sg when =add neg- get _lost -V2.give-1sg-neg=nmlz.sg I would never get lost. 18 _nrr _03.015 . hou, ka eko=ca m-pham-me-ŋ-ga-nǃ i=na=le? excla 1sg one =add neg- help -npst-1sg.P-2.A-neg what =nmlz.sg=ctr Man, you do not help me even with one (word, line); what is going on? (a complaint uttered while singing a song) 07 _sng _01.16
summary:
Additive focus in Yakkha is marked by the clitic =ca, which attaches to constituents of any type, including adverbial clauses. It signals that content is added to something presupposed or that a participant is included in a previously established set, and it can also mark question words to yield exhaustive or free-choice readings like “any” or “ever.”  

The marker can further express scalar meanings akin to “even,” though these are rare in the corpus, and it combines with verbal negation to convey exhaustive negation, often corresponding to English “any.”

text: The emphatic particle =pa is typically attached to the inflected verb or to other sentence-final elements, like the dislocated phrase in . The function of this marker is to indicate that the hearer should be aware of the propositional content already, or to emphasize its truth, paraphrasable with German doch , or English of course . The particle is found on assertions (affirmative and negated), imperatives, hortatives and permissive questions, but never on content or truth-value questions (see ). In assertions, it occus mutually exclusive with the nominalizers =na and =ha in sentence-final position. Its function seems similar to these nominalizers, except for its occurrence on imperatives and hortatives, and its absence on the above-mentioned question types (see the ungrammatical examples in ). Etymologically, the particle might have developed from the nominalizer =pa. . .a-ppa=ŋa et-u-ci=ba, samundra=be=pa 1sg.poss- father =erg apply [3sg.A;pst]-3.P-3nsg.P=emph ocean =loc=emph My father used them (the fishing rods), in the ocean. 13 _cvs _02.024 .nhe, uk=ka u-cya=ci mohan=ŋa hiŋ-ma=ci=ba. here 3sg.poss=gen 3sg.poss- child =nsg Mohan =erg support -inf[deont]=nsg=emph Here, her children, of course Mohan has to care for them. 28 _cvs _04.145 . kucuma=ŋa co-i-ks-u=ha? khem=ba! dog =erg eat -compl-prf-3.P=nmlz.nc before =emph A: Did the dog eat up? B: Already before! . .*man=ba? exist.neg[3]=emph Intended: There is none? .*khiŋ=ba? this _much =emph Intended: This much? .*heʔna khy-a=ba? where go [3sg]-pst=emph Intended: Where did he go? Example shows =pa =ba in permissive questions. Here, it implies that the speaker expects a positive answer (see ). In imperatives, the marker is employed to make commands and requests more polite, occurring in a fixed sequence of the focus marker =i (often realized as [e]) and =ba (see ). . .ca-ŋ-so-ŋ=ba? eat [3.P]-1sg.A-V2.look[3.P]-1sg.A[sbjv]=emph May I try and eat it? 17 _cvs _03.301 . na=be yuŋ-ma leŋ-me=pa? this =loc sit -inf be _alright [3sg]-npst=emph Is it allowed to sit here? . .yokmet-a-ŋ=eba tell -imp-1sg.P=emph Please tell me about it. 19 _pea _01.005 . co=eba eat [imp]=emph Please eat it. The emphatic particle =pa also frequently combines with other particles. The particles =le and =ba are combined in a fixed expression that is shown in . It can attach to the emphatic particle =maŋ and to the restrictive focus particle =se when it attaches to constituents in predicative function. . . i=na=le=ba what =nmlz.sg=ctr=emph watchamacallit, what to say .mi=na=maŋ=ba! small =nmlz.sg=emph=emph It is so small! 36 _cvs _06.225 .hen khiŋ se=ppa today this _much restr=emph Today it is this much only.
summary:
The emphatic particle =pa is usually attached to the inflected verb or other sentence-final elements and signals that the hearer should already know the proposition or that its truth is being emphasized, similar to German *doch* or English *of course*. It occurs with assertions, imperatives, hortatives, and permissive questions, but not with content or yes/no truth-value questions; in assertions it is mutually exclusive with the nominalizers =na and =ha in final position.

It also makes imperatives and requests more polite, and in permissive questions it can imply that a positive answer is expected. The particle commonly combines with others in fixed sequences, and it may historically derive from the nominalizer =pa.

text: The emphatic particle =i is frequently found in assertions that emphasize the truth value of some propositional content (see ), usually following the clause-final nominalizers =na and =ha (see nmlz-uni-3), but never attaching to clauses that are marked by =pa. The focus particle is most likely related to the phonologically unbound question marker i that occurs in truth-value questions (see below). . . khaʔla, eŋ=ga ceʔya=i chak=ha=i, chak=ha! like _this 1pl.poss=gen language =emph difficult =nmlz.nc=emph difficult =nmlz.nc It is like this, our language is difficult, difficult. 36 _cvs _06.544 .menna=i, paip cok-se khe-me-ŋ=na=i cop.neg=foc , pipe do -sup go -npst-1sg=nmlz.sg=emph No, I will go to fix the pipe. This particle is also found in a negative construction with an infinitival form preceding the finite verb. The construction expresses exhaustive negation not at all . . .pheŋ-ma=i m-pheks-a-ma-n=na. plough -inf=emph neg- plough [3sg]-pst-prf-neg=nmlz.sg It is not ploughed at all. 06 _cvs _01.081 .ka ni-ma=i n-nis-wa-ŋa-n=na. 1sg[erg] know -inf=emph neg- know -npst-1sg.A[3.P]-neg=nmlz.sg I do not know (any songs) at all. 06 _cvs _01.104 .ni-ma=i men-ni-ma=na yapmi=be? know -inf=emph neg- know -inf=nmlz.sg person =loc (Getting married) to a person one does not know at all? 36 _cvs _06.325
summary:
The emphatic particle =i is used to reinforce the truth of assertions, typically appearing after clause-final nominalizers =na and =ha, but it does not occur on clauses marked with =pa. It is probably related to the unbound question marker i used in truth-value questions.  

The same particle also appears in a negative construction with an infinitival form before the finite verb, where it expresses exhaustive negation meaning “not at all.”

text: The particle =le carries a strongly contrastive notion. It is functionally equal to the Nepali particle po, which indicates that some new information stands in a strong contrast to the expectations, or was not part of the presupposed knowledge (see ). Thus, it expresses a certain amount of surprise on part of the speaker. The particle is often accompanied by the mirative rahecha raecha (borrowed from Nepali), and the functions of both markers are indeed related. The particle is not restricted to marking contrastive information from the perspective of the speaker. In , the assertion stands in contrast to the adressee's expectations, as this assertion belongs to an argument about a particular patch of farming ground. . . are, heʔne khy-a-ŋ=na=lai, ka? lambu=go naʔmo=le sa=na ohǃ? where go -pst-1sg=nmlz.sg=excla 1sg way =top down _here =ctr cop.pst[3sg]=nmlz.sg Holy crackers, where did I go? The way was down here! 28 _cvs _04.027 . na=go aniŋ=ga=le kham! this =top 1pl.incl.poss=gen=ctr ground (But) this is our ground! 22 _nrr _05.007 . ka=go a-sap=le thakt-wa-ŋ=na 1sg=top 1sg.poss-[stem]=ctr like -npst[3.P]-1sg.A=nmlz.sg But I like it (in contrast to the other people present). As one can see in the examples in , the marker also occurs in questions, marking the constituent that is focussed on. The marker expresses that the speaker is particularly clueless about the possible answer, i.e. that nothing is presupposed. In , the speaker mistook the image quality of the Pear Story film Chafe1980The-Pear for snow. In , the protagonists of the narrative arrived in some unknown place after fleeing from their enemies. . .hiuŋ=le wai-sa=em i=le wai-sa=em? show =ctr exist [3sg]-pst=alt what =ctr exist [3sg]-pst=alt Was there snow, or what was it? 19 _pea _01.004 . heʔne=le ta-i=ya m-mit-a-ma=hoŋ uŋci m-maks-a-by-a-ma=ca where =ctr come -1pl=nmlz.nsg 3pl- think -pst-prf=seq 3nsg 3pl- be _surprised -pst-V2.give-pst-prf=add They were surprised, wondering: Where in the world did we arrive? 22 _nrr _05.030
summary: The particle =le has a strongly contrastive meaning, comparable to Nepali po: it marks new information that sharply contrasts with expectations or with what was previously presupposed, often conveying surprise. It often appears with the mirative rahecha raecha, and it can mark contrastive assertions from either the speaker’s or the addressee’s perspective. In questions, =le focuses the questioned constituent and signals that the speaker lacks a presupposed answer.

text: The particle =maŋ is another emphatic marker, as the examples in illustrate. It attaches to constituents of any kind, whether arguments or adverbs or clause-initial conjunctions. It is paraphrasable with just or right in English, but its function is not fully understood yet. . . i cok-ma? yakkha ten=be khaʔla=maŋǃ what do -inf Yakkha village =loc like _this =emph What to do? After all, it is just like this in a Yakkha village! .nhaŋ=ŋa=maŋ ŋ-ikt-haks-u, ... and _then =ins=emph 3pl.A- chase -V2.send-3.P[pst] , ... And right then, they chased him away, ... 18 _nrr _03.011 .nna jeppa=maŋ eko mem-muʔ-ni-ma=na len sa-ya. that really =emph one neg- forget -compl-inf=nmlz.sg day cop.pst[3sg] That really was an unforgettable day. 41 _leg _09.069 .ma, na=ci=ga niŋwa=maŋ om mother sister =nsg=gen mind =emph cop Of course, it is just the concern/love of my mother and my sister. Context: a child pondering about being scolded for doing dangerous things. This example is exceptional in not displaying the obligatory possessive marking that is usually found on kinship terms. The reason might be that both participants are highly topical in the narrative, and had been mentioned several times before. 42 _leg _10.048,
summary: The particle =maŋ is an emphatic marker that can attach to constituents of any kind, including arguments, adverbs, and clause-initial conjunctions. It is roughly translatable as “just” or “right” in English, but its exact function is not yet fully understood. The passage illustrates its use in several examples and notes one exceptional case involving kinship terms, possibly due to the participants’ high discourse topicality.

text: The criterion for a marker to be classified as epistemic is that it expresses the commitment of the speaker to the reality of an event. Evidential markers, on , purely indicate the source of the information Cornillie2009_Evidentiality. Yakkha distinguishes evidential and epistemic markers. Furthermore, the notion of mirativity has to be distinguished from both evidentiality and epistemic modality. It expresses the unexpected status of some information DeLancey1997Mirativity.
summary: The passage states that epistemic markers express the speaker’s commitment to the reality of an event, whereas evidential markers indicate only the source of information. It notes that Yakkha distinguishes between evidential and epistemic markers, and that mirativity is a separate category from both, expressing the unexpected status of information.

text: The reportative particle conveys a purely evidential notion, namely that the source of the information is not the speaker but someone else. The source of information can be either unspecific (translating as It is said. , see ) or a specific, quotable source, as in . The particle is frequently found in narrations of legends and myths, as they are a prime example of hearsay know -ledge. It mostly occurs sentence-finally; it usually attaches to the finite verb, but it can also attach to any other constituent (including adverbial clauses, see ), also more than once per sentence (see ). . . nam wandik=ŋa lom-meʔ=niŋa kam cok-ni-ma sa=bu sun tomorrow =ins come.out [3sg]-npst=ctmp work do -compl-inf cop.pst=rep It is said that he had to have the work completed when the sun would rise on the next day. 11 _nrr _01.007 .nna puŋdaraŋma=cen, eko maŋme leks-a-ma=na=bu that forest _goddess =top one eagle become [3sg]-pst-prf=nmlz.sg=rep That forest goddess, she became an eagle, it is said. 22 _nrr _05.108 . u-milak khokt-a-by-a bhoŋ=bu, ŋkha desan-masan n-da-ya, n-nis-wa-n-ci-n=ha=bu. 3sg.poss- tail cut -sbjv[3sg]-V2.give-sbjv cond=rep that scary _ghosts 3pl- come -sbjv neg- see -npst-neg-3nsg.P-neg=nmlz.nsg=rep If one cuts their (the dogs') tails, they do not see the scary ghosts coming, it is said. 28 _cvs _04.213 . .lu, abo, hamro yakkha, eh, aniŋ=ga ceʔya=ŋ=bu chem lum-biʔ-ma=na=lai init , now our Yakkha, oh, 1pl.excl=gen matter =ins=rep song tell -V2.give-inf=nmlz.sg=excla Alright, in our Yakkha, oh [switching to Yakkha], now we have to sing a song in our language, she said. 06 _cvs _01.102 .a-na=bu khe-meʔ=na=bu, 1sg.poss- sister =rep go [3sg]-npst=nmlz.sg=rep My sister has to go, she (my sister) says. 36 _cvs _06.558 In , the constituent that is marked by =bu is in focus. The speaker remembers that she was asked to sing a song in her language, and not in Nepali, and hence she puts the reportative marker on the focussed constituent aniŋga ceʔyaŋ(a) in our language . Occasionally, the reportative marker =bu is followed by an utterance predicate, as in . Its occurrence is, however, not obligatory on complements of predicates that embed speech in Yakkha (cf. utterance-pred). . hiʔwa=ga hiʔwa wait=na=bu ŋ-gam-me wind =gen wind exist [npst;3sg]=nmlz.sg=rep 3pl- say -npst They say that he only lives in the air. 21 _nrr _04.052
summary: The reportative particle is a purely evidential marker indicating that the information comes from someone other than the speaker, either from an unspecified source or from a specific quotable one. It is common in legends and myths, usually appears sentence-finally, and typically attaches to the finite verb, though it can also mark other constituents and may occur more than once in a sentence. When attached to a focused constituent, it highlights that element, and it can sometimes be followed by an utterance predicate, though this is not required.

text: This particle expresses that the speaker assesses the content of the proposition to be likely, but not an established fact, very much like the English adverbs maybe , probably , possibly . It generally comes sentence-finally. Etymologically, it is a combination of the marker loSynchronically, it only exists as a clause linkage marker in Yakkha, see adv-cl-int. In Belhare, there are a comitative marker lok and a focus marker (k)olo that could be related to Yakkha lo Bickel2003Belhare. and the irrealis particle =pi (see below). Examples are provided in . This particle is also found in questions (see ) and in counterfactual clauses (see adv-cl-count). . . kaʈhmandu=ko men=na loppi, men=na. Kathmandu =top neg.cop[3sg]=nmlz.sg probably neg.cop[3sg]=nmlz.sg It was probably not in Kathmandu [pondering] - no. 36 _cvs _06.311 .bappura isa=ga u-cya loppi? poor _thing who =gen 3sg.poss- child probably Poor thing, whose child could it possibly be? 01 _leg _07.292
summary: The particle expresses that the speaker judges the proposition as likely but not certain, like English *maybe*, *probably*, or *possibly*, and it usually appears sentence-finally. Although it is historically related to other elements, synchronically it functions in Yakkha as a clause-linkage marker, and it also occurs in questions and counterfactual clauses.

text: The marker =pi (realized as [bi] after nasals and after vowels) is found mostly on counterfactual conditional clauses, but also on hypothetical clauses. In counterfactual clauses, it attaches to the inflected verb of the main clause and to the clause linkage marker of the subordinate clause, either cotemporal =niŋ(a) or sequential =hoŋ. There actually are sequences of clause linkage marker, topic particle =ko and irrealis marker =pi, in all examples in . The verbs in counterfactual clauses are always marked for the Past Subjunctive (see mood). . . ɖiana=ca piʔ-ma=hoŋ=go=bi cond-a-sy-a=bi=baǃ khatniŋgo man-ninǃ Diana =add give -inf[deont]=seq=top=irr be _happy [3sg]-sbjv-mddl-sbjv=irr=emph but neg.cop-3pl We would have had to give them (fish) to Diana, too, she would have been happyǃ But there aren't any. 13 _cvs _02.056 .nniŋ=ga ten a-sap n-thakt-u-ŋ=niŋ=go=bi, ka n-da-ya-ŋa-n=bi. 2pl.poss=gen village 1sg.poss-[stem] neg- like -3.P-1sg.A[sbjv]=ctmp=top=irr 1sg neg- come -sbjv-1sg-neg=irr If I had not liked your village, I would not have come. .ŋ-gind-a-by-a-masa-n=niŋ=go=bi ikhiŋ n-leks-a=biǃ neg- rot -sbjv-V2.give-sbjv-pst.prf-neg=ctmp=top=irr how _many 3pl- become -sbjv=irr If they (the apples) were not rotten, how many would we have! The particle =pi does not only occur on counterfactual clauses. It can also mark clauses referring to hypothetical situations where it expresses the speaker's assessment about the unlikelihood of an event. In example , the hypothetical situation that it will rain stands in opposition to the more likely, but also yet unrealized scenario of a hail storm, as judged by the speaker. In this example, the particle expresses the speaker's assessment of the likelihood of an event. The speaker is 99 percent sure that it will hail and thus uses a counterfactual clause for the proposition that contains the event of raining. .wasik=se ta-ya=hoŋ=go=bi, ucun leks-a sa=bi, khatniŋgo phom ta-meʔ=na loppi rain =restr come [3sg]-sbjv=seq=top=irr nice become [3sg]-sbjv cop.sbjv=irr but hail come [3sg]-npst=nmlz.sg probably If it just rained, it would have been nice, but it there will probably be hail. The interaction between the irrealis marker and the clause linkage markers it attaches to is nicely illustrated by the following clausal minimal pair of hypothetical and counterfactual information in . Both sentences are inflected for the Past Subjunctive (which is in many forms homophonous with the past tense), but the clause linkage marker =niŋ in establishes a simultaneous relation between the clauses while =hoŋ establishes a sequential relation, indicating that the event must have occurred prior to the main clause, and thereby implying that it has not been realized. . .makalu nis-u-ŋ=niŋ=go=bi cond-a-sy-a-ŋ=bi Makalu see -3.P-1sg.A[sbjv]=ctmp=top=irr be _happy -sbjv-mddl-sbjv-1sg=irr If I could see Mt. Makalu, I would be happy. .makalu nis-u-ŋ=hoŋ=go=bi cond-a-sy-a-ŋ=bi Makalu see -3.P-1sg.A[sbjv]=seq=top=irr be _happy -sbjv-mddl-sbjv-1sg=irr If I had seen Mt. Makalu, I would have been happy.
summary: The marker =pi, pronounced [bi] after nasals and vowels, occurs mainly in counterfactual conditional clauses and also in hypothetical clauses. In counterfactuals it attaches to the inflected main-clause verb and to the subordinate clause linkage marker (=niŋ(a) for cotemporal or =hoŋ for sequential), with all such clauses also marked by Past Subjunctive verbs; =pi can also signal the speaker’s judgment that a hypothetical event is unlikely. The contrast between =niŋ and =hoŋ shows that cotemporal clauses express hypothetical meaning, while sequential clauses imply that the event is unrealized and therefore counterfactual.

text: The Nepali mirative rʌhechʌ raicha, Diachronically, it is a perfective form of the verb rahanu to remain . was borrowed into Yakkha and is used as a sentence-final marker of surprise about the propositional content, for instance when the speaker shares newly discovered information. In , the speaker discovers that something must be wrong with the water pipe. In the speaker remembers something that she had not been aware of at first, only after someone reminded her. . . maŋcwa mi=na rahecha water small =nmlz.sg mir The water got less. 13 _cvs _02.071 .ka ŋkhaʔla bhoŋ tutunnhe bhauju=ghe wa-ya-masa-ŋ=na raecha, tunnhe=ba. 1sg like _that cond up _there sister-in-law =loc exist -pst-pst.prf-1sg=nmlz.sg mir up _there =emph If it is like that, I had been uphill, at my sister-in-law's place, I see, uphill. 36 _cvs _06.399 Mirativity in Yakkha is not restricted to surprise at the time of speaking, and it does not just indicate the speaker's surprise. The mirative particle is frequently found in narratives, where the notion of unexpectedness either relates to some point in the time line of the story or to the hearer's state of mind, as the one who tells the story can rarely be surprised of what he tells himself. The function or the mirative marker in narratives rather is to draw the attention of the hearer to the plot than to signal surprise. Further examples from narratives are provided in . In , the speaker reports about the events she saw in the Pear Story film Chafe1980The-Pear. . .cokcoki-netham=be, eko maɖa oʈemma kham wait=na rahecha star-bed =loc one big plain ground exist [3sg;npst]=nmlz.sg mir In the place called Bed of Stars, there is a huge plain area! 37 _nrr _07.049 .pak=na baŋna mi=na phalubaŋ, na huture sa-ma raecha. younger =nmlz.sg called small =nmlz.sg Phalubang this a _clan cop.pst-prf mir The younger one, the smaller one, Phalubhang, he was a Huture. 22 _nrr _05.074 .khus-het-u=ha raicha. steal -V2.carry.off-3.P[pst]=nmlz.nsg mir He stole them and carried them off! 20 _pea _02.015 As these examples have shown, the mirative prefers nominalized sentences as hosts (see nmlz-uni-3). Another marker often found together with the mirative is the focus marker =le (see above) that signals contrast to presupposed content, or the absence of presupposed content.
summary: The Nepali mirative *rʌhechʌ raicha* was borrowed into Yakkha and functions as a sentence-final marker expressing surprise or newly discovered information about the proposition. In narratives, however, it often marks unexpectedness relative to the story line or the hearer’s knowledge rather than the speaker’s own surprise, and it serves to direct attention to the plot. The marker typically appears with nominalized clauses, and it is often used together with the focus marker *=le*, which signals contrast with presupposed content.

text: The function of the sentence-level particle lai (always in sentence-final position) is to add a certain vigor and force to assertions and exclamations (see ), to rhetorical questions as in , and to deontic statements, as in . It can in most cases be paraphrased with the Nepali particle ni, or with English just and of course . It bears its own stress, but it can also be cliticized in fast speech. . . ikhiŋ chiʔ=na yapmi laiǃ how _much greedy =nmlz.sg person excla What a greedy personǃ . om lai! cop emph Yes, of course! . koi khaʔla lai! some like _this excla Some are just like this! 13 _cvs _02.10 . . A: hetne wei-ka=na? - B: paŋ=be lai. tuʔkhi ca=se i kheʔ-ma lai? A: where live [npst]-2=nmlz.sg - B: house =loc excla trouble eat -sup what go =inf excla A: Where do you live? - B: Just at home. Why should I go to suffer (in a marriage)?! . n-da-ci bhoŋ=go im-m=ha=ci lai, ca-m=ha=ciǃ 3pl.A- bring -3nsg.P[sbjv] cond=top buy -inf[deont]=nmlz.nsg=nsg excla eat -inf[deont]=nmlz.nsg=nsg If they bring some (fish), we would definitely have to buy and eat them! 13 _cvs _02.056
summary: The sentence-final particle **lai** adds force or emphasis to assertions, exclamations, rhetorical questions, and deontic statements. It can often be paraphrased by Nepali **ni** or English **just** and **of course**, and although it bears its own stress, it may be cliticized in fast speech.

text: The particle =ʔlo is used frequently in colloquial speech, signalling a certain lack of patience on the side of the speaker, and possibly also a frustrative notion. It occurs in assertions, imperatives, and questions alike. The marker is always bound, attaching to the sentence-final constituent, which is often another discourse particle, such as =ha (see nmlz-uni-3), emphatic =ba or contrastive =le (see ). When =ʔlo attaches to other particles, the resulting units become independent words regarding stress (e.g. haʔlo, baʔlo, leʔlo/laʔlo, which are always stressed on the first syllable), but not with regard to the voicing rule. The most commonly heard particle is haʔlo (see ). . .i=ʔlo? what =excla What (the heck)? (also used as a filler, like watchamacallit ) . wa-ni haʔlo. n-da-me-n=na bhoŋ, n-da-nin-ni haʔloǃ exist [3sg]-opt excla neg- come [3sg]-npst-neg=nmlz.sg cond neg- come [3sg]-neg-opt excla It is alright! It attaches to the final constituent of the clause, often other discourse particles such as =ha, =ba, or =le, producing independent stressed forms like haʔlo, baʔlo, and leʔlo/laʔlo, and a dialectal variant =kho is also attested.

text: Another exclamative particle is hau. It is generally found at the end of a sentence, turning assertions into exclamations (see ). Judging from the available examples, it also carries a mirative notion, expressing that the speaker is emotionally involved by making a discovery. It generally bears its own stress, but it can also occur cliticized, thus reduced to mere [au] or even just [u]. Occasionally, the particle is also found at the beginning of sentences in order to draw the attention of the hearer to the propositional content, for instance when the topic is changed , or when an exciting discovery has been made, as in . . .sal=go mund-i-ŋ=na=i hau! year =top forget -compl-1sg.A=nmlz.sg=emph excla I just forgot the year (of my birth), ha! 06 _cvs _01.034 . taŋkheŋ ka-ya=na hau! sky call [3sg]-pst=nmlz.sg excla It thundered! 13 _cvs _02.062 .mun-nhe sombare daju=ge ŋ-waiʔ=ya-ci=bu hau, jeppa! down _here Sombar brother =loc 3pl- exist =nmlz.nsg=nsg=rep excla really Down here at brother Sombar's house they have them (fish) for sale, I have heard, really! 13 _cvs _02.057 . .hau, salle=be heʔne wei-ka=na? excla Salle =loc where exist -2=nmlz.sg Hey, where in Salle do you live? 06 _cvs _01.090 .hau, kha=go, eŋ=ga yapmi loʔa=ci=ca excla these =top 1pl.incl.poss=gen person like =nsg=add Really, they are like our people, too! 22 _nrr _05.044
summary: The exclamative particle **hau** typically occurs at the end of a sentence and turns assertions into exclamations; it also appears to have a **mirative** meaning, indicating the speaker’s emotional reaction to a discovery. It usually carries its own stress, but can be cliticized to **[au]** or **[u]**. Less often, it can appear sentence-initially to draw the hearer’s attention, especially when the topic changes or an exciting discovery is being introduced.

text: The question particle i marks truth-value questions, as in . In most cases, the clause it attaches to is nominalized by =na or =ha. The marker may carry its own stress, but it also occurs phonologically bound, the alternation probably just being conditioned by fast speech. If it occurs independently, a glottal stop is prothesized, as it typically is in vowel-initial words in Yakkha. The marker is most likely ety -mo -lo -gi -cally related to the (bound) emphatic marker =i that has been described above. . . raksi=ŋa sis-a-ga=na=i? liquor =erg kill [3sg.A]-pst-2.P=nmlz.sg=q Are you drunk? . ka i? 1sg q I? .yakthu i? enough q Did you have enough? 36 _cvs _06.248 . nis-u-ga=na=i? know -3.P[pst]-2.A=nmlz.sg=q Do you know it?
summary: The question particle **i** marks truth-value questions and usually attaches to a clause nominalized with **=na** or **=ha**. It can appear either stressed or phonologically bound, with independent forms preceded by a glottal stop, and it is probably historically related to the bound emphatic marker **=i**.

text: The insistive particle is found on imperatives and on hortatives, adding force and emphasis to these speech acts (see ). Possibly related to this marker is a vocative that is found occasionally, as shown in . . .ah, so-se ab-a-ci, au? yes look -sup come -imp-du insist Yes, please come to look (at the bride), will you? 36 _cvs _06.416 .lu, haku=chen pog-i, au? alright now =top raise -1pl[sbjv] insist Alright, now let us get up, will we? 36 _cvs _06.556 .a-na=u! 1sg.poss- eZ=voc He, sister!

text: Yakkha has a closed class of interjections, such as hoʔi, bhela and yakthu (all meaning Enough! ), om yes , menna/manna no (identificational and existential, respectively), and issaŋ, the latter being pronounced with a rising intonation. It stands for I do not know or I have no idea , just like the Nepali interjection khoi. Examples are provided in . Interjections are usually employed as sentence replacements, but in Yakkha it is still possible to additionally express a topic, as in . The affirmative and the negative interjections also have copular function (see also cop-infl and cop). Interjections, like sentences, can host further discourse particles such as in . In the Ankhinbhuin dialect, om has an alternant ommi. . .ka=ca hoʔi. 1sg=add enough I also had enough. .yakthu=i? enough =q Did you have enough? .men=na, nna=maŋǃ cop.neg=nmlz.sg that =emph No, it is that oneǃ .heʔne khet-u haʔlo, issaŋ laʔlo! where carry _off -3.P[pst] excla ign excla Where did he take it - I have no idea! 20 _pea _02.031 .om=ba! yes =emph Yes, of course! A particle lu (borrowed from Nepali) can be found sentence-initially (see example lu) or replacing sentences. It is employed to initiate an action, both in commands and in hortatives. There is no expression for thank you in Yakkha. Common greetings are sewayo, and semeʔnenna, which is the verb greet with 1>2 inflection I greet you . Geomorphic interjections, prompting the addressee to look in a particular direction (tu for Look uphill! , mu for Look downhill! and yu for Look over there! ) have been discussed in geodeixis.
summary: Yakkha has a small closed class of interjections, including forms for “enough,” “yes,” “no,” and “I do not know,” and these typically replace full sentences, though they can still co-occur with a topic or discourse particles. The affirmative and negative interjections can also function copularly, and some interjections have dialectal variants or borrowed equivalents such as Nepali *lu*, which can appear sentence-initially or stand in for a sentence to launch an action. The passage also notes that Yakkha lacks a conventional expression for “thank you,” has common greetings, and includes directional “geomorphic” interjections like *tu*, *mu*, and *yu* that direct the addressee’s attention.

The bet required the Linkha to complete a series of tasks by sunrise, but one cow ran away and a rooster crowed, causing them to lose; as a result, the sun cursed them with restrictions such as not facing doors eastward, not planting banyan trees or building resting places, and not placing children in bamboo cradles.

summary:
This oral narrative tells how a Linkha clan sister went to Mamling after marrying into Canuwa and requested the bagdata, but also insisted on taking a particular stone said to belong to them from ancient times. Her companions eventually gave her the stone, warning that it had to be carried all the way home without being set down, or it would not truly be theirs.

The story then describes the difficult journey with the stone: the group crossed to Mulgaun and Coilikha, where the girl’s stomach hurt and she had to wait until dawn. The passage ends as one person runs uphill carrying the stone to Okhyu in Mulgaun.

summary: The passage recounts a legend about stones that could not be lifted or made to stand upright, including a special high rock called Dewan stone in Mulgaun. This stone was said to travel to a mythical place called Yaksigum or the Bed of Stars at night and return upright before sunrise, where it could be seen from the plains below. The story ends with the girl failing to move the stones and the Dewan stone falling, causing a landslide that buried the ground.

summary: The passage describes a myth in which stones brought from Namthalung fall and cause misfortune in the surrounding area: people in the village become ill, the adults lose strength, and the weather alternates between drought and destructive rain. The people identify the cause as the Namthalung stone, which had been brought and set upright in the village, and they conclude that it must be worshipped. The text then explains the ritual requirement that a Linkha clan sister, or alternatively a Linkha sister who is not marrying out, should perform the worship.

summary: This personal narrative by Shantila Jimi describes a childhood trip with her mother and elder sister to dig a field, where the children suffer from intense sun, thirst, and a lack of shade or water. On the way to fetch water from a stream, the narrator sees and eats fruit from a fig tree, then discovers an owl and its nest with two eggs; when she tries to take the eggs, the owl attacks and pecks her head.

summary: The passage narrates a first-person episode in which the speaker, while trying to climb down a tree, is frightened, trapped, and repeatedly pecked by an owl until his mother and elder sister find and rescue him. Afterward, he is scolded and learns not to be naughty or disobey his elders, and he says that even now the sound of an owl makes him feel as if it is still pecking his head.
